Sports.title: Battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars: Conor Benn takes on troubled Ryan Garcia after burning Eddie Hearn with $10MILLION payday in his sights - but here's why Briton's fate rests solely in the hands of his narcissistic American rival
Sports.content:
‘Who ya like buddy?’ It’s the most asked question in casino-ville as the hours tick down to this Saturday’s world title fight between two angry young men.

One, America’s extravagantly gifted but troubled world welterweight champion. The other, the ever-persistent English challenger who never stops throwing punches whether they connect or not. As if in manic obsession with defeating not only opponents but also his demons and a sceptical outside world.

So, Ryan Garcia or Conor Benn?

When the denizens of this neon gambling Strip in the Nevada desert ask that question they don’t’ want to know which of these two combatants you like personally more than the other. It is their way of trying to find out who you might be betting on to prevail in the atmospheric T-Mobile Arena.

Their inquiries are even more numerous than usual on such occasions as this. Because neither the Americans nor the Mexicans who are thronging here in support of their blood brother by heredity know very much about Benn. Other than the fact he is the son of a fabled icon of the British ring.

On his two previous US visits Benn Jr made hard work of beating men who looked more like nightclub bouncers than professional boxers. Of his exploits back home only the pair of fights against Chris Eubank Jr evoked any interest whatsoever on either side of this border.

What they are aware of is the two positive tests for performance enhancing drugs and the protracted legal battle to technically clear his name which kept him out of the ring for months. Just as they know about Garcia’s conviction and suspension for a similar finding.

Conor Benn is locked in the battle of boxing's most unlikeable stars in Las Vegas

Benn is lining up a $10m payday after burning his bridges with promoter Eddie Hearn

So, what’s to like?

There can be no doubting Benn’s work ethic. He trains like a dervish to manufacture the maximum possible out of however much natural-born ability he inherited from Nigel the Dark Destroyer. Nor does he ever give up. Eubank Jr had to go beyond the normal limits of even this battle-hardened business to inflict the only defeat of Conor’s career thus far. A loss he avenged, albeit in partly contrived and contentious circumstances.

Eubank the Younger was perilously drained in the rematch by a clause in the contract which prevented him rehydrating fully after struggling to cut poundage to meet the agreed catchweight.

What goes around comes around. If not in a full measure of the irony. Benn has had to sweat and strain down by almost a stone from middleweight to make the welterweight championship limit of 147 lbs. As he puts it: ‘Five weeks in hell.’

To say his body looks shredded is putting it mildly. But he has not been subjected to rehydration limitations following his Friday morning visit to the scales.

Eubank was handsomely rewarded to put his health on the line, and now Benn has been lured into similar jeopardy by the fortune – some reports say ten million dollars – he is receiving from UFC boss Dana White to be one of the first poster boys for his venture into boxing.

Benn tells it otherwise: ‘I’m doing this because I relish challenges. Have always wanted to strap on the same green WBC belt my dad was so proud to wear. To start getting the world titles that will leave a legacy for my kids. And to prove wrong everyone who doesn’t give me a chance of winning. That puts all the pressure on him, not me.’

Hearn backed the British fighter during his controversial doping ban saga

Ryan Garcia stands in his way of the WBC title, who is the more talented of the fighters

WEIGH-IN VERDICT: After all the brouhaha Conor Benn made the weight with a full pound to spare After what he described as 'five weeks of hell' dieting down by two divisions he scaled 146 lbs in readiness to challenge world welterweight champion Ryan Garcia here this Saturday night. He did so with a told-you so smile. Throughout the speculation as to whether he could shed the best part of a stone in his training camp journey from middleweight Benn had assured one and all that he would be comfortable at his long-ago weight. Good as his word he came in only half a pound heavier than Garcia. Although he is leaner of hip the muscle is still there on arms and torso. Complete with a six pack as a reminder of his constant work ethic. The slightly taller part/Mexican great white hope of American boxing does look more natural at the weight. But Benn does not appear stressed from all his exertions. Even so Garcia is still a solid odds on favourite in the Vegas betting

Whether or not Benn can take in sufficient liquids and pasta before entering the ring, the dangers to him are greater than those with which Eubank struggled. Garcia, one year the younger at 28 but the riper in championships experience, has authentic one-hit-knockout power.

Benn goes into his first world championship fight reliant on the cumulative effect of his non-stop output. The problem with this is that King Ry is probably the best counterpuncher in the world right now and Benn’s headlong style will likely suit him nicely, thank you.

To complicate the evaluation, both have blotted their copybooks as people. Garcia, the handsome heartthrob, burnished his bad-boy rock-star image by trashing a five-star hotel room. He also needed his family’s help with overcoming mental problems aggravated by a passing fancy for social drugs and booze.

Benn invited mockery for claiming initially that he failed his drugs tests because of eating enough eggs to fill the shelves of all the Tescos in London. Then, in order to collect his bonanza from Mister UFC, he unceremoniously dumped his long-time promoter Eddie Hearn who had bankrolled his hefty legal costs and loaned him half a million quid to help sustain his flamboyant lifestyle through that crisis.

Not much to like there.

So, when it comes to the fight, who ya like? The answer is not Conor Benn’s to give. Because the real question is which Ryan Garcia turns up.

If it is the narcissist whose arrogant complacency has cost him a couple of big fights, it may not be totally beyond the bounds of possibility that Conor could pull off one of the major upsets by a British boxer abroad.

If it is King Ry fully prepared and ready to unfurl all the majesty then we can only hope the son of Nigel is not seriously hurt.

Sports.title: Ricky Hatton's mother recalls last hug with boxing champion three days before he took his own life a year ago as parents speak out for first time
Sports.content:
Ricky Hatton's mother recalls last hug with boxing champion three days before he took his own life a year ago as parents speak out for first time

Ricky Hatton's mother has recalled her last hug with him three days before he took his own life one year ago as his parents speak out for the first time.

Carol and Ray Hatton have urged people to tell their friends and family they love them before it's too late after the boxing champion hanged himself on September 14 last year.

One year on from Ricky's death, aged 46, his mother has revealed the last time she embraced her son.

Just days before he took his own life, the boxing champion had been in an argument with his parents but the family were 'building bridges'.

Carol decided to make an unplanned visit to his gym in Hyde and gave him a 'real proper hug'.

She told ITV News: 'I pulled up on the car park because I saw his car. He asked if everything was okay.

'I said "yeah, everything's fine". I said I'd like to see a bit more of him.'

Ricky's mother said he told her he wanted to see his father Ray the next week. However Ricky died three days later.

Former world boxing champion Ricky Hatton died by suicide in September last year aged 46

Ray and Carol Hatton (pictured at their son's funeral) have urged people to tell their friends and family they love them before it's too late

Ricky had previously opened up about his struggle with drug and alcohol addiction and had become estranged from his parents before the reconciled

She added: 'I'm so glad (I got to see him) because nobody knows when it's the last time you're going to see somebody.'

Ray, the boxer's father, said: 'You tell your grandkids how much you love them, you tell your wife how much you love them but I think, especially with men, don't ever be afraid of getting hold of your son and telling him you love him.'

Ricky had become estranged from his parents for around a decade before he reached out to patch up their relationship several years before his death.

He had survived previous suicide attempts and struggled with drug and alcohol addiction.

Ricky fell out with his parents over money and despite the dispute he still allowed Carol and Ray to see his newborn daughter Millie.

However the boxer became upset when his girlfriend Jennifer was not invited to a Christmas Day party.

Months later he received letters from his parents' lawyers saying they wanted to see their granddaughter.

But he told Manchester Evening News in 2013 that he responded by saying: 'I replied to my parents, through solicitors, and said we did not want them to have contact with Millie.'

Carol Hatton wipes a tear from her eye while reading a statement at her home after Ricky's death

Ricky had survived previous suicide attempts before he died in September last year

'We have never stopped them seeing her, as far as I was concerned they had just not been ******.

'I know that sounds harsh and I am sure they see it differently, but it is how I feel.'

He added that the situation 'was a mess', describing the family feud as 'bitter and horrible', referring to back-and-forth letters between his and his parents' lawyers.

This culminated in his father attacking him in a car park fist fight.

Angry about 'all that stuff you've written about your mum in that solicitor's letter', Ray then punched his boxing champion son in the face before Ricky hit back and his father then drove off.

But Ricky's parents are still struggling to come to terms with his death and Carol said the couple 'have to move forward' but will continue 'remembering him and loving him'.

Carol and Ray have now called for a statue of Ricky to be erected in Manchester, saying it would be a 'fitting tribute' to their son who 'brought a lot of pride' to the city.

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury looks set for CARDIFF - at 2am: Welsh venue set to waive curfew to take boxing's biggest fight away from Wembley and New York
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury looks set for CARDIFF - at 2am: Welsh venue set to waive curfew to take boxing's biggest fight away from Wembley and New York

Cardiff's Principality Stadium now looks set to be the unlikely winner of the venue war for boxing's biggest fight - by hosting Anthony Joshua vs Tyson Fury in the early hours of the morning.

The local authorities could today approve lifting the stadium's 10.30pm curfew to host the fight - stepping in after rows over holding it at Wembley Stadium or Madison Square Garden in New York.

Cardiff has history of hosting late-night boxing. Joe Calzaghe fought Mikkel Kessler at the Principality in 2007 at 2am. Fury and Joshua could fight at a similar time to satisfy broadcaster Netflix's huge audience in the United States.

Netflix had wanted the fight in New York to suit their prime timezones, while Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn pitched Wembley to host under the guise that Britain's biggest fight of the century should be hosted in the UK - and he has refused to budge unless contracts are rewritten with upgraded financial offerings.

Cardiff now appears to be the compromise. The Principality Stadium has an 80,000 capacity and a retractable roof - unlike Wembley - which could be useful in late November or December. A date of Saturday, November 28 has been mooted.

The Times report a press conference is tentatively scheduled for next week pending the approval.

Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua could now be set to fight in Cardiff, Wales in November

Joshua and his camp wanted the fight in the UK - while broadcasters Netflix wanted a US host

Wembley looked an ideal venue for the fight but the strict 11pm curfew has been a sticking point, despite London mayor Sadiq Khan saying he wanted to ensure allowances were made to host the fight.

Boxing dealmaker Turki Al-Sheikh has been insistent on a start time of 2am.

Netflix have been running s for Fury-Joshua as recently as Thursday night, clearly confident an agreement will be struck.

The streaming giant has yet to sign off on Cardiff but American sportswriter Dan Rafael last night reported he had asked Netflix if they would approve, with a source telling him: 'I think they're OK.'

A spokesperson for the Welsh Rugby Union said: 'We'd be delighted to host this fight.

'We are very keen to attract more boxing to the stadium, which has a rich history in the sport, enhanced by its closable roof, unrivalled sight lines and unique city-centre location.'

Joe Calzaghe trains at the Principality Stadium before his 2am fight there in 2007

Joshua has fought in Cardiff twice previously, beating Carlos Takam and Joseph Parker in the Welsh capital in 2017 and 2018.

While Joshua has left Hearn to do the talking on his side of the deal, Fury has been publicly speaking and threatening that the heavyweight contest will be called off.

This week he suggested he will no longer be fighting Joshua in another social media rant as rows over the location and contract surrounding the fight continued.

'So it looks like AJ has s*** his pants yet again,' Fury said on social media on Sunday. 'After 11 years, he's finally s*** his pants yet again.'

Last week, Fury, who regularly takes to social media to express his views on potential opponents, was keen to make clear he feels Joshua is not motivated by a love of his country. Earlier this year Daily Mail Sport revealed Joshua had in fact quit the UK to move to Dubai – even as thousands tried to flee amid rising panic in the Middle East warzone.

And Fury, a tax exile to the Isle of Man himself, brought up a 2020 speech at a Black Lives Matter march, where Joshua read out a letter from his friend Reece Campbell to urge attendees to stop spending money with white-owned shops and businesses.

'Show them where it hurts', Joshua had said. 'Abstain from spending your money in their shops and economies, and invest in black-owned businesses.'

Fury re-posted the video of the speech, writing: 'This is the man who loves England, absolute s*** bag! Total piece of s*** bully with zero guts! Don't let them deceive you! & Living in Dubai.'

Provided Cardiff hits no further stumbling blocks, the Welsh capital may now offer the solution to get the fight on at last.

Sports.title: Mercedes aims to end pole drought with upcoming Malaysia F1 upgrades
Sports.content:
Mercedes has confirmed its next big Formula 1 car upgrade will arrive at the forthcoming grand prix in Malaysia, where it hopes to get back into contention for pole.

The Silver Arrows is the runaway leader of the 2026 championship with a 145-point advantage over second-placed Ferrari, despite its last major upgrade package being Montreal in May.

Mercedes has instead preferred to fit minor race-specific updates whereas its nearest challengers Ferrari and McLaren have been significantly more aggressive with developments.

So although Mercedes won the first six grands prix, it has since won four of the last eight as McLaren and Ferrari have closed their respective gaps taking two wins each in that time.

But the German outfit is hoping to reestablish its dominance during the Malaysian weekend on 2-4 October, the race after Baku, as the Asian country replaces Bahrain to make its F1 return.

Speaking on the Nu Silver Arrows Radio Show podcast, trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin said: “We haven't got much new coming to Baku, but actually that's a circuit that's more about drag than downforce.

“So the car was good in Monza, hopefully it will work well in Baku. But, you need a car that can have a good straight line speed.

Toto Wolff, Mercedes, James Allison, Mercedes, Andrew Shovlin, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

“There's other things, though, you need in Baku, like the sort of street circuit nature, almost that Monaco-esque being able to deal with the low speed, keeping all the wheels on the ground.

“And then the updates, well, they're going to come Malaysia onwards and hopefully we'll make a decent step.

“I don't think we're going to be out front by miles, but hopefully we'll be back into a position where we can really go into qualifying, knowing that we're fighting for pole.”

Although Mercedes has won the last two races - Monza and Madrid - via the dominant Kimi Antonelli, it hasn’t actually claimed pole since the Italian went quickest at Spa in July.

So that is a run of four, three of which saw McLaren’s Lando Norris take pole, marking a far cry from the start of 2026 where the Silver Arrows took pole for each of the opening 10 rounds.

“Early in the season, we tended to go thinking, we have a car that if we do a really good job, it should be on pole,” added Shovlin.

“We should be fighting for a race win. Whereas now the margin between finishing first and finishing sixth is one or two tenths and it's difficult to predict because Monza is a unique track.

“It needs a car that's quite slippy with low drag and then new circuit like Madring couldn't be more different. But we just focus on getting the most out of the car and if we win, awesome.”

Sports.title: Cadillac F1 owners Mark Walter and TWG Global face class-action lawsuit
Sports.content:
Cadillac Formula 1 shareholder Mark Walter has officially become the subject of a class-action lawsuit, while a concurrent investigation into potential fraud between his insurance companies is ongoing.

The class-action lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida, and the complaint alleges that Walter used his firms - TWG Global, alongside Delaware Life Insurance and Group 1001 - to execute a scheme aimed at concealing federal investigations and diverting billions of dollars from policyholders' funds.

The lawsuit claims that insurance companies affiliated with Walter used money from annuity policyholders to finance a broader business network.

This network enabled the mogul to acquire stakes in sports franchises like the Los Angeles Dodgers and the Los Angeles Lakers, before expanding into motorsport through TWG Motorsport (a division of TWG Global) by acquiring Andretti Global and partnering with General Motors to launch the Cadillac F1 team.

Media outlets report that instead of maintaining low-risk investments, the insurers funneled approximately 42% of their assets - around $17 billion - into Walter’s private network of business interests.

The lawsuit was brought by 67-year-old Florida resident Ira Rosner, represented by law firm Robbins Geller Rudman & Dowd, who alleges that the insurance companies intentionally withheld key financial disclosures.

Valtteri Bottas, Cadillac Racing Photo by: Alex Bierens de Haan / LAT Images via Getty Images

USA Today reported receiving a response from a spokesperson for Group 1001 Insurance, who acknowledged awareness of the suit while emphasizing: "No court has ruled that Group 1001 Insurance or Delaware Life Insurance Company did anything wrong, and we intend to defend the case vigorously, consistent with our long track record of serving policyholders with integrity."

TWG Global plays a vital role in Cadillac F1's organizational structure, acting as both an investing partner and an operational entity for the team.

While the civil lawsuit does not directly halt track operations and no criminal charges have been filed against executives, the controversy raises questions about the future of Walter's sports holdings. Walter recently agreed to sell his stakes in both the Lakers and Premier League side Chelsea - the latter case a combined 25% holding with Todd Boehly, for which the pair have received almost $1 billion from private equity firm Clearlake.

Just this past August, amid rising scrutiny over Walter's business practices, the team's parent company took a firm stance on Cadillac F1's future, issuing a statement to deny any plans to offload its Formula 1 assets.

"TWG is not considering a sale of the Cadillac team or any other part of TWG Motorsport," the company stated categorically during the Dutch Grand Prix.

Sports.title: How Antonelli's luxury problem is causing Wolff and Mercedes grey hairs
Sports.content:
For better or for worse, there seems to be no slowing down Kimi Antonelli.

Just ask Pete Bonnington, who channelled his inner schoolteacher in Madrid as he relentlessly had to remind the 20-year-old Italian to pay attention to track limits.

Having benefited from an earlier virtual safety car on a circuit where overtaking proved impossible, all Antonelli had to do was to keep it clean until the finish line, with Max Verstappen and Lando Norris resigned to following him home.

Bonnington and Mercedes had already suffered a scare earlier in the race with what almost sounded like a prank call from the young Italian.

Antonelli: "Check the car!"

Bonnington: "Which corner?"

Antonelli: "No I didn't touch any wall, but the steering feels weird..."

But with five laps to go, despite little genuine pressure from behind, Antonelli did tag one of the many concrete walls lining the challenging Madring circuit. "I touched the wall on the entry to Turn 7," Antonelli yelled.

Despite being in control, it was another race where Antonelli had been dangerously flirting with the track limits, much to the dismay of his father Marco and team boss Toto Wolff. There's just no slowing Antonelli down.

"I just discussed it with his father and we were joking: 'What an idiot!'. No, that's just Kimi,” the Mercedes boss said after the race. “The white lines, we had to drum it into his head that he shouldn't go over the white lines. Even in Monza, he still went over the white lines and [risked] the car. And the same with track limits.

"At a certain stage, I said to him: 'Don't you see out of the car? Do we need to sit you that high up so that you have [avoid] those track limit things? We had a laugh about it.

"And today, six laps to the end or whatever it was, he says: 'Check the car, I just brushed the wall.' What?! He's causing us grey hair. But maybe he's like this and maybe that's what's making him so quick."

Wolff added: "He had to hit the wall again because he wants to go fast. Sometimes for me, he's an inch too cool."

Kimi Antonelli is giving Toto Wolff a few grey hairs Photo by: Anni Graf - Formula 1 via Getty Images

Antonelli's flat-out approach appears to be a trait that Wolff and Mercedes are going to have to live with for now, at least until it goes wrong one day. Could that day come when Antonelli starts thinking about the big prize at the end as he careens towards a maiden world championship?

Wolff is adamant that won't be the case, despite Antonelli being by far the youngest driver to ever be in that position. "I promise you he's not thinking about it," Wolff insisted. "The way this kid is able to compartmentalise and be the young kid and then get into the car and be the mature racing driver...

"If Kimi says to himself: 'I'm not thinking about the championship', then he's not thinking about the championship. We are also trying, the parents and myself, the team is saying: 'You know, this is not finished.'

"There are black swan events. They can come and you're losing something out of your hands when you didn't think it was possible to lose. So, he's not going to think about it. We're too grown up and mature for this. We think about worst-case scenarios. He doesn't think about it."

Building on the lessons of a troubled debut year in 2025, Antonelli feels he has the right support system around him to carry him through to the finish line, whether that be in Abu Dhabi or at an impromptu home race in Imola near his native Bologna.

Kimi Antonelli has a strong support network in the paddock Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

"I’m lucky to have really good people around me," Antonelli explained. "I have an incredible team that supports me, a great family. Especially my dad is the one who keeps me on the ground. Especially when he sees that I might lose a little bit the way, he doesn’t [hesitate] to tell me off or to just tell me to come back to the ground.

"On my side, as I said many times, I just try to do my best every race, trying to really drive as fast as I can whenever I go in the car. And then we’ll see where we end up at the end of the year. But definitely I don’t want to over-complicate things or just drive worrying about championship or results. Just driving, doing my best."

Driving as fast as he can all the time, is certainly working for Antonelli right now. As far as his team is concerned, almost to a fault.

Sports.title: Former Mercedes F1 tech chief Elliott joins Alpine as CTO
Sports.content:
Alpine has appointed Mike Elliott as chief technical officer of its Formula 1 team, further bolstering the Enstone-based team's technical structure.

Alpine announced on Thursday that Elliott will "oversee the technical and engineering functions at the team's factory at Enstone" in what is a newly created position as CTO.

For the 52-year-old Briton, it presents a return to Enstone after serving as the team's principal aerodynamicist in its Renault and Lotus days.

Elliott then went on to join Mercedes as its head of aerodynamics, helping the team make a head start on the 2014 regulations. Elliott rose to the position of technical director and chief technical officer, trading positions with James Allison, before leaving the Brackley squad in 2023.

"He has a proven track record in the sport, having contributed to an impressive eight constructors' and eight drivers' championships," Alpine stated.

Pierre Gasly, Alpine Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

"Elliott's arrival at Enstone strengthens the team's technical capabilities as the team looks to build on the improved performances on track and close the gap to the top four teams."

Current executive technical director David Sanchez is understood to be reporting into Elliott, who is overseeing the entire technical area of the outfit.

After sacrificing last year, Alpine has made a strong start to the 2026 regulations, fighting Racing Bulls for fifth in the constructors' championship. The 2026 campaign is Alpine's first as a customer team of Mercedes.

Sports.title: Tsunoda's in-depth look at why he failed to master Red Bull’s F1 car in 2025
Sports.content:
It seems almost unfathomable for a title contender's team-mate to end up 17th in the Formula 1 drivers’ standings, yet that’s what happened to Yuki Tsunoda alongside Max Verstappen at Red Bull in 2025.

In a way, it was unprecedented – the closest modern example perhaps was Felipe Massa lying a lowly 16th eight rounds into the 2012 season while Ferrari team-mate Fernando Alonso comfortably led the championship, but the Brazilian somewhat turned the situation around.

Equally, Tsunoda’s case was unique. Having decided to release an underperforming Sergio Perez, Red Bull picked Liam Lawson over Tsunoda for a 2025 promotion, believing the New Zealander’s lack of experience would be offset by his allegedly higher potential.

Lawson didn’t get much time to prove himself. After two grands prix in which he was eliminated in Q1 and failed to score any points, he was sent right back to Racing Bulls, with Tsunoda finally getting his chance at the main team.

At the time, the Japanese was actually quite bullish about his odds of succeeding where so many others had failed.

“People often say Red Bull cars tend to have strong front-end grip. I personally love cars that turn aggressively, and in the past, I adapted my driving style to that kind of set-up,” Tsunoda said ahead of his Red Bull debut.

Liam Lawson, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Red Bull Content Pool

“Racing Bulls traditionally had cars that understeered a bit more, which was challenging for me at first, but I got used to it, and it eventually became my norm. Now, the key will be adjusting to Red Bull’s characteristics again, but considering my past experience, I’m not too worried about it.”

Perhaps he should have been. While Verstappen won eight grands prix – more than anyone, including 2025 champion Lando Norris – Tsunoda failed to take a single podium finish, with his highest result an underwhelming sixth in Baku; he scored 30 points to his team-mate’s 385 over their time together.

In 27 qualifying sessions (sprints included), Tsunoda made it to Q3 eight times, was out in Q2 on nine occasions, and was eliminated as early as Q1 on 10 occurrences. He outqualified his team-mate just once and was 0.6s slower on average.

So, what was the problem with Red Bull’s RB21 F1 car? To some extent, Tsunoda remains at a loss to explain it.

“Normally I'm able to understand the car, what I'm driving, what kind of characteristic,” Tsunoda detailed on the Beyond The Grid podcast, “but it feels like even after Abu Dhabi, I didn't know what kind of car I was driving. I still don't understand what was the issue and what things made me very struggle to learn about this car and get used to the car.

“I thought confidence was there, but some race I just somehow lost the confidence. I still don't understand the car, to be honest.”

Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Mark Thompson / Getty Images

Still, Tsunoda has fascinating insight to provide. He openly admits he refrained from tweaking his driving style, believing that’s just what works for him. However, he did end up trying out Verstappen’s set-ups – and that experiment just failed.

“One thing about myself: I have big enough ego to not change my driving style,” Tsunoda admitted. “I know what I'm doing in terms of driving and I believe in myself. So, I never try to change my driving style to another driver’s, even though the driver is competitive and fast.

“Obviously for Max, it's a different case. He's a world champion, he proves a lot of things and I still learn a lot of things from his driving.

“My core driving is the same. And at some time, probably the first year out of any years since I started, I thought about changing driving style and trying to do something similar to Max. But in my perspective, if I just look at data, I didn't really see a huge difference in terms of driving.

“What I did most – and what I think now was the biggest mistake last year – was to try to replicate the set-up, what he's doing; even knowing that sometimes, if I feel the car very oversteer, Max's [set-up] in theory makes the car worse, more sensitive in the direction change, or makes the car slide more.

"I tend to choose the set-up, even though I'm already struggling with oversteer. It can happen sometimes the opposite way as well: even though I'm struggling with understeer, his car is more understeer. I try to replicate that.”

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing Team Photo by: Zak Mauger / LAT Images via Getty Images

Tsunoda is not the first driver to unsuccessfully attempt to use Verstappen’s set-up. Alex Albon also struggled alongside the Dutchman, for a year and a half, in 2019-20.

Back in 2023, the Anglo-Thai reminisced in the High Performance Podcast: “[Verstappen] has quite a unique driving style, it’s not that easy to get along with. Everyone has a driving style; I would say my driving style is a bit more on the smooth side, but I like a car that has a good front end, so quite sharp, quite direct. Max does too, but his level of sharp and direct is a whole different level – it’s eye-wateringly sharp.

“To give people kind of maybe an explanation of what that might feel like, if you bump up the sensitivity [on a computer game] completely to the max and you move that mouse and it’s just darting across the screen everywhere, that’s kind of how it feels. It becomes so sharp that it makes you a little bit tense.”

This metaphor was brought up to Tsunoda, but he wasn’t convinced it was particularly relevant to the RB21. Asked if he could relate, the Japanese racer said: “Yes and no. First, the car is a lot different to when Alex was driving and I’ve never driven Alex's car.

“It's sensitive, but I didn't feel that sensitive. But at the same time, like I said, it was very up and down. Some tracks I'm driving more sensitive car than him, some tracks he was driving more sensitive. On average, probably he was driving a bit more sensitive car, more like a sharper car than me.

“What he was definitely better at was, even though the car was sensitive or even numb… In a corner, there's always one phase or one moment that the car naturally reacts to, or tries to kind of respect its own behaviour. You know what I mean? Like, always in the corner, as soon as I turn in or whatever, that car does its own thing. That can be like a sensitive, sharp rotation or, I don't know, the front slides or something. He’s able to use that and he can smell that kind of behaviour probably much faster than me. And he was able to maximise that kind of behaviour throughout the corner.

“It's not necessarily my driving style that I'm doing, but if I have that kind of moments, sharp turn-in or rotation or the front slide, I tend to force the car how I want to drive. I normally respect how the car wants to drive through the corner, or I’m able to use that kind of natural behaviour from the car. But I wasn’t able to use that ability much in the Red Bull.”

Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Zak Mauger / LAT Images via Getty Images

As soon as he first drove the RB21 in free practice at Suzuka, Tsunoda’s early optimism gave way to caution; he reported the car was “feeling a bit more tricky” than on the simulator.

With hindsight, it was a sign of the ordeal to come.

“Even though I said, yeah, I thought I had confidence, probably it was not enough, as much as the VCARB car that I drove for four years,” Tsunoda said. “Red Bull is still a car that was completely different, which I felt as soon as I stepped into that car in Suzuka.

“There's some confidence level I was able to build up, but to maximise that whole performance, I think that was probably something I was missing, and trying to find that confidence throughout the year.”

Tsunoda eventually found out in Qatar, at the penultimate round of the season, that he would not be retained as a race driver and would act as a reserve in 2026 – no huge surprise given his results, and the campaign had been so draining that the news actually was a relief to him.

“I still remember the moments,” he recounted. “Initially, what I got told was from Helmut [Marko, then Red Bull’s motorsport advisor].

“In the end, Helmut is the person that brought me into Formula 1, brought me even to the Red Bull junior programme. We were together since when I was 17, 18. I remember he was also pretty disappointed about that.

Yuki Tsunoda, Red Bull Racing, Helmut Marko, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Mark Thompson - Getty Images

“And when I got told, I still remember, I didn't feel that much of huge disappointment or devastated feeling.

"Obviously I was still disappointed and pretty sad that I'm not driving next year. But not as I expected because I don't know why, somehow in a way, I fought really hard. I fought more than ever in that 2025 year and even if I look back now, I don't have much regret. I gave everything.

“In a way, honestly, my heart was just saying, ‘Okay, now I can be relaxed’. Because it was so stressful, the second half of the 2025 season, where I fought hard with a lot of pressure. Like I was never able to kind of breathe out much.”

Sports.title: Autosport magazine: Antonelli and a Can-Am celebration
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli’s rise to become Formula 1 world championship favourite and a celebration marking 60 years of Can-Am feature in the October issue of Autosport, out today (17 September).

It’s not just his substantial points lead that makes Antonelli the likely 2026 world champion. His consistent level of performance, with a reducing list of apparent weaknesses as each week passes, makes him seem impregnable.

Antonelli’s remarkable victory from 19th on the grid at Monza was a brilliant demonstration of patience and speed when required. Yes, the strategy fell Antonelli’s way, but the win must have been a psychological hammerblow to George Russell.

The Briton is perhaps in the hardest position of all. If McLaren, Ferrari or even Red Bull can find a technical advantage and put on a charge – a challenge that Jake Boxall-Legge also explores in this issue – then Lando Norris, Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen can start racking up wins and eating into the gap, potentially with a team-mate to help.

But any Mercedes improvement will, of course, benefit both Russell and Antonelli. Russell will have to start consistently outperforming Antonelli – or hope the Italian has an unbelievable amount of misfortune.

As well as Stuart Codling’s look at the long wait for an Italian world champion and Antonelli’s challenge, we assess the role of the reserve driver in the modern era, and Ronald Vording listens to Honda’s chief engineer and trackside general manager Shintaro Orihara open up on the troubles Aston Martin’s engine partner has faced this season.

Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Federico Basile

It’s 60 years since the famous Can-Am series for big banger sportscars began and we celebrate the category that briefly outpaced F1 this month. Pete Lyons, Autosport’s Can-Am reporter from the period, outlines what made it so special, we recall a McLaren that proved unbeatable, and Gary Watkins argues that the championship’s second era shouldn’t be ignored.

Looking ahead, Tom Howard hears from the World Rally Championship’s new promoters to understand their vision for the future of rallying, while Marcus Simmons charts Ash Sutton’s inexorable charge to a fifth British Touring Car crown in our Donington Park and Croft debriefs.

Two very different machines also star in our 25-page National section: a rallycross supercar and a UK club racing icon set to return to competition at the Goodwood Revival.

Sports.title: Bruising F1 2026 will not be the end for Russell - Wolff
Sports.content:
Toto Wolff is confident that George Russell can overcome a bruising 2026 Formula 1 campaign and still become world champion in the future.

The Mercedes driver is second and 81 points behind his dominant team-mate Kimi Antonelli with just nine rounds remaining, meaning a maiden crown for the 20-year-old is a matter of time.

It comes despite Russell entering 2026 as the heavy title favourite as he maximised the W16 last year with fourth in the standings and 169 points ahead of seventh-placed Antonelli.

Very few expected Antonelli to make such a strong leap into his sophomore season after a very up-and-down rookie campaign, but he is the one to have capitalised upon the rocket ship Mercedes has delivered for 2026.

“You can have good races, bad races, good years and bad years, but we're talking about the driver that has won everything that you could have potentially won before,” said Wolff of Russell at the Spanish Grand Prix.

“Every single karting championship, Formula 3 in his rookie year, Formula 2 in his rookie year, went into the Williams. We're talking about the top driver.

“We need to find out what is it for him to be able to unleash that potential and of course, there's the psychological side. If you have a run like him this year, you're taking a beating.

“But the great ones, they recover. And I think that George has all it needs to fight for championships and even if that one has maybe sailed, there will be more.”

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images

The Spanish Grand Prix was where Antonelli took his second consecutive victory after Monza, which was particularly damaging for Russell as the Italian started 19th with his team-mate on the front row.

It has all led to Russell effectively conceding that “I don’t think I am in the fight” for the title, as eight-time race winner Antonelli is romping towards becoming F1’s youngest ever champion.

A high-pressure situation that Wolff doesn’t think will affect Antonelli, especially thanks to his support network that ensures he remains level-headed for the years to come.

“Kimi from his personality, so grounded, 100% racer, not distracted from anything outside, super family situation and that's why I see no risk that he's losing the plot because he's so dominant,” added Wolff.

Read Also: Formula 1 Russell and Hamilton concede F1 2026 title chances as Antonelli dominates

“Over the next few years, it's something that we will always have our discussions like we have now. What is it that could distract him? What is it that's good for him? What kind of environment he needs? That is the discussion we have.”

“I promise you he's not thinking about it. The way this kid is able to compartmentalise and be the young kid and then get into the car and be the mature racing driver, that's why if Kimi says to himself, I'm not thinking about the championship, he's not thinking about the championship.

“And we are also trying, the parents and myself, the team is saying, you know, this is not finished. There is black swan events. They can come and you're losing something out of your hand when you didn't think it was possible to lose. So he's not going to think about it.”

Sports.title: Haas confident of getting 2027 F1 budget closer to cap with new partner talks
Sports.content:
Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu says the team is making "positive" progress with his team's search for new sponsorship, as the American Formula 1 team seeks to start pushing its yearly budget towards the cap.

F1's smallest team, Haas employs just north of 400 people and has been operating well below the budget cap in both of its iterations. Although the team currently has a title sponsorship deal with Toyota's Gazoo Racing arm, which took over from money transfer company MoneyGram for this year, it is currently looking to further augment its sponsorship portfolio.

Rumours have surfaced that the team is in talks with BWT, currently Alpine's title sponsor, which will move on the team next year as Alpine has a new title partnership with fashion house Gucci planned for 2027. This is not the first time that Haas has been linked to BWT; the Austrian company was suggested as one of its destinations after it ended its deal with Aston Martin at the close of 2021, before it moved to Alpine in search of more pink livery space.

Earlier this year, Komatsu told Sky Sports that a lack of budget was stopping the team from increasing its headcount, and from improving its tooling and infrastructure, and that his job was to find more revenue by attracting new partners to the team.

Speaking over the Madring weekend, Komatsu provided an update and stated that the team was in talks with a few different prospective partners to help bring the team's budget closer to the $215 million cap.

"We're talking to so many prospects; it's getting there. I'd say very positive about next year's budget," Komatsu stated.

"It just helps massively. But I think slowly and surely we are getting our story out there and finding great people. So, yeah, it's good so far."

Asked about the BWT rumours, Komatsu stated that "we're not going to have pink cars, if that's what you are saying!"

Komatsu added that he was not looking to prospective future drivers to make up the shortfall, and that the team was still in a position where it could focus on selecting its 2027 line-up based on performance.

Ayao Komatsu, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

Ryo Hirakawa, Leonardo Fornaroli, and Rafael Camara have been conducting tests in previous cars for Haas, as the team assesses potential future drivers; Komatsu estimated that there were five in the running, presumably including current incumbent Esteban Ocon (whose performances have improved of late) and Yuki Tsunoda.

Asked if any commercial factors would have a bearing, Komatsu stated that it would only enter the picture if he had two drivers who were largely inseparable in terms of pace.

"If it's within a tenth, for instance, very, very close, then affiliation package does come into play for sure. I don't think [that will be the scenario]. I think we can choose by performance; we haven't finished the whole programme yet.

"We really want two fast drivers because that's the best way to grow this team. It doesn't matter if it's two Ferrari drivers or two Toyota drivers or two McLaren drivers.

"I mean, Fornaroli, he's a McLaren driver, right? But honestly, it doesn't matter. Whoever is the fastest, that's the best for the team.

"Again, for everybody, 400 people working here, they need to know that we've got the best driver choice that we can get hold of so that these two drivers are getting the best out of the car. Imagine taking somebody half a second off, but extra money. That's not going to be very motivating.

"And also, one position in the championship. That's quite a lot of money, right? For us, like I said, I'm staying consistent. I've always said we take drivers by performance. That's what we're doing."

Sports.title: Hearn Risks Matchroom’s Future for Aging Joshua
Sports.content:
Eddie Hearn may have secured Anthony Joshua’s preferred country for the Tyson Fury fight, but Roy Jones Jr. believes the Matchroom promoter has damaged his position with the people controlling boxing’s richest events.

Joshua and Fury had agreed to fight November 20 at Madison Square Garden. Hearn resisted the New York venue because Joshua’s contract required the contest to take place in Britain. The heavyweight clash is now likely to land at Principality Stadium in Cardiff on December 11.

That gives Hearn a victory he can sell to the British public, but the reported 2 a.m. local start removes much of its meaning. Seventy thousand paying spectators may be asked to remain inside the stadium until early morning so Netflix can show the fight during American prime time.

If Jones is correct that American viewers have little interest in Fury–Joshua, the compromise becomes harder to defend. Britain provides the crowd, ticket money and atmosphere while the broadcast schedule caters to an audience that Jones says does not care.

Jones applauded Hearn for resisting the combined pressure from Turki Alalshikh, Sela, Netflix, Dana White, TKO and Team Fury. He also offered a much darker forecast for Matchroom.

“Hearn has won a battle, but he’s gonna lose the war. I just think it’s because Turki has enough money to do whatever he wants to do. Whoever has his ear is gonna win the war, because he’s got the money to keep it going. But my hat goes off to Eddie for fighting, because Eddie knows that war is not the best thing for boxing,” Jones told Parimatch Slots Site, via BoxingScene.

The concern reaches beyond a disagreement over one venue. Alalshikh has the financial resources to outlast any traditional promoter. If he decides TKO and Frank Warren are easier partners, Matchroom can be removed from major cards without leaving the Saudi operation short of alternatives.

Warren has remained aligned with the Riyadh group while showing flexibility over the Fury–Joshua date and location. That may leave Queensberry better placed for future Saudi events as Hearn returns to a far more limited DAZN schedule.

Dana White and TKO present another danger. White wants a more centralized boxing structure with tighter control over fighters and purses. Hearn has built his reputation by securing the largest possible payments for his boxers. The two approaches were always likely to collide, and this dispute may have given TKO another reason to work around Matchroom.

Hearn has made that stand for a 36-year-old Joshua whose career is nearing its conclusion. Joshua helped build Matchroom Boxing into an international company, so the promoter’s loyalty is understandable. However, Jaron Ennis, Diego Pacheco, Conor Benn and Matchroom’s younger fighters will need access to major financial opportunities long after Joshua retires.

It is too early to state that Hearn’s relationship with Alalshikh is finished. Neither side has announced a permanent split. Jones nevertheless sees the imbalance clearly. Hearn enforced Joshua’s contract and preserved the British venue, but he challenged a group with enough money, fighters, and promotional partners to continue without him.

Joshua may receive the home fight he demanded. Matchroom’s younger stable may inherit its cost.

Sports.title: Can David Morrell Recover at Light Heavyweight?
Sports.content:
David Morrell has disappeared from the boxing conversation since Zak Chelli stopped him in the 10th round on May 9. Once presented as a future star at super middleweight, the Cuban now sits at 12-2 with no confirmed return date and serious questions about his future at 175 pounds.

Chelli accepted the fight on two weeks’ notice and was trailing before hurting Morrell in the ninth and finishing him with 36 seconds left in the final round. It was not merely a shocking defeat. It exposed a technical weakness that had followed Morrell throughout his professional career.

When pressured, Morrell retreats in straight lines until his heels reach the edge of the ring. He then squares his upper body, raises both gloves, and waits for the attack to end.

The guard protects parts of his head, but widening his torso gives opponents access to his liver and ribs. He also provides no angle for an escape. Instead of stepping around an orthodox fighter’s lead foot, Morrell remains directly in front of him.

David Benavidez exploited that behavior over 12 rounds in February 2025. Morrell dropped Benavidez in the 11th, but those isolated successes could not erase the long stretches he spent absorbing combinations along the ropes.

Chelli found the same opening. Once Morrell’s legs faded, the guard became a hiding place rather than an active defense.

Morrell remains dangerous when he has room to select his shots. His straight left hand, counter right hook, and short two-punch bursts are fast enough to punish careless entries. The trouble begins when an opponent survives the first attack. Morrell rarely follows with the sustained combinations needed to hold the center of the ring. His style still carries the rhythm of amateur boxing: land the cleaner single shot, reset and wait for another opening. Professional pressure fighters do not always grant that reset.

An opponent willing to walk through one or two hard punches can force Morrell backward and beat him through activity. Morrell does not have a developed inside game that allows him to fight for position once the distance has disappeared.

Elite fighters who become trapped along the ropes usually clinch, pin an arm or turn the attacker before leaving. Morrell does little of that.

He stands behind his forearms and allows opponents to complete their combinations. Even when most of the punches strike his gloves, judges see one fighter attacking and the other merely surviving.

That passivity is more exhausting at light heavyweight. Morrell was physically stronger than most of his opposition at 168 pounds. At 175, naturally larger fighters can drive their weight into him and force his legs to support both bodies.

Holding a turtle guard under that pressure drains the shoulders, back, and thighs. It helps explain why Morrell’s energy vanished so rapidly against Chelli in the ninth and 10th rounds. Morrell reportedly relocated to Orlando and changed his training setup after the Chelli defeat. A new camp will only help if it changes his reactions when another fighter presses him.

He needs lateral escape steps, an offensive clinch, and combinations long enough to make opponents reconsider walking forward. Returning to super middleweight would reduce the physical burden, although making 168 again may no longer be practical.

Matchmaking presents another issue. Morrell remains too powerful to become an easy opponent for a rising prospect, but his two defeats have stripped away much of his bargaining power. A soft return fight will bring criticism, while another aggressive volume puncher may push him farther from the top level. Morrell is only 28, and his speed, power, and amateur background still give him valuable tools.

His future depends on accepting that the defense which carried him through 168 pounds does not work against strong light heavyweights. If he returns with the same straight-line retreat and stationary high guard, Chelli’s victory will no longer look like an isolated upset. It will look like a blueprint.

Sports.title: Moses Itauma Exposed as Three Round Fighter
Sports.content:
Moses Itauma’s explosive offense carried him into an IBF heavyweight title fight at 21, but Filip Hrgovic exposed the costly machinery underneath it. George Groves now describes Itauma as a “three-round fighter,” a label that rings true once the sheer physical toll of that early assault is broken down.

Itauma held the speed advantage, tagging Hrgovic with sharp, clean punches during the initial minutes. Rather than establishing control, he pursued the knockout as if Hrgovic were simply another fragile victim waiting to fold. The Croatian veteran absorbed the initial storm, forced the prospect into sustained manual labor, and closed the show in round nine.

“At the moment, he’s a three-round fighter. That’s the sad fact of it,” Groves told Sky Sports.

Groves saw the deterioration developing long before the stoppage. The tactical failure began with Itauma completely discarding distance management. Instead of flicking out light, probing jabs to displace Hrgovic’s guard, he loaded up on heavy hooks from the opening bell. Dozens of those shots crashed harmlessly against Hrgovic’s gloves, yet Itauma continued torqueing his entire core into every strike as though the target were exposed.

Bludgeoning a tight defense with maximum leverage wrecks the back and shoulders. Itauma made that deficit worse by firing extended combinations at top gear. He was emptying championship-level reserves on leather while Hrgovic waited calmly behind his shells.

Top-tier heavyweights pace their attacks. They dial back the force on four punches to mask the fifth, dislodging a guard to create genuine openings. Itauma approached every swing like an executioner. That blitz dismantles limited gatekeepers, but it burns through the reserve tank when a stubborn veteran stays upright.

His movement created a parallel physical leak. Itauma employed an active, darting bounce to step into range and pull away before Hrgovic could fire back. It caught the eye, but that bounce placed relentless strain on his calves.

The moment that bounce disappeared, his posture came apart. Itauma stood straight up, his head movement vanished, and his jaw drifted onto the center line. He quit pivoting off the ropes, retreating instead in straight lines. Hrgovic stopped having to track a mobile target because Itauma planted himself directly in the path of the right hand.

The most glaring flaw was Itauma’s lack of defensive resting skills. Elite fighters know how to steal breathers. Tyson Fury leans his massive frame into clinches to crush a man’s legs, while Oleksandr Usyk circles just outside reach to run thirty seconds off the clock. Itauma attempted to punch his way through suffocating fatigue. Rather than wrapping Hrgovic up, leaning on him or establishing a break in the action, he kept firing wild salvos.

A mental unraveling accompanied the bodily exhaustion. Having grown accustomed to early knockouts, Itauma looked rattled when Hrgovic absorbed his hardest punches without blinking. Lacking a fallback strategy, his shot selection deteriorated into desperate swings, speeding up his own demise.

Rebuilding Itauma requires a far more precise touch than feeding him a passive punching bag. Another two-minute knockout would decorate the highlight reel while leaving the critical flaws unaddressed. He requires an opponent whose defensive habits punish impatience without offering Hrgovic’s devastating counterpunching.

Hughie Fury provides the ideal stylistic puzzle. He fights ugly, stays elusive, ties up inside and refuses to grant young punchers the firefights they crave. Itauma would have to operate behind a steady jab, trap a retreating target along the ropes, and accept that an immediate finish is off the table.

Muscle fiber composition and cardiovascular ceilings are largely genetic. Fighters who carry dense, explosive, fast-twitch muscle mass do not wake up at 28 with the engine of an endurance athlete. George Foreman was an explosive wrecking ball who blew his tank against Muhammad Ali in Zaire at 25, and he never magically transformed into a high-output distance machine. He solved it later in life by stripping away almost all wasted motion, pacing himself to a crawl, and walking men down behind a heavy, thudding jab.

The hard truth for Itauma is that human physiology does not work backward. As heavyweights move out of their early twenties, their bodies naturally thicken, absolute fast-twitch snap dulls, and carrying 240-plus pounds over twelve rounds becomes more taxing on the heart and lungs, not less. If a fighter is hyperventilating and losing his legs after three hard frames at 21, running more miles on the road will not rewrite his DNA.

Right now, Itauma operates like a sports car redlining in first gear. Every punch is loaded with full hip and shoulder torque, every movement is an explosive leap into range, and he has zero concept of how to make an opponent carry his weight when he gets tired. That is catastrophic fuel economy.

If Itauma remains married to that style, he is permanently locked into being a dangerous three-round frontrunner who will get dragged out into deep water and finished by any durable contender with a pulse and a chin. He only stretches his effectiveness to six or seven rounds if he accepts a radical tactical lobotomy:

Sports.title: Joe Louis Crushes Bob Pastor in Detroit Rematch
Sports.content:
Joe Louis settled an old score on September 20, 1939, knocking out Bob Pastor in the 11th round before 33,868 spectators at Briggs Stadium in Detroit. Pastor had escaped him for 10 rounds two years earlier. Louis made certain that the same tactics would not save him again.

Their first meeting took place at Madison Square Garden on January 29, 1937. Pastor, a former New York University fullback, conceded roughly 25 pounds and was listed as a 10-to-1 underdog. He survived by circling, retreating, and refusing to remain within punching range.

The unanimous decision belonged to Louis, but Pastor celebrated reaching the final bell. Sections of the 18,864 crowd booed the winner and treated the challenger’s survival as a moral victory. Their reaction irritated the future champion, who believed Pastor had reduced the contest to a footrace.

By the rematch, Louis (39-1, 35 KOs) was making his eighth defense of the heavyweight championship. Pastor (38-4-4, 17 KOs) had developed into a leading contender. Both men were 25, though Louis held a 17-pound weight advantage at 200 pounds.

Pastor’s camp requested a 20-round fight, believing the extended distance would test the champion’s stamina. It was a disastrous calculation. Pastor prepared to ration his energy across a marathon. Louis attacked from the opening bell as if the fight had been scheduled for three rounds.

A different pursuit strategy also separated the rematch from their 1937 encounter. Instead of following Pastor around the perimeter, the champion used shorter diagonal steps and moved across his escape lane. Pastor repeatedly found his opponent waiting for him.

The adjustment produced four knockdowns in the opening round and another in the second. Yet that early destruction presented Louis with a test of his own. He had spent heavily trying to force the stoppage, and Pastor’s refusal to fold left the champion less explosive through portions of rounds three through six.

There was no reckless chase for the knockout after the early assault failed to finish Pastor. The champion lowered his output, recovered his breathing, and resumed the methodical work of taking away the challenger’s legs. Body punches during close exchanges reduced Pastor’s lateral bounce without wasting energy on punches aimed at an absent target.

Pastor had trained specifically to avoid Louis’s left hook. Trainer Jack Blackburn turned that preparation against him. The champion showed the left, occupied Pastor’s vision with throwaway jabs and drove his right hand through the opening. Pastor’s habit of slipping outside the left placed his head in the route of the punch he truly needed to avoid.

The challenger produced his strongest work in the eighth. Pastor planted his feet, backed Louis toward the ropes, and connected with jabs and short combinations. The sequence exposed a flaw in the champion’s defense. Louis held a high guard but offered limited upper-body movement, allowing an active jab and quick inside punches to reach him before he regained his punching position.

That success carried a price. To back Louis up, Pastor had to abandon the movement that had protected him. Every planted combination created a stationary target. The champion remained calm, absorbed the surge, and continued attacking the body rather than trying to silence Pastor with one wild counter.

A short right badly staggered Pastor in the tenth. By then, the left hand had become a range finder and visual distraction. Pastor was still reacting to the hook, while Louis was measuring him for the right.

Back in the corner after the tenth, the champion told Blackburn that the next round would be the last.

Pastor opened the 11th by jabbing and attempting to circle left along his familiar escape route. Louis extended the left to obstruct his view and close the lane. Pastor moved to evade the punch he expected, and the right hand came over the top.

He never saw it. Pastor crashed to the canvas and remained there for referee Sam Hennessey’s count. The knockout came 38 seconds into the round, after the challenger had been dropped six times.

The victory paid Louis $118,400 from a gross gate of $347,870, while Pastor received $51,800. More importantly, it erased every complaint left behind by their first fight. Pastor had survived by making him chase in New York. In Detroit, the champion cut off the ring, attacked the challenger’s habits, and used the punch Pastor had spent the entire night helping him find.
