By this point, eight women had been found dead.

There would be another discovery less than 48 hours later.

9. Jabulile Ntimba – 17 September

The ninth body was found in Dawn Park, Boksburg, on 17 September.

Police added the case to the investigation into the deaths of women across Ekurhuleni, taking the official number to nine in two months.

The woman was found in an open area in Villa Liza.

Police initially said the victim had not been identified and that preliminary information suggested she may have been killed elsewhere before her body was left at the scene.

The victim has since been identified as Jabulile Ntimba.

The Dawn Park case has also produced one of the biggest developments in the investigation so far.

On Monday morning, SAPS announced that the Gauteng Murder and Robbery Unit had arrested one man and two women over the weekend in connection with the murder.

The trio are expected to appear in the Boksburg Magistrate’s Court on Monday, 21 September.

SAPS said the arrests relate to the ninth case.

Police have not announced that the three suspects are responsible for any of the other deaths.

Are the nine Ekurhuleni murders linked?

That question has followed the investigation from the moment the number of bodies began rising.

Police have looked for connections, but investigators have not concluded that all nine women were killed by the same person or group.

Cachalia addressed the speculation directly on Sunday.

He said investigators had not confirmed that they were dealing with a serial killer because the cases were “not all necessarily linked”, with indications of different methods and motives in some cases.

Parliament’s Portfolio Committee on Police chairperson Ian Cameron issued a similar warning earlier in the investigation.

“We must be careful not to claim links that investigators have not established,” Cameron said after the Kwa-Thema discovery.

He said SAPS had deployed specialist detectives, forensic experts, tracking capability, K9 resources and investigative psychology to the cases.

What police have confirmed is that the nine deaths now sit before a multidisciplinary investigation team.

Investigation escalated as death toll rose

The scale of the police response has grown with the number of cases.

Acting Gauteng police leadership initially drove the investigation, but national police structures have since become more heavily involved.

Cachalia announced on Sunday that Crime Intelligence head Lieutenant-General Dumisani Khumalo and KwaZulu-Natal police commissioner Lieutenant-General Nhlanhla Mkhwanazi would assist the investigation, which falls under senior detective and forensic leadership.

Cachalia also confirmed that investigators had called three persons of interest in for questioning. Police later confirmed that these were the same three suspects arrested in connection with the Dawn Park murder case.

President Cyril Ramaphosa has directed authorities to give the Ekurhuleni killings the highest level of attention, while government has increased police visibility in affected areas.

For the families, however, the investigation is about far more than a running number. It is about Busisiwe. Itumeleng. Nomfesane. Gracious. Tsontso. Dineo. Jabulile.

Police are still trying to establish who killed them, why they were killed and which of their deaths — if any — connect.

World.title: Tshwane’s prepaid meter crackdown: Fines of up to R75k
World.content:
Homeowners in Tshwane who have prepaid electricity are being warned that tampering or bypasing can cost them up to R75 000 in fines as the metro fights against power theft. However, it seems some law-abiding residents are also being caught in this.

WHAT EXACTLY IS THE PROBLEM?

The City of Tshwane says its enforcement operations have found 2339 manipulated prepaid meters. 494 of the 2339 are reportedly linked to repeat offences. Tampering has cost Tshwane more than R78 million so far. Guilty households face the fine as well as billing adjustments to recover electricity allegedly used without proper metering. In an attempt to curb the problem, the metro is replacing older meters with smart prepaid units that are harder to interfere with.

Howver, the problem is national. Eskom recorded R8.15 billion in non-technical losses from theft between April 2025 and the end of February 2026. The Department of Electricity and Energy estimates that about 1.7 million customers use illegal connections or tampered meters. Non-technical losses, including illegally generated prepaid tokens known as ghost vending, cost up to R23 billion in revenue a year.



GROWING COMPLAINTS

The Freedom Front Plus (FF+) said they are receiving a growing number of complaints from residents who claim they were wrongly accused. According to the party, technicians responding to fault reports sometimes arrive without spare parts and temporarily bypass the meter to restore supply. Inspectors then visit and accuse the household of tampering. The party also says some residents were told a fine could disappear in exchange for cash. Two residents have reportedly opened criminal cases with the police.

“In many cases, residents claim that these fines are unfounded and legally questionable…when residents report power problems, technicians often arrive without spare parts and bypass the meters to temporarily restore power,” said FF+.

“Shortly afterwards, inspectors visit the same residents’ properties and accuse them of having tampered with the meters,” said FF+.



HOW DID THE CITY OF TSHWANE RESPOND?

City of Tshwane said that officials and technicians may never solicit or accept cash to cancel fines or alter meter records. Fines must be charged to the account under gazetted tariffs, not paid through cash transfers or messaging apps. Anyone who receives such a demand should open a criminal case with SAPS. Formal disputes can be lodged by email or at the Client Service Centre in the Isivuno Building.

Take a look at home appliances that could be draining your electricity here.

World.title: Caught on camera: the threat that triggered a SANRAL probe (Video)
World.content:
SANRAL is investigating Moriel Infrastructure Group after its executive chairman was filmed threatening women: Image via X

The South African National Roads Agency (SANRAL) has confirmed it is investigating one of its own contractors, Moriel Infrastructure Group.

This follows footage showing its founder and then-executive chairman threatening women at a Johannesburg restaurant.

Lawrence Chamurwa Mudzinganyama was filmed confronting a group of women at Vlamo Restaurant in Sandtonon 19 September.



The footage has since gone viral.

It prompted a criminal case, ministerial intervention, and his removal from the company entirely.

WHAT ACTUALLY HAPPENED AT THE RESTAURANT

According to widely circulated footage, the confrontation began near the restaurant’s ladies’ restroom.



The women reportedly rejected Mudzinganyama’s advances beforehand.

In the video, he is heard making direct threats of violence against the women.

A case was opened with SAPS on Saturday, 20 September, and Mudzinganyama now faces an intimidation charge.



Mudzinganyama has since issued a personal statement.

He apologised “unreservedly” to the women involved, saying his “aggressive and threatening language was unacceptable and unjustifiable, regardless of the circumstances that led to the disagreement.”

He said he should have removed himself from the situation and sought help from restaurant management instead.



Mudzinganyama also committed to completing a conflict-management programme, while cooperating fully with any law enforcement investigation.

Vlamo Restaurant confirmed the incident occurred on its premises.

It clarified that Mudzinganyama has no ownership, employment or affiliation with the establishment.



He was removed once management became aware of the confrontation.

WHY THIS HAS BECOME A GOVERNMENT MATTER

The fallout moved quickly beyond the restaurant itself.

Transport Minister Barbara Creecy instructed SANRAL’sboard to investigate how Moriel Infrastructure Group secured its government contracts in the first place.



SANRAL has confirmed it holds two active contracts with the company, covering projects on the N1 and N2 national roads.

SANRAL’s Acting CEO, Lehlonolo Memeza, said the investigation would determine whether Moriel was lawfully appointed and whether it’s meeting its contractual obligations.

He added pointedly that “no South African can allow women to be threatened and insulted with impunity,” given the country’s ongoing gender-based violence crisis.



SANRAL has also confirmed it’s consulting lawyers over reputational damage.

It is also reviewing its tender documentation.

The goal is to add a clause specifically excluding companies whose directors or senior managers are implicated in gender-based violence.



SANRAL is now inviting other public and private construction-sector entities to adopt this same approach.

Separately, Minister of Women, Youth and Persons with Disabilities Sindisiwe Chikunga publicly called on Mudzinganyama to hand himself over to police.

“The law will find him no matter how rich he is,” she said.



WHERE THINGS STAND NOW

Moriel Infrastructure Group has since terminated its association with Mudzinganyama entirely.

The company confirmed he has been removed from both his roles.

He will no longer represent, speak for, or act on behalf of the company in any capacity.



Property group Steyn City has also reportedly terminated his lease.

It’s a genuinely striking example of how quickly consequences can move once footage like this becomes public.

A company, a government contract, a personal apology and a criminal case, all unfolding within a matter of days.



Do you think SANRAL’s proposed blacklist for GBV-implicated executives should become standard across the construction industry?

Let us know in the comments below…

World.title: Confirmed: When Springboks will name team to face Wallabies
World.content:
Springbok coach Rassie Erasmus is expected to make several changes to the team to face the Wallabies in a one-off Test, with the likes of Handre Pollard, Franco Mostert and Canan Moodie among those due to return.

With the match taking place on Sunday, it has been confirmed that Erasmus will reveal his matchday 23 on Tuesday at 10:30 SA time.

The match itself kicks off at 11:45.



HOW THE SPRINGBOKS COULD LINE UP AGAINST WALLABIES

SPRINGBOKS (possible selection) – 15 Aphelele Fassi, 14 Edwill van der Merwe, 13 Canan Moodie, 12 André Esterhuizen, 11 Ethan Hooker, 10 Handre Pollard, 9 Grant Williams, 8 Cameron Hanekom, 7 Elrigh Louw, 6 Paul de Villiers, 5 Franco Mostert, 4 Cobus Wiese, 3 Thomas du Toit, 2 Johan Grobbelaar, 1 Boan Venter.

Subs: 16 Jan-Hendrik Wessels, 17 Gerhard Steenekamp, 18 Zachary Porthen, 19 Lood de Jager, 20 Ben-Jason Dixon, 21 Morne van den Berg, 22 Manie Libbok, 23 Quan Horn.

Careful planning

Erasmus and captain Siya Kolisi have both said the Springboks are bracing themselves for a completely different challenge against the Wallabies.

“They’ll be really fresh and they’ve won four out of five of their recent matches, while we come off a tough series against New Zealand. But RGR and this match have nothing to do with each other. This is a completely different challenge,” Erasmus commented.

Kolisi agreed with Erasmus and said: “You always adjust for each team, but our core values are going to remain the same. Australia is completely different to New Zealand, so we’ll have to readjust certain things. It’s going to be a big challenge.”

This past weekend it was also confirmed that utility forward Pieter-Steph du Toit and centre Damian de Allende have been released from camp to spend time with their families after a demanding workload during RGR, but the rest of the squad remains intact.

World.title: Will the Reserve Bank hike rates?
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - It’s a week of reckoning for interest rates.

Economists are weighing whether the South African Reserve Bank will raise interest rates, as central banks around the world respond to persistent inflationary pressures.

Last week, the US Federal Reserve raised its policy rate by 25 basis points, marking its first increase in three years.

The decision, together with elevated oil prices and their impact on inflation, has strengthened the case for further rate hikes.

South Africa’s latest inflation data is expected ahead of the Reserve Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee announcement.

Annual inflation eased to 4.3 percent in July, from a two-year high of 5 percent in June.

However, both figures remain above the Reserve Bank’s 3 percent inflation target.

The current prime lending rate in South Africa is 10.5 percent, affecting consumers paying off home loans and vehicle finance.

World.title: Iran economy contracts during US war: official statistics
World.content:
TEHRAN - Iran's economy contracted by more than 10 percent during the Middle East war, which began with US-Israeli attacks in late February.

The country's gross domestic product (GDP) shrank by 10.1 percent year-on-year from late March to late June, a period known in Iran as the first quarter of the Persian calendar, according to the Statistical Center of Iran on Sunday.

Iran has been at war with the United States since late February, when US-Israeli strikes killed the Islamic republic's supreme leader and senior military officials at the start of a vast offensive.

The strikes sparked Tehran's retaliation in blocking the Strait of Hormuz -- causing global oil prices to surge -- as the conflict spread in the Middle East.

Aside from this, Iran's economy has long struggled with hyperinflation and devaluation of its currency, caused in large part by economic sanctions.

World.title: Thousands march in France against 'licence to kill' draft law
World.content:
PARIS - Thousands of people marched in Paris and other French cities on Sunday against a proposed law on the legitimate use of force that critics say would be a "licence to kill" for police and gendarmes.

In July, deputies in the National Assembly approved the bill, which says that any law-enforcement official who uses force is assumed to have acted legally when using their weapon. It now faces a vote in the Senate.

Politicians, rights groups and other activists joined the Paris demonstration, among them Mathilde Panot of the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party.

"The police kill already," Panot told the crowd, calling for the bill to be voted down in the Senate.

"In the Republic there can be no organised police impunity," she added. "In the Republic, there cannot be a category of citizens who have the right of life or death over other citizens."

World.title: Horror movie 'Resident Evil' tops North American box office
World.content:
LOS ANGELES - "Resident Evil," a horror movie based on a video game franchise, swept the North American box office with a $60 million opening weekend, industry estimates showed Sunday.

The Sony-distributed movie is directed by Zach Cregger and stars Austin Abrams, who plays a medical courier battling mutant creatures to deliver a package to a remote hospital.

"Resident Evil" displaced last week's top performer, Warner Bros' "Practical Magic 2," a long-awaited sequel starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, into a distant second place.

The story of the modern-day witches, who face a curse that sees any man they fall in love with doomed to an early death, took $12.2 million after last weekend knocking Sony's "Spider-Man" from its weeks-long perch at the top.

Spidey took another $6.5 million this weekend, bringing its total take in the United States and Canada to $944.5 million. It was followed by another of 2026's strongest performers, "The Odyssey," which took $4.9 million.

For the second consecutive weekend, "Coyote vs Acme" took fifth place, with Will Forte and an animated Wile E. Coyote snaring another $4.5 million for Falling Forward Films.

World.title: Evenepoel wins record 4th straight world time-trial title
World.content:
MONTREAL - Olympic champion Remco Evenepoel etched his name into the history books with a dominant fourth successive world time-trial victory in Montreal on Sunday.

The 26-year-old Belgian came into the race as the overwhelming favourite and he did not disappoint.

Evenepoel was already more than half a minute ahead of the rest by the second intermediate time-check just over half way through the race.

By the finish, the Belgian had put almost a minute into second-placed Filippo Ganna with Paul Seixas taking third another 15 seconds back.

Evenepeol became the first man to win the time-trial world title four times in a row, while also equalling the record number of overall titles held by German Tony Martin and Swiss Fabian Cancellara.

"It's amazing. It was obviously the goal to come and win here for the fourth time in a row. It was a big motivation," said Evenepoel.

"I'm super happy. It was a wonderful experience."

Already the Olympic champion in both this discipline and the road race, Evenepoel has not lost a time-trial since the 2025 Tour de France.

He has enjoyed his best season to date, winning the Amstel Gold Race, Clasica San Sebastian and Grand Prix de Quebec, as well as finishing second behind Tadej Pogacar at the Tour de France.

His next objective will be to win a second road-race world title next Sunday, and become the first man to do the double in the same year.

"There's quite some time to rest now and enjoy this special course," he said. "Full focus on Sunday from Tuesday."

Ganna had started slowly and was only 10th at the first time-check, but by the third, he had moved up into second spot.

But he could not make any headway into Evenepoel, who did not stop increasing his lead from the start to the finish.

Young Swede Jakob Soderqvist, the under-23 champion in this discipline last year, was second to Evenepoel at the first two time-checks but faded over the last 10km and finished fifth.

Teenage French starlet Seixas, gauged his effort better and put in a strong ride over the final 10km to finish third.

World.title: Joe 'Ferrari' Sibanyoni to face Madlanga Commission again
World.content:
PRETORIA - Businessman and taxi boss Joe “Ferrari” Sibanyoni is expected to return to the Madlanga Commission on Monday.

During his first appearance before the commission, Sibanyoni was questioned about the taxi industry and alleged links to the so-called Big Five cartel.

Sibanyoni and three co-accused face charges of extortion and money laundering in connection with allegations of a protection racket in Mpumalanga.

He and his co-accused are currently out on bail.

World.title: Alleged serial rapist arrested in KZN after 16 years on the run
World.content:
DURBAN - A 36-year-old man was arrested in Ncotshane, Nongoma, on Sunday in connection with the alleged rape of 14 women across KwaZulu-Natal and Gauteng.

Police say the suspect allegedly began his rape spree in 2010 in Mhlabathini. He was arrested but later released on bail.

He subsequently absconded from court, prompting the issuing of a warrant for his arrest.

While out on bail, he allegedly raped seven women in Pongola, four in Primrose and Germiston, and one woman each in the Paulpietersburg and Magudu policing precincts.

According to police, the suspect targeted women who were home alone.

He allegedly broke into their homes through windows or doors before threatening them with knives and raping them.

He is expected to appear in the Mahlabathini Magistrate’s Court on Monday in connection with his 2010 failure to appear in court.

He will then face formal charges relating to the other 13 alleged rapes.

World.title: IFP puts water at heart of election plan
World.content:
DURBAN - South Africa needs credible, qualified, and ethical leaders to run municipalities and deliver services.

That’s according to IFP leader Velenkosini Hlabisa.

He unveiled his party’s local government elections manifesto at Princess Magogo Stadium in KwaMashu, Durban.

Hlabisa detailed the organisation’s five-point plan, emphasising water provision.

The IFP wants to govern well-run municipalities that can provide basic services with ease.

“IFP municipalities will adopt a clear, fixed-basics approach. We will address visible service failures before they become a crisis," said Hlabisa.

"Our approach will be that maintenance must come before a crisis occurs. Municipalities under the IFP will prioritise preventative maintenance and timely repairs. Water, sanitation, electricity, roads, and refuse collection must be priorities in budgets, in operational plans and maintenance schedules.”

As he outlined the party’s five-point plan, Hlabisa also addressed the country’s gender-based violence and femicide crisis.

He called on men to take the lead in protecting women and children.

“The time has come to call men of South Africa, working together with government, civil society and all stakeholders, to lead the war against gender-based violence and femicide. That time is now, and men must take the lead against femicide,” said Hlabisa.

“We cannot continue to pick up bodies of women and issue statements of regret. This is a national crisis. To say, ‘not in our name,’ is no longer enough because it continues in our name. Now we must say it ends here and now.”

Hlabisa spoke about a climate of fear, frustration and disappointment.

However, as he and his party set their sights on the 4 November local government elections, he urged South Africans to remain hopeful.

World.title: The Sh5tr blind spot: No visibility as billions disappear through government funds
World.content:
‎Controller of Budget (COB) Dr Margaret Nyakang'o makes her submissions before the Committee on Finance and National Planning Chaired by Molo MP Kimani Kuria.[Elvis Ogina, Standard]

Controller of Budget Margaret Nyakang'o has said her office has no visibility over billions of shillings collected through key government funds and levies, including the National Infrastructure Fund and the Sovereign Wealth Fund, renewing fears about transparency in the Ruto administration's multibillion-shilling financial vehicles.

Speaking on Citizen TV, Nyakang'o said the Office of the Controller of Budget (CoB) cannot track how money collected through these standalone funds is spent because they operate outside the Consolidated Fund, the government's central account.

World.title: Ndindi Nyoro, Kinangop MP clash over alleged threatening message
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro arrives at St Paul ACK church in Engineer Town for the service on September 20, 2026. [James Munyeki, Standard]

There was drama at St Paul ACK church in Engineer Town during service on Sunday after Kiharu MP Ndindi Nyoro clashed with Kinangop MP Zachary Kwenya Thuku over an alleged threatening message.

Thuku, who is allied to the Kenya Kwanza government led by President William Ruto, is said to have warned Nyoro against attending the service.

"Yesterday, I received a message from the MP for Kinangop, Kwenya Thuku, warning me not to attend the church service. If I am lying, let him come here and read the message he sent me," Nyoro said.

He challenged the Kinangop MP to read the message aloud to the congregation.

"If anything happens to me today, Kenyans will judge whoever will be responsible," said Nyoro.

The Kiharu MP challenged Thuku to face him at a public rally at Engineer Trading Centre.

When he rose to speak, the Kinangop MP said he would not address the matter in church.

Instead, he said this was a political issue that the leaders would resolve.

"Let us solve this matter amicably. We are all brothers in this political journey," he said amid cheers from the congregation.

Recently, Nyoro added his voice to the growing political realignment in Mt Kenya, openly acknowledging the political tightrope he now walks as he distances himself from his former allies in the ruling party.

In a candid interview, he admitted that his previous close ties with President William Ruto and the Kenya Kwanza administration have left him vulnerable to suspicion from both sides of the political divide but insisted his decision to abandon the ruling party, United Democratic Alliance (UDA) was deliberate, difficult, and necessary.

World.title: Ruto leaves for New York ahead of UN General Assembly
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Ruto leaves for New York ahead of 81st UN General Assembly. [PCS]

President William Ruto has departed for New York, United States, to attend the 81st United Nations General Assembly.

Ruto is expected to push Kenya’s investment agenda and advocate for increased financing for Africa.

According to a statement from State House, Ruto will use the global gathering to seek partnerships in energy, infrastructure, manufacturing, health, agriculture and technology.

He will also advance Kenya’s agenda on artificial intelligence and Africa’s participation in the global digital economy.

Ruto is expected to co-chair roundtables hosted by the Africa Finance Corporation (AFC) and Global Africa Business Initiative (GABI), alongside industrialist Aliko Dangote.

A key focus will be the planned Sh2.2 trillion East Africa Refinery in Lamu, which the government says will have a capacity of 700,000 barrels per day and create more than 60,000 jobs. The project is scheduled to break ground on September 30, 2026.

On artificial intelligence, Ruto and Finland President Alexander Stubb will co-lead the AI Middle Powers Initiative, which seeks to enable countries to pool computing resources, data and talent to build AI capabilities.

Kenya will also advance the Africa Development Bank-backed AI 10 billion initiative, which aims to mobilise up to 10 billion dollars by 2035 for investment in Africa’s artificial intelligence sector.

The President is further expected to sign a global declaration and roadmap on child online AI safety alongside leaders from Spain, the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia.

He will also launch an Africa Resilience Compact that will use artificial intelligence, satellite earth observation and predictive technologies to strengthen preparedness for El Niño and other climate shocks.

During his address to the UN General Assembly, Ruto is expected to champion an Africa-financing-Africa approach, calling for reforms and international guarantees to unlock more African capital for infrastructure and enterprise.

Ruto will also highlight Kenya’s National Infrastructure Fund, which the government says is designed to mobilise up to 40 billion dollars without adding to public debt.

On the sidelines of the General Assembly, the President is expected to hold meetings with heads of state and government, multilateral institutions and global corporations to discuss trade, investment and diplomatic cooperation.

He will also engage Kenyans living in the United States as the government advances a Diaspora Investment Platform intended to channel diaspora capital into productive investment in Kenya.

World.title: Inside Parliament's probe into secondary school fees and capitation
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Pangani Girls School Chief Principal Dr Millicent Odhiambo before the National Assembly Public Investments Committee on Governance and Education. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

Parliament’s scrutiny of the Auditor-General’s report on public secondary schools has exposed inconsistencies in capitation funding, student enrolment figures and the National Education Management Information System (NEMIS).

The National Assembly Public Investments Committee on Governance and Education has raised concerns over the impact of funding shortfalls on school operations and called for discussions with Ministry of Education officials to address the challenges.

The committee is also exploring whether the secondary school fee structure should be reviewed amid concerns that current capitation is insufficient to meet rising operational costs.

Chaired by Luanda MP Dick Maungu, the committee raised the concerns after the Auditor-General’s report showed that several national schools (C1) had sought additional fees from parents above the approved Sh53,000 annual amount, citing rising costs and inflation.

MPs also questioned disparities between capitation disbursements and the actual number of students in schools, which principals said had contributed to underfunding.

For the first time, administrators of national schools appeared before a parliamentary committee to respond to audit queries, with several saying discrepancies between NEMIS figures and actual school records had affected the amount of capitation they received.

Chief principals from Alliance High School, Alliance Girls, Bishop Gatimu Ngandu Girls, Limuru Girls, Mang’u High, Kenya High School, Pangani Girls and Kabare Girls, among others, said they had experienced difficulties validating learner data on NEMIS.

They said capitation received by their schools did not cover all students, with principals reporting that they receive less than the Sh22,244 expected per learner annually. The amount, they said, averages about Sh15,000.

Schools defend additional fees

During the committee’s examination of Alliance High School’s audit report, the Auditor-General flagged the irregular increase in school fees, including Sh17.6 million collected from parents.

“The school charged fees of Sh68,554 whereas the fees as per the Ministry’s guideline is Sh53,554 and the school thus raised fees by Sh15,000 per student annually contrary to Regulation 44 of Basic Education Regulation 2015, which states that no public school or institution shall issue alternative fee structure other than that approved by the Cabinet Secretary,” the auditor read. ‎Alliance High School's Principal David Kamau before the National Assembly Public Investments Committee on Governance and Education. [Elvis Ogina, Standard]

Alliance High School Chief Principal David Kamau admitted that the school had sought alternative funding but said the initiative came from parents.

He said the approved Sh53,000 fee was insufficient to sustain the school’s budget amid rising costs and expectations of maintaining the institution’s standards.

“We have a certain lifestyle we have to maintain and that is why parents came in – in fact it was their idea – and asked us to maintain that. They came in and suggested they can do a budget support so that we maintain the same standards. For us, to acquire the results, we have to do a lot of activities to make sure we give a holistic education associated with the school over the years,” he explained.

“Parents approve that at an Annual General Meeting and we write to the Ministry but that letter of authority has never been granted. We have followed the process to the letter in terms of seeking approval for extra levies from parents,” he added.

The audit also flagged fee arrears in almost all the schools, with Alliance High School reporting arrears amounting to Sh36 million.

Kenya High School Chief Principal Rev Edith Koech was also required to respond to an audit query over unapproved fees under the parents’ association support programme, through which parents were charged Sh25,000 above the set amount per student without approval from the county education board.

Koech said the school had written to the Ministry seeking approval and, although it did not expressly receive authorisation at the time, it had since obtained it.

She said additional funds were approved during annual general meetings, where two budgets were presented — one based on Ministry guidelines and another reflecting what parents felt should be covered.

“Kenya High has its standards, for instance we have tea three times a day and they eat githeri once, they will burn the school if we change,” Koech explained.

Kiminini MP Kakai Bisau said the issue of additional levies had emerged in many schools, with principals arguing that the funds were necessary for students’ wellbeing.

“Looks like this issue is conflicting the law yet public participation is conducted among parents of respective schools. This is something we need guidance on and embedded in policy,” he said.

Other MPs questioned what happens to students from poor backgrounds who cannot afford the additional charges.

Lungalunga MP Chiforomondo Munga said principals had been entrusted with following the law, which states that public schools should not issue alternative fee structures without approval.

“I was a parent of Alliance but all said and done, you have done contrary to the law because approvals must come from the CS and I can assure you there is nobody who will approve that because they know they will be breaking the law and will be held accountable,” he said.

He said the situation presented a dilemma because schools were expected to maintain certain standards while operating within existing regulations.

Embakasi West MP Mark Mwenje said the issue of additional fees had existed for years, noting that he had paid about Sh40,000 while he was an Alliance High School student about two decades ago.

“We just need to sit down with the Ministry because it is becoming obvious that this money is no longer sufficient but we need to inform the principal that whenever such things are happening, there should be concurrence of the Principal Secretary but when we meet with the CS that issue should come out because we can no longer bury our heads in the sand,” Mwenje said.

Igembe Central MP Daniel Karitho described the issue as a “tricky” one, given rising inflation and the need to comply with the law.

“We cannot allow parents from any institution to just sit down and agree because there are those who are voiceless. This is an issue that needs to be discussed even in the House on the fees structure and if there is something that needs to be done, even on the basic regulation so that we can have a level,” Karitho said.

Alliance principal, however, maintained that the school’s process was transparent, with parents being provided with budget documents during annual general meetings and informed why additional funds were required.

“We tell the parents that is their decision to make and if they want to stick to the Sh53,000 but what we can offer as a school will reduce. I can assure we are conscious of the needy and we do not send anyone away because of the fees, either for statutory or additional,” he explained.

Kenya High echoed similar sentiments, saying additional contributions were based on public participation among parents and that no child was sent home over fees. The school also has endowment funds, it said.

NEMIS discrepancies

In another case, MPs questioned how Limuru Girls High School received an additional Sh785,946 in capitation after discrepancies emerged between its student enrolment records and figures captured in NEMIS.

The committee noted variances in Limuru Girls’ records and those of other national schools for the financial years 2020/2021 to 2024/2025.

The Auditor-General’s report for the year ended June 2024 showed that NEMIS recorded 2,099 students at the school in September 2023, 2,300 in January 2024 and 2,354 in May 2024.

However, records presented by the school showed enrolment of 2,062 students in September 2023 and 2,253 students in both January and May 2024.

The difference resulted in Sh785,946 in excess funding, raising concerns over whether the variance affected service delivery in other schools that did not receive capitation and made it difficult to confirm value for money.

Limuru Girls Chief Principal Susan Kariuki acknowledged the discrepancies but attributed them to differences between physical enrolment records and learner information captured in NEMIS.

“The difference arose from variations between the school’s physical enrolment records and the learner information captured in NEMIS at the respective reporting periods. The school did not intentionally provide inflated enrolment figures,” Kariuki said.

“So, because you are given more money, where do you take it?” Maungu posed.

Kariuki, however, said the school had not received the full amount of capitation due per learner and therefore did not consider itself overfunded in the ordinary sense. She said the Government was expected to provide Sh22,244 per learner but the school had been receiving about Sh15,000.

Narok Woman Representative Rebecca Tonkei questioned how Limuru Girls received higher funding for learners who were not captured in NEMIS, noting that other schools appearing before the committee had complained of underfunding caused by incomplete NEMIS records.

Maungu questioned the reliability of NEMIS, saying a system used to determine public funding should be predictable, consistent and dependable.

“This is not a good system. A good system should be predictable, consistent and dependable. But this system gives some people less and others more, sometimes the data is missing,” Maungu noted.

Starehe Girls raises fresh questions

Starehe Girls presented a different case that the committee said contained several grey areas after it emerged that 70 per cent of the school’s 776 learners are fully sponsored while the remaining 30 per cent are self-sponsored.

The school explained that all learners receive about Sh16,000 in Government capitation. For the 70 per cent, their upkeep is sourced through the board of trustees, while self-sponsored learners cover their own costs.

“Being a C1 school, by law it should pay Sh53,000. Instead, some are paying Sh150,000 meaning Sh96,000 extra to take care of the vulnerable. On this other side, you are saying they have a sponsor who take care...are you seeing the kind of confusion because they are already sponsored?” posed Maungu.

Despite the school’s unique funding arrangement, the committee said Starehe Girls remained a public institution and should therefore be audited.

The committee noted that not all financial years had been covered in the audit, unlike other C1 schools, and directed the institution to present all relevant documents for review.

Meanwhile, Mang’u High School surprised the committee when its administration said the school also faced challenges posed by snakes and hyenas that sometimes invade the institution.

World.title: Ruto faults Uhuru for undermining his government
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto join traditional dancers in Homa Bay on September 17, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has renewed his public criticism of former President Uhuru Kenyatta, accusing his predecessor of undermining the government and urging him to withdraw from active political mobilisation.

Ruto said he had supported Uhuru throughout their political partnership and expected reciprocal support when he sought the presidency.

“I stood by you through four elections; I stood by you, helped you, took care of you, and worked for you.”

Ruto claimed the two had discussed an arrangement in which each would serve as president for ten years. He accused Uhuru of failing to honour that understanding, saying:

“When the time came for you to help me, after you said ‘ten years for you, ten years for me,’ not even for a single day did you support me.”

Ruto also appealed to Uhuru to respect the position of former President and withdraw from political activities that he said were aimed at destabilising his administration.

“A former president! Surely, my brother, you are lowering the dignity of the office of the former president. You are a retired president respect your office, go and relax. Let us plan for this country of ours, Kenya,” Ruto said.

Ruto made the remarks on Thursday, September 17, 2026, in Sindo, Homa Bay County, as he concluded a four-day development tour of Nyanza.

The tour covered Kisumu, Siaya, Migori and Homa Bay and focused largely on roads, markets, housing, water and other development projects. The Star+1

The latest confrontation adds another chapter to the complicated political relationship between the two leaders.

Ruto served as Uhuru's deputy from 2013 to 2022, after the two politicians formed a political alliance that won the 2013 and 2017 presidential elections.

Contemporary accounts describe their original arrangement as involving support for Kenyatta for two terms, followed by support for Ruto's presidential ambitions. The Washington Post

The President nevertheless acknowledged Uhuru's democratic right to oppose his government but urged the former president to respect the office he once held.

“You are running schemes to sabotage the government. You are a retired president respect your office, go and relax. Let us plan for this country of ours, Kenya,” he said.

His criticism centred instead on what he described as continued political mobilisation against his administration.

He said his administration had stabilised the economy and pointed to investments in education, housing, markets and infrastructure. During the Homa Bay leg alone, the government highlighted a Sh3.5 billion plan for 21 modern markets.

World.title: Five killed as bandits ambush police search team in Isiolo
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Five people, including two police officers killed by bandits at the troubled grazing field of Gotu in Isiolo County on Wednesday.

The victims are a senior police officer, a police constable who was the driver of the vehicle that was ambushed by bandits, a livestock farmer and two National Police Reservists (NPR). The police officers were attached to an Anti-Stock Theft Unit (ASTU) located near Gotu trading centre.

The victims were part of a search team that was looking for an elderly man who reportedly went missing within the Gotu area and was last seen around Madho Gurba Huka, a grazing area in Chari Ward in Merti sub-county.

Isiolo County Police Commander Isaac Sang said the mentally challenged man from Barambate sub-location, Kulamawe location was reported missing a day ago.

The Isiolo camel keeper, reported to be related to the man who went missing, had requested police to search for him.

The mission turned tragic when the group was ambushed by armed bandits, killing all five on the spot.

The incident took place near the junction of Lososia-Merti road and Gotu-Merti route.

Mr Sang said the bodies of the officers and other victims were removed to Isiolo County Teaching and Referral Hospital awaiting postmortem.

"A reinforcement (of security personnel) had been sent to the area which includes an armoured vehicle to pursue the attackers," said the police chief.

The police boss called for calm and cooperation from the residents while police pursue the suspects.

He said that investigation into the incident had commenced.

On Wednesday afternoon, a gunfight was reported between police reservists and the bandits on the western bank of the river.

"The reservists in the area pursued the attackers minutes after reports of the killings that led to an exchange of gunfire. We are told an unknown number of people have been injured," said a herdsman from Gotu who sought anonymity for security reasons.

A source from Isiolo County and Teaching and Referral Hospital revealed that two ambulances had been sent to Gotu to attend to the injured persons.

Gotu, along with Kom in Merti sub-county is a bandit hotspot in Isiolo that is attributed to competition over scarce pasture by rival herders from Isiolo, Samburu East and parts of Marsabit with local leaders calling for eviction of pastoralists from outside the County. Several people have been killed in the two locations since last year and hundreds of livestock stolen.

On August 1, two people were killed in the Garse Dabata area in Gotu and nearly 700 goats and sheep were stolen. Nearly all the stolen animals were recovered in operation undertaken by a multi-agency security team stationed in various locations along the Isiolo-Meru border.

Interior CS Kipchumba Murkomen on two occasions called for an operation in parts of Isiolo, Laikipia, Samburu and Meru Counties that had experienced frequent cases of banditry and rustling.

However, leaders fault the CS for failure to take decisive action on insecurity that keeps on recurring in parts of Isiolo and Meru Counties. The leaders including Governor Abdi Guyo want herders from outside Isiolo who are in Kom and Gotu areas to be evicted.

World.title: Muthaiga Golf Club restores access after KFS standoff
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Muthaiga Golf Club has restored access to a section of its course that was temporarily taken over by the Kenya Forest Service (KFS), hours after the agency moved into the area, claiming it forms part of Karura Forest.

The disruption affected the Front Nine, covering Holes Two to Nine, before the club’s board intervened to restore normal operations.

In a statement issued Tuesday, Muthaiga Golf Club Chairman Dennis Mwirigi said the board had taken the necessary steps to facilitate the resumption of activities after the temporary disruption.

“We are pleased to confirm that access to the affected part of the course has been restored and members may proceed with their scheduled activities as usual,” Mwirigi said.

He said the board remained committed to protecting the club’s interests, assets and members while addressing the matter through the appropriate channels.

The development follows an earlier communication to members informing them that KFS had taken over access to the affected section, claiming it was part of Karura Forest.

The club had initially said the Front Nine would not be accessible until further notice as it sought to resolve the matter. The driving range and parking areas were not affected.

The incident sparked criticism over the manner in which KFS handled the dispute, with Prof Karanja, Chairperson of Friends of Karura Forest, urging the agency to pursue dialogue and legal channels.

Prof Karanja said KFS should have first engaged the club’s management and clearly explained its claim over the disputed land instead of deploying dogs, guns and heavy security.

“If they don't agree that it was your land, go to court. The court will determine,” he said.

He questioned whether KFS had adequately demonstrated that the disputed section was forest land or explained how it was allegedly acquired by Muthaiga Golf Club.

“They should have come publicly and said, look, Muthaiga, that area and that area belong to the forest,” Prof Karanja said.

He said KFS should identify the specific portion of land it claims belongs to the forest and explain the basis of its claim before taking further action.

Prof Karanja argued that the dispute should be resolved through established legal procedures rather than force. “Trees are not protected by guns,” he said.

He described the deployment of armed personnel as the wrong way of resolving a land dispute and called for engagement between KFS and the golf club.

Prof Karanja also warned that actions by government agencies could have wider implications for the administration of President William Ruto, saying confrontational conduct could lead members of the public to associate such actions directly with the government.

“When government departments behave like this, everybody now starts thinking, oh, it's Ruto's whatever,” he said.

He further recalled a previous dispute involving Friends of Karura Forest, where he said armed personnel were deployed and the group removed from an area before senior government officials intervened.

According to Prof Karanja, officials from the Treasury and forestry departments eventually intervened and encouraged dialogue to resolve the matter.

He urged KFS to adopt a similar approach in the Muthaiga dispute, saying the agency and the club should present their respective claims and seek a court determination if they cannot agree.

For now, the restoration of access means members can resume their scheduled activities, while the underlying dispute over the contested section remains subject to further engagement between KFS and the club.

World.title: Juja couple's surprise blessing of five babies
World.content:
Mercy Kanini, 28, from Juja, Kiambu County, gave birth to five children at Thika Level Five Hospital. [Gitau Wanyoike, Standard]

A couple from Juja, Kiambu County, is celebrating the unexpected arrival of five babies after scans during pregnancy showed they were expecting quadruplets.

Mercy Kanini, 28, delivered four girls and a boy through normal delivery at Thika Level Five Hospital, in a rare case believed to be among only a handful of quintuplet births recorded in Kenya.

World.title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani to meet with President Trump in New York City
World.content:
New York — New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani will meet with President Donald Trump on Monday ahead of the United Nations General Assembly, Mamdani’s office said Sunday.

The meeting will take place at Gracie Mansion, the mayoral residence in Manhattan, marking the first time Trump will meet with Mamdani on his home turf.

A spokesperson for Mamdani said the meeting would “focus on issues affecting New York City and New Yorkers.”

Trump is scheduled to speak at the UN General Assembly in the city on Tuesday. The White House confirmed the meeting with the mayor but did not offer additional details.

Monday will mark the third time Mamdani and Trump have met in person. Their first meeting was held in the Oval Office in November 2025, shortly after Mamdani’s election, followed by a second meeting in February.

Mamdani has said when he speaks with Trump, it’s always focused on the needs of the city.

“When it comes to the president, we continue to have a conversation about how best to deliver for this city,” he told reporters. “That is a conversation that has been done in person, it’s been done over the phone, and it will continue so long as either of us have the ability to deliver for the city.”

Despite their opposing politics, Trump and Mamdani have had surprisingly amiable meetings. Staffers for Mamdani argue the mayor has chosen a diplomatic approach with the president, which has proved advantageous for the city. New York has been spared from the large-scale immigration enforcement Trump threatened during the mayoral campaign and, despite threats that he would “take over,” the president has been surprisingly complimentary of Mamdani’s stewardship of his hometown.

The mayor’s staffers declined to say exactly what Trump and Mamdani will discuss, but the president’s immigration agenda has been a consistent pressure point. Just last week, Mamdani announced a lawsuit against the Trump administration over its expansion of a rule that would make it harder for some immigrants to get green cards.

While Mamdani and Trump are ideologically opposed, the mayor’s aides point to concrete outcomes from his previous discussions with Trump as evidence that the meetings are politically favorable.

During the February gathering, Mamdani demanded the release of Elmina Aghayeva, a Columbia University student who was detained by federal immigration agents inside her university residence. After meeting with the president, Mamdani said Trump called him to inform him Aghayeva would be released.

During that same meeting, Mamdani pitched Trump on a massive housing project in Queens that would require billions in federal grants. The mayor brought visual props to make his case for what could be the biggest federal investment in housing in 50 years, including a mock-up of a New York Daily News front page bearing the president’s face and the headline: “Trump to City: Let’s Build.”

While no progress has been made on the project, aides to Mamdani said both parties agreed to continue discussions.

Monday’s meeting also gives Mamdani an unusually prominent spot on the international stage. With world leaders and journalists gathered in New York for the UN General Assembly, the encounter at the mayor’s residence is likely to draw significant attention beyond the city.

Mamdani’s aides say the mayor’s ability to keep his policy differences from the president while also extracting commitments is evidence that maintaining a relationship with Trump can produce results for New York. Whether that approach continues to produce results will be closely watched after Monday’s meeting.

Trump has referred to Mamdani as “my little communist” and has tried to use the mayor, a democratic socialist, as a foil, linking his politics to Democrats across the country. During his campaign, Mamdani said he would “become Donald Trump’s worst nightmare.”

Despite the rhetoric, Trump also referred to Mamdani as a “very rational person” and said he was “very comfortable” with the mayor running New York City following their first Oval Office meeting.

“The better he does, the happier I am. I will say there’s no difference in party. There’s no difference in anything, and we’re going to be helping him to make everybody’s dream come true — having a strong and very safe New York,” Trump said after the meeting.

Presidential visits to New York City’s mayoral residence are rare. Presidential records show the last president to visit was Ronald Reagan, who visited Gracie Mansion and presented then-Mayor Ed Koch with a prop check as a sign of the Reagan administration’s commitment to an infrastructure project in Manhattan.

President John F. Kennedy visited Gracie Mansion in 1962 to deliver a speech on medical care before a group of US mayors. President Jimmy Carter and first lady Rosalynn Carter were overnight guests at the mansion in 1978. Carter made the visit during an official trip to New York City and a bill signing ceremony at City Hall alongside Koch.

The Monday meeting at the mayor’s residence also comes days before Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is scheduled to address the United Nations on Thursday. Mamdani, an ardent critic of the Israeli government, has said he does not plan to participate in any planned demonstrations against Netanyahu.

This story has been updated with additional information.

World.title: Beyond Ukraine: Why Europe is preparing for a wider conflict
World.content:
Something is spooking Europe.

This week, Belarus, Russia’s closest military ally, conducted large exercises near the Suwałki Gap, the narrow corridor connecting the Baltic states to the rest of NATO. The geography that has long made it one of NATO’s most vulnerable points.

French President Emmanuel Macron summoned France’s political leaders for a confidential intelligence briefing, then announced new measures to protect critical infrastructure from intensifying Russian hybrid attacks.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk went further, warning that Russia may launch drone or missile attacks against NATO countries and disguise them as accidents.

The UK has told citizens to start preparing for the possibility of war, and to stockpile canned foods and drinking water. Its chief of defense said Britain faced the “most dangerous” period in decades.

Germany is preparing its hospitals for a possible Russian attack. Its Chancellor, Friredrich Merz, warned of “decisive moments” in “defending the freedom and peace of our continent.”

Even the famously neutral Switzerland adopted a new national security strategy calling for greater resilience and an ability to defend itself against an armed attack.

President Donald Trump, meanwhile, suddenly announced progress toward establishing a permanent US Army base in Poland. Two weeks ago, he dispatched the CIA Director on a secret mission to warn Moscow against attacking NATO territory.

Countries on both sides of the Atlantic seem alarmed that Russian President Vladimir Putin might soon widen his war beyond Ukraine.

Russia’s widening battlefield

The United States got a glimpse of the threat this week.

Federal prosecutors charged five people allegedly working with Russian intelligence in a network plotting attacks and murders around the world, including inside the US. Prosecutors also allege the network commissioned attacks against civilian and military infrastructure in European countries.

The charges fit a broader pattern Europeans have confronted for years: cyberattacks, sabotage, arson, drones and attacks against critical infrastructure. Last month, Germany blamed Russia for a drone attack at a civilian airport.

The strategic challenge for NATO is that Russia can conduct such operations without clearly crossing the threshold into conventional war.

Fly a drone into NATO airspace, disrupt an airport, sabotage infrastructure, conduct murders through criminal networks — all deniable “gray zone” operations.

Putin uses ambiguity and denial as a weapon, testing NATO resolve, while recognizing that NATO is divided on how best to respond, or to respond at all.

But what if Putin decides to go further?

The Gap

The Suwałki Gap offers one answer.

It is a roughly 65-mile border between Poland and Lithuania and the only land connection between NATO’s Baltic states—Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia—and the rest of NATO.

Lithuanian soldiers secure the area where Italian fighter jets shot down a drone during NATO’s Baltic Air Policing Mission near Pratkunai village, located north of the capital Vilnius, Lithuania, on September 15. AP

Imagine a crisis in which Russia, perhaps operating with Belarus, moves forces into a portion of the corridor. It’s not an explicit invasion of a NATO state, such as tanks rolling into Poland. Putin would claim a limited incursion if he said anything at all, and that Russia did not seek escalation.

Russia would also claim through non-official channels that a NATO response risked nuclear war.

The purpose is less about the Gap and severing NATO’s Baltic flank, than undermining NATO and its mutual defense commitments altogether.

Would 32 NATO countries agree to fight Russia to recover a small strip of territory? Would an American president risk escalation with a nuclear power over Lithuania? Would Germany and France?

Nobody can say for certain, and that plays into Putin’s hands.

NATO’s Secretary General Mark Rutte was asked this year about a war game involving precisely such a Russian move against the Suwałki corridor. His response was that NATO regularly exercises against such scenarios and that an attack would produce a devastating response.

Does Putin believe him? With Washington at loggerheads with its closest allies, including Canada — perhaps not.

Learning from Ukraine

Ukraine has provided Europeans with a brutal tutorial in what modern war requires.

Countries need more than military materiel. They need electrical grids that can survive attacks, hospitals capable of handling mass casualties, redundant communications, functioning transportation networks and governments able to operate under sustained pressure.

Most importantly, they need societies capable of absorbing costs without collapsing or polarizing.

Anatolii Fedoruk, mayor of Bucha, brings a candle to pay tribute at the memorial installation for the victims of attacks and executions by Russian troops on the fourth anniversary of the liberation of the town of Bucha outside Kyiv, Ukraine on March 30. Gleb Garanich/Reuters

This week, NATO publicly released updated requirements for national resilience, covering everything from continuity of government and energy supplies to food, water, health care and communications during “crisis and conflict.”

NATO officials are studying how Ukrainians have kept essential services functioning under sustained Russian attack.

It’s an extraordinary turn of events. Ukraine is no longer simply receiving lessons from NATO — NATO is also receiving lessons from Ukraine.

In doing so, the alliance aims to deter not just by promising a devastating response to aggression — but by demonstrating to Putin that his aggression won’t work.

Preparedness itself becomes part of deterrence. That is one reason for the slew of headlines this week.

Questions about Washington

There is also an American factor behind Europe’s urgency.

The US is simultaneously deployed in Europe, fighting Iran in the Middle East and deterring China in the Indo-Pacific. Air defenses, naval forces, intelligence platforms, and depleting munitions cannot be everywhere at once.

Trump has done much to strengthen NATO, but his commitment to its mutual defense clause is uncertain.

Moscow knows this.

Russia remains bogged down in Ukraine. But Putin does not need another invasion on the scale of Ukraine to challenge NATO. He can move up an escalation ladder: sabotage, cyberattacks, assassination plots, drone or missile attacks — and then a limited military operation designed to test whether NATO still means what it says.

Military personnel from Poland, Lithuania, and France take part in training exercises during Operation Brave Boar 26 at the Orzysz Land Forces Training Center near the Suwalki Gap in Poland, on June 17. Damian Lemanski/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Ask yourself whether Trump would go to war with Russia over a patch of land called the Suwalki Gap? Would Americans be ready for such a thing? The question answers itself.

And that alone undermines deterrence.

In Europe, an end to illusions

For three decades after the Cold War, Europe allowed national preparedness to atrophy. Risks of war seemed remote. Spending on militaries and recruitment plummeted. Civil defense was a relic of the past. And the US was presumed to be there in a pinch.

That era is over.

Europe is preparing for war because its leaders increasingly understand an uncomfortable truth: deterrence depends on what Putin believes, and America’s response to a widening war would be uncertain.

The Belarusian exercises near the Suwalki gap are raising alarms because, despite Russia’s struggles in Ukraine, the deterrence equation has atrophied.

The best way to prevent a widening war is to make certain Putin believes it will fail.

And judging by the urgent moves now underway across European capitals, there is growing concern that he may believe the opposite.

World.title: Trump vows to create ‘AI Force’ and appoint czar amid calls to regulate technology’s development
World.content:
President Donald Trump said Saturday he plans to create an “AI Force” and name an AI czar as the government faces growing calls to impose guardrails on the rapid development of artificial intelligence.

The president, writing on Truth Social, repeated his assessment that fears over AI amount to a hoax and also seemed to acknowledge some of the risks the technology presents, saying, “we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System.”

“For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ — Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Trump said in the post.

CNN has reached out to the White House for more details on the AI czar’s duties, whether the president has anyone in mind for the role, and whether the “AI Force” will be a branch of the military, like the Space Force. Trump’s creation of the Space Force in 2019 marked the first new US military service since 1947.

Trump’s announcement comes as the White House and Congress have faced pressure in recent weeks to enact AI safeguards. The president has downplayed concerns, claiming that a “SICK conspiracy” was afoot to undermine AI.

“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry,” Trump said in his post Saturday. “We are leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way!”

Trump has made clear that he considers outpacing China and preserving AI-driven economic gains a higher priority than addressing growing public concerns. The issue has quickly come to dominate political debate in the United States, after industry leaders called for a global slowdown in development.

AI’s meteoric growth has led to major stock market gains and buoyed the manufacturing sector through the construction of data centers — which Trump calls “the golden goose.” Yet fears about the technology’s potential to eliminate jobs and AI data centers’ impact on communities have led to a souring in public sentiment.

Democrats have been more vocal in their calls to slow AI development, with former President Barack Obama urging potential Democratic presidential candidates to put AI at the center of their agendas in 2028.

“My view this week has been it is good that some of the leading companies have said we need to slow this down, and we should encourage that,” Obama said Friday during a fireside chat at Colgate University, according to excerpts of his speech obtained by CNN. “There have been some on the left who’ve said we shouldn’t allow them to make that decision. I agree that that can’t be a long-term solution. Government has to be regulating this.”

Venture capitalist David Sacks served as Trump’s AI and cryptocurrency czar until March, when he stepped down after reaching his time limit as a special government employee. He now chairs the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.

Meanwhile, conversations surrounding AI regulation are expected to play a key part in multiple diplomatic gatherings next week.

The Trump administration will convene a high-level event on AI on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, multiple sources familiar with the matter previously told CNN.

A day later, several technology executives — including OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang and Google’s Sundar Pichai — will attend a state dinner at the White House as part of Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington, according to a White House official.

CNN previously reported that Trump officials were contemplating a meeting with major technology and AI chiefs on the sidelines of the high-stakes summit, though nothing has been finalized.

A White House official also said that AI safety would be “on the agenda” when Trump meets with Xi.

This story has been updated with additional developments.

World.title: A delivery company founded by Arabs takes on its competition in Israel
World.content:
Deep inside the labyrinthine alleys of Acre’s Old City – home to a 700-year-old Crusader fortress – Muhammad Hani could not order a takeaway pizza. Delivery drivers struggled to navigate the maze of tightly packed ancient buildings, narrow alleyways and winding streets – leaving many of the Arab citizens of Israel there cut off from such services.

“Only the residents like us know how to get around these neighborhoods,” the 27-year-old said.

And even if a driver could find the house address, another barrier remained. Many Arab citizens could only pay with cash, while delivery companies such as Wolt, the leading operator in Israel, only accept card payments. “Most people here don’t have a bank card,” Hani explained.

Launched in 2019, Haat set out to tackle some of the barriers that left communities like Hani’s on the margins of Israel’s high-tech society. Not everyone in the country known as the “Startup Nation” could reap the rewards of cutting-edge services from the latest applications.

At first, the idea for Haat was simple: combine technology with the old-fashioned convenience of cash. But the technology ultimately found uses far beyond its initial goal, helping the Israeli postal service map villages and allowing small, local restaurants to grow a customer base far beyond their neighborhoods.

A view of old town of Israel’s coastal city of Acre, where many Arabs like Muhammad Hani used to struggle to order takeaway food. Menahem Kahana/AFP/Getty Images

Founded by Hasan Abasi in the Arab-majority town of Umm al-Fahm in Israel, Haat now offers its services across 50 cities, working with more than 10,000 restaurants and markets, and employing more than 500 couriers. Its success has earned the app a valuation of more than $100 million, according to the company’s PR and Communications lead, Aida Kaddan.

Abasi’s creative strategy with Haat also helped him nab a place on Globes’ 40 Under 40, an annual list by one of Israel’s leading business newspapers recognizing promising young Israelis.

Abasi came up with Haat – Arabic for “bring” – while working for Google in Switzerland. The 36-year-old returned to Umm al-Fahm from Zurich as his wife was expecting a second child. One evening, he tried to order a pizza, but the courier kept getting lost.

Hasan Abasi founded Haat in the northern Arab-Israeli town of Umm-Al Fahem, pictured, with the business subsequently growing to offer services across 50 cities. Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images

The experience helped Abasi recognize a wider problem – and an opportunity. He launched Haat with five others, starting in Umm al-Fahm before expanding to neighboring Arab towns. Demand exploded during the Covid-19 pandemic, when lockdowns kept people at home and online orders boomed.

Abasi was also aware of the systemic issues around banking in Israel, particularly in the Arab sector, where, according to a 2024 study from The National Insurance Institute of Israel, more than 37% live in poverty. Many lower-income families simply don’t have electronic payment options, especially in Umm al-Fahm, according to Mayor Samir Mahamed, making cash the most convenient form of payment.

Like a ‘90s Domino’s delivery

Haat combined the convenience of shopping and dining through a smart phone application with an old-school pay-by-cash option.

This option proved useful beyond Arab communities and has caught on in mixed neighborhoods like Jaffa, where many people do not have bank cards, Kaddan said.

Haat has since expanded its services to allow users also to pay utility and phone bills with cash.

In neighborhoods like Jaffa in Tel Aviv, home to the city’s famous flea market, many residents rely on cash because they do not have bank cards. Simon Beni/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty Images

“The cash option came from answering the needs of the society. It has now become one of Haat’s most significant advantages in every area where it operates,” she said.

As Haat focused on reaching those underserved by other delivery applications, its work to turn previously unnavigable streets into mapped-out towns advanced.

Uncharted territory

In some Arab neighbourhoods in Israel, not only were the maze of densely built homes a challenge for delivery services, but streets also often lacked formal names or had unnumbered houses.

A man cycles through the Old city of Acre.“Only residents like us know how to get around these neighborhoods,” Muhammad Hani told CNN. Odd Andersen/AFP/Getty Images

“Navigation relied heavily on neighborhood names, family compounds and local landmarks, which posed considerable challenges for postal distribution, commercial deliveries and emergency services,” said Mahamed, the Umm al-Fahm mayor.

Over the past six years, Haat has helped redraw the map of underserved cities. By tracking courier routes and using machine learning to identify roads, neighborhoods, buildings and entrance points overlooked by conventional navigation services, the company says its maps now include 30% more streets in the areas it serves than other mapping platforms.

According to Samir Sobhi Mahamed, mayor of Umm al-Fahm, many lower-income families in his town do not have access to electronic payment options. Oded Balilty/AP

This was particularly useful for residents in Umm al-Faham, a city of more than 57,000. The mayor said Haat helped support a city-wide project carried out by the local authority to name streets and number houses.

CNN has reached out to Israel’s postal service for comment.

Beyond word-of-mouth

The improved access to Arab neighborhoods also opened up new markets for restaurants and shops overlooked by the wider community, something Haat said “democratizes visibility.”

Krunchy Chicken began as a single fried chicken restaurant in Baqa al-Gharbiyye, an Arab town in northern Israel near the border with the occupied West Bank.

The restaurant has since opened two more branches in the Israeli Triangle – a concentration of Arab towns and villages on the Green Line, which demarcates the boundary between the West Bank and Israel.

At first, Krunchy Chicken relied largely on word-of-mouth advertising, according to manager Sharif Masarweh. But the online exposure of Haat helped greatly, Masarweh told CNN, as did the convenience of different payment options.

“The fact that there is an option for cash also allowed more people to use the application and to order food from our restaurant and others. It helped a lot, because not everyone prefers to pay using a bank card,” he said.

Haat recently expanded into Tel Aviv, taking on Finland’s Wolt, the dominant player in Israel’s food delivery market. Wolt motorbikes zipping along the streets and weaving through dense traffic are an ubiquitous sight in the beachside city.

Now the local competitor is trying to build its own foothold in Tel Aviv using its strengths. “Haat reads the needs of local people because we are local and operate from within,” Kaddan said. “We see what is missing and try to fill those gaps with technology.”

World.title: Trump’s sanctions, inflation and a collapsing economy leaves Iran’s sick exposed
World.content:
When 35-year-old Sima walked into a Tehran pharmacy, her eyes raced across the shelves behind the counter, searching for the box that would keep her kidneys from failing. Without it, she was running out of time.

She finally found the medication in the seventh pharmacy she visited, in a wealthy Tehran neighborhood. Her relief faded when the pharmacist told her that the price had once again gone up, leaving her with no choice but to underdose the lifesaving medication.

As US sanctions suffocate Iran’s economy, ordinary people with chronic conditions and serious illnesses are struggling to find the medicine they depend on to survive. With severe shortages and daily price increases, many, like Sima, have been forced to cut doses, postpone doctor visits or self-medicate.

“They’ve stopped using cancer medication for people who they say are terminal or far along,” said Sima, who did not give CNN her real name so she could speak freely. “They only use it for those who are in the very early stages.”

A mother in Tehran who lost her only daughter has been forced to change her antidepressant medication to a less effective locally produced version. Seasonal flu vaccinations have been called off this year after the government failed to procure them from Europe. Cancer patients are selling their televisions and refrigerators to buy overpriced medication.

A 55-year-old cancer patient, who asked to remain anonymous, said she, too, is running out of options.

“I’ve asked if people who come visit or come back from abroad can bring my medicine back, especially the things we can’t find here or get access, too,” the patient, who lives in Tehran, told CNN. “Between the illness and uncertainty of the war I have a hard time knowing what to do.”

Pharmacies in Iran contacted by CNN confirmed shortages and price increases across several categories, including heart medication, which is now offered as a local generic rather than the prescribed brand, cholesterol-lowering pills, which are available but far more expensive, and migraine drugs, which have completely vanished from shop shelves.

Iran media reports, however, suggest the shortages are far more wide-reaching, affecting everything from antidepressants to insulin and pregnancy medications. Other drugs are completely unobtainable, leaving Iran’s sick facing astronomically higher prices or a less effective generic version.

The shortages have affected almost 800 medications, the head of the Iranian Pharmacists Association Shahram Kalantari told a press conference last month, with pharmacies unable to procure alternatives due to the rising costs.

“Everyone says we’re brave,” the cancer patient added in a telephone call. “But I don’t know if being brave means anything when you’re dying.”

Mounting debt

Iran now manufactures more than 97% of its medicines by volume, Mehdi Pirsalehi, head of the country’s Food and Drug Organization, said in February. Hardest hit are imported specialty drugs that must be paid for in foreign currency. Shortages of these drugs have grown under US President Donald Trump’s maximum-pressure campaign, which has intensified scrutiny of Iran’s banks and impeded exports of oil – the main source of the foreign currency for the Islamic Republic.

As well as inflated pricing, pharmacies are experiencing shortages of vital medications. Majid Asgaripour/Wana News Agency/Reuters

“This high level of domestic production does not necessarily mean complete self-sufficiency,” said Peivand Bastani, Senior Lecturer at Flinders University and co-author of research examining the effects of sanctions on pharmaceutical procurement in Iran. “Local manufacturing can still depend on imported materials, equipment and technology, while some specialized and high-cost medicines must be imported.”

Pharmacies cannot replenish their inventories because insurance companies have stopped paying them, according to Iranian officials. With millions of Iranians covered by insurance, presenting an insured prescription at a pharmacy usually produces nothing, or requires the patient to pay out-of-pocket.

Rampant inflation, the collapse of insurance payments, and the government’s inability to sell oil and obtain the foreign currency needed to repay pharmacies have fractured the supply chain.

More than 18,000 private pharmacies across the country are now waiting to get paid by insurance companies, officials from Iran’s Pharmacists Association said at a news conference last month, with insurance debts owed to pharmacies reaching almost 800 trillion rials ($300 million)

“These pharmacies can no longer afford to continue investing their own capital and then wait a year to receive their outstanding payments,” the head of the association, Shahram Kalantari, said at the time.

War destruction

US and Israeli airstrikes on Iran earlier this year damaged more than 40 pharmaceutical companies, equipment suppliers and distributors, the spokesman for Iran’s Food and Drug Administration, Mohammad Hashemi, told Iranian state-affiliated media in June.

In late March, Israel struck the factory of a major Iranian pharmaceutical company, Tofigh Daru, which produced active ingredients for anticancer drugs and anesthetics. The Israeli military claimed the company provided fentanyl to an Iranian entity conducting “research and development of chemical weapons” – something the company denied.

Airstrikes also damaged the historic Pasteur Institute, founded more than a century ago. The Lancet, a medical journal, reported that the attacks had flattened “crucial reference laboratories, including those for genomic surveillance, rabies, HIV/AIDS, viral hepatitis, and vector-borne diseases.”

Last month, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced that the US would clamp down on the complex network built by Iran over years to allow its entities to evade Washington’s wide-ranging sanctions – a move designed to add pressure on Iran amid a lack of diplomatic resolution.

Washington has permitted transactions involving “agricultural commodities, food, medicine, or medical devices to Iran,” but have added some safeguards to ensure such goods are “not diverted by the Iranian regime to fund its nefarious purposes.”
