World.title: From waste to wealth: Europe’s textile opportunity
World.content:
A new season for Europe’s fashion industry

Turning fashion from a linear industry into a circular one is an ongoing, complicated process. For the Ellen MacArthur Foundation, a circular economy for fashion is where clothing, shoes and accessories are used more, made to be recycled and created from recycled or renewable inputs.

European post-consumer textile waste is currently more likely to be downcycled, landfilled or incinerated rather than recycled in Europe due to a lack of financial incentive and a clear regulatory pathway — meaning the EU is discarding material it could use, while exporting environmental impacts and industrial value elsewhere. Right now, it is more affordable for producers to use virgin materials rather than recycled ones, but it doesn’t have to be that way.

The demand for secondhand is clearly not growing as fast as the waste, and the waste being received is of lower quality. The centers have to handle more without being able to extract the value, so they’re being overwhelmed.” Patrik Frisk, CEO of Reju

In the Netherlands, the government recently awarded Reju a €135 million grant to build and operate its first industrial-scale textile Regeneration Hub in Chemelot. Reju is a textile-to-textile regeneration company focused on turning European post-consumer polyester textile waste into new high-quality recycled polyester. Once the Chemelot Regeneration Hub is up and running, the company expects to process approximately 64,000 tons of textile waste, representing 300 million items, to produce close to 40,000 tons of recycled polyester material annually.

Textile sorting is still usually done by hand in sorting centers run by non-profits. “The demand for secondhand is clearly not growing as fast as the waste, and the waste being received is of lower quality. The centers have to handle more without being able to extract the value, so they’re being overwhelmed,” says Patrik Frisk, CEO of Reju. “As the business matures over the years, and regulations come into force to help build the upstream system that is required to scale up, only then will we have a self-sufficient economy. The regulation framework has to be coordinated and without this the entire Extended Producer Responsibility infrastructure will not attract outside capital.”

Supporting locally made, circular textiles will not only help the EU pursue the Sustainable Development Goals but will also support regional manufacturing during a difficult economic time. The clock is ticking: Each EU member country must establish its textile EPR scheme by April 16, 2028, and the forthcoming Circular Economy Act is expected by the end of the year.

World.title: Why the far right lost: 11 lessons for Europe from Sweden’s election
World.content:
Amid reports of recriminations within the SD, Åkesson may take time away from frontline politics, but insists he won’t resign.

Jimmie Åkesson’s final rally takes place in Stockholm on Sept. 12, 2026. | Tim Ross/POLITICO

The disappointing outcome for the SD is a rarity these days in European politics: A far-right populist party making a name for itself campaigning against immigration, but then falling back instead of grasping power.

POLITICO spoke to experts and key players, including outgoing center-right Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and his likely Social Democrat replacement Magdalena Andersson, to draw some lessons from the campaign.

The far right allied with the center — and lost

The SD’s vote share fell from 20.5% in 2022 to 17.5% this year, even though it had supported Kristersson’s center-right coalition within the parliament for four years. Although Åkesson’s party succeeded in pushing Kristersson’s administration to adopt tougher policies on crime and immigration, their electoral result was ultimately worse.

Kristersson’s Moderates party, meanwhile, increased its support and overtook the SD to become the second-largest force in the parliament. That outcome will have drawn the notice of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats and the far-right Alternative for Germany, for example, as well as of Britain’s Conservative Party and Reform UK.

It’s OK to blame voters, if it fits your story

Åkesson’s explanation for the SD’s disappointing result was bang on brand for an anti-migrant populist. At a Friday press conference he claimed the Social Democrats and their allies on the left had been “very good at mobilizing the Islamist voters who previously had other parties to vote for.”

World.title: Russia’s secret plan to supercharge kamikaze drone production
World.content:
The U.S. House Select Committee on China has reviewed the documents and determined they are authentic, according to a U.S. government official familiar with their contents. The Ukrainian government has also reviewed the documents and confirmed their authenticity, a Ukrainian official said. Both officials were granted anonymity as they were not authorized to speak on the record.

Russia's drone war expands

In May, the Russian government approved Rosatom’s plans to build the new line at its Alabuga-Volokno factory “for the production of chemical fibers and threads” to produce up to 500 tons of carbon fiber per year, according to official approval for the construction project.

Satellite images between May and July show land earmarked for the expansion project adjacent to Alabuga-Volokno’s current carbon fiber factory in Tatarstan being cleared for construction, said the Ukrainian official. The images provided by the USCC show “proof that it is already growing,” this official said.

The foundation of the new factory “is being prepared,” said weapons expert David Albright, founder and president of the Washington-based Institute for Science and International Security think tank, who independently obtained satellite images of the site from August. The timeline for the factory’s completion in 2027, he said, “requires rapid construction.”

Drones allow Moscow to “launch these massive volleys and put pressure on deep targets within Ukraine at many different locations, and ensure that they can saturate the defenses,” said Stacie Pettyjohn, a former adviser in the Office of the Secretary of Defense who researches drone warfare at the Center for a New American Security in Washington. “It's been a very good coercive tool and critical to Russia's deep strike campaign.”

Rosatom’s plans to grow its capacity to feed Russia’s demands to increase weaponized drone production isn’t just a concern for Ukraine as Moscow’s fifth year of all-out war drags into another winter.

World.title: EU wants ‘closest possible’ relationship with Canada, Costa tells POLITICO
World.content:
Costa told POLITICO that the EU wants to develop “the closest possible” relationship with Ottawa. When asked to define “associate membership,” Costa said: “This concept means basically that we want to do more and act as much as possible with Canada,” adding that “there is just this small problem that geographically they [Canada] are not a European country” and cannot apply for EU membership.

The EU and Canada signed a landmark trade agreement in 2016. CETA, as it was known, took effect the following year but wasn’t ratified by 10 EU countries, including France, Italy and Belgium.

Costa said the EU “can do much more with them [Canada] than only trade. We can work on defense and security. We can work on investment in AI, quantum, the new technological challenges.”

“We can work with them to strengthen democracy, because we are like-minded and reliable partners,” he added.

Costa pointed to the upcoming EU-Canada Summit in Montreal Oct. 29-30 as a key moment to define the future relationship with Ottawa.

In a further sign of warming relations, Costa will co-host a public event on multilateralism with Carney and Kenyan President William Ruto in New York on Monday on the margins of the U.N. General Assembly.

World.title: EU budget needs taxes governments aren’t already raising, Costa says
World.content:
“If we don’t create new own resources, we need to ask [for] more money from the member states,” Costa said. “We know that we need to keep the national contributions at a reasonable limit. For this, we need to have a credible basket of new own resources.”

However, some of the options on the table — such as a tobacco tax — are being challenged by governments because they would tap into revenue that is already being collected domestically.

Tobacco is already taxed nationally in all EU countries, Costa said, meaning an EU tax could simply reduce national revenue. But newer products such as vapes and e-cigarettes are not taxed in many countries.

“If you are taxing the same thing or a different thing” it matters, Costa said. If it’s a different thing, “then it’s really new money. Then it means it’s easier [to secure an agreement.]”

Costa indicated that some proposals on the table can be "fine-tuned" to address concerns from EU governments.

“At the end, we need to have a basket, enough balance between all member states,” he said.

World.title: Merz vows to stay on as chancellor despite ‘disaster’ in another German regional vote
World.content:
AfD leaders hailed their victory — party national co-leader Tino Chrupalla called the Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania result a “sensation” — while also putting the pressure on a profoundly weakened Merz to step aside and abandon his party’s policy of maintaining a “firewall” around the far right.



“Friedrich Merz is the wrong chancellor for the CDU and is dragging the CDU down with him,” national co-leader Alice Weidel told German public television. “So the CDU must ask itself, above all else, does it want to continue with this chancellor and with these left-wing policies?”

Merz took the unusual step of convening CDU leaders at the party’s Berlin headquarters on Sunday night in an effort to rally their support ahead of what he knew would be another humiliating election defeat. Merz’s approval ratings are among the lowest ever recorded for a German chancellor at this point in their tenure, prompting internal CDU discussions about a possible change at the top—Kanzlertausch.

“Of course, the mood isn’t exactly lighthearted,” Ines Claus, a CDU politician who took part in the leadership meeting, told ARD. “If you ask me now whether one might prefer to just pull the covers over one’s head, well, that might be the case. But that’s not what responsibility is about; stability is what’s required now.”

Ahead of the election, one CDU official told POLITICO that “all hell breaks loose” in the party if the conservatives fail to make it into Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania’s state parliament — an outcome that remained distinctly possible as of 10 p.m. on election night.

Just 1% of voters — and 1% of CDU supporters — said Chancellor Merz had helped his party’s election performance in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, according to a poll by public broadcaster ZDF.



“We can’t sugarcoat the results in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania,” Merz said after the polls closed Sunday. “It’s a disaster.”



The CDU also saw its support decline in a separate regional vote in Berlin, finishing second with around 19%, according to a preliminary count, behind the Left party, a far-left force which won 25.5% and is now poised to take over the capital’s mayoralty from Merz’s conservatives in coalition with center-left parties.

‘Reform chancellor’

Merz has staked his chancellorship on a reform agenda he argues will boost Germany’s competitiveness and restore growth to the EU’s largest economy, and has urged voters to be patient as the reforms kick in.

World.title: US has deported 25,000 people to third countries under secretive deals, report shows
World.content:
The United States has deported more than 25,000 people under secretive agreements with 35 countries to take migrants with no ties to those nations, according to an investigation published on Monday.

 

Since US President Donald Trump took office in January 2025, Washington has been signing deals with developing countries to take migrants who cannot legally be sent home.

The investigation by Forbidden Stories found the administration has earmarked $410 million (€357 million) to be paid directly to the receiving countries or to UN agencies to facilitate the returns.

At least 25,447 people had already been deported to third countries by 31 August 2026, according to data compiled by Forbidden Stories with a consortium of international journalists.

The vast majority, around 20,000, were sent to Mexico, but the rest were dispersed to 27 other countries across Latin America, Africa and the Pacific, and agreements have been finalised with seven more.

The deals vary, including over which nationalities can be deported and whether people with criminal records can be accepted.

An investigation by the AFP news agency earlier this year found Washington is using visa bans and restrictions on African countries to strongarm them into accepting deportees.

Lawyers told AFP that deportees were being thrown into a "legal black hole," held without charge in countries where they have no ties and few if any rights.

Forbidden Stories said 49 of Africa's 54 countries had been approached about accepting third-country deportees.

A little-known State Department division called the Office of Remigration, created in May 2025, has handled most of the negotiations and payments, according to Forbidden Stories.

The office is headed by Christian Jove Ehrhardt, a 41-year-old diplomat who previously worked as a security officer.

The report details his visits to Cameroon, which signed a memorandum of understanding with the US in December on accepting deportees. A week later, it also signed a five-year health assistance programme worth nearly $400 million (€348 million).

A handcuffed migrant stands by before he is deported by ICE agents in McAllen, 13 March, 2026 AP Photo

The following month, the State Department said it would provide a further $30 million (€26 million) to the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) in Cameroon to "facilitate the voluntary return of refugees and combat illegal immigration."

The first plane carrying deportees arrived in Cameroon on 14 January.

Payments

Other agreements have involved direct payments to governments.

Palau, a small Pacific island nation with a population of under 18,000, signed an agreement in December 2025 to accept up to 75 third-country nationals in return for $7.5 million (€6.5 million).

However, only three people have so far been sent under the agreement.

In Eswatini, 32 people have arrived since July 2025 out of a possible 160 under an agreement worth more than $5 million (€4 million). It has accepted deportees with criminal records, the investigation found.

Of the $410 million planned for the agreements, internal State Department records showed that $81 million (€70 million) was earmarked for signatory governments.

A group of undocumented migrants is deported by ICE agents across the McAllen–Hidalgo–Reynosa International Bridge in McAllen, 13 March, 2026 AP Photo

The rest was intended for aid organisations, including more than $178 million (€155 million) for the UN's International Organisation for Migration and $123 million (€107 million) for UNHCR.

The agencies have faced criticism over their involvement, although UNHCR told Forbidden Stories that it was not party to the bilateral agreements and that US funding was being used in line with its mandate to strengthen asylum systems.

An IOM spokesperson told Forbidden Stories that the agency's decisions to accept funding rested "on a single question: whether our engagement will improve the lives of the migrants affected. In these instances, we believe strongly it does."

World.title: Lisbon hosts Europe’s largest exhibition of models built with Lego bricks
World.content:
For children and adults, enthusiasts or simply the curious. At Europe's largest exhibition of LEGO models, there's room for everyone. The only limits are those set by the imagination.

 

The numbers speak for themselves: two thousand square metres packed with models built from the famous colourful bricks.

More than 15 million bricks have been used to build over 120 models, including four "super-models". According to Lukas Siwiec, who is in charge of the exhibition, these are structures "made from more than half a million LEGO bricks" and are therefore far more imposing than the rest.

One of them is a replica of Air Force One. The exact number of bricks used to build this Boeing 747 at a scale of 1.7 is not entirely known. It is estimated that around one million bricks support the structure, which took half a year to build by a team of six people. According to the organisers, the model is nearly 11 metres long, 10 metres wide and three metres high.

Air Force One replica took half a year to build Euronews

Impressive as it is, this aircraft is not the only attraction. At the exhibition, currently hosted at Cordoaria Nacional in Lisbon, visitors can see the "King of the Seas", a model inspired by a cruise ship whose intricate details are sure to fascinate anyone. More than 700,000 bricks were used to raise the structure.

Euronews

Visitors will also find the "Great Red Dragon", a figure inspired by a medieval dragon, and a Spinosaurus, a structure built from 900,000 bricks.

But these are only the largest models; there are structures of every kind, covering a wide range of themes.

"We also have several themed areas dedicated to the worlds of cinema and sport, to Star Wars and to educational displays about geography, biology and other sciences," the organiser explained.

Visitors can find numerous structures from the Star Wars universe Euronews

The exhibition, which has already visited 11 European countries, has now arrived in Lisbon for a season. "After Lisbon we will probably tour the Iberian Peninsula. If we don't go to Porto first, we may head straight to Madrid or Barcelona and even other major cities in Spain," said Lukas Siwiec.

Most of the models on display were conceived, designed and built by the organisers themselves.

At this exhibition you can do more than just look. The so-called Fun Zone is divided into three areas and is open to visitors of all ages, giving them the chance to let their imagination run wild and build their own creations.

Alongside the model exhibition there is also the 3D Trick Gallery, a dedicated area for photographs and optical illusions, which is only accessible for an additional fee.

The exhibition is open to visitors until 10 January.

World.title: ‘A disaster’ – Merz’s migraine-triggering electoral defeat
World.content:
Trouble in Europe’s centre: Germany’s final state elections of 2026 occurring over the weekend have reshaped the political landscape, with the Left securing the strongest position in the state of Berlin and the far-right anti-immigration Alternative for Germany (AfD) topping the polls in the northern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

 

The results are expected to shake German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) to its core, with the party’s stunning losses directly tied to the swelling gains of the AfD.

Merz described the results in Berlin “reasonable” but the Macklenburg-Western Pomerania political outcome as “a disaster”. The CDU recorded its worst result in the state's history in the latter state with just 4.9%, meaning it has not met the threshold to enter parliament. For a drill-down into the numbers, my Berlin-based colleague Johanna Urbancik has this must-read story.

Despite the data, Merz has promised resolve: “What needs to be done now requires backbone, steadfastness, and patience,” he said in a statement shortly after the exit polls were announced Sunday night. “I will demonstrate these qualities as chairman of the CDU and, above all, as chancellor of our country.”

The results also follow a similarly bruising result in Saxony-Anhalt, forcing many political spectators to wonder whether the chancellor’s time may soon be up.

Sabrina Repp, German Member of the European Parliament of the Group of the Progressive Alliance of Socialists and Democrats (S&D), just told Europe Today that the far-right has risen in Germany since the most recent European Parliament elections in 2024. “You can see, especially in the eastern part of Germany, an increase in the results of the AfD of over 30%,” she said. Watch.

New York minute: Meanwhile, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen alongside a top team of EU officials are in New York for the United Nations General Assembly.

Today, she is expected to meet the Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese alongside European Council President António Costa. Could this be about potential associate membership for Europe’s far-flung ally, as winked at by European Parliament President Roberta Metsola last week? The European Commission spokesperson Arianna Podestà poured cold water on Canberra potentially joining the fold last Friday, telling reporters she would not speculate.

Carney-villesque: But the meeting of middle powers doesn’t stop there, with von der Leyen attending a multilateral-themed meet-up alongside Kenyan President William Ruto, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, and none other than Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. In an combined opinion piece for the Financial Times newspaper, the leaders outlined their pitch for a new middle power partnership, aiming to “renew and strengthen” the multilateral system, “not replace it”.

On top of this, von der Leyen said last week she would use her time in the US to emphasise that Europe is steadfast in its support for war-torn Ukraine. “Now others must step up their support too,” her online statement says. Canada has already expressed desire to participate in the EU’s €90 billion support loan for the war-battered country, but only time will tell whether other nations join the call.

Also in New York, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he would meet US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the UNGA. "We agreed to meet in New York, and this meeting could change a lot. There is diplomatic momentum," Zelenskyy wrote on social media platform X. It comes as the mayor of Moscow decries that Ukraine launched its "largest-scale attack" on Russia’s capital since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began.

Federico Borsari, fellow with the Transatlantic Defense and Security Programme at the Centre for European Policy Analysis, just told Europe Today, that he is not optimistic Russia could lessen its assault on Ukraine despite the political pressure and fresh assault from Kyiv.

“There will definitely be an attempt by Russia to destroy and damage — even more — the power grid and the critical infrastructure in Ukraine,” he said.

Back to Brussels: The EU’s 27 ambassadors are meeting in the Belgian capital this morning to thrash out a deal to renew the individual sanctions on Russia before they expire at midnight on Tuesday, Jorge Liboreiro writes. Failure to do so would free Vladimir Putin, Sergey Lavrov and over 2,600 names from the blacklist. As Moscow escalates the war, no one wants to portray weakness.

“We have a very tight deadline,” a senior diplomat said. “All our efforts are focused on reaching an agreement on Monday.” But the picture looks increasingly thorny.

First, Slovakia wants the removal of Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, a long-held request. Second, France wants the removal of Usmanov to secure the release of several French prisoners held in Azerbaijan. And finally, Luxembourg says that if Usmanov is removed, then Fridman should be removed too. Fridman is seeking compensation from the Grand Duchy over the freezing of his personal assets, estimated at $16 billion.

How to square the circle? Until now, Ireland, the country that holds the rotating presidency, has been loath to propose delistings. The majority in the room is against removing the high-profile oligarchs. If the puzzle proves intractable, ambassadors may once again agree to a one-week extension to buy themselves more time. But a longer wait risks inviting fresh requests.

Brussels to keep ban on Arctic oil and gas drilling despite Norwegian pressure

A ban on new oil and gas drilling in the Arctic will remain the European Commission’s official position in a revised strategy Brussels is due to unveil, a Commission spokesperson told Euronews, despite fierce pressure from oil-rich Norway to drop the ban.

The revised version of the EU’s 2021 Arctic strategy will be announced on 20 October, as the region gains increasing strategic importance for the bloc’s defence and climate ambitions.

“Moving forward, our approach on the moratorium will remain unchanged: our policies have objectives to address climate change and environmental degradation and support sustainable economic development,” the Commission spokesperson said.

For the Commission, new Arctic fossil fuel development is incompatible with its climate goals. Maintaining the moratorium underscores Brussels’ determination to uphold that position, despite calls from the International Energy Agency to reconsider it and pressure from Norway, a key energy supplier and ally, as the bloc faces an energy crunch.

Marta Pacheco has the story.

World.title: 'Primetime', M83 and obsolete tech: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
World.content:
Comedy, drama, artistic masterpieces — this week's lineup has it all (with some dream pop thrown in).

 

Highlights include the release of Primetime, starring Robert Pattinson as American TV host Chris Hansen, and the 10th album release from French band M83.

Elsewhere, new exhibitions in London and France explore obsolete tech and ancient fragments, while Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson bring us some comic relief with new Apple TV+ show Brothers.

Keep scrolling to find out more.

Exhibitions and events

Jenkin Van Zyl: ‘Enclosure’

Enclosure (2026) film still. Somerset House/Jenkin van Zyl

When: 24 september - 29 november 2026

Where: Somerset House (London, UK)

British artist Jenkin Van Zyl's new film and installation is a sensory trip inside the world of obsolete technologies that have outlasted the society that created them. Set within a decaying facility, the film follows a former actress who allowed her body to be replicated for tourists to inhabit. Once this replica becomes outdated, she decides to terminate it — unleashing chaos. Ambient with neon and the eerie remains of an older world slipping away, it's a richly imagined world that contemplates self-preservation and commodification. Find out more here.

Broken: The Power of the Fragment

Genova Scala. Palazzo Strozzi, Florence

When: 25 September 2026 - 24 January 2027

Where: Palazzo Strozzi, Florence Opening on 25 September and running until 24 January 2027

Fragments contain stories. Whether relics from an ancient civilisation or symbols of artistic expression, the broken pieces that people and places leave behind become tethers to the past — and transformation. The Palazzo Strozzi's new exhibition explores this with extraordinary detail, featuring works from masters like Giovanni Pisano, and Michelangelo alongside sculptures by contemporary artists Louise Bourgeois, Huma Bhabha and more. There are more than eighty works and artefacts on display in total, including ones loaned from prestigious museums across the globe. Together, these form a powerful exploration of shifting symbolism that questions: how does meaning change when something is broken? Find out more here.

Bonus highlight: The Musée d’Orsay is hosting an exhibition and immersive virtual reality experience that pays tribute to 19th-century French sculptor Auguste Bartholdi (who famously created the Statue of Liberty). On until 31 January 2027.

Movies

Primetime

Where: Cinemas across France (with a staggered release across the rest of Europe).

When: 23 September

The 2000s were a wild time for TV, but one of the more shocking was To Catch a Predator. The reality-based American series centred around sting operations, where adults would pose as minors online to lure predators back to a house filled with cameras. Robert Pattinson plays the show's unnervingly calm host, Chris Hansen, in a big screen dramatisation that delves into the show's peak success and darker history; exposing the greed lurking beneath its facade of justice. Musician Phoebe Bridgers, Merritt Wever (Christy) and Anna Faris (Scary Movie) also star.

Bonus highlight: A new revival of Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and George MacKay, is out at cinemas from the 25 September (with staggered dates across Europe).

TV series

Brothers

Where: Apple TV+

When: 23 September

Here is a fact you might not know about actors Matthew McConaughey and Woody Harrelson: they might actually be brothers. Well, half-brothers. After McConaughey's mother revealed she had known Harrelson's father (in a tone that seemed to insinuate something), the pair began speculating on the timeline and worked out they could indeed be related. While they've never done an official DNA test, they have created a TV series inspired by it — a goofy, Texas-set comedy in which the actors play fictionalised versions of themselves. As McConaughey would say, "alright, alright, alright".

Bonus highlight: The 13th season of anthology series American Horror Story streams from 25 September on Disney+.

Music

M83 – I Wrote You A Letter

When: 25 September

It's 25 years since Anthony Gonzalez released M83's self-titled debut album — and the French band's ambient, shoegaze sound has continued to lure listeners since. 'I Wrote You A Letter' marks the occasion, aptly drawing on nostalgia to create an immersive and cinematic experience that's textured with the more unpredictable, punk energy of their earlier works. This will be a promising sign for fans, many of whom still miss the band's peak successes in the early 2010s. The world is weird and confusing, take us back to Midnight City!

Bonus highlight: Ruddy hell, it's Soft Cell! The '80s chart-topping duo are releasing their sixth — and apparently final — studio album, ' Danceteria'. Out 25 September.

World.title: Venezuelan man shot and injured by ICE agent in Texas, officials say
World.content:
A Venezuelan national was shot and wounded by a US immigration agent, Texas officials said on Sunday, as they voiced outrage and demanded a thorough investigation.

 

Tasked with enforcing Trump's immigration crackdown, heavily armed and often masked US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents have faced nationwide backlash for aggressive and often violent tactics, including the shooting of American citizens.

The man, identified by his lawyer as 28-year-old Venezuelan national Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, was taken to a hospital in Texas's capital city Austin in a serious but stable condition after being shot in the torso, officials said.

The wounded man's lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said on X that Garces Perez had been shot by an ICE agent while making "a DoorDash delivery."

The shooting took place during a "significant increase, almost overnight" of ICE operations in the Texas capital, Mayor Kirk Watson told a press conference.

The Department of Homeland Security said Monday it was leading an investigation into the officer involved in the shooting with the help of the FBI.

The department said in a post on X that the man had "illegally entered our country under the Biden administration and had a final order of removal."

Authorities deploy non-lethal weapons near a demonstration where a man was shot in his vehicle by an ICE officer in Austin, 20 September, 2026 AP Photo

"The illegal alien's condition is stable, and he is in federal custody pending removal," it added.

Watson said he was "very angry and extremely disappointed that a person was shot on the streets of Austin by ICE."

He said local law enforcement should be involved in the investigation.

"The credibility of ICE doing some form of investigation just by itself and excluding others would not be appropriate," he said.

Texas Democratic Representative Greg Casar echoed that sentiment, telling reporters that "ICE has not been truthful in shootings in other cities."

Casar cited the January shooting of Renee Good in Minneapolis in which video footage belied ICE accounts that she had attempted to run over a federal agent.

"It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep," he said. "A few weeks ago as we saw the ICE surge come...I and others said that ICE needed to leave before someone was shot."

The House Democrat called for the release of body camera footage of Sunday's incident.

People protest at the site where local authorities say an ICE officer shot and wounded a man in Austin, 20 September, 2026 Aaron E. Martinez /Austin American-Statesman via AP

Deportation threat

A few hours later, Casar said Garces Perez had been "taken out of the hospital and into ICE custody."

"If ICE deports him, the key witness to their shooting disappears," the lawmaker added. "He must not be removed from this country and he must receive proper medical care."

Lincoln-Goldfinch said her client was placed "into custody, but we still don't know his location."

The shooting sparked outrage in the community with video footage posted by local news outlets to social media showing several dozen people protesting at the alleged shooting site.

Protests broke out following the shooting. Via Alejandro Serrano on X

Donald Trump campaigned for president in 2016 and again in 2024, on a promise to expel millions of undocumented migrants, and has taken a series of dramatic actions since returning to the White House aimed at speeding up deportations and reducing border crossings.

Nearly 51,000 undocumented migrants were arrested in the United States in August, according to Department of Homeland Security figures.

Ruben Ray Martinez, a 23-year-old was shot by ICE in March 2025, in what the Texas Tribune said was the first known killing by immigration agents of an American in Trump's second term.

World.title: Sweeping raids leave Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community fearing what comes next
World.content:
Turkey has jailed dozens of people pending trial as a sweeping crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups widens, prompting international condemnation and protests outside Turkish embassies on Friday.

Advertising

By Thursday, courts in several provinces had jailed at least 82 people following raids on LGBTQI+ organisations, clubs, cafes and homes.

The cases include LGBTQI+ activists and members of rights groups as well as people accused of prostitution, drug offences and other crimes. Not everyone jailed is accused of gay rights advocacy.

The United Nations human rights office has called on Turkey to uphold human rights without discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity and to immediately release anyone arbitrarily detained.

Protests were held outside Turkish embassies in cities including Paris, Brussels, London, Oslo and Washington on Friday.

The crackdown began on Saturday, when police carried out coordinated raids targeting nine LGBTQI+ organisations. Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said legal action was being taken against 162 people, nine associations and 13 businesses in 15 provinces.

Turkey arrests dozens in ongoing crackdown on LGBTQI+ groups

Mass detentions

The raids prompted protests across Turkey, including outside Istanbul’s main courthouse on Tuesday. Police broke up the demonstration and detained more than 100 people, including journalists. They were later released.

“I am here because I want to say that LGBTQ+ friends are not alone in this country,” said Ayse, a protester who asked to be identified only by her first name.

“I want to support them and to stay in solidarity with them, which is not easy these days in Turkey, but they are not alone, and we are not alone, and we will be here until the end.”

Opposition DEM Party parliamentarian Ozgul Saki remained at the protest, protected from arrest by parliamentary immunity.

“This oppression against LGBTQ+ people is an attempt to compress society into a single type; to build an Islamist, Turkish, racist society,” Saki said. “Those who are here say, 'No! Society will live equally, freely and honourably with all its diversity,' and that's why they were all detained.”

The operations have been defended by Gurlek, from President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s conservative Justice and Development Party (AKP).

“No criminal organisation, abuse network or illegal activity which targets children, youths or families will be tolerated,” Gurlek posted on social media.

Among the organisations affected was Istanbul-based SPoD, which provides psychological support to LGBTQI+ people.

“As a community, we were expecting that such an operation would come one day. But we didn't imagine it as that violent, that much unlawful,” said a SPoD representative who asked to remain anonymous.

“They raided our office; I think four or five have been detained, and they are still in custody. What will happen to the LGBTQ+ community after this day? Like they can implement a kind of informal criminalisation upon our community, so my personal feeling is an immense feeling of uncertainty.”

Surge in anti-LGBTQ disinformation targets Pride in Europe

Obscenity allegations

Homosexuality has been legal since the foundation of the Turkish republic in 1923, but authorities are using an obscenity law as part of the crackdown.

“All of our board members are detained due to the allegations of obscenity,” said Yildiz Tar of Ankara-based KAOS GL, Turkey’s leading LGBTQI+ news portal.

“They look into our social media account, and our news articles are seen as obscene because, for example, there is one picture of two women kissing, and they see that it's obscene. So that is why they have been detained.”

The measures resemble actions taken against LGBTQI+ communities in Russia and Egypt, Tar said.

“It's very similar to Russia and Egypt, like the things they want to do is very similar to anti-gay propaganda laws, and there were huge operations, and people got detained,” Tar said.

“So it's very similar to both countries. And actually, like the Turkish government is very fond of Putin's way of dealing things.”

The crackdown has also drawn condemnation from the European Union and international human rights groups.

“It's an attempt to show LGBTQ+ people as immoral and against the family. But in fact, none of this does anything to protect the family at all,” said Emma Sinclair-Webb, who leads Human Rights Watch’s Turkey office.

“It's all about discrediting and stigmatizing people for their sexual orientation or gender identity.”

Turkey marks a decade since the coup that never was, but never really ended

Wider crackdown

The arrests form part of a broader crackdown on people regarded as opposing the government, Sinclair-Webb said.

“This operation should be set in the context of a very wide crackdown on anybody who is regarded as oppositional to the government, whether in terms of being politically or in terms of their lifestyle or their outlook… there is a general attempt by the government to impose as well as, you know, ideological conformity on people, lifestyle,” Sinclair-Webb said.

President Erdogan routinely refers to LGBTQI+ people as perverts and has stepped up his rhetoric ahead of much-rumoured early elections. Gurlek has called on prosecutors to increase investigations into the LGBTQI+ community, fuelling fears of further arrests.

The crackdown has also prompted condemnation across Turkish civil society, with trade unions, doctors’ associations and opposition parties voicing their opposition.

For Tar, that support offers some hope amid fears over what could follow for Turkey’s LGBTQI+ community.

“If this attack won't be stopped, it would mean a lot of maltreatment and torture; it can also cause hate crimes; it incites hatred inside the country too,” Tar said. “And it will mean that you cannot be openly queer; if they succeed in their operation, that is a really, really hellish scenario.”

World.title: A doubleheader feast!
World.content:
This week on The Sound Kitchen it’s a doubleheader: you’ll hear the answers to TWO quiz questions, as well as TWO “Listener's Corner" with Paul Myers, and of course, Erwan Rome’s “Music from Erwan”. So sit down, relax, and join the banquet! Just click the “play” button above to join the feast.

Advertising

Hello everyone!

As noted on the show, I am retiring on 1 October. Unfortunately, The Sound Kitchen is retiring too – I will not be replaced.

We’ve had a great time together all these years, haven’t we?

Click here to listen to past Sound Kitchen podcasts.

I know you will all stay loyal to RFI English – our service has so much to offer. We’re small, but my colleagues are firebrands!

For example, we have wonderful podcasts: Spotlight on France, with journalists Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas; Melissa Chemam’s insightful Spotlight on Africa, and our International Report, usually sent to us by one of our foreign correspondents. We also have an award-winning bilingual series – an old-time radio show, with actors (!) – to help you learn French, called Les voisins du 12 bis.

Remember, podcasts are radio, too! As you see, sound is still quite present in the RFI English service. Please keep checking our website for updates on the latest from our team of journalists. You never know what we’ll surprise you with!

To listen to our podcasts from your PC, go to our website; you’ll see “Podcasts” at the top of the page. You can either listen directly or subscribe and receive them directly on your mobile phone.

And don’t forget, in addition to our audio bilingual series, you can also learn French through our website “Le Français facile avec rfi”. In addition to online lessons, there are news broadcasts in slow, simple French, with exercises to practice what you’ve heard.

Go to their website and get started! At the top of the page, click on “Test level”, and you’ll be advised on the best-suited activities for your level, according to your score.

Do not give up! As Lidwien van Dixhoorn, the head of the “Le Français facile” service, told me: “Bathe your ears in the sound of the language, and eventually, you’ll get it”. She should know – Lidwien is Dutch and came to France hardly able to say “bonjour,” and now she heads this key international award-winning RFI department – so stick with it!

For the quiz on 24 January: I asked you a question about the Africa Cup of Nations, and an article sent to us by Paul Myers, who was there. You were to re-read his article “Senegal outwit Morocco to claim 2025 Africa Cup of Nations”, and send in the answer to this question: At the 2026 World Cup, which took place in the United States, Mexico, and Canada in June, in which group did Morocco play, and in which group did Senegal play?

The answer is, to quote Paul’s article: “Morocco will play in Group C against Brazil, Scotland and Haiti.

Senegal will feature in Group I with France, Norway, and the team that emerges from the intercontinental play-off in March.”

In addition to the quiz question, there was the bonus question: “What is your favorite day of the year? Why? What is it about that day that makes it your favorite?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Dipita Chakrabarty from New Delhi, India. Dipita is also the bonus question winner.

Also on the list of lucky winners this week are Muhammed Naved, a member of the International DX Radio Listeners Club in West Bengal, India; Muhammad Abdullah, a member of the RFI Online Visitors Club in Sahiwal, Pakistan; RFI Listeners Club member Rodrigo Hunrichse from Bio-Bio, Chile, and last but not least, RFI English listener Sakila Musarrt from Chapainawabganj in Bangladesh.

Congratulations winners!

For the quiz on 31 January: You were to listen to our podcast “Spotlight on France”, the brainchild of my colleagues Alison Hird and Sarah Elzas. I hope you listen to it regularly, it’s really quite good.

On their programme number 138, Alison reported on La Ménardière, an alternative living arrangement for seniors in the village of Bérat, close to the southern French town of Toulouse. The aim of the project is for seniors to live and grow old together, contributing to society for as long as possible, and to delay – or avoid – the moment when people are forced into institutional care.

The answers you were to send in were: How many residents can live at La Ménardière, and what is the selection process?

The answer is, to quote Alison: “La Ménardière can house up to 20 residents. The selection process to become one is rigorous. Candidates stay for trial weekends and, if they decide to join, they must then complete a six-month probation period.”

The bonus question you answered that week – suggested by Murshida Parvin Lata, the co-chairman of the Sonali Badhan Female Listeners Club in Bogura, Bangladesh – was: “Which daytime temperature do you prefer: cold or hot? Why?”

The winners are: RFI Listeners Club member Father Steven Wara, who lives and serves in the Cistercian Abbey in Bamenda, Cameroon. Father Steve is also the winner of this week’s bonus question.

There’s long-standing RFI Listeners Club member Zenon Teles, who is also the president of the Christian – Marxist – Leninist – Maoist Association of Listening DX-ERs in Goa, India, as well as another faithful Sound Kitchen listener – and club member – Radhakrishna Pillai from Kerala State, also in India.

Moving over to Bangladesh, Anjana Parvin – she’s the secretary of the very active Shetu RFI Listeners Club in Naogaon. And last but not the least, club member and my fellow dinosaur, Alan Holder, from England’s Isle of Wight.

Congratulations winners!

Here’s the music you heard on this week’s programme: “Take the A Train” by Billy Strayhorn and Duke Ellington, performed by Duke Ellington and his orchestra; the “AFCON 2025 Official Intro Theme – Africa Cup of Nations Morocco 2025” by Othmane Laaouina; “What a Wonderful World” by Bob Thiele and George David Weiss, sung by Louis Armstrong; “The Cakewalk” from Children’s Corner by Claude Debussy, performed by the composer, and “Étincelles”, Op. 36, No. 6 by Moritz Moszkowski, played by Alexander Zhou.

I’ll talk to you next week, 26 September, for our final Sound Kitchen together. You’ll hear the answers to the questions about the Grammy Awards Lifetime Achievement Awards and the Benin Bronzes, as well as your responses to the bonus questions on "The Listener’s Corner" with Paul Myers, so be sure and tune in.

Until then, fare thee well!

World.content:
09/21/2026 September 21, 2026 Kerala flash flood: Death toll rises, more rain expected

Search and rescue authorities in the southern state of Kerala found three more dead bodies on Monday morning, taking the death toll from a flash flood to at least five.

Six people were swept away on Sunday evening in the scenic town of Nilambur when the Kottapuzha River rose due to rainfall higher up in the landscape, local media reported. The search for the sixth person is still on.

Floods and rain-triggered landslides are a common occurrence in Kerala during the monsoon months, between June and November.

The state's Chief Minister VD Satheesan is set to arrive in the town shortly.

Meanwhile, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued orange alerts for six districts in the state on Monday morning, warning of more downpour.

An orange alert is the second highest in IMD's four-stage color-coded system, sitting just below the red warning. It tells local authorities and residents to 'be prepared' for heavy to very heavy rainfall in the region.

World.title: Japan: Typhoon Dujuan sparks flood, landslide warnings
World.content:
Hundreds of flights have been canceled in Japan, which is in the middle of a five-day holiday. The storm could dump record levels of rain on the country.

A powerful typhoon was nearing Japan's eastern coast on Monday, triggering warnings of floods and landslides and prompting hundreds of flights to be canceled.

Dujuan is forecast to pass close to the Tokyo metropolitan area later in the day.

What do we know about Typhoon Dujuan?

Typhoon Dujuan was packing winds at speeds of 144 kilometers (89 miles) per hour as it lingered some 110 kilometres from Hachijojima, one of Tokyo's most remote islands.

Parts of the Izu Islands and the Chiba prefecture near Tokyo already saw heavy rainfall over the weekend.

The ⁠Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) has cautioned that weather conditions could worsen rapidly.

"The total rainfall through Tuesday could exceed the average monthly rainfall for September, resulting in record-breaking heavy rain," the JMA said.

Authorities have also warned of a possibility of ⁠linear ​rain bands forming over central Japan and the Kanto region — which includes Tokyo and surrounding prefectures — that could raise the risk of rain-related disasters like flash floods and landslides.

Linear ‌bands cause heavy torrential rainfall ​over a narrow area for several hours.

Dujuan is Japan's 25th typhoon of the year Image: Ichiro Ohara/AP Photo/picture alliance

How have Japan's regions been affected by the incoming storm?

Over 4,000 households in Chiba were without power.

In the central prefecture of Aichi, which is currently hosting the Asian Games, an equestrian eventing competition was postponed until Tuesday.

The Tokyo Game Show, one of the world's biggest video game trade fairs, was shut down ahead of its final day on Monday.

Dujuan could also scupper travel plans during Japan's "Silver Week" holiday, which has just begun and which normally sees a surge in domestic travel.

On Monday, Japan Airlines canceled 120 domestic and 15 international flights, while All Nippon Airways canceled 140 domestic flights.

Some railway services were suspended on some lines in Tokyo and its neighboring areas.

World.title: US: Man wounded in Texas after being shot by ICE agent
World.content:
An ICE agent shot and wounded a man in Austin, Texas. The city's mayor has called for an independent investigation into the shooting.

A man has been hospitalized in Austin, Texas after being shot by an officer of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), local officials said Sunday.

Austin's Mayor Kirk Watson expressed his anger over the shooting, calling for the involvement of the local police in a "clear-eyed" investigation into the incident.

What do we know about the ICE shooting in Austin?

The man suffered one gunshot wound in his torso during a brief foot pursuit in the Texan capital's north side shortly before 1 pm local time, Austin officials said at a press briefing.

He is at a local hospital in a serious but stable condition, the officials said, adding that the information on the incident was "very preliminary."

City police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said.

Who is the man wounded by ICE agent?

The officials did not name the man or release his age and nationality but an immigration lawyer, representing his family, identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan.

Attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch said in a video published on her Instagram account that she believed he had no criminal history and had no final order to be removed from the country.

The Associated Press later cited Goldfinch as saying that she did not know his current immigration status.

There is yet to be a statement on the shooting from ICE or the Department of Homeland Security that oversees the immigration agency.

Meanwhile, a group of about 100 protesters gathered at the site of the shooting and demonstrated against ICE's actions.

Demonstrators protest at the scene of the shooting Image: Kaylee Greenlee/REUTERS

The protest was held across the street from a blue Toyota Corolla which had damage to its ​passenger-side door, news agency Reuters reported citing local TV, as ICE agents stood nearby.

The damaged car was towed away Image: Jesse Bedayn/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

Austin Mayor rails against 'rogue' ICE, calls for independent probe

Sunday's shooting is the latest in a slew of incidents involving ICE, which has become the face of an immigration clampdown by US President Donald Trump's Republican administration.

Watson, a Democrat, told the media that the shooting occurred amid a "significant increase, almost overnight" of ICE operations in Austin.

"While I'm angry and disappointed, I'm not surprised. This has happened in other cities. With the rogue nature of ICE and the chaos we're seeing fomented by ICE, there's no reason to be surprised," the Austin mayor wrote on X.

He called for an independent investigation into the shooting, with the Austin Police Department (APD) having a role in the probe.

He said that the people of Austin had a "right to know what happened" and "a right to feel safe in their community".

"Though APD was not involved in the shooting, I believe that there needs to be an investigation that APD assures is clear-eyed, as complete as possible, and independent," Watson said.

He added that police chief Davis had deployed the APD's Special Investigation Unit at the scene, elaborating that the unit is the one responsible for probing Austin's officer-involved shootings.

Watson said that Davis has also asked the Texas Rangers to help out in the investigation.

'Horror has come to our doorstep,' says Congressman

On Sunday, US Representative Greg Casar — a Texas Democrat — called for transparency as the shooting is investigated.

He accused ICE of not being "truthful" in shooting in other cities.

"It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep," Casar said.

"A few weeks ago as we saw the ICE surge come ... I and others said that ICE needed to leave before someone was shot," he told the media.

World.title: Iran closes language center in Tehran, France vows response
World.content:
In response to the Iranian authorities' decision to close a French language center affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, France vowed to take appropriate measures.

Paris will summon Iran's ambassador and take appropriate measures in response after Iranian authorities closed a French language center affiliated with its embassy in Tehran, the French Foreign Ministry said on Sunday.

"This new attack against France's cultural presence in Iran, following the assault on two staff members of the French embassy last July, is unjustifiable and ​unacceptable," the ministry's spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said in a statement.

What do we know about the center's closure?

Earlier on Sunday, Iranian authorities announced the closure of a French language center in Tehran following a judicial order from the prosecutor's office.

"The illegal center affiliated with the French embassy in Tehran, which has operated for years under the guise of language instruction, was closed," the judiciary's Mizan news website said, referring to the French Language Center (CLF).

The Iranian judiciary accused the center of conducting "illegal acts that violated diplomatic conventions".

It also accused the center of having "abused its status as a language training facility" and of having sought to "identify and build networks among the country's elite figures while facilitating their departure."

Tensions between Paris and Tehran

France has previously dismissed such allegations. The country claims that there has been a pattern of intimidation in recent months as it has sought to increase support for and contact with Iran's civil society following the crackdown on protests at the beginning of this year.

Tensions between Tehran and Paris have been escalating in recent years. Last month, France expelled two Iranian diplomats in response to the brief detention and prohibition of two French envoys to the Islamic Republic. Tehran accused the diplomats of interfering in its internal affairs.

Diplomats said Iran was also upset by a recent social media post from French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot commemorating the fourth anniversary of Mahsa Amini's death, which sparked protests nationwide.

In response, on Friday, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi called the post "crocodile tears" and accused Paris of slaughtering 1.5 million Algerians during Algeria's war of independence.

The two ministers are scheduled to meet on Tuesday at the United Nations' annual gathering of world leaders.

World.title: Canada, France agree to closer ties in defense, economy
World.content:
Amid strained relations with the US, French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced closer economic and defense ties.

French President Emmanuel Macron and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney announced deeper cooperation between their countries in many areas, including defense, energy, and business.

The two leaders made the announcement on Sunday from Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a small French territory just off the Atlantic coast of Canada.

According to a statement from Carney's office, the leaders discussed aerospace, energy, critical minerals, and advanced technologies, such as quantum computing, satellites, and supercomputing.

This move is another step in Canada's accelerating turn toward Europe, as both countries are experiencing strained relations with the US.

The meeting between Macron and Carney follows up on Carney's visit to Brussels, during which the EU offered Canada "associate member" status.

Canada's PM welcomes EU associate membership idea To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did the leaders say?

"We both believe that our countries are two great, independent nations who want to remain so," Macron said at the joint news conference, adding that France and Canada would work together for closer ties on fishing, security and energy.

"We both believe in democracy, the rule of law, respect for free and fair trade, the science on which our decisions are based, and the strategic autonomy that we defend," Macron said. "And this is what very deeply unites Canada and France, Canada and the European Union."

Meanwhile, Carney said: "The time has come to tighten our links between Canada and France, between Canada and the European Union — links based on the values we share."

"History remembers those who... defend their sovereignty, those who stay true to their values," Carney stressed in his speech.

However, he also proposed that France, Canada, the United States and China work together on artificial intelligence.

How could Trump react to Canada-EU association plan? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Where is Saint Pierre and Miquelon?

Saint Pierre and Miquelon, a French overseas territory, is located off the coast of Newfoundland and has a population of fewer than 6,000 people.

It is France's only remaining possession in North America and a remnant of its former vast territories in what are now Canada and the United States. One of Canada's provinces, Quebec, has French as its sole official language.

Macron's three-day visit to Saint Pierre and Miquelon is the first by a French president in over a decade. Carney is the first Canadian prime minister to visit the territory.

The leaders' meeting comes at a time of strained relations with the US. Ottawa has strongly rejected President Donald Trump's repeated remarks about making Canada the 51st US state.

Last Monday, Trump posted a map of North America on social media. The map depicted Canada, Greenland, Mexico, much of Central America and the Caribbean, and Iceland in the colors of the US flag.

Several French overseas territories were also included in the image, such as Guadeloupe, Martinique, and Saint Pierre and Miquelon.

However, upon his arrival in the territory late Saturday, Macron reaffirmed its status as French territory and dismissed "strange ideas" on the subject.
