World.title: Lika Residents Ask One Thing After Waste Scandal: Are We Infected?
World.content:
September the 21st, 2026 – Furious and deeply concerned Lika residents have been asking one very valid question following the shameful hazardous waste scandal was uncovered: Are we infected?

In wells in the Gospić settlement of Krpani, downstream from the illegal waste dump in Bilajska Street, PFAS compounds, which are so-called forever chemicals, have unfortunately been found. One of the wells is about 600 metres from the dump, HRT reported. The latest findings have further alarmed residents who have for years been using local springs and wells and are engaged in livestock farming and agriculture. Index reports that the Croatian Institute of Public Health published the results of extraordinary sampling of 43 private water facilities in the Lika area – 38 wells, three cisterns and two springs. PFAS was found in two wells in the immediate vicinity and downstream from the illegal dump.

In one of them, the sum of PFAS compounds amounted to 0.3018 micrograms per litre, more than three times above the maximum permitted value of 0.1 micrograms. In the other 0.0265 micrograms per litre was measured, which is below that limit.

serious concerns about the water in lika

Residents of Krpani warn that the groundwater from their settlement does not remain only in the area of the wells. “This water that flows through here goes into the well, and that well now has PFAS, it now has those compounds,” said OPG owner Marko Štimac for HRT. Resident Mate Krpan claims that these are groundwaters that are connected to local watercourses and warns of the possibility of further spread of the pollution. The exact direction and extent of the movement of the pollution through the groundwater still needs to be professionally determined.

“are we infected?”

The wells were once an important source of water for residents, and the new findings have caused fear because of possible long-term exposure.

“Are we infected or not, we’ll see. Who knows, who knows,” said resident Božo Krpan. “Of course I’m afraid for the children, there’s always the thought whether this has already affected their health, and our health in general,” said Josipa Krpan. PFAS is a large group of very persistent chemical compounds that are difficult to break down in the environment, which is why they are often called forever chemicals.

family farms fear for their livestock and produce

Particularly concerned are local farmers whose livestock used water from that area. “The livestock may be infected, I don’t know, that needs to be tested. I won’t sell calves and think whether I’ll infect someone with that,” said Štimac. Tomislav Krpan fears that the findings could completely destroy the market for local producers from Lika. “What we’ve been raising will obviously all go to ruin, and we will no longer have a market, nor will we be able to sell our products, neither lambs, nor calves, nor kids, nor potatoes,” he said. Their fears so far do not mean that the livestock or food from their farms is indeed contaminated. Separate tests would be needed for such a conclusion.

HZJZ this week published the results of testing 32 samples of locally produced food from 13 locations up to a kilometre away from the dump. The Institute states that the findings so far do not show general contamination of local food, and in seven samples tested for PFAS the values were below the limit of quantification.

public health authorities say the water is safe…

It is important to emphasise that the disputed wells are not part of the public water supply system. HZJZ states that residents of that area are connected to the public water supply and that the water from the two wells in which PFAS was found is not used for drinking. The Institute concludes that the results so far point to pollution of a local character, in a narrower area downstream from the dump. Analyses of the public water supply so far have not shown PFAS above the limit of determination. By 16 September a total of 93 samples of water from the public system in the Lika-Senj County and Pag area were analysed, and all were health-safe.

Earlier expert examinations carried out for USKOK already established PFAS compounds in the waste and groundwater immediately next to the illegal dump. HZJZ published that the compounds established in the waste match those found in the groundwater in its immediate vicinity.

Biologist and ecotoxicologist Branimir K. Hackenberger warned for HRT that the findings from different polluted wells are not the same. “The chemical fingerprint is completely different in those wells, which means that the source of pollution is also not one, and we cannot link all three wells to that one nearest source of pollution that is located there,” he said. For that reason, he is calling for a detailed hydrogeological investigation.

“Experts from the Institute and other institutions must absolutely go out into the field as soon as possible, see what the traffic of that water is like, what the hydrodynamics are, what the directions are, etc., so that anything further can be responsibly claimed on the basis of such analyses,” said Hackenberger.

covering this waste up is nowhere near enough of a solution

The citizens’ initiative Gospić is Our Home considers that the planned temporary covering of the waste can no longer solve the groundwater problem.

“That solution made sense a year ago, but now, as we know, the influence of groundwater cannot be prevented,” said Darija Dođen from the initiative. In the area of the former PPK Velebit complex in Gospić around 37,000 tonnes of mixed waste were illegally dumped. USKOK is conducting an investigation against a larger number of persons on suspicion that they committed criminal offences against the environment and the economy as part of a criminal association. The latest findings from private wells now open the question of how far the pollution has spread through the underground karst system and what additional tests are needed to assess its actual reach.

World.title: Number of Foreign Tourists in Croatia Falls With More Growth Elsewhere in Mediterranean
World.content:
September the 21st, 2026 – The number of foreign tourists in Croatia has actually fallen, with much more growth seen elsewhere across the Mediterranean.

Croatia recorded only 0.5 percent more tourist overnight stays in the first six months of this year than in the same period last year, according to the latest comparable Eurostat data. Index reports that this is one of the weakest results among Mediterranean tourist countries and the lowest growth among those that finished the first half of the year in positive territory. Looking at tourist accommodation in Croatia from January to the end of June this year, just under 26 million overnight stays were recorded, about 120 thousand more than a year earlier. Index reports that by comparison, at the level of the entire European Union, the number of overnight stays across Croatia rose by 1.7 percent.

albania, malta and slovenia grew several times faster

Among Mediterranean competitors Portugal had growth of 0.9 percent, Greece 1.4 percent, Spain 1.5 percent, Montenegro also 1.5 percent, and Italy 3.1 percent. Significantly stronger results were achieved by Slovenia, with growth of 5.7 percent, Albania with 9.1 percent and Malta with 9.9 percent. Two countries from that group were in negative territory: Bulgaria with a fall of 1.7 percent and Cyprus with a fall of 7.7 percent. As such, Croatia was at the bottom among the Mediterranean countries that achieved growth.

fewer overnight stays from foreign visitors

Even more interesting is the structure of the Croatian result. The number of overnight stays by domestic guests in the first six months rose by as much as 7.7 percent, while foreign tourists recorded 0.6 percent fewer overnight stays than last year. In neighbouring Italy, overnight stays by foreign tourists simultaneously rose by 4.4 percent, in Slovenia by 6.9 percent, in Malta by 11.7 percent, in Albania by 8.7 percent, and in Greece and Spain by 1.7 and 1.4 percent respectively. Domestic guests thus practically pulled the Croatian first-half result out of the red.

DZS data also shows just how quickly the situation changed during the pre-season. After the first five months Croatia had as much as 8.6 percent more commercial overnight stays than last year. But in June the number of overnight stays fell by 6.1 percent, and overnight stays by foreign tourists by as much as 7.5 percent. This brought the cumulative growth by the end of June down to only 0.5 percent.

july and august improved things, but the overall growth is still small

July brought a recovery. DZS recorded 25.3 million commercial overnight stays, 1.2 percent more than in July last year. In the first seven months growth was thereby raised to 0.8 percent, while overnight stays by foreign guests were only 0.2 percent above last year’s. Data for August also doesn’t show a major acceleration. According to the eVisitor system, which has a broader coverage than Eurostat’s commercial accommodation statistics, Croatia had 17.5 million arrivals and 90.5 million overnight stays in the first eight months. Both arrivals and overnight stays rose by around one percent. On the Adriatic alone the growth in overnight stays was 0.5 percent.

In August itself, 31.4 million overnight stays were recorded, only 0.5 percent more than last year. HTZ data also show differences among types of accommodation. In commercial accommodation by the end of August 78.6 million overnight stays were recorded, about 0.5 percent more than last year. Hotels had around 20 million overnight stays and growth of 2.7 percent, while almost 34 million overnight stays in household facilities were approximately at last year’s level.

croatia still clings onto july and august

The figures are particularly interesting in the context of the multi-year goal of extending the Croatian tourist season beyond July and August. Eurostat published that Croatia is the most seasonal tourist country in the entire EU. As much as 54.5 percent of all Croatian tourist overnight stays in 2025 were recorded only during July and August. The EU average was 31.1 percent, in Greece 41.6 percent, and in Bulgaria 43.4 percent. The difference between the main season and the rest of the year in Croatia is also the largest: last August as many as 41 times more overnight stays were recorded than in January. This means that Croatia, despite years of announcements about strengthening the pre-season and post-season, still depends significantly more than its competitors on two summer months.

europe is growing faster, and tourists are paying more and more attention to value for money

The broader European trend also shows that the weaker Croatian growth cannot be explained only by a general slowdown in tourist demand. The European Travel Commission in its July report states that international tourist arrivals in Europe this year grew by around five percent, and the number of overnight stays by 4.8 percent. At the same time it warns that travellers, due to weaker consumer confidence, are increasingly choosing destinations according to the price-quality ratio and are showing greater interest in travel outside the main season.

Price competitiveness was precisely one of the main topics of Croatian tourism before and during this season. Tourism Minister Tonči Glavina already at the beginning of the year warned that guests on the key German market are extremely sensitive to the price-quality ratio. The overnight stays statistics themselves, however, do not show why Croatia is growing more slowly than its competitors, so it cannot be concluded from those figures that prices are the only or main cause.

higher invoice values

On the other hand, physical traffic is not the only measure of the tourist season. The Ministry of Tourism states that in the first eight months €7.41 billion was fiscalised, 17.6 percent more than in the same period last year, while the number of invoices rose by 5.7 percent. According to the latest published HNB data for the first quarter, revenues from foreign tourists amounted to €945.2 million, 9.2 percent more than one year earlier.

World.title: Landlords in Split Rebel Over More Charges and Higher Costs
World.content:
September the 21st, 2026 – Landlords in Split have rebelled against more charges and higher costs, accusing the powers that be of choosing large hotels and resorts over local families.

The association Let’s Save Small Family Landlords (SMOi) has submitted an official statement to the City of Split on the proposal of the new Destination Management Plan. Morski reports that in the statement, they sharply criticise the expert basis prepared by the Institute for Tourism, claiming that without clear evidence and scientific arguments, it simply favours hotel chains and campsites, while private accommodation run by locals is unjustifiably pushed off the market by restrictions.

According to the disputed Plan proposal, an increase in the share of hotels and campsites of as much as 65 percent is envisaged, while private accommodation is presented in an extremely negative light – despite the fact that data from the document itself state that more than 85 percent of tourists are extremely satisfied with the quality of private accommodation.

the paradox of domestic demand

The Association points out an obvious paradox in the explanations of the public scientific institute. While the competent Ministry of Tourism and the Croatian Tourist Board emphasise the key importance of domestic tourists, the data of the Plan show that in Split in just one year arrivals of domestic guests in private accommodation grew by 30.5 percent, and their overnight stays by 20.9 percent. At the same time, overnight stays of domestic guests in hotels recorded a decline of 1.6 percent.

“What scientific criteria were used to conclude that the hotel segment should be strongly increased and private accommodation restricted? The Plan in no way proves a cause-and-effect link between private accommodation and problems in the city, nor does it analyse the consequences that these measures will have on the livelihood of citizens and the local economy,” stated Hana Matić, the vice-president of the SMOi association.

the income of local families is under threat

The association emphasises that these decisions do not only shape tourism statistics, but directly affect the standard of citizens. As many as 36.1 percent of respondents in the Plan stated that their families generate their main or additional income precisely from tourism. The restriction of family accommodation will also be felt by local craftsmen, caterers, shops and various service activities that indirectly live from small landlords. They particularly consider the thesis that private accommodation is to blame for the crisis of affordable housing to be contentious. They warn that the Plan itself mentions the potential for the construction of almost 15,000 new apartments, while on the other hand unused city and state properties are completely ignored.

“Institutional properties are being turned into hotels, student dormitories are being rented to tourists in summer, and private investments in hotels are being co-financed with public money. On the other hand, citizens’ private property is to be restricted. If one wants to manage the impact of tourism, the criteria must apply equally to everyone. A tourist bed cannot be a problem when it belongs to a citizen, and desirable when it belongs to a hotel,” emphasised Vedran Tomić, president of the SMOi association.

the mayor must now make the difficult choices

Small landlords emphasise that everything is now on Mayor Tomislav Šuta and the city authorities. Depending on whether they accept such a Plan, they will make a purely political decision – whether they will restrict the livelihood of their own citizens in order to open space for the growth of large hotel capital. Before any bans, the SMOi association demands from the Split city administration solid evidence, a detailed analysis of the economic consequences and equal treatment for all participants in tourism.

World.title: Croatian Prices Rise Once Again in August
World.content:
September the 20th, 2026 – Croatian prices rose once again this August, with restaurants, housing and fuel in particular all climbing up.

The prices of goods and services for personal consumption, measured by the consumer price index, in August 2026 compared to August 2025 (on an annual basis) were on average higher by 4.2%, while compared to July 2026 (on a monthly basis) they were on average higher by 0.4%.

Morski reports that when observed according to the main groups of the ECOICOP classification, ver. 2, on an annual basis, the largest increase in consumer prices on average was recorded in the groups Transport, by 13.5% (contribution to the increase of +1.88 percentage points), Housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels, by 10.8% (+1.62 percentage points), Restaurants and accommodation services, by 6.1% (+0.34 percentage points), Health, by 5.1% (+0.14 percentage points), Alcoholic beverages and tobacco, by 3.9% (+0.19 percentage points), Insurance services and financial services, by 3.6% (+0.07 percentage points), Personal care, social protection and miscellaneous goods and services, by 2.8% (+0.14 percentage points), Information and communication, by 2.7% (+0.16 percentage points), and Recreation, sport and culture, by 2.4% (+0.09 percentage points). The increase in prices on an annual basis was mitigated by a fall in prices in the groups Clothing and footwear, by 5.1% (contribution to the fall of -0.36 percentage points), Education services, by 2.0% (-0.01 percentage points), Food and non-alcoholic beverages, by 0.6% (-0.16 percentage points), and Furnishings, household equipment and routine household maintenance, by 0.3% (-0.02 percentage points).

According to the main components of the index (special aggregates), an increase in prices on an annual basis was recorded in the components Energy, by 17.6%, Services, by 7.2%, and Food, beverages and tobacco, by 0.1%, while a fall in prices is observed in the component Industrial non-food products excluding energy, by 1.3%. An increase in prices on a monthly basis was recorded in the components Energy, by 3.9%, and Services, by 0.1%, while a fall in prices appeared in the components Industrial non-food products excluding energy, by 0.9%, and Food, beverages and tobacco, by 0.2%.

The prices of goods and services for personal consumption, measured by the harmonised index of consumer prices, in August 2026 compared to August 2025 (on an annual basis) were on average higher by 3.7%. Compared to July 2026 (on a monthly basis) they were on average higher by 0.3%.

World.title: FlixBus Expands Network to 258 Destinations in Croatia
World.content:
September the 20th, 2026 – The popular coach service FlixBus has expanded its already enviable network to 258 destinations in Croatia.

Croatia is an important part of the Flix Europe East region, and Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe are among the areas with great potential for further development, says Michal Leman from Flix. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that a decade of FlixBus operations in Croatia has now officially been marked. The company began providing services back in 2016 in four Croatian cities and in cooperation with four bus partners, and today in the wider Flix network it has more than 258 connected destinations in Croatia and 390 cities across Europe.

Michal Leman, Vice President Europe East of Flix, emphasises that the anniversary is not only a look back. “Croatia is now entering a new chapter in which we want to further develop domestic and international connectivity, in cooperation with our local partners. Croatia is an important part of the Flix Europe East region, and Central, Eastern and Southeastern Europe are among the areas with great potential for further development.

We therefore see the future not only in new lines, but in even stronger partnerships, better connected markets and a greater number of opportunities for passengers,” Leman says. In the first ten years of operations, FlixBus in Croatia has transported 16.3 million passengers, and the growth of the network is best shown by the connectivity data: the number of direct connections to and from Croatia increased from 375 in 2016 to 4,471 in 2026.

The number of bus partners simultaneously rose from four to 15, while during 2026 FlixBus records an average of around 9,100 departures per month. Today a total of 128 lines operate from and to Croatia. Ten years of development has not meant only an increase in the number of lines and destinations, but above all growth in opportunities for passengers – from a greater choice of destinations and travel times to stronger linking of Croatian cities with neighbouring countries and the rest of Europe.

From the very beginning Croatia, was part of a wider story of regional connectivity. Only a year after entering the Croatian market, in 2017, FlixBus expanded to Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serbia and Slovenia, thereby laying the foundations for stronger connectivity of Central and Southeastern Europe. Flix sees particular potential in Southeastern Europe, where stronger domestic and international connectivity can further bring individual markets closer together, but also better connect them with the rest of the European network.

World.title: The Croatian Bell Tower That Offers Views into Three Countries
World.content:
September the 20th, 2026 – There’s a Croatian bell tower hidden away in an old Istrian town which, on clear days, offers spectacular views into three different countries.

A trip to the gorgeous old settlement of Buje is a perfect combination of history, untouched nature and excellent gastronomy, and nearby are the Momjan castle and the unusual Istrian desert of Piski. Putni kofer/Ivana Vasarevic writes that for all their abundant beauty, very few parts of Croatia look as fairy-tale-like as the interior of Istria. Astonishingly beautiful towns surrounded by untouched nature never cease to delight us, and one of them is certainly Buje. Situated on a fertile hill, in the firm embrace of centuries-old vineyards and olive groves, this Istrian gem was already inhabited in the Bronze Age and today has around 3,000 inhabitants. It is only 13 kilometres from the crystal-clear Adriatic Sea (Umag), and the Slovenian border is also very close.

the guardian of buje

Picchio4ever, Daniele Kovacic – Opera propria

Its ancient population once lived in a fortified hillfort, of which there are as many as about 20 remains in Buje and the surrounding area! A labyrinth of paved streets full of charm will take you to the core of the old town and Freedom Square, where the magnificent Church of St. Servulus and the 15th-century bell tower will greet you. From it, in fine weather, there is a fantastic view of as many as three neighbouring countries: Slovenia, Italy and Austria. This beautiful bell tower is one of the tallest in Istria, and given that it stands at 222 metres above sea level, it was once a lookout and watchtower, so it received the nicknames guardian of the town and watch of Istria. In addition, its image also adorned the town seal from the 13th century.

IT wAS FIRST MENTIONED IN DOCUMENTS AS EARLY AS 981 AS CASTRUM BUGLE

And there is also the bell tower that proudly stands next to the Church of Our Lady of Mercy (St. Mary of Mercy). It dates from the 17th century, is 22 metres high, is adorned with a clock, and at its base there is a characteristic passageway, opposite which is the ethnographic museum. At the same time, in the aforementioned church you can see the sculpture of Our Lady of Mercy, one of the most beautiful wooden statues in Istria. In the Iron Age, the wider area around Buje was inhabited by the Histri, the first documented people to settle on the Istrian peninsula, and the Romans also had their colonies in Terra Magica. In the Middle Ages a fortified medieval town developed, and it is first mentioned in documents, i.e. in a charter of the German-Roman Emperor Otto II, as early as 981 as Castrum Bugle.

THE MAGNIFICENT TOWER wAS ONCE PART OF THE VENETIAN WALLS

At the beginning of the 15th century the entire Buje area came under the rule of the Venetian Republic, and over the next four centuries the magnificent bell tower, the impressive Church of St. Servulus (the town’s patron saint) and the town loggia, which was located on Freedom Square, were built there. To this day, the Tower of St. Martin, which was part of the Venetian walls, has been preserved from that period. And after the fall of the once mighty Venetian empire in 1797, the French, the Austro-Hungarian Monarchy and the Kingdom of Italy successively ruled in Buje. After the end of the Second World War, the town and its surroundings ended up in the Free Territory of Trieste. Its status was settled only in 1954, when it was agreed that the northern part of the Territory, Trieste and the surroundings, would belong to Italy, and the southern part, including Buje, to the then Yugoslavia.

THE ETHNOGRAPHIC MUSEUM iS HOME TO AN OLIVE PROCESSING PLANT AND AN OLD BLACKSMITH’S WORKSHOP

If you find yourself in Buje, also take a look at the aforementioned ethnographic collection in the local museum, which preserves handicrafts of folk material culture from the entire Buje area. It is located in a magnificent four-storey building, and tools, furniture and everything that made up a typical old household, once oriented towards agriculture and ancient crafts, are exhibited in it. Down in the basement, you will find a blacksmith’s workshop and an old olive processing plant, i.e. a press, millstone and stone vessels with wooden lids in which olive oil was stored. Traditional Istrian cuisine and valuable pottery items are exhibited on the first floor, and the greatest attraction of this part of the museum is the hearth, the lifeblood of every Istrian household.

NEARBY LIE THE MEDIEVAL MOMJAN CASTLE AND THE ISTRIAN DESERT OF PISKI

The second and third floors are reserved for a loom and antique carved chests in which clothes and other personal items were kept. In addition to all of the above, the third floor is often used for occasional exhibitions of an ethnographic and historical character. Near Buje are also the picturesque settlement of Momjan with its imposing medieval castle above the Dragonja River and the Istrian desert of Piski, a unique natural phenomenon, i.e. marl dunes, one of the greatest attractions of northwestern Istria that really looks impressive.

tHE HOME OF BEER MISU!

Momjan – Fraxinus Croat

And after sightseeing this magical little town, it is time to explore the wine and olive oil roads of the Buje area. Enjoy the delicious Istrian cuisine and excellent wines, but also the excellent local beer that has been produced since 2013 at the San Servolo brewery in Buje. Only four ingredients are responsible for its perfect taste: barley malt, hops, yeast and natural water from the St. John spring, which is located in the valley of the Mirna River. In the pub you can also taste dishes such as beer soup or beer misu.

World.title: Croatian Military Special Forces Take 1st Place at FPV Drone Pilots Competition
World.content:
September the 20th, 2026 – Croatian military special forces have won 1st place at an international FPV drone pilots competition.

Members of the Croatian Special Forces Command of the Armed Forces recently won first place at the international military competition for FPV drone pilots in the TACTICAL category. Morski reports that this win means they have achieved an outstanding result in competition with international military teams.

The competition was held from the 13th to the 18th of September at the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst in the UK. Called the international military competition for FPV drone pilots “British Army Tactical Drone Competition – BADCT and Military International Drone Racing Tournament – MIDRT”, the Croatian team certainly wowed. Croatia was represented at the competition by members of the Special Forces Command of the Croatian Armed Forces who, thanks to an exceptional level of training, professionalism and teamwork, won first place in the TACTICAL category. Second place was taken by Ukraine, while Germany came third.

an extremely demanding competition

The competition brought together more than 80 competitors, members of the armed forces from several countries, and during the multi-day programme the participants demonstrated a high level of knowledge and skills in controlling FPV drones. In the first part of the competition, a contest in the tactical use of drones was held, which included an obstacle course, dropping a bomb with a drone and intercepting another aircraft in the air, in which the members of the Special Forces Command achieved an enviable result in an international military environment. The continuation of the competition included FPV drone races.

In addition to Croatia, Ukraine and Germany, representatives of Australia, Australian cadets, the United States of America, the United Kingdom, American veterans, New Zealand, Sweden and France also took part in the competition. This result represents significant recognition for the members of the Special Forces Command of the Croatian Armed Forces and confirms their knowledge, skills and ability to apply modern technology in a demanding international environment.

World.title: Estonian trade unions call for a labor court
World.content:
The Ministry of Economic Affairs wants to make the resolution of labor disputes by labor dispute committees more efficient. Trade unions, however, want Estonia to establish a separate labor court.

Those who do not want to go to court can instead initially turn to a labor dispute committee to resolve a workplace dispute. Last year, the committees received nearly 2,500 applications, most commonly because an employer had failed to pay the agreed wages.

The committees should operate as efficiently as possible, but the Ministry of Economic Affairs acknowledges that this is not always the case. A number of shortcomings and bottlenecks have emerged in recent years, which the ministry now wants to address.

Liis Tõnismaa, an adviser on employment relations and the working environment at the Ministry of Economic Affairs, said a number of situations arising in employment disputes, for example, are not currently regulated in sufficient detail.

"Labor dispute committee chairs often find themselves in situations where they don't actually know whether they are acting correctly or how they should proceed. That can cause proceedings to drag on," Tõnismaa said.

Proceedings can be delayed, for example, when an employer or employee fails to attend a hearing without good reason or does not respond to requests. To save the parties time, the ministry now wants to give labor dispute committees the right to issue default decisions in justified cases.

"At the moment, every procedural step has to be carried out from beginning to end. Even if the other party doesn't respond, you have to wait for them to do so. This can take a very long time and the labor dispute committee can't do anything in the meantime," Tõnismaa said.

The Estonian Trade Union Confederation supports allowing decisions to be made by default. Nelli Loomets, a lawyer for the confederation, noted that employees account for the majority of those who turn to labor dispute committees with their concerns.

"I can give one specific example where an employee filed an application with a labor dispute committee. The employer was informed of the hearing but didn't show up. Everything had been sent to the employer and they were aware of it, but they didn't come. In a case like that, the employee could get a decision more quickly and take it to a bailiff sooner," Loomets said.

However, trade unions would actually prefer Estonia to establish a separate labor court. In their view, this would allow similar disputes to be resolved much more quickly.

"If we had an independent labor court, its decision would be a court ruling. At the moment, if a labor dispute committee issues a decision and it is appealed in court, the proceedings start again from scratch. So we have four levels for resolving labor disputes: the labor dispute committee, district court, circuit court and Supreme Court. If we had a labor court ruling, the next stages would be the circuit court and the Supreme Court, giving us three levels of court," she explained.

ERR was unable to obtain a comment from the Estonian Employers' Confederation, but the organization said it believes the ministry's plan for resolving labor disputes is moving in the right direction.

World.title: Margus Tsahkna: Is the UN Charter a rule or merely a recommendation?
World.content:
Estonia will push for changes that would strengthen the UN's ability to uphold international law and respond to aggression, particularly Russia's war in Ukraine, at the upcoming UN High-level Week, writes Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna.

As the leaves begin to turn yellow in Estonia, the time is ripe for the world's annual fall gathering in New York. Estonia heads into the UN High-level Week with one clear question: If the UN Charter states that national borders cannot be changed by force, is that a rule or merely a recommendation?

I have just spent three days in Ukraine where Russia is flagrantly violating the principles of the UN Charter. Air raid alerts sounded day and night because of drone and missile attacks as Russia's aim is to use relentless aerial terror to sow fear, disrupt everyday life and break Ukrainian resistance.

If Russia succeeds and manages to change borders by force without facing consequences, the entire body of international rules on which Estonia's independence also rests will become fragile.

As a small country, we cannot afford a world in which international law applies only until a major power decides to trample over it. Estonia is therefore heading into the UN High-Level Week with two objectives: first, to make clear that supporting Ukraine is also in the interests of countries farther removed from the war and, second, to work with our partners to take concrete steps to more effectively uphold the rules enshrined in the UN Charter.

An aggressor must not be allowed to block decisions regarding it

First and foremost, we are looking to the UN Security Council where the UN's inability to defend its own Charter is most starkly apparent. Russia, a permanent member of the Security Council, is both the criminal and the cop: On the one hand, its war of conquest violates the UN's most fundamental principles, while on the other, its veto power allows it to prevent the UN from responding effectively to its own aggression.

Article 27, paragraph 3 of the UN Charter stipulates that a party to a dispute should abstain from voting on certain decisions. Yet, over more than four years of war, there has still not been sufficiently serious international debate about applying this principle.

Estonia wants to change how Article 27 is understood. Together with our partners, we want to establish an international practice under which a country that has launched an act of aggression could not use its veto power to block decisions concerning its own aggression under the framework of Chapter VI. This would be a concrete step toward making the Security Council more effective and restoring its credibility.

At the same time, we want the UN General Assembly, where all member states have equal representation, to assume greater responsibility for maintaining peace and security and to act in situations where the Security Council has been paralyzed by a veto.

Estonia and our partners want General Assembly resolutions to be more than mere political statements. They should help coordinate the actions of member states, increase pressure on the aggressor and keep violations of international law in the spotlight. The use or threat of a veto in the Security Council must not lead to a situation in which UN efforts to achieve a just and lasting peace in Ukraine are completely paralyzed.

In addition, we expect discussions surrounding the selection of the next UN secretary-general this fall to focus not only on who gets the job, but first and foremost on what kind of secretary-general today's world needs.

We need a secretary-general whose moral and political compass is the UN Charter and who is prepared to defend it even when doing so is inconvenient for a major power. The secretary-general cannot replace member states or the Security Council. But the secretary-general can use the office's political weight, shine a light on violations of the rules and consistently stand up for the principles the UN was created to defend in 1945.

Estonia, together with other like-minded countries, has worked for years to make the process of selecting the secretary-general more open and transparent and this year we are seeing tangible results from that work. Although there is still a long way to go, we have taken a step closer to ensuring that the choice is not made behind closed doors, but that candidates are nominated publicly and have the opportunity to present their vision for the role of secretary-general to all UN member states.

More countries must be mobilized in support of Ukraine

In addition to reforming the UN as an organization, High-level Week gives Estonia an opportunity to actively engage with countries with which we lack regular contact because we do not have embassies there. One of the most important goals of this engagement is to mobilize support for Ukraine.

There are still countries that view Russia's aggression as something distant. In reality, the effects of Russia's aggression extend to food and energy security and there is no doubt that if Russia succeeds in changing national borders in Ukraine, the stability of borders elsewhere will also be at risk and the security situation will become more dangerous worldwide.

But we must also remember everything that tends to become mere statistics amid the constant stream of news: that civilians, including children, are killed in Russian attacks every day, that many Ukrainians face a winter without heat, electricity or water and that Russia has separated approximately 20,000 children from their families and homeland and deported them to Russia.

Bringing the deported children home is one of Estonia's most important priorities and we are actively working with international partners to ensure that every child can return to their roots. Ukraine's reconstruction is also an area in which countries that, for various reasons, cannot provide military assistance, for example, can contribute to supporting Ukraine. UN High-level Week provides an opportunity to deepen international cooperation both on bringing deported children home and on preparations for the Ukraine reconstruction conference to be held in Estonia in January.

At the same time, UN High-level Week gives us an opportunity to listen more closely and engage with the challenges facing other countries. Countries in Africa, Latin America, Central Asia and other regions have their own security concerns, economic problems and expectations of the international system. We must identify shared interests and opportunities for cooperation with all of them. Only then can we ensure that others listen when we speak about the issues that matter most to us.

One issue that unites countries from the Baltic Sea to the Mediterranean and the Indian and Pacific oceans is maritime security, the threats posed by the shadow fleet and the protection of critical undersea infrastructure. Estonia will host a discussion on maritime security in New York, giving us an opportunity to deepen cooperation in this field with countries from different regions of the world.

This year, Estonia's chairmanship of the Nordic-Baltic Eight (NB8) cooperation format provides an additional opportunity to mobilize support for Ukraine and to discuss our own security. This is a group of countries that speaks with one voice on most major foreign and security policy issues. While that common voice already resonates strongly in Europe, as chair we are working to ensure that it is also heard farther afield, including during UN High-level Week in New York.

Rules need protecting

The UN stands at a crossroads today and every UN member state bears responsibility for choosing the organization's future direction.

Estonia wants a world in which the right of both large and small countries to exist independently is equally protected and a UN capable of defending internationally agreed rules. I believe that most UN member states ultimately want the same and that, together with our partners, we can bring about concrete change.

First, we must limit an aggressor's ability to use its veto power to shield its own actions. Second, we must strengthen the role of the UN General Assembly. Third, we must support international accountability and broaden the coalition of countries supporting Ukraine beyond Europe.

Because for Estonia, international law — and the UN, which was created to uphold it — is part of our security.

World.title: Tallinn Airport awards €67-million deal to double passenger capacity
World.content:
Tallinn Airport has awarded its terminal expansion contract to Tallinna Ehitustrust OÜ/Ehitustrust OÜ for nearly €66.6 million. Major work begins next year.

The expansion of Tallinn Airport's passenger terminal is one of the largest ever investments in Estonia's aviation infrastructure, aimed at boosting capacity and making it possible to serve up to five million passengers a year.

The original figure announced late last year had been €75 million.

Tallinn Airport CEO Riivo Tuvike said passenger numbers are growing and several areas of the passenger terminal have reached the limits of their capacity. The terminal was designed for 2.8 million passengers a year, but the airport is already serving nearly a million more than that.

"The expansion will provide more space, shorten waiting times and improve service while preserving the comfortable and homely travel experience characteristic of the airport," Tuvike told ERR.

Under the plan, construction will last 31 months and will be carried out while the airport remains operational, with both the passenger terminal and air traffic continuing to function. The full program runs from 2025 to 2029, with preparatory work this autumn and major construction inside the terminal from early 2027.

Kaido Somelar, chairman of the management boards of Tallinna Ehitustrust OÜ/Ehitustrust OÜ, which has the contract, said the companies will not only erect a new section of the terminal but also connect it to the existing building, while several existing areas will also be reconstructed.

"Between 2025 and 2029, approximately 16,500 square meters of new space will be added to the passenger terminal, while around 18,000 square meters of existing areas will be renovated," Somelar said.

As part of the expansion, a new section of the terminal will be built on the site of the present-day parking lot between the passenger terminal and the public transport terminal. It will include a baggage claim area for arriving passengers, new baggage carousels, shops and restaurants, and two boarding gates. To serve the new gates, the aircraft parking and servicing area next to the terminal will also be expanded.

The terminal's border control and gate areas will also be expanded to improve handling of non-Schengen flights and reduce queues at peak hours. Existing retail and dining areas will be renovated.

"The passenger terminal will remain open and air traffic will continue throughout the construction period, but passengers should expect temporary changes and some inconvenience," Tuvike added.

The historical terminal building, replaced by the current terminal ahead of the 1980 Olympics, was set for demolition in the original plans but met with pushback from the heritage board.

The Estonian state has also set new targets for Tallinn Airport: at least 60 regular destinations and five million passengers a year by 2030, up from around 3.5 million last year.

The nearby Ülemiste hub is set for a €500 million transformation, and the airport is close to the under-development Rail Baltica terminal.

The current airport terminal was built for the 1980 Moscow Olympics and later named after Lennart Meri, Estonia's first post-independence president; the site has hosted an airport since the interwar period.

World.title: Russians in Estonia cast State Duma election votes at Tallinn embassy
World.content:
Voting for Russia's State Duma elections went ahead at Russia's embassy in Tallinn over the weekend, permitting Russian citizens residing in Estonia to vote.

Some of those who turned out said taking part was still important, despite the lack of any real democratic choice and with one major liberal party banned in Russia from running.

"I don't trust the results, but I feel it is important not to lose the habit," said Anna, who voted. "I believe in some kind of better future. I don't want to think that I don't matter and that there is no point in voting. I want to keep that habit," she told "Aktuaalne kaamera."

"Let's put it this way: I knew exactly which parties I did not want to vote for, and I based my decision on that," said another voter, Nina. "Since I don't like the direction the country is currently heading in and it is causing difficulties for me personally, I did not vote for United Russia."

Of the alternatives on the ballot, the Communists were seen as an option by some voters in Tallinn.

Russian speakers and others were far from unified on the topic. A small protest was held opposite the embassy, whose participants called the elections illegal.

"While we were protesting here, several pensioners, Russian citizens, came up to us and said that we are fascists, that we are traitors, that Ukrainians are fascists too," said protester Daniil. "It is really interesting to see how many strongly pro-Russian people there still are in Estonia."

Yabloko, the only registered party openly critical of the war, was removed from the ballot by Russia's Supreme Court last month. Observers were turned away at polling stations, and Russia did not invite the OSCE, Europe's main election-monitoring body.

A total of 333 polling stations opened in 152 countries worldwide Sunday; in Tallinn, the embassy was the venue and Police and Border Guard Board (PPA) personnel were on hand to verify and document voter IDs.

"The checks are very strict. You know, of course we all understand the situation, but it is unpleasant. Unpleasant," said one Russian voter.

There were few surprises in the three-day elections, according to early indications, which showed Vladimir Putin's party, United Russia, virtually devoid of opposition. The voter franchise was around 111 million people, with results including those from the four occupied easternmost oblasts of Ukraine and illegally annexed Crimea.

While not a presidential election, the vote to the Duma — the Russian legislature — is widely seen as part of Putin's tightening grip on power at a time when the war in Ukraine is not going well for him.

Voting continued at some embassies and consulates in time zones further west, including in the US.

World.title: Estonia's defense agency takes Datasel dispute to Swiss arbitration
World.content:
The disputes are being heard under the rules of the International Chamber of Commerce (ICC), according to ERR's information. The RKIK has taken disputes over several contracts to international arbitration, with one joint contract dispute before Harju County Court — together worth a reported €59.8 million.

"Arbitration fees alone — the fees ultimately paid to the arbitrators and the arbitration institution for administering the proceedings — amount to hundreds of thousands," said lawyer Paul Keres, who is among the arbitrators representing Estonia at the ICC. Experts and lawyers' fees will add significantly more, he added, though the payoff is a faster and more specialized decision.

Keres said Swiss arbitration was a good choice. "Swiss arbitration is by no means a bad option: they are efficient and very good. I have been there myself, and everything is very well organized," he said.

Keres said taking disputes to arbitration is as yet not particularly common in Estonia.

Paul Keres. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"It is not as common as in some countries that have enjoyed democracy for longer. But there are more and more of these disputes, and they are becoming bigger and more interesting. Estonia is also gaining more representatives who know arbitration proceedings and are competent in the field. So I think we are moving in the right direction," Keres said.

Contracts often name the court in advance; without such a clause, cases go where the defendant is based. Datasel is incorporated in Italy, though its owners are Indian.

"What may cause confusion is who the owners are. If it is an SRL, I believe it is still an Italian company registered in Italy — by that logic, the case would have to be brought in Italy. But if it is an Indian company, you would have to go to India. I am glad for my colleagues that they do not have to deal with it. It is so confusing and fragmented, really very complicated," Keres said.

According to Keres, a case can end up in arbitration in two ways: "Firstly, it may have been agreed in advance — the contract contains a separate arbitration clause stipulating that the parties will resolve their dispute through arbitration. A proper arbitration agreement also specifies where the arbitration will take place, which institution will administer it, how many arbitrators there will be, and so on. Secondly, it is also possible to reach such agreements after a dispute has arisen. The contract may not provide for arbitration but, for example, for the jurisdiction of an ordinary court, yet the parties may decide that, for whatever reason, it would be more practical to resolve the dispute outside the courts, usually through arbitration," Keres explained, adding that an arbitrary award has the same legal force and is just as binding and enforceable as an ordinary court judgment.

RKIK signage. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"There are simply elements of speed and perhaps specialization that may persuade the parties that arbitration makes more sense," Keres said.

"Usually, the parties have greater control over the proceedings, starting with who adjudicates the case — they can choose the arbitrators themselves. The course of the proceedings is more under the parties' control, generally confidential and usually faster than national courts. In addition, some institutions that administer arbitration, such as the ICC, offer particularly strong supervision and intensive review of drafted awards," Keres said.

This review ensures the award is well reasoned, logical and free of errors, and cannot later be challenged even on the narrow grounds on which arbitrary awards may be contested.

Keres declined to speculate on the outcome: "It could turn out that the Estonian state has to pay additional money, or it could turn out that the advance payment is recovered. Both sides have filed claims: there is a claim and a counterclaim."

Background

Datasel, an Italian firm acquired in 2024 by Indian-owned Neco Defense Munitions, signed four contracts with RKIK to supply artillery shells for Ukraine with roughly €70 million paid up front, but delayed and substandard deliveries led the RKIK to terminate the agreements and pursue legal action; none of the ammunition reached Ukraine.

The RKIK has now rejected Datasel's proposal for a joint working group, saying the European Peace Facility funding period has expired and it has no budgetary resources to accept further ammunition, while Datasel's lawyer insists the company has the resources and supply chain to fulfill its obligations — the two sides also remain at odds over whether the terminations were valid.

The fallout contributed to Defense Minister Hanno Pevkur's resignation on September 2, alongside wider accounting and oversight problems at the Defense Forces.

Auditor General Janar Holm said the defense scandals pose no security threat and that open discussion makes Estonia stronger, but warned several problems are systemic and money flowing into the sector is increasing confusion.

World.title: Giant pumpkin, 14kg cabbage draw 20,000 to Paunvere fair
World.content:
A 53-kilogram pumpkin and a cabbage weighing 14 kilograms were among the attractions as the Paunvere exhibition, in Jõgeva County over the weekend.

The fair, held for the 27th time, showcased giant and unusual vegetables, while growers reported a mixed year shaped by weather and cheap imports. and fair drew 20,000 people to Palamuse, population around 550.

The most interesting exhibits were the unusual, strange or giant vegetables. The 53-kilogram giant pumpkin was on display at the Palamuse cuteness contest. According to its owner, growing a winter squash of these proportions requires not only rich soil but also a lot of love.

"You still have to go and pet it, water it. It won't grow weeds, because the pumpkin is so big. But especially cabbage, because cabbage worms are so industrious," said Toomas Puusepp, cultivator of the giant pumpkin.

His giant fruits — a 53-kilogram and a 42-kilogram pumpkin and a 14-kilogram cabbage — arrived at the exhibition on a lawn tractor. The oversized produce found new homes at the fair's auction.

While some real giants could be seen in the "cute tent" (Nunnutelk), this year's vegetable harvest offered mixed feelings for gardeners.

"You can't complain. Compared to last year, we had quite a harvest this year. Everything grew. I could complain about today's sale, there aren't as many people as there have been in previous years," said vegetable grower Tatjana.

However, cool and rainy spring weather almost completely ruined the open-field cucumber and tomato harvest, while the marketing of domestic vegetables is being made more difficult by cheaper imported goods.

"The year was not very productive. There are half as many cucumbers as last year. While we used to pick 300 kilos of cucumbers in the spring, now we only take a total of 300 kilos to Tartu stores. Previously, we took 300 kilos to one store and 300 kilos to another," said vegetable grower Igor.

Meanwhile, a more exotic fruit managed to defy the local cold. Southern Estonian watermelon grower Raimo harvested a whopping four tons of watermelon.

"We grow them in the open field, so that we have them under plastic and in the spring you bury them beautifully with a covering and keep them warm and under a blanket like you would yourself, and that's how they grow," he said.

The Paunvere exhibition was held for the 27th time.

World.title: Attempted kidnapping in Tallinn of Australian tech billionaire was hatched in Moscow
World.content:
A 2024 plan to kidnap Australian-born IT billionaire in Tallinn's Old Town was hatched in Moscow, Eesti Ekspress reported .

In july 2024 men were sent to Estonia to abduct Yolo Group founder Tim Heath as he entered his home on Rataskaevu, posing as painters to attack him in the stairwell.

The gang intended to force him into a van and drive him to a rented sauna house near Kakerdaja bog, around 60 kilometers from Tallinn, where they would have demanded the keys to his cryptocurrency wallet.

Heath resisted forcefully, something which caught the assailants by surprise, and they fled without him; first to Riga and then further afield.

On Thursday, Harju County Court convicted Oleg Marco, one of the attackers, after he agreed to a seven-year prison sentence under a plea bargain.

Marco, from Moldova, was brought from prison to the hearing wearing a T-shirt reading the slogan "Never give up."

His accomplices had already been convicted: Azerbaijani Allahverdi Allahverdiyev received seven and a half years, and Georgian citizen Ilgar Mamedov eight years and nine months.

The fourth member of the gang, Azerbaijani Najaf Najafli, led the kidnapping attempt but will not stand trial in Estonia as Azerbaijan does not extradite its citizens.

Questioned by Azerbaijani authorities, Najafli said he became involved because of debts, was deployed to Tallinn by a Chechen figure in Moscow's criminal underworld, and while he realized something was not right, he was in too deep to refuse.

The gang had reportedly used well-known platforms to rent accommodation and transport, making tracking them down easier.

Heath, 48, arrived in Estonia in the early 2000s, built the IT company Yolo Group from scratch, and has been estimated by Australian business media to be worth €1.4 billion

World.title: International interest mounts in Estonian scientists' drug-detection meter
World.content:
Researchers in Estonia have developed a portable drug analyzer that can identify both the substance taken and the amount, returning results in as little as 15 minutes.

Developers at Tallinn University of Technology (TalTech) and startup SafePAS say the "Narcometer" device has drawn international interest, and they now aim to make it smaller and drug detection as easy as a breathalyzer test.

When police or ambulance crews need to determine possible drug intoxication at the scene, they currently rely primarily on rapid tests, but whose accuracy often leaves much to be desired. To determine the exact substance present in a sample and its quantity, positive samples need to be sent to the lab for further testing. However, it can sometimes take days to receive those lab results.

If police can find time for additional testing as part of investigative procedures, every minute counts when assessing a person's medical condition. This is particularly important with substances that break down rapidly in the body, for example GHB, commonly known as a date-rape drug.

TalTech researchers and the startup SafePAS have for more than a decade now been developing an analytical device with the English name Drug Hunter, whose aim is to take accurate and rapid drug testing beyond the laboratory. The researchers' analyzer can identify both a narcotic substance and its quantity in just about 15 minutes.

Up to now now, the tech has been tested in close cooperation with the Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), but this summer the team also worked with organizers of major events, such as festivals. According to Jekaterina Mazina-Šinkar, an assistant professor at TalTech and the SafePAS founder, the aim was to understand how the device could be used by private individuals themselves. "A saliva test can be carried out on people who, for example, suspect that a narcotic substance has been put into their cocktail. Or someone may have taken something and feel very unwell but not know what it was," the researcher explained.

SafePAS co-founder Jelena Gorbatšova and older and newer versions of Drug Hunter. Source: Jekaterina Mazina-Šinkar

An ever-changing black market

The device uses capillary electrophoresis technology, which is also used to analyze DNA. "This is a very sensitive method in which we first separate all the substances present in the sample, excite them and detect them with a detector. We then not only identify the substance but also quantify it," Mazina-Šinkar, said, describing how the device works. Positive samples will always undergo additional testing under laboratory conditions too, she noted.

Drug Hunter can at present detect common narcotic substances such as cocaine, amphetamine, methamphetamine and MDMA (ecstasy). The device can also identify tramadol, codeine and morphine, as well as THC.

However, the prevalence of narcotic substances varies considerably by time and place, meaning researchers must constantly keep up with developments on the illicit drugs market. "Research is underway into new narcotic substances, their metabolism and how they can subsequently be detected in the human body. At the same time, so-called classic drugs account for 97 percent of all cases of use, while only three percent involve new narcotic substances," Mazina-Šinkar noted.

The Drug Hunter device tested at festivals and in the course of traffic enforcement is about the size of a computer printer. A year ago, however, the development team received €2.5 million in funding from the Estonian Business and Innovation Agency (EIS) to make the device more compact. The next-generation model, which was tested for the first time in August this year, is already down to about the size of a shoebox.

"The biggest challenge is not simply making the device smaller, but ensuring the reliability of the final result. We tested not only the technology, which we already know works, but also the analyzer's ease of use. We looked for aspects that could be further improved or simplified," Mazina-Šinkar went on.

The next generation Drug Hunter device is considerably smaller than its predecessor. Source: Jekaterina Mazina-Šinkar

From lab to international market

The TalTech researchers say their next goal is to render drug detection as simple and reliable as using a conventional alcohol breathalyzer is today. "Technologically, we are already quite close to that, but a distinction has to be made between the technology itself and its official adoption," the researcher said, stressing the role of legislation.

She also noted that greater complexity lies behind even the humble breathalyzer.

"When we think of a breathalyzer, it seems a very simple thing to us today: a person blows into it, the device displays a number and a decision can be made based on that. In reality, this is backed by decades of scientific knowledge and established threshold values. With narcotic substances, it is even more complex because there are different substances with different effects, metabolism and concentrations," she added

All this means that when entering foreign markets, the device's parameters must be adapted precisely to local laws and threshold values in force in the target country. There is, in any case, undoubtedly international demand for fast and reliable analysis. Over the past year, SafePAS has shared its experience with police in England, forensic experts in Germany, and experts in Spain and the Czech Republic. According to Mazina-Šinkar, bringing a research-intensive device out of the lab and into practical use has provided important lessons. "A good scientific result is not yet a finished product," she said, summing up more than a decade of development work. While researchers always seek maximum sensitivity and accuracy, end users are primarily concerned with maintenance, speed of analysis and reliability, she noted.

"Our goal is not simply to bring out yet another rapid test," Mazina-Šinkar stressed. "Our goal is to bring reliable instrumental measurement out of the laboratory and directly to where decisions need to be made."

World.title: Iraq Oil Ministry clarifies September crude exports average 2.6M bpd
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s Ministry of Oil clarified on Monday, September 21, 2026, that the country’s daily crude export average for September stands at approximately 2.6 million barrels per day, refuting recent media reports suggesting that export volumes had surged to 4 million barrels per day.

In an official statement received by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the ministry explained that the four-million-barrel figure was an exceptional single-day peak rather than a sustainable daily benchmark, resulting from a confluence of scheduled tanker loadings occurring simultaneously.

The ministry noted that the isolated spike occurred when the State Organization for Marketing of Oil (SOMO) executed an offshore lift outside the Strait of Hormuz carrying Qayyarah heavy crude, coinciding with scheduled vessel liftings from southern maritime export terminals and northern outlet shipments aggregated into commercially viable tanker parcels.

Officials emphasized that daily tanker movements naturally fluctuate based on maritime loading schedules, vessel laycans, and parcel batching, which can periodically create transient volumetric spikes that do not reflect normalized monthly baselines.

The Oil Ministry underlined that maintaining an average export rate of roughly 2.6 million barrels per day through late September represents a major operational achievement under prevailing geopolitical and logistics headwinds, most notably the continued closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Authorities reiterated that energy logistics teams remain focused on sustaining export continuity through diversified operational corridors, aiming to maximize petroleum sales and secure vital foreign exchange revenues for the federal treasury amid tight liquidity constraints.

World.title: Jameel Motors enters Iraq with new OMODA & JAECOO showroom in Erbil
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Jameel Motors has officially joined the Iraqi automobile industry by opening a new OMODA & JAECOO showroom in Erbil.

The new store will serve OMODA and JAECOO consumers as Jameel Motors establishes a foothold in Iraq, a market recognized as critical to the company’s regional expansion strategy.

Jameel Motors, part of the international mobility sector brand of Saudi Arabia’s Abdul Latif Jameel, stated that it hopes to build a long-term presence in Iraq, with plans that go beyond car sales to include local alliances, customer service, and more investment in the country’s automotive industry.

The company also hinted that other brands and showrooms may follow as it increases its Iraqi business and the variety of automobiles offered to local purchasers.

Jameel Motors executives also met with Mohammed Shukri, Chairman of the Kurdistan Regional Government Board of Investment, to explore investment prospects and the economic climate in the Kurdistan Region.

Yousef Hussein, CEO of Jameel Motors’ Middle East and Levant division, KRG Minister of State for Component Affairs Aydin Maruf Selim, Erbil Chamber of Commerce Vise President Kamaran Salah Bajger, dealers, and other industry officials attended the event.

As competition in Iraq’s automobile industry heats up, Jameel Motors has partnered with OMODA and JAECOO, two Chinese automotive firms extending their worldwide reach.

The Erbil showroom represents the first step of Jameel Motors’ growth in Iraq, with the business contemplating more investments as it expands its local dealer and customer network.

World.title: Iraq-Kuwait security cooperation seizes of 700,000 Captagon pills
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Security cooperation between Iraq and Kuwait has resulted in the recovery of 700,000 Captagon tablets, as the neighboring nations ratchet up efforts to fight cross-border drug trafficking.

Kuwait’s Interior Ministry stated on Sunday that the operation was carried out in conjunction with Iraqi officials and resulted in the arrest of two individuals at livestock farms in Kuwait’s Kabd region.

The suspects, one an Arab citizen and the other designated by Kuwaiti officials as an unlawful resident, were discovered with a significant consignment of Captagon tablets, the ministry said.

Authorities claimed the two confirmed after interrogation that the narcotics were theirs and had been prepared for trafficking. They were submitted to appropriate authorities for future legal action.

The operation demonstrates growing security coordination between Baghdad and Kuwait City on narcotics trafficking, which has become a growing concern for Iraq as authorities seek to disrupt regional smuggling networks and prevent the country from being used as a transit route for illegal drugs.

Iraq has increased its anti-narcotics activities recently, including collaboration with neighboring nations to share information and pursue transnational trafficking networks.

Kuwait’s Interior Ministry said that the recent seizure proved the significance of international security cooperation in identifying traffickers, halting their activities, and curbing the transportation of drugs throughout the region.

World.title: Iraq joins Trump-GCC talks in New York focused on Iran
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraq will participate in high-level meetings between US President Donald Trump and Arab leaders in New York this week, placing Baghdad at the center of regional debates over Iran, armed groups, and the future of the Middle East war.

The conference will take place on the fringes of the United Nations General Assembly, and officials from Gulf nations, Iraq, and Jordan are likely to attend, according to The National.

Egypt is also scheduled to participate.

The negotiations take place at a very difficult time for Iraq.

The US-led coalition will conclude its military operation in Iraq on September 30, marking a significant shift in Baghdad’s security relationship with Washington.

The future of strong Iran-aligned Iraqi militias is also anticipated to play a significant role.

Prime Minister Ali Falih Al-Zaidi has been working to put weaponry under state control, although numerous powerful forces have opposed disarmament.

The problem has grown more pressing as drones fired from Iraqi territory recently targeted Saudi Arabia, putting further pressure on Baghdad to prevent armed organizations from pulling Iraq into the larger conflict between Iran and its regional enemies.

Trump’s meetings with Arab leaders are anticipated to be mainly focused on the battle with Iran and Tehran’s regional network, which includes the Houthis in Yemen, whose recent strikes on Saudi Arabia have further destabilized the region.

Trump has said that he is reaching a key decision on the course of the Iran issue and is seeking feedback from regional states.

Al-Zaidi is traveling to New York to address the UN General Assembly and meet with Trump as Iraq aims to redefine its relationship with Washington around investment and economic cooperation in the aftermath of the coalition pullout.

The meeting follows Al-Zaidi’s visit to the United States earlier this year, during which Baghdad inked substantial deals with American corporations and encouraged investment in Iraq’s energy, infrastructure, technology, and other areas.

The New York meetings come as Baghdad seeks to keep Iraq out of the escalating regional conflict while shifting its relationship with the United States from military cooperation to longer-term economic ties.

World.title: Asia stocks rise on AI, US-China trade talks optimism
World.content:
Hong Kong – Asian stock markets mostly rose on Monday morning, boosted by global demand for artificial intelligence technology and positive signals from trade talks over the weekend between Chinese and US officials.

Global stocks had finished last week mixed as central banks made moves to curb inflation, including the US Federal Reserve’s decision on Wednesday to lift interest rates.

US and Chinese economic officials met on Sunday for closely watched talks on trade and AI, ahead of a planned summit on Thursday with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said that following lengthy conversations, the two countries had discussed setting up a channel to communicate about AI issues called the “US-China AI dialogue”.

Chinese state media described the talks as “candid, in-depth and constructive”.

Hong Kong’s main index was up half a percent one hour after trading started on Monday morning.

South Korea’s tech-heavy benchmark surged 1.5 percent, while shares in Shanghai gained 0.5 percent.

Tokyo was closed for a public holiday, while Sydney’s main index was down slightly.

“Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng have already laid the groundwork (for the Trump-Xi meeting) in New York, with trade, investment and artificial intelligence on the table, but this is not a market waiting for a grand bargain,” wrote Stephen Innes at Quintex Intel.

“It is waiting to see whether both sides can keep the next trade grenade in the drawer,” he added.

Pressure has increased on monetary authorities around the world in recent months as oil prices remain elevated due to the war between the United States and Iran, which shows little sign of ending anytime soon.

In a widely expected move, the Bank of Japan raised interest rates on Friday to a three-decade high, but the yen sank against the dollar on fears the pace of hikes might be slower than expected.

That followed earlier tightening this month by the European Central Bank and the US Federal Reserve.

Oil prices fell on Monday morning, adding to Friday’s declines on hopes that Saudi Arabia was moving to restore about half of crude shipments within days after they were disrupted by the stoppage of its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea.

But both major crude contracts remain around $100 a barrel, significantly higher than pre-war levels.
