World.title: Powerful Typhoon Dujuan zeroes in on Tokyo area
World.content:
Typhoon Dujuan brought heavy rains to the Izu Islands and the Kanto region on Monday, with advisories and evacuation orders issued for some areas as Japan marks its Silver Week holidays.

The Japan Meteorological Agency urged residents in the Izu Islands and Kanto, as well as Pacific coastal areas of Tokai and Tohoku, to remain on high alert for landslides and violent winds, as well as flooding in low-lying areas, swollen or overflowing rivers and high waves.

One person in Miyazaki Prefecture was confirmed dead as a result of the typhoon, and another sustained minor injuries, according to a report released Monday afternoon by the Fire and Disaster Management Agency.

Northern parts of the Izu island chain received a Level 5 landslide warning, while other areas in the Kanto region received Level 4 warnings for heavy rain, landslides and flooding.

At a news conference Monday afternoon, Takuya Hosomi, director of the weather agency’s forecasting division, warned that “in areas corresponding to Level 4, a major disaster could occur at any time,” and urged those in affected areas to check the level of disaster risk in their current location and carefully review the evacuation information issued by local municipalities.

People in urban areas are advised to remain on the alert for flooded roads and to avoid underground facilities where water could accumulate and vehicles could become trapped.

The powerful typhoon’s arrival has coincided with Silver Week, which runs through Wednesday, with the storm likely to disrupt transport networks and wreak havoc on cultural events.

As of 3:45 p.m. Monday, the year’s 25th named storm was located about 60 kilometers southeast of Miyakejima in the Izu island chain, moving northeast at 30 kph. It had an atmospheric pressure of 960 hectopascals at its center, with maximum sustained winds of 40 meters per second and maximum gusts of up to 55 meters per second.

In the 24 hours through 3:50 p.m. Monday, 657.5 millimeters of rainfall was recorded in Izu Oshima in the Izu chain, while the Sakahata area of the city of Kimitsu, Chiba Prefecture, saw 301 mm of rain, according to the weather agency.

In the subsequent 24 hours through 12 p.m. Tuesday, rainfall could reach up to 250 mm in the Tokai and Kanto regions and in the Izu Islands, while Tohoku could see 150 mm, the agency said.

The Tokyo Game Show, which began Thursday, announced the cancellation of Monday’s program, shortening the five-day video game extravaganza by a day.

The storm also saw Japan Airlines cancel 120 domestic flights and All Nippon Airlines cancel 140 flights, according to NHK.

East Japan Railway announced partial and full-day suspensions of operations on some lines in Chiba and Ibaraki Prefectures as well as western Tokyo on Monday.

World.title: A century on, search continues for Nagoya’s missing ‘blue-eyed dolls’
World.content:
Next year will mark a century since Japan and the United States exchanged dolls under a project aimed at improving relations that had deteriorated at the time.

Through the efforts of American missionary Sidney Lewis Gulick and Japanese industrialist Eiichi Shibusawa, about 12,000 American dolls were sent to Japan in 1927 as tokens of friendship, while Japan reciprocated by sending 58 traditional Japanese dolls to the United States the same year.

The exchange took place amid worsening relations between the two countries following the passage of a revised U.S. Immigration Act in 1924, which effectively barred immigration from Japan.

World.title: Ukrainians are bracing for worst wartime winter of airstrikes
World.content:
Ukrainians are already drawing up contingency plans for what threatens to be the worst wartime winter yet.

Under near-constant attack since Russia’s invasion of February 2022, residents are well-versed in getting through cold periods during airstrikes and regular blackouts. But last winter’s prolonged subzero temperatures brought a new level of hardship as a result of weekslong disruptions to heating, water and sewage services in major cities including Kyiv.

With the trauma of that experience still fresh, coupled with Russia’s increasingly sophisticated drones and a critical shortage of interceptors, many are bracing for what’s to come. Some are considering relocating or even moving abroad. Others are stocking up on firewood or buying equipment and clothing to help cope.

World.title: Five takeaways from Germany’s regional elections
World.content:
Elections in two German states on Sunday resulted in severe losses for the country’s leading Christian Democrats, whose Chancellor Friedrich Merz is facing pressure to keep the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party at bay.

Here are five takeaways from regional elections in the northeastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Germany’s capital, Berlin.

The results mark a major setback for Merz and his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) party, whose voters have flocked to the AfD, increasingly doubtful the 70-year-old can revive Germany’s economy and bring down the cost of living.

World.title: Japan raises the bar on residency. Cue the outrage.
World.content:
From the U.S. green card to the U.K.’s “indefinite leave to remain,” permanent residency in a country that’s not your own can be a prickly issue. Japan is now getting choosier about who gets to stay for good.

Under Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, the country has tightened various rules around immigration, including higher renewal fees for visas and stricter enforcement of overstayers. The latest proposal is to raise the bar on permanent residency, adding requirements for minimum salary and Japanese language ability.

Critics, and some residents, are up in arms at the suggested changes. The Asahi Daily deemed them “a revision that will doom the dreams and enthusiasm of foreigners.” Some liken the moves to anti-immigration crackdowns taken by the Trump administration and other right-wing governments. “Japan should not shut the door on permanent residents,” said the Mainichi.

World.title: Three South Korean soldiers injured in DMZ blast
World.content:
Three South Korean military officers were injured in an explosion during an operation near the heavily mined border with North Korea, Seoul’s military said Monday.

The incident occurred south of the Military Demarcation Line (MDL) inside the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ), one of the world’s most heavily fortified and mined frontiers.

Two of the injured officers were evacuated by helicopter, while a third was due to be transported by road before being airlifted, the Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) said.

It was not immediately clear whether the explosion was caused by a North Korean mine, a South Korean mine or another explosive device.

The three officers “were injured by an explosion of unknown cause while conducting an operation at a location south of the MDL,” the JCS said in a statement.

The military did not immediately provide details on the severity of their injuries.

The DMZ is a 248-kilometer-long and roughly 4-km-wide buffer zone that has divided the Korean Peninsula since the 1953 armistice that halted the Korean War.

While the zone itself is officially demilitarized, its northern and southern boundaries are among the world’s most heavily fortified frontiers and remain littered with landmines.

Around 800,000 mines are estimated to be buried around the area, according to military data cited by Yonhap news agency, many dating to the Korean War although mine-laying has continued in recent years.

Since 2024, after North Korean leader Kim Jong Un designated South Korea as his country’s “principal enemy,” Pyongyang’s military has laid mines and built anti-tank barriers along the border as part of efforts to permanently seal off the frontier.

South Korea’s military has previously said several North Korean soldiers were killed or wounded in accidental mine explosions during those works.

Landmine incidents have previously heightened tensions between the two Koreas.

In 2015, two South Korean soldiers were seriously wounded when a landmine exploded on the southern side of the DMZ, with one losing both legs.

Seoul concluded that North Korean troops had crossed the MDL to plant the mines, an accusation Pyongyang denied.

The incident prompted South Korea to resume anti-North Korea loudspeaker broadcasts along the border.

The latest incident comes as South Korean President Lee Jae Myung has repeatedly called for unconditional dialogue with the North, overtures that have so far gone unanswered by Pyongyang.

World.title: Trump gets caught in a dilemma over a Saudi plea for military help
World.content:
For two weeks, the question of whether to yield to pleas from Saudi Arabia and order the U.S. military to strike targets in Yemen controlled by the Iran-backed Houthis has bedeviled President Donald Trump.

A decision to go forward could open another front in the war against Iran that Trump started but has been unable to end as it spreads economic shock around the globe.

The president had wavered for weeks over the Saudi appeals for help in fighting the Houthis, who took advantage of the instability in the Middle East and reignited their war with the kingdom this summer.

World.title: Elderly warned of accidents involving nursing beds, wheelchairs
World.content:
Ahead of Respect for the Aged Day in Japan on Monday, the National Institute of Technology and Evaluation warned of accidents involving nursing beds or wheelchairs and urged elderly people to review proper usage with their families and care workers.

According to NITE, there were 43 nursing bed accidents affecting elderly people between 2016 and 2025, including 23 cases in which users’ bodies were caught in handrail and other gaps.

There were 23 fatal accidents. In June 2022, a woman in her 80s died in Shizuoka Prefecture after her neck was trapped between a bed’s handrail and its mattress.

NITE calls for checking the year of manufacture to prevent accidents involving such beds. In 2009, safety standards were revised to narrow handrail gaps to reduce the risk of slipping into them.

During the same 10-year period, there were 59 wheelchair accidents involving elderly people, including 26 cases in which users fell into roadside ditches and rivers. Among 34 fatal cases, a man in his 80s fell into a waterway and died in Ehime Prefecture in April 2024.

About 75% of the wheelchair accidents were caused by misuse or carelessness, according to NITE. It calls for identifying dangerous places, such as railway crossings and side ditches, and also repeating practices to learn how to use wheelchairs properly.

Other types of accidents involving elderly people include cases in which they mistakenly drink detergent due to cognitive decline or get burned while cooking due to impaired vision. NITE also warns against using deteriorated canes.

“We want people to check safety measures for familiar products so that elderly people can live safely,” said a NITE official.

World.title: Hong Kong Ballet to move to city’s first dedicated dance venue in 2027
World.content:
Hong Kong Ballet will relocate to the city’s first dedicated dance art venue for at least five years, starting in April 2027, according to the institution and the West Kowloon Cultural District (WKCD)

The move to the “Dancehouse” at the soon-to-be-finished WestK Performing Arts Centre will follow the ballet company’s departure from its base of 16 years at the government-run Cultural Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui.

An announcement last December that the city’s flagship ballet company would be departing the Cultural Centre prompted concerns that the group would be left without an appropriate venue.

In an interview with the South China Morning Post ahead of the announcement, Hong Kong Ballet artistic director Septime Webre expressed relief at being able to finally reveal the news of the move. The move is expected to take place in April next year.

World.title: Once the world’s most-visited city, Hong Kong now converts hotels into student dorms
World.content:
Late last month, an open tender for Hotel Cozi Harbour View in Kwun Tong was announced, with interested parties given until October 15 to submit bids.

The 598-room hotel, located in Hong Kong’s eastern Kowloon Peninsula, a former industrial area, was taken over by Nanyang Commercial Bank for HK$1.87 billion (US$238.4 million) in 2025, with the bank now looking to dispose of the asset to the highest bidder.

Just a week after the announcement of the tender, Nina Hospitality, one of the largest hotel operators in Hong Kong, unveiled the completion of the HK$120 million (US$15.3 million) renovation at Nina Hotel Island South.

The refurbishment transformed the hotel’s lobby and guestrooms and launched both balcony suites and family rooms.

World.title: Over 11,000 applicants for new Hong Kong taxi, ride-hailing test
World.content:
More than 11,000 residents have applied to take the joint examination for taxi and ride-hailing car driver permits, exceeding the Hong Kong government’s expectations, the city’s transport minister has said.

Secretary for Transport and Logistics Mable Chan also gave more details on Monday about a separate scheme that would allow mainland Chinese yacht owners to sail their vessels into city waters, saying they had achieved a good passing rate for the relevant test.

Hong Kong recently passed legislation to regulate ride-hailing services in the city, capping the number of vehicle permits for such services at 10,000.

World.title: Hong Kong to review stray dog handling policies after woman dies in suspected attack
World.content:
Hong Kong’s environment chief has vowed to review stray dog handling policies following a cyclist’s death in a suspected canine attack in Yuen Long, months after shelters warned of pets being abandoned in the New Territories amid land resumption operations.

Secretary for Environment and Ecology Tse Chin-wan made the promise on Monday morning, hours after the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department (AFCD) , which operates under his bureau, said it had worked with police to capture three stray mongrels near Pok Wai South Road on Sunday evening.

The capture operation followed the death of a 27-year-old woman along the same road on Saturday after she was chased by dogs.

The victim suffered lacerations to her head, face, neck, arms and legs, with the wounds to her head and neck believed to have been fatal. Aside from stray dogs, officers also spotted wild boars in the area.

World.title: Nearly 50% rise in drug seizures by Hong Kong customs in first half of year
World.content:
Hong Kong customs recorded a nearly 50 per cent year-on-year rise in drug seizures during the first half of 2026, driven by notable increases in smuggling activities via air and sea routes.

The Customs and Excise Department confiscated 5,704kg (12,575lbs) of illegal narcotics in the first half, a 49 per cent increase year on year, according to figures seen by the South China Morning Post.

Nearly two-thirds of the seized narcotics, or 3,408kg, were found at the airport, a 46.6 per cent year-on-year increase at that port of entry. Those on sea routes accounted for one-third, or 1,954kg, representing a 55.6 per cent rise. The remaining 342kg were confiscated at land checkpoints and other parts of the city.

Cannabis and ketamine accounted for about 60 per cent of the drugs seized in the first six months, marking a rise of 40 per cent and 78.8 per cent of those substances, respectively. The number of drug cases detected by customs and the number of arrestees also recorded a slight increase.

World.title: Barristers dismiss calls for solicitors to gain senior counsel status in Hong Kong
World.content:
The professional body for Hong Kong barristers has dismissed as “premature and largely academic” calls by solicitors for legal changes so fellow lawyers can gain recognition as senior counsel and rights to represent clients in higher-level courts.

The Law Society, the governing body for the city’s solicitors, is calling for the higher status for its members as lawmakers scrutinise the latest round of omnibus legislative updates in Hong Kong.

But the Bar Association, the body for barristers, questioned the need for such changes, noting that the city had about 100 solicitor advocates with such representation rights, but most of them had not exercised the privilege in the past two years.

“A review of judgments handed down from the beginning of 2024 to the end of 2025 shows that the number of judgments where a solicitor advocate has exercised higher rights of audience in open court as lead or sole advocate is fewer than 15 cases,” the association said.

World.title: ‘His love for Hong Kong was profound’: Tung Chee-hwa honoured at state funeral
World.content:
Chinese President Xi Jinping and other top leaders sent condolences from Beijing as Hong Kong bade farewell to the city’s first postcolonial leader, Tung Chee-hwa, at a sombre yet poignant state funeral on Sunday.

A report by the official Xinhua News Agency praised Tung, who died on September 8 at the age of 89, as “an outstanding contributor to ‘one country, two systems’, a renowned patriot, an outstanding social activist and a close friend of” the Communist Party of China.

“While Tung was critically ill, the central authorities expressed deep concern over his condition,” it said. “Xi Jinping and other central leaders instructed the [liaison office in Hong Kong] to convey best wishes and demanded all-out efforts to treat Tung.”

Xinhua also reported that following Tung’s death, Xi, Premier Li Qiang and other members of the leadership “expressed their deep grief in various forms and extended sincere condolences to [Tung’s] family”.

World.title: Hong Kong secures expanded equal treatment and investment guarantees across Asean
World.content:
Hong Kong firms will benefit from expanded non-discriminatory treatment and investment guarantees in 10 Asean states after a protocol amending an investment agreement with the bloc was signed on Sunday.

The protocol was signed in Manila – where Asean economic ministers are meeting – ahead of dedicated trade consultations between Hong Kong and the bloc.

Undersecretary for Commerce and Economic Development Bernard Chan Pak-li signed the protocol for Hong Kong, alongside Philippine Trade Secretary Cristina Roque and Thailand’s Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Commerce Suphajee Suthumpun.

The protocol enables local enterprises to enjoy treatment no less favourable than that accorded to domestic or foreign enterprises in the 10 Asean states.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019031/From Paris to Hangzhou: The $9m Quest to Return China’s Lost Encyclopedia
World.title: From Paris to Hangzhou: The $9m Quest to Return China’s Lost Encyclopedia
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019031/From Paris to Hangzhou: The $9m Quest to Return China’s Lost Encyclopedia
World.content:
Over six centuries, the Yongle Encyclopedia has all but disappeared. Commissioned by the Ming emperor Zhu Di and compiled by more than 3,000 scholars, it once contained over 11,000 volumes on science, poetry, philosophy, medicine, and law. Today, less than 4% survives — fires and foreign invasions consumed the rest.

So when Weng Lianxi at Beijing’s Palace Museum received word in 2020 that two volumes would be auctioned in France, he was skeptical. Fakes were common, and with the pandemic grounding most international flights, he was unable to fly out to inspect them firsthand.

The researcher had only 39 JPEG images, a lifetime of handling ancient books, and a set of exacting criteria for the type of binding and paper used in the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). The photos checked every box, and the sellers were descendants of a French naval officer stationed in China in the late 1800s.

Convinced of their authenticity, Weng contacted businessman and book collector Jin Liang, who ultimately secured the volumes at auction for 8.12 million euros ($9.31 million), 1,600 times the starting price. This June, Jin donated them to the China National Archives of Publications and Culture (CNAPC).

Yet the journey of these “national treasures” from a Parisian attic, where they had sat unread for 140 years, to their new home in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province, was anything but simple.

Cultural compendium

Weng first heard about the auction at Beaussant Lefèvre & Associés from a friend in June 2020, but he didn’t get his hopes up. “So many purported volumes of the Yongle Encyclopedia have emerged in recent years, and so few have been real,” he explains.

The original work was commissioned in 1403. After a first draft failed to meet his expectations, Zhu Di — aka the Yongle Emperor — ordered eminent scholars and calligraphers from across the realm to assemble and compile knowledge, “grouped by category and organized by rhyme.”

The final version approved in 1407 consisted of 22,877 manuscript rolls across 11,095 volumes, with between 370 million and 450 million Chinese characters, according to estimates by various academics. The book was first stored at the Ming Palace in Nanjing, which served as the nation’s capital from 1368 to 1421. It was later moved to the Forbidden City in Beijing, now the Palace Museum.

After a fire in 1557, the Jiajing Emperor ordered that the encyclopedia be reproduced, creating what’s known as the “Jiajing copy.” All known surviving volumes come from this edition.

The two copies were kept separately at the Forbidden City’s Belvedere of Embodying Benevolence and the nearby imperial archive, Huang Shi Cheng. When the Ming dynasty eventually fell in 1644, the belvedere was burned down, and the fate of the original became a mystery.

Between 1723 and 1735, the Jiajing copy was moved to the elite Hanlin Academy, just east of the Forbidden City. However, Qing dynasty inventory records from 1794 show that 1,154 volumes were already missing.

With the imperial court consumed by conflict with foreign powers as well as internal strife, fewer than 5,000 volumes remained by 1875. Within the next 25 years, nearly all of the Yongle Encyclopedia had been lost, largely because of corruption among Qing officials and looting by the invading Eight-Nation Alliance.

China today holds just 241 volumes, including the two purchased by Jin, with most housed at the National Library in Beijing.

Weng, a senior member of China’s Ancient Books Preservation and Conservation Association, says what first caught his attention in 2020 was the volumes’ provenance. “According to the collector, they were passed down through the family,” he says. “One ancestor was a French naval officer who had close connections with several Chinese officials in the 1870s and received many gifts, including these volumes.”

But what mattered most was determining their authenticity.

Having seen genuine excerpts from the ancient encyclopedia, he was confident he could easily spot a fake up close. But with many air routes suspended because of the pandemic, traveling to Paris wasn’t an option. He could only base his judgment on 39 photos taken by a friend in France.

First, Weng examined the volumes using conventional authentication criteria. The Yongle Encyclopedia uses wrapped-back binding, a traditional Chinese method in which a hard cover is added for protection after the pages are bound. The cover, made of high-quality xuan paper and silk, has a book label comprising blue silk under a smaller layer of yellow silk, and a manuscript roll label in the upper-right corner carrying indexing information.

Pages measure 50.3 centimeters by 30 centimeters, with a text frame of roughly 35.5 centimeters by 23.5 centimeters and hand-drawn border lines on all four sides.

“All these text frames had to be drawn by hand. To ensure speed and quality, line spacing was controlled using pinpricks,” Weng says, explaining that the compilers would pierce a stack of paper before drawing the lines.

In addition to the binders’ fine craftsmanship, another way to verify authenticity is through the display text. The Jiajing copy was written entirely in red and black ink, with the main text in Ming ministerial-style script.

To fix errors and omissions, the transcribers used a splicing technique that involved cutting out the erroneous section with a knife at a 45-degree angle and applying a patch, carefully aligning the paper’s fibers. Repairs are only visible when held up to the light.

Over about two weeks, Weng forensically examined each photo for clues and ultimately determined the volumes were real. Soon after, he called Jin, his longtime friend. “I told him there were no problems with the books. We just needed to prepare the money,” he recalls.

Pearls of wisdom

With the sale fast approaching, Jin, a textiles tycoon in his late 50s from Zhejiang’s Taizhou City, immediately set aside 100 million yuan ($14.9 million) of his personal finances. “That figure came from discussions with experts,” he says. “More importantly, it was all I could afford.”

On July 7, 2020, he used three phone lines to call the French auction house, just in case one got disconnected. The bidding began at 11:10 p.m. Beijing time, an hour later than scheduled because of the larger-than-expected turnout.

The starting price was just 5,000 euros. “We learned that despite taking China’s growing economic prosperity into account, the auctioneers expected a final sale price of only 200,000 euros. They obviously underestimated the value of these two volumes,” Jin says.

After the first round, bidding had already reached 4 million euros.

“Things started to slow down after it reached 5 million. Once it reached 6 million, I thought that was it, because people started to become a bit hesitant, and it finally ended at 6.4 million,” he says. With VAT and commission, the final price came to 8.12 million euros.

Jin immediately called his friend Weng to give him the good news.

“People and books are brought together by some kind of fate,” muses the entrepreneur. “When I was bidding for these volumes, if it hadn’t been for the transportation difficulties caused by the pandemic, many experts from around the world could have attended and recognized their authenticity at a glance. The government would also have arranged for experts to authenticate the volumes and applied for funding to make the purchases.”

However, purchasing them had been the easy part. Now Jin had that challenge of getting them back to China.

The first obstacle was France’s export review process for cultural property. Jin believes that, as the Chinese government was paying close attention to the matter, the French Ministry of Culture became “extra cautious.” The businessman had to apply twice to get an export permit.

When approval finally came almost five months later, China’s cultural and customs authorities and security transportation agencies drew up a plan for the volumes’ return. “We received considerable guidance from the National Library of China and the CNAPC,” Jin says. “We had to carefully consider the process to avoid any errors.”

In early 2021, employees from China Shipping Group accompanied the relics from the auction house’s storage facility in central Paris to the city’s Charles De Gaulle Airport, where they were loaded onto a China Eastern Airlines flight to Shanghai.

After clearing customs, the volumes were initially stored at the bonded warehouse in the Shanghai Free Trade Zone before being entrusted to Hangzhou’s Zhejiang Library for safekeeping.

On July 30, 2022, the CNAPC opened specialized storage facilities for ancient books in Beijing and Hangzhou, as well as Xi’an, capital of the northwestern Shaanxi province, and Guangzhou, capital of the southern Guangdong province. The new volumes of the Yongle Encyclopedia were deposited at the Hangzhou CNAPC soon after.

At the official donation ceremony in July this year, Jin expressed relief at having this weight lifted from his shoulders and joy at safely returning two “national treasures.”

“If they had remained in a private collection, their true value wouldn’t be fully realized,” he tells Jiefang Daily. “The CNAPC has done extensive research on these volumes. That’s why I donated them to the institution. … books are simply a vessel for research.”

Jin has donated 3,337 items to the Hangzhou CNAPC, but the Yongle Encyclopedia is “so important, so precious,” he says, describing it like a giant gene bank preserving thousands of years of Chinese civilization.

In terms of content, this monumental work contains a vast number of lost texts from the Song (960–1279) and Yuan (1279–1368) dynasties, and informs researchers on manuscript production in the Ming era.

“Unlike the ‘Complete Library of the Four Treasuries’ compiled in the Qing dynasty, which strictly adhered to Confucian principles, teasing out all the materials that were irrelevant or fell outside the content, the Yongle Encyclopedia showed far less parochialism,” says Zhang Pu, deputy director of the Hangzhou CNAPC.

The Ming-dynasty book provides a wealth of firsthand materials for research, everything from a prescription by a physician in the central Hunan province to detailed rules for the game pitch-pot.

“There are just so many things to look into,” says Zhang, whose team has already published eight theses on the new volumes and discovered 22 previously unknown poems. “Every one is like a pearl left behind by history.”

Reported by Li Chuyue.

A version of this article originally appeared in Original (Jiefang Daily). It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019041/Ticket to Trouble: Scalping Row Disrupts Shanghai Comedy Show
World.title: Ticket to Trouble: Scalping Row Disrupts Shanghai Comedy Show
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019041/Ticket to Trouble: Scalping Row Disrupts Shanghai Comedy Show
World.content:
An incident at a Shanghai stand-up show in which customers who bought tickets through unofficial channels were denied entry because of the venue’s ticket identity-verification requirements has sparked public debate over China’s ticket scalping market.

The topic has surged to Chinese microblogging platform Weibo’s trending list, receiving over 57 million views as of Friday. Many argued that making exceptions for scalped-ticket holders is unfair to legitimate buyers and could further fuel the practice.

The show, held Sept. 11 at the city’s Majestic Theatre, was headlined by Fu Hang, a comedian known for his high-energy performances and distinctive delivery. To combat ticket scalping, show organizer Standby had implemented a system requiring attendees to present their ID cards and undergo real-name checks upon entry.

The scene quickly became chaotic, as ticketholders whose ID cards did not match the identity information provided at the time of purchase were not allowed entry. Videos of the incident circulating online showed a large crowd gathered outside the theater, demanding entry, and delaying the show’s start time. Because of the disorder, all ticket holders were eventually allowed in, and Fu extended his performance for 20 minutes to make up for the delay.

Chinese law prohibits ticket scalping for profit, which can result in administrative penalties, including detention and fees. In 2023, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism and the Ministry of Public Security jointly issued a notice requiring shows with a capacity over 5,000 to adopt real-name ticket purchases and admission.

Ulala Li, a Shanghai resident and comedy fan who bought her ticket through an official channel, told Sixth Tone she felt overlooked by Standby. “Shouldn’t the audience members who entered the venue properly and were left waiting for 20 minutes have received an apology and compensation?” she said.

“I think there’s a legitimate place for a secondary market. But when there are too many professional scalpers, they can seriously disrupt the healthy functioning of the market,” she added.

Tickets for Fu’s show were priced between 280 and 580 yuan ($42 to $86). According to domestic media, one attendee told Fu that he had paid 3,500 yuan for a scalped ticket — roughly seven times its original price.

Event organizer Standby said on Sept. 12 that it would cover documented losses caused by the delayed performance, including cancellation, train and flight ticket change fees, and additional accommodation expenses.

A day later, Shanghai police announced that three scalpers who bought 104 tickets to the show and resold them at higher prices had been placed under criminal coercive measures. The three reportedly made more than 18,000 yuan in illegal profits.

Three others also received administrative penalties for reselling eight tickets they had purchased through official channels, making more than 570 yuan in profit, the police added.

An audience member was also punished for starting a widely spread rumor online that “80% of the show’s tickets were sold through scalpers.”

Internet celebrity and stand-up comedy commentator Luo Yonghao criticized Standby’s actions in a popular Weibo post on Saturday, saying that “ticket scalpers can never be completely eliminated.” He suggested introducing regulated secondary ticketing platforms to legalize ticket resales and called for legislation on the issue.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019015/How I Brought China’s Vibe-Coding Revolution to Rural America
World.title: How I Brought China’s Vibe-Coding Revolution to Rural America
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019015/How I Brought China’s Vibe-Coding Revolution to Rural America
World.content:
As the car chugged up a dark, winding mountain road in eastern China’s Fujian province, I began to worry that I had made a huge mistake.

I had come to this remote mountainside to explore China’s push to harness the rise of artificial intelligence to drive growth in the countryside — a campaign I believed could offer some interesting lessons for the rest of the world.

A few days earlier, at a tech event in Shanghai, a contact had mentioned that a village in Fujian was about to host the country’s first “rural hackathon.” The idea immediately intrigued me. I had attended several hackathons in Silicon Valley over the years, but these events were typically sleepless, caffeine-fuelled contests where expert coders would team up to hammer out hundreds of lines of code over a few days.

To many in the Bay Area, the idea of holding a hackathon outside of a major tech industry hub — let alone in a tiny village — would have seemed like an outlandish proposition. Non-coders tended to be viewed as afterthoughts at best, or dead weight at worst.

But China seemed to be taking a different approach, leaning into the potential for new AI tools to lower the barriers to creating and running online businesses. Curious to learn more, I’d booked a ticket for the event — and jumped on a train from Shanghai.

But Longtan Village turned out to be even more remote than I’d imagined. Getting there involved taking a sleek high-speed train to neighboring Zhejiang province, then a much slower “green train” to the city of Ningde in Fujian, followed by an hourlong car ride up a snaking mountain track.

They weren’t really planning to host a hackathon here, were they?

My doubts eased somewhat once I arrived at the village. A brightly lit hall stood out like a beacon in the darkness, where a couple of young volunteers were welcoming latecomers with care packages, farmer’s hats, and directions to a hotel offering free accommodation, where I’d be sharing a room with another participant I hadn’t yet met.

As the only foreigner joining the event, I was first asked whether I could speak Chinese. I acknowledged a shaky command of the language, collected my things, and trudged off through the dark to find my room, as I nervously wondered how I would pitch a startup entirely in Mandarin.

But I was excited to get an up-close look at China’s vibe-coding revolution. As someone with family in rural Michigan, I have long had a keen sense for how accelerating technological change has deepened class and regional inequalities — and tried to find ways to bridge those divides.

Since college, I have tried to use my experience in the tech industry to drive social change, working on a range of projects to empower local communities. My trip to China was part of that effort, as I hoped to gain new ideas from the dynamic tech scene here.

Longtan, it turned out, offered an interesting case study. The village was no ordinary Chinese farming community — it was more like a social experiment, driven by a combination of government policy and youthful idealism.

Over the past few years, Longtan has seen a growing influx of young people looking to escape the intense pressure of life in China’s major cities. The local authorities have encouraged the inflow, seeing it as a way to revive the local economy after decades of urban migration.

The new residents moved into renovated buildings alongside the original villagers, and set up a non-hierarchical online cooperative known as the DAO to manage their affairs. They made a living by painting, running hotels and cafés, or as digital nomads.

Now, the village was jumping on a new trend in China: people setting up one-person companies, or OPCs, using a mix of AI models and agents to launch and run startups on their own. The village hoped the OPC wave would create new jobs and attract more newcomers, lifting the local economy.

As I strolled towards the assembly hall for the opening ceremony, it was easy to see why people wanted to come here. A river ran through the center of town, weaving downhill over gentle rapids past boutique shops and footpaths. Rows of souvenirs sat unattended, and passersby could simply take what they wanted and pay by scanning QR codes.

At the ceremony, I found most participants were young people from around China, plus a contingent of “new villagers” who had moved here permanently. The original villagers, by contrast, were mostly the ones serving Fujianese soups in local restaurants, operating small convenience stores, or helping to run the guesthouses.

It was a dynamic worth sitting with. The new villagers had undeniably created something — opportunities, foot traffic, a reason for outsiders like me to show up — but the question of whom all this development was meant for lingered at the edges of every conversation. Perhaps the hackathon was meant to start answering it.

We could submit up to two projects and join two teams, but I spent the bulk of my time pursuing the OPC route with my own idea. Since the U.S. had pulled the last vestiges of the Peace Corps out of China during the pandemic, I used AI agent Vercel’s v0 tool to vibe code a website for something I’d dubbed “Compass Corps”: a bilateral alternative to the Peace Corps, whereby mixed American and Chinese teams would engage in service projects in one another’s countries before going out into the world together to tackle global problems.

The competition had multiple tracks, and many teams built conventional tech products like those you might see at traditional hackathons. But artists were building complex apps at the same rate as engineers, thanks to the leveled playing field that vibe coding had enabled. Both American and Chinese AIs were heavily used, with America’s Claude Code by Anthropic still extremely popular despite the rise of domestic open-weight models.

After a five-minute pitch to a panel of village leaders and guest judges, my individual project ended up claiming joint third prize. It may have been a pity vote for the lone foreigner, who stumbled through a presentation in basic Mandarin, though I’d like to think the concept has some merit of its own.

After the weekend, I left the village to continue my tour of China. Beyond Shanghai and Longtan, I also spent a week in the southern city of Shenzhen exploring the nation’s tech renaissance and made multiple trips to Hangzhou in the east to establish a local counterpart to my American-registered robotics teleoperation project. But it was the hackathon in Fujian that stayed with me most.

Prior to the AI revolution, organizing a hackathon in a place like Longtan would have been a questionable proposition. Even New York City hadn’t had anywhere near as many hackathons as Silicon Valley, despite having a population many times larger than the Bay Area’s.

But this event in rural China, with its preponderance of non-coders, made me realize how much things could change. If AI has enabled anyone to build, what’s stopping us from bringing hackathons to the masses? In my home country, why haven’t we been showing the average American how they can make ideas come to life in front of their eyes?

The idea grew after I returned to the U.S. and visited family in Michigan. Back in LeRoy, a small town where I spent the best parts of my childhood, I noticed local Amish families had started installing solar panels on their homes in surprising numbers. Connection to the electrical grid was apparently still taboo, but electricity itself no longer was.

If the Amish — an insular and extremely traditional ethnoreligious group — could leapfrog into the future on their own terms, I felt reasonably confident leveraging my Longtan experiences to organize Michigan’s first rural hackathon.

I started by renting the fellowship hall of an old church on the edge of town. The original congregation had dwindled until it ceased to be functional, and the building had since been converted into a rentable community space. The caretaker was an energetic military veteran of my mother’s generation who had relocated to her husband’s home state after a career in the nation’s capital. To my surprise, she had worked in IT and knew exactly what a hackathon was.

Although I’d privately faulted the Chinese hackathon for largely excluding the village’s original residents, I began to see that the knowledge gap was a real issue. My host mentioned that members of a local committee were frightened by the word “hackathon” — they worried that local services or businesses would get “hacked” or otherwise disrupted by our event.

But I still believed that locals needed to be at the forefront of reshaping their own communities. Although the town was due to celebrate its annual festival that day, I wrote up a schedule and decided to use the first hour of the daylong event to walk participants through the general ethos of a hackathon, how vibe coding works, and how they might use it to solve everyday problems.

I posted flyers on the public bulletin boards of local restaurants, banks, and post offices, and then put up signs and set out snacks and soda pop at an outdoor registration table on the day of the event.

Turnout was slow at first, and the people who stopped by seemed more curious than committed. An old Amish couple even rode past on a horse and buggy, visibly perplexed by the word “hackathon,” before saying hello and continuing on their way.

For a while, I wasn’t sure whether I had only learned something theoretical in China, or whether the concept could travel beyond its country of origin and the specific demographic of young urbanites who had come down to Longtan.

True to startup tradition, I decided to pivot. I left the community center and walked to the center of the village, telling attendees of the town’s annual fair that I was running a new type of competition.

They could enter the contest by submitting their best ideas for improving the town — new businesses, public infrastructure, apps, nonprofits, or anything of interest. I would then feed each idea into an AI vibe coding tool, build something to best express each concept, and eventually invite our small panel of judges to pick a winner.

Rather than simply coming to town, teaching people to vibe code, and hoping for a hundred technological flowers to bloom, I really had to start somewhere more fundamental: people first needed to learn that it was possible to participate in the process of solving local problems, and only after that realization might they have an interest in leveraging AI tools to amplify their impact.

One resident said that the village was a “laundry desert” and that she adamantly wanted to solve this problem. Many families in modular homes and trailers had no washing machines and thus had to drive 40 minutes round-trip to nearby Cadillac or down the freeway to Reed City to locate a laundromat. Even my grandfather’s house, where I was staying, itself lacked a washer or dryer.

After reviewing submissions ranging from splash pads to car washes, the judges reached their verdict: the biggest opportunity for scalable impact was solving the aforementioned laundry problem. The winner received a grocery store gift card and a promise we’d build something more comprehensive in response to her problem statement.

After a few hours of perfectionist prompt engineering via v0’s natural language interface, we had something that actually solved her problem: a community tool that we’d dubbed “WashMapper.”

It was a simple concept: a peer-to-peer laundry marketplace where neighbors with a washer and dryer can list open time slots, and anyone needing laundry done can book a slot nearby. Whether WashMapper takes off in any meaningful way remains to be seen, but at the very least it exists, and people started thinking about what a solution might look like.

Just like LeRoy, I’d need to return to Longtan to see whether anything we’d built had found practical use. Interestingly enough, washing machines also came up during my conversations with business owners in the Chinese village, which made me feel that we humans aren’t so different.

Sitting with my learnings from Longtan and LeRoy also made me rethink a tenet I’d first learned while living in Silicon Valley. Everything needed the ability to scale nationally, if not globally. But these towns didn’t need a scalable platform; they needed solutions rooted in local networks, like clean laundry.

Although most hackathon projects soon go dormant after the initial event, perhaps one or two ideas will have taken root, and that makes all the difference. Similarly, if WashMapper never takes off in LeRoy, maybe another town will run with it, or be inspired to host its own hackathon, or whatever they want to call it.

And even if the average Longtan resident didn’t join the hackathon, they couldn’t have missed it. Banners hung throughout the village, there were frequent gatherings in the town square, and people coded in the coffeehouses. Anyone walking through saw an unavoidable display of energy, possibility, and something resembling hope.

Honestly, we need more of that in the world. We can’t simply throw up our hands and hope that the future treats us kindly. AI isn’t going to solve all the world’s problems, and it’s noticeably creating a few new ones. But it’s worth paying attention to how powerful technologies can be harnessed for the common good, even if it’s as simple as a clean pair of jeans.

(Header image: Visuals from the author and Shijue/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019036/Marriage Proposal at Beijing Concert Hits Sour Note With Fans
World.title: Marriage Proposal at Beijing Concert Hits Sour Note With Fans
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019036/Marriage Proposal at Beijing Concert Hits Sour Note With Fans
World.content:
Against the backdrop of tens of thousands of fans singing “Southern Girl” by popular Chinese folk singer Zhao Lei, a man in the audience drops to one knee, a woman in a wedding dress rises to her feet, and the two begin hurling wedding candies into the crowd.

But soon the audience turns, and instead of congratulating the happy couple, they start shouting, “Sit down” and “That’s enough,” drowning out Zhao’s singing and requiring several security guards to intervene.

The scene, which occurred at Zhao’s Sept. 12 concert at Beijing’s National Stadium, soon was heavily criticized after being posted on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. Related topics on microblogging platform Weibo have been viewed over 130 million times as of Thursday.

Proposals at concerts are common in China, but pushback has grown in recent years. A 2025 survey of over 800 young Chinese by online tech news platform youth36kr found that over one-third of respondents ranked wedding proposals at concerts as “unwelcome” and “disruptive.”

Concert ticket prices are also climbing, making some feel that on-site disturbances come at a personal cost to their experience. Data from October 2024 showed that average concert ticket prices were nearly 525 yuan, up from roughly 485 yuan the previous year. In May 2025, average ticket prices climbed to nearly 750 yuan.

Many argued the couple had overstepped the bounds of acceptable public behavior. One online comment read, “I came for the concert, not your proposal.” Another user posted, “I paid to watch a performance, not to be the backdrop for your little sideshow.”

The discussion intensified on Monday when the video’s original poster, surnamed Xie, told domestic media that a user claiming to be the fiancé featured in the video had messaged him demanding he delete it. Xie said the user apologized for disrupting the concert but said the video infringed on the couple’s portrait rights, that they had filed a police report, and that they would pursue legal action if it was not removed.

Zheng Xiaoqiang, a senior partner at Beijing Tiantai Law Firm, told Sixth Tone that privacy claims usually fail in large public venues such as the concert arena where the incident took place. “They chose to actively draw attention (to themselves) in a public setting with tens of thousands of people present,” Zheng said.

However, he said that close-ups, repeated edits, or mocking captions of the incident reposted online may cross into portrait rights infringement. He added that the minor disruption to audience members is rarely compensable in court.

Other recent concert marriage proposals have similarly sparked controversy in China. In 2023, at a Beijing concert for the popular Taiwanese rock band Mayday, a couple in wedding attire took photos in front of the stage, sparking jeers that drowned out the music. Many said they disrespected both the audience and the performers.

Wang Yao, a concertgoer who proposed to her partner at pop singer Zhang Jie’s 2025 Beijing concert, told Sixth Tone that audiences differ depending on the music genre. Folk fans tend to value immersive musical experiences, while pop fans are more tolerant of interruption, she said.

Those who witnessed her own proposal sent her their videos, which Wang then posted on social media, earning hundreds of thousands of likes. “The proposal was brief, and people mostly cheered and wished us well,” she said.

“A concert proposal can be a touching surprise, but it ultimately shouldn’t disturb other audience members,” she added.

A university student from Wuhan, capital of the central Hubei province, surnamed Chen, told Sixth Tone she and her friends oppose marriage proposals during concerts, but used to support them. “As consumers, our sense of agency and public order has grown,” she said. “Singers and fans put a lot of effort into performances, and proposers piggyback on that at no cost. That’s selfish and insincere.”

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo and Xiao Chuhan; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot of a video of the viral marriage proposal at Zhao Lei’s concert in Beijing. From Douyin)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019030/Pension Paradox: China’s Delivery Riders on a Rocky Road to Retirement
World.title: Pension Paradox: China’s Delivery Riders on a Rocky Road to Retirement
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019030/Pension Paradox: China’s Delivery Riders on a Rocky Road to Retirement
World.content:
At just 19, retirement feels light-years away for Lin Yi. Hunched over a plate of fried noodles, the takeout delivery rider’s face goes completely blank when asked about his pension plan. “I haven’t paid into anything,” he says, before hungrily returning to his lunch.

The same goes for his colleague, Hai Liang, who is 42, though for him it’s simple arithmetic: “Pay nearly 900 yuan ($135) a month into a pension? That’s four days of deliveries for me. Can I bring myself to part with that?”

Gig workers like Lin and Hai have for years sat on the fringes of China’s social insurance system, either by choice, or because they simply don’t understand how the system works.

For the past 17 months, domestic on-demand services platform Meituan has been attempting to bring more part-time couriers into the system through a subsidy program first piloted in Quanzhou, in the eastern Fujian province, and Nantong, in the eastern Jiangsu province. Takeup has been extremely low, yet local government service centers say they receive gig workers every day asking about pensions, suggesting this group is highly interested in planning for retirement.

So why are so many opting out?

Tough sell

Lin and Hai are among about 150 riders working out of the Puxi Wanda delivery station, one of the largest stations that Meituan operates in Quanzhou.

Most riders take their meals at a small restaurant nearby, a de facto canteen with an eat-now-pay-later policy for cash-strapped customers. The owner, 35-year-old Luo Kai, welcomes a string of exhausted, sweat-soaked couriers throughout the day.

“Most of these guys have to eat on credit. How realistic is it to talk to them about paying into a pension fund?” he asks.

China’s social insurance system covers five core benefits: pension insurance, medical insurance, unemployment insurance, work-related injury insurance, and maternity insurance. Contributions are mandatory for workers with labor contracts, but not for those with service contracts, which applies to gig workers, who are mostly managed by temp agencies and third-party enterprises.

In addition to recent efforts to expand medical insurance and work-related injury insurance to freelancers, gig workers, and the self-employed, the central government has been running a flexible-employment pension system since 2005, with contribution bases adjusted according to the regional average monthly salary.

Working with local authorities, Meituan began running its own program in November, targeting part-time employees after a seven-month pilot in two eastern cities. The program encourages couriers to pay 50% of their state pension contribution, with the Beijing-based tech company promising to cover the rest.

To qualify for the Quanzhou pilot, launched in April 2025, riders had to be aged 16 to 60 (50 or 55 for women, depending on their role), and must have earned at least 4,433 yuan for three of the previous six months. Although average monthly earnings at the city’s delivery stations have fallen in recent years, most workers could easily meet the requirements. Yet fewer than 20 riders at the Puxi Wanda station signed up, and the number has not even reached double digits this year. Meituan has not released national enrollment data.

Wu Xiaohua, who manages the station, suggests the low takeup there is linked to high turnover. “It’s normal in this line of work,” he says, adding that in the run-up to the Chinese New Year holiday in February, nearly 80 gig workers quit, including some of those first 20 signees.

“It’s not that we haven’t tried to promote the program,” Wu adds. “There’s just something contradictory about asking people who want to make quick money to pay for pension insurance they won’t use for decades.”

According to recent research by Nankai University, the average age of a food-delivery rider in China is 33. With the country’s retirement age set to rise by 2040 to 63 for men and 55 for women in blue-collar jobs, low-to-medium-salary gig workers could be forgiven for “earning for now.”

“We deliver food to cover the basics,” says 25-year-old rider Wang Xu, who eats the cheapest set menu at Luo’s restaurant twice a day, every day. “Does pension insurance count as a basic?”

Pay to receive

In 2024, a team led by professor Zhang Dandan at Peking University’s National School of Development surveyed more than 30,000 riders for a major food-delivery platform about their views on social insurance. The study found that more than half wanted a pension, but few had interest in paying for it, while 23% said they wouldn’t enroll even if contributions were mandatory.

Just under 40% were willing to contribute less than 5% of their monthly income, and fewer than 10% agreed with the prevailing rate for gig workers, the poll showed.

When Meituan launched its pilot, many riders initially believed that the company would cover 100% of their monthly pension contributions. After several rounds of promotion and discussion, representatives for both sides agreed to a 50-50 split.

Yet many remain wary of allowing money to be drawn directly from their salary.

“They don’t understand that the contributions go directly into the state social security system. They worry that the platform is trying to take a bigger share of their earnings,” says Jin Luhui, a courier team leader who signed up to Meituan’s subsidized pension program in April 2025.

Jin explains that his daughter was due to start elementary school in September, and that Quanzhou’s enrollment rules require parents to have paid at least six months of social insurance. With the program, his family was able to meet the criteria.

Repeated information sessions have helped clear up some confusion among riders, such as whether a pension is tied to where they work rather than their hometown (many gig workers in big cities are rural migrants), or whether their contributions would no longer count if they stopped working as a takeout courier.

For many people, especially the younger generation, food delivery is a seasonal gig — something to do when other industries are quiet. In Quanzhou, for example, local shoe factories pay much higher wages at peak times, attracting many riders to make the switch.

The survey by Zhang’s team showed that takeout couriers stay in the job for only about six months on average. This means many could struggle to meet Meituan’s pension subsidy requirements.

In Quanzhou’s busy shopping district, roughly 50% of the more than 30 Meituan riders that reporters spoke with had been in the industry only about three months. Few knew about the company program in any detail; instead, conversations invariably turned to earnings, order volumes, and whether the grueling work is still worth it.

“I used to make more than 50 deliveries a day. Now I’m lucky to hit 35,” says Wang, who rotates between running his own business, working full-time jobs, and delivering food. He recently returned to couriering after more than a year away and believes the job has gotten a lot harder.

“When orders are down, asking riders to pay social insurance is a tough sell,” says Jin. “But I still mention at team meetings that the Meituan app has a complete guide on how riders can contribute.”

Meanwhile, some are “just bad at managing their finances,” according to station manager Wu. The app allows workers to withdraw their earnings three times a month, yet he says he advances around 20,000 yuan each month to staff who are running low on cash.

Risks and rewards

For most, the decision over whether to contribute to pension insurance ultimately comes down to whether they feel it’s the best use of their money, especially in the face of more immediate risks.

“Once I’ve saved enough from deliveries, I’ll use it to open a restaurant. If business is good, won’t the returns be better than a pension?” asks Jin Cailin, a Shanghai-based delivery rider in his 30s. He says he’d only consider pension contributions after turning 45.

Li Min, 27, has been delivering food in Quanzhou for barely a week. For him, receiving benefits 30 years down the line feels abstract. He’s far more interested in saving to buy a new electric bike and a Samsung smartphone, as well as to pay for orthodontic treatment costing 16,000 yuan. “I prefer seeing the results of my labor right away,” he says.

Zhu Tian, a researcher involved in Meituan’s rider protection initiatives, suggests a mismatch between riders’ micro daily realities and the platform’s macro view of their needs. In principle, a social security system for riders should address short-term risks such as work-related injuries before extending to retirement. However, Meituan’s internal research suggests otherwise.

In-house surveys have found that 70% of the company’s riders hold rural household registration, with the vast majority already covered by basic medical insurance programs in their hometown. Traffic accidents also come under the platform’s mandatory occupational injury insurance, while some riders have commercial accident insurance on top of that. Zhu says that this leaves pensions as the most prominent gap in the system.

At the same time, Meituan’s data shows that its highest-earning, most active riders are among the least willing to pay social insurance contributions. “Those who push themselves hard to earn more are often under pressure from household expenses or debt,” Zhu explains. “What they need is money now.”

“We had hoped pension subsidies would help us retain more riders long term, but they haven’t been very effective,” he adds.

The subsidy program is part of Meituan’s broader efforts to build a more stable workforce through stronger employment protections. In Zhengzhou, capital of Henan province, and Jiangsu’s Wuxi City, full-time riders are now offered comprehensive social insurance coverage. Yet the company has struggled to fill these positions.

This points to a deeper disconnect between China’s social insurance system, which was designed for conventional employment, and gig workers, who move to a different rhythm: they count their earnings monthly or even daily, move easily between industries, and can stop or start working at any time.

“Gig workers tend to focus more on immediate earnings, but giving them the option to pay into a pension may encourage some of them to start planning longer term,” says professor Zhang Dandan.

Zhao Qing, an associate professor at Wuhan University’s School of Political Science and Public Administration, believes gig work sits uneasily with the current pension system, which requires sustained contributions. “The system needs to be more flexible,” she says.

After spending more than a year promoting Meituan’s program, Wu has found that the best strategy is not to oversell or pressure riders but to respect what they decide. “Sometimes understanding why they won’t pay is as valuable as getting them to sign up,” he says.

For example, Hai, a twice-married father of two, is his family’s sole breadwinner. He rents a room without air conditioning for 300 yuan a month and, until recently, wore a work uniform that had turned black with grime. “He won’t listen when we tell him to slow down,” says Wu. “He just keeps working, trying to make as much as he can.”

Although he would like a pension, Hai has moved frequently among food-delivery platforms, taking advantage of the salary incentives offered to riders as the market intensified, so he doesn’t yet meet the requirements for Meituan’s program.

In July, Wu handed Hai a brand-new uniform, one of the prizes from a recent Riders’ Day event that Hai didn’t have time to attend. Wu feels that a small, immediate comfort is sometimes all someone needs to keep going.

(Due to privacy concerns, Lin Yi, Luo Kai, Zhu Tian, and Li Min are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Yang Shuyuan and Wu Kaiwen.

A version of this article originally appeared in Original (Jiefang Daily). It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Chen Yue; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019029/Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.title: Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019029/Token of Trust: Beijing Links AI Usage to Company Loans
World.content:
A zone in Beijing has launched a program asking several banks to extend billions of yuan in credit to multiple companies across the AI industry chain, partly based on their token usage.

Termed “token loans,” the financing scheme was recently implemented by the Beijing Economic and Technological Development Zone, also known as Beijing E-Town, in the city’s southeast, and involves extending nearly 2 billion yuan ($300 million) in credit to several AI companies, domestic media reported Monday.

A token is the smallest unit of data an AI large language model can process. In March, the National Data Administration officially adopted “ciyuan” — combining “word” and “currency” — as the Chinese term for “token.” The move was largely seen as putting an economic spin on AI-led computing power.

In June of this year, China’s daily token consumption already exceeded 500 trillion, according to data from the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology. A Saturday report by the China Telecom Research Institute estimates that that number could rise to 100 quadrillion, or 200 times that figure by year-end.

Six domestic banks, including the Agricultural Bank of China, China CITIC Bank, Industrial Bank, Bank of Beijing, China Minsheng Bank, and Huaxia Bank, provided the loans. The credit is intended for AI companies with “high research investment and high technological barriers,” as well as growing computing needs, but without the physical assets or profits typically required to obtain bank financing.

In addition to token consumption, the banks also awarded the loans based on technological barriers, team strength, and companies’ business development prospects.

Guoqi Zhikong, a developer of automobile-focused connected cloud platforms and autonomous driving vehicles, received a 30-million-yuan credit line from China CITIC Bank. Meanwhile, Shenzhou Guangda, which provides computing infrastructure and enterprise-level AI agent solutions, received the same credit amount from Industrial Bank.

The rapid growth of the AI industry has created a dilemma for tech startups, which often struggle to obtain traditional loans, an anonymous staff member from Beijing E-Town’s business and finance bureau told domestic media. Conventional lending models rely heavily on collateral and corporate profit statements, so even companies with strong technological capabilities often lack physical assets to pledge. In contrast, their opportunities for technological development and business expansion are constrained by profits that have yet to fully materialize.

In August, Bank of China’s branch in the southern city of Guangzhou launched the country’s first token loan scheme. Aimed at small- and medium-sized computing companies, it covers token supply, applications, and related services, with successful applicants eligible for up to 30 million yuan in credit.

Looking ahead, Lou Feipeng, a researcher at the Postal Savings Bank of China, said that before such loans can be adopted more broadly, the country must address several major issues, including exaggerated token-use data, inaccurate assessments of computing power consumption, and overestimation of borrowers’ repayment ability.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018999/From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.title: From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018999/From Monkey Kings to Little Demons: China’s New Age of the Supporting Character
World.content:
In the classic Chinese novel “Journey to the West,” little demons are nobodies. They serve powerful demon kings, perform menial tasks, and are easily dispatched by heroes like Sun Wukong, better known as the Monkey King. Most do not even have names.

But increasingly, these once-forgotten characters are moving to the center of the story. Across Chinese films, TV shows, games, and books, little demons are being transformed from anonymous supporting characters into protagonists in their own right.

Take Black Myth: Wukong, the Chinese AAA video game that became a global hit. The game features a compendium of 203 supernatural creatures, including 90 classified as “little demons,” each with its own biographical profile. It is almost like an archive assembled from the gaps in “Journey to the West,” a who’s who of forgotten characters.

Another example is 2024’s “The Great Nobody,” a Chinese comedy series spinoff that grew out of the variety show “Amazing Night.” In it, a group of little demons living on the fictional Flower Neck Mountain waits in vain for the monk Tang Sanzang and his disciples to arrive on their pilgrimage to retrieve Buddhist scriptures. The reworking of the classic tale becomes a commentary on supporting comedians struggling to make their mark in the entertainment industry.

But perhaps the most striking example is “Nobody,” a Chinese animated film that grossed 1.7 billion yuan ($240 million) at the box office last summer. Expanded from the first episode of “Yao-Chinese Folktales,” an animated anthology series released on the video platform Bilibili in 2023, the film follows a “knock-off” pilgrimage team of demons comprising a pig, a toad, a weasel, and a gorilla.

Seen in the broader history of “Journey to the West” adaptations, this renewed interest in little demons represents the third major approach to interpreting the classic since the turn of the millennium.

The first was what might be called “post-revolutionary interpretations.” Emerging in the late 1990s, this approach is represented by Stephen Chow’s “A Chinese Odyssey” (1995) and the online novel “The Legend of Wukong,” which began serialization in 2000. These works focused on Sun Wukong’s struggle for individual autonomy, symbolized by his decision over whether to don the golden headband, a device used by Tang Sanzang to rein in his mischievous nature. At their core was the tragic rebellion of the neoliberal individual against the grand narrative of the pilgrimage, as well as a playful deconstruction of earlier “revolutionary” interpretations of “Journey to the West.”

The second consisted of “gothic interpretations,” represented by films including “Journey to the West: Conquering the Demons” (2013), “The Monkey King 2” (2016), and “Journey to the West: The Demons Strike Back” (2017). Through digital spectacle, these films created fantastical worlds and recast the classic as a monster movie. Their dark, horror-filled atmosphere can be seen as a cultural expression of the crisis of neoliberalism.

The third approach is what I call “system-based interpretations.” These works portray the Heavenly Palace and Vulture Peak, the respective seats of the Taoist and Buddhist hierarchies, as parts of a vast network of relationships. Tang Sanzang and his disciples’ pilgrimage to obtain the scriptures becomes a meticulously planned project, while the 81 trials they encounter along the way are recast as conspiracies orchestrated by the powers that be.

Ma Boyong’s bestselling novel “The Annoyance of the Gods” (2023), for example, portrays Taibai Jinxing, a deity associated with the planet Venus, as a project manager exhausted by office politics. In doing so, the novel reframes the pilgrimage as an internal struggle within a sprawling bureaucracy characterized by maneuvering, competition, and checks and balances.

The focus on little demons emerged from this same “system-based” approach. Rather than subverting the logic of the original text, these works stand in the shadows of its grand narrative and construct detailed accounts of the lives of those who remain nameless.

This interpretation is closely connected to the current social mood. Since 2020, growing uncertainty has weakened faith in nixi, or the idea that ordinary people can beat the odds and dramatically improve their fortunes. As economic growth has slowed, such aspirations have increasingly given way to greater empathy for ordinary workers simply trying to get by.

If the era in which little demons were ignored corresponded to a period of economic expansion, when workers believed they too could “retrieve the scriptures and achieve Buddhahood,” then the era of empathizing with them belongs to the period after that peak. Ordinary people stuck on the periphery of systems recognize themselves in these little demons: operating at the margins, with limited control over events, and little guarantee that their efforts will be rewarded.

Take “Nobody,” for example. Close-ups of the little demons’ vacant eyes and sluggish expressions reflect the mental state of some workers today. Their circumstances , to a certain extent, closely mirror contemporary workplaces: routine and often modest tasks, represented by scrubbing pots and making arrows; shifting expectations and promises that do not always materialize; and the risk of being treated primarily as a functional part of a larger operation.

Identification with these little demons reflects a changing sense of where ordinary workers locate themselves within larger systems. Rather than always imagining themselves as protagonists destined to rise above their circumstances, they may find greater resonance in supporting characters who navigate constraints, make compromises, and carve out limited forms of agency within the roles available to them.

This sense of being a supporting character also underlies the popular idea that “the world is just a ragtag troupe.” Some individuals may struggle to fully identify with the current situation while also finding it difficult to imagine viable alternatives. For those who remain within these structures, a common response is to learn how the rules operate and navigate the available room within them in order to maintain a workable position.

This shift toward accepting a supporting role has already manifested in forms of spectatorship common online. “Roasting” other people’s stories allows individuals to mock them from a safe distance while releasing some of the psychological pressure they themselves face.

Posting “bullet comments” that scroll across videos in real time creates a more distanced form of viewing while giving spectators a sense of collective belonging. “Eating melon,” a Chinese internet expression for following gossip and online drama as a bystander, similarly turns public events into spectator entertainment. Rather than emphasizing individual agency, these forms of spectatorship encourage people to watch from the sidelines.

This consciousness has also spread into contemporary cultural production, with little demons being just one example. In the 2024 web novel “The Diary of a Female Zombie’s Hiking Adventure,” the protagonist has no desire to become involved in other people’s storylines and instead chooses simply to observe. Meanwhile, in the animated film “Chang An” (2023), the figure who guides the audience through the splendor of the Tang dynasty (618–907) is the diligent and orderly poet Gao Shi rather than Li Bai, the personality who most fully embodies the era’s poetic spirit. Through Gao Shi’s eyes, Li Bai’s wildness and romanticism are viewed with a sense of incomprehension and detachment.

The audiences for these works are people navigating rapid social change, uncertainty, and shifting forms of connection. They are not merely digital natives, but individuals searching for a sense of place and meaning in this “era of supporting characters.”

Translator: David Ball.

(Header image: Visuals from Douban and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)
