World.title: After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019024/After Beijing Bowel Accident, Hyrox Changes Its Rules
World.content:
Update: Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk apologized Thursday for continuing to race after she soiled herself midway through a Hyrox event in Beijing last week. In a statement, Wietrzyk said she regretted not exiting the course and said she would retroactively withdraw from the race and give up the points she earned. On Sept. 16, Hyrox said athletes whose races took place between 2:40 p.m. and 8:40 p.m. the day of the event would be eligible for full refunds.

Hyrox has amended its official rulebooks after the winner of a recent Beijing event experienced bowel incontinence mid-race yet continued competing. The incident sparked widespread debate in China over sportsmanship and the organizer’s handling of potential hygiene risks.

On Monday, Hyrox updated its online rulebook to state that a race director may withdraw an athlete if their “blood, vomit, urine, or faeces pose a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers.”

The change comes in the wake of controversy surrounding the women’s solo elite race on Saturday, in which Australian athlete and Hyrox world record holder Joanna Wietrzyk finished first with a time of 1:01:23. Footage circulating online showed fecal matter staining Wietrzyk’s clothing and legs as she performed various exercises.

Hyrox has recently surged in popularity across China. Founded in Germany, the sport features eight 1-kilometer runs, each followed by strength training stations including sled pulls, rowing, and burpees. China’s first official race was held in Beijing in 2024 and drew 1,700 entries. Participants at this weekend’s Beijing event exceeded 11,000, with standard individual registration costing roughly 800 yuan ($125).

Competitors and social media users questioned organizers’ decision to let Wietrzyk continue racing. The Women’s Pro division won by Wietrzyk began at 2:40 p.m. Saturday, with other heats scheduled until 8:40 p.m. and another full day of competition Sunday.

“As someone who works in the public health sector, my biggest concern is that if she had a bacterial or viral infection, contamination like this could spread pathogens very quickly,” a Beijing-based athlete in her 20s, surnamed Wang, whose race began about an hour after Wietrzyk, told Sixth Tone.

Toilets were available at the venue, she noted, but using the bathroom counts toward an athlete’s total race time.

In a post made via its official account on microblogging platform Weibo Saturday night, Hyrox’s China division said organizers had “immediately” closed and disinfected affected areas and removed contaminated equipment. Wang said she had seen nothing “noticeably unusual” on the course.

Wietrzyk later posted an Instagram Story of herself receiving an intravenous infusion from what appeared to be a hospital. An accompanying caption read: “a win is a win.”

This drew further criticism from some Chinese social media users, who saw the remark as dismissive of concerns over other competitors’ health and safety.

Italian Hyrox pro-athlete Sara Gandola, who competed in the same race, told Sixth Tone that Wietrzyk should not be blamed for the incident.

Gandola said the responsibility of athletes is to perform at their highest level within the rules, while “it is the sport’s responsibility to set those rules and define what is acceptable.”

“If you disagree with the rules, debate the rules,” she said. “But attacking an athlete for doing exactly what elite athletes are supposed to do is completely backward.”

On Monday, Hyrox’s global headquarters issued a statement on Instagram, describing the incident as an “unforeseen situation” and adding that those who threatened its athletes would be permanently banned from future events.

However, Chinese social media users criticized their stance for not directly acknowledging failures in how it handled the incident at the time.

Later that day, Hyrox China admitted on Weibo that the incident exposed “shortcomings” in its competition rules and said it had proposed revisions to its global headquarters. The previous Hyrox rulebook imposes a two-minute penalty for littering, spitting, or blowing one’s nose onto the floor, but does not address fecal incontinence.

Hyrox China added that the venue’s carpets had been replaced and that the entire venue had been deep-cleaned overnight, pledging to disinfect both venues before future events and any shared equipment.

Hyrox co-founder Moritz Fürste also issued an apology via Instagram on Monday, admitting that “Hyrox made a mistake by not reacting immediately during the race.”

In a Sunday commentary, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV said the incident highlighted a growing tension between the “rapid expansion” of commercial sporting events and “gaps in competition rules.”

Additional reporting: Xie Anran; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

World.title: Join #MoveCebu 2026 public forum, workshops for a liveable city
World.content:
Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH is returning to Cebu for #MoveCebu: Sugbo alang sa Sugboanons, a three-day civic empowerment roadshow set for October 14 to 16, 2026

MANILA, Philippines — How can local citizens shape Cebu’s future as a liveable city?

Rappler, through its civic engagement arm MovePH, is returning to Cebu City for a series of community activities following its provincial roadshows there in 2012 and 2018.

#MoveCebu: Sugbo alang sa Sugboanons, the civic empowerment roadshow, will kickstart with a public forum on Wednesday, October 14 at the University of San Carlos – Downtown Campus from 1 pm to 4 pm.

The forum aims to define and assess urban liveability through the lens of local Cebu realities and key challenges like urban flooding, waste management, and disaster recovery following Typhoon Tino (Kalmaegi) and the 6.9 magnitude earthquake in 2025, among others.

It also seeks to put the spotlight on the role of the community as civic watchdogs and empower local civic leaders and residents to define the agenda for a liveable Cebu.

This event is supported by the Government of Canada through its Canada Fund for Local Initiatives and by the Journalism for Nation Building Foundation.

It is organized in partnership with the University of San Carlos (USC), including the USC Political Science and Governance Department, School of Law and Governance, Carolinian Political Science Society, Department of Communication, Languages, & Literature, School of Arts and Sciences (SAS), and The Scire; the University of the Philippines Cebu (UP Cebu), including its College of Communication, Art, and Design (CCAD) and Office of Student Affairs (OSA); JCI Cebu; and Cebu Citizens Initiative.

This page will be updated with the full program. Refresh this page for updates.

Tickets to the public forum are free, but seats are limited.

Register below until Monday, October 9:

Ahead of the forum, attendees must download the Muni app, available on Google Play and App Store, to actively collaborate in the conversation during and even after the forum.

The public forum is the first of several activities under #MoveCebu, bringing together citizens, civic leaders, young journalists, and community organizations to translate conversations into community action beyond the event.

Be more involved by joining the MovePH network

MovePH is also opening applications for the Movers Program, a volunteer network of changemakers that seeks to bring meaningful change to their community through storytelling and civic action.

Movers help tell stories from their communities, organize civic initiatives, and connect with other people and organizations working on local issues. Through the program, community journalists and leaders can develop their storytelling and community organizing skills while also amplifying local voices and initiatives.

Those interested to be a Cebu Mover may apply here.

Shortlisted applicants will be contacted and must attend the online sessions on October 2 and 9; and on-site training/workshops in Cebu City on October 15 and 16 at the University of San Carlos.

During the Move workshops for Movers, participants will learn the ropes of effective storytelling or reporting and organizing community advocacies, including connecting with possible collaborators; and ultimately, inspiring courage. Certificates will also be provided.

Connect with local organizations

#MoveCebu will also be organizing a partners’ gathering on Friday, October 16 at 1 pm. Representatives of local community organizations who are interested in collaborating with MovePH may indicate their interest through the public forum registration form above.

From the public forum to the Movers workshops and partners’ gathering, #MoveCebu aims to create spaces for Cebu residents and civic groups to exchange ideas, build connections, and find ways to take civic action in their communities.

Interested in partnering with us or want Rappler to visit your region? Email move.ph@rappler.com – Rappler.com

World.title: Saclag gets golden shot, Alvarez bags bronze as MMA fighters shine in Asian Games
World.content:
FIGHTERS. Filipino mixed martial arts standouts Jean Claude Saclag (right) and Carlos Alvarez in action in the 2026 Asian Games.

Jean Claude Saclag advances to the final as he earns a chance to either match or surpass the silver medal he won in wushu in the 2014 edition, while Carlos Alvarez secures a bronze despite falling in the semifinals

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino mixed martial artists (MMA) contributed to the Philippines’ medal cause in the Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, as Jean Claude Saclag earned a shot at the gold, while Carlos Alvarez bagged bronze on Monday, September 21.

Saclag will fight for the top prize after a unanimous decision win over home bet Daisuke Murayama in the semifinals of the men’s traditional -65kg class at the Nagoya City Inae Sports Center.

A three-time Southeast Asian Games in kickboxing, Saclag will face Tajikistan’s Otabek Rajabov in the final on Tuesday, September 22.

By reaching the finale, Saclag — a pride of Kalinga and Benguet — gets a chance to either match or surpass the silver medal he won in the 2014 edition in Incheon, South Korea, where he represented the country in wushu.

Meanwhile, Alvarez secured a bronze despite a technical knockout loss to Kazakhstan’s Yerkingali Burkutalin in the semifinals of the men’s traditional -77kg division.

Alvarez assured himself of a medal by making the final four following a victory over Indonesia’s Ananda Wahyu Setyo Prabowo in the quarterfinals.

The Philippines officially now has two bronzes, the first one coming from the women’s soft tennis team of Bien Zoleta, Princess Catindig, Hilary Paas, Shyryn Salazar, Christy Sañosa. – Rappler.com

World.title: Before ASEAN gold, Baguio spent 60 years fighting smoke
World.content:
FIGHTING SMOKE. Baguio City workers install a sign reminding residents and visitors that smoking and vaping are prohibited under the city’s smoke-free ordinance.

In its long history of tobacco control, Baguio City has treated tobacco use as the public health issue that it is, and not merely as an enforcement issue

BAGUIO, Philippines – Long before Baguio won gold from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) for keeping its public spaces smoke-free, the city was already telling people where they could not light a cigarette.

That story began in 1966.

Sixty years later, a succession of ordinances, tougher enforcement, community participation, and public health programs has turned what began as a smoking ban inside theaters and movie houses into one of the region’s recognized local tobacco-control programs.

The latest recognition came last September 10, when Baguio received the Gold Award at the second ASEAN Smoke-Free Awards.

It capped a remarkable run that includes a World Health Organization Healthy Cities award for the Smoke-Free Baguio campaign in 2021, a Bloomberg Philanthropies tobacco-control award in 2025, the WHO World No Tobacco Day Award in 2026, and, just days before the ASEAN ceremony, another WHO Healthy Cities award for the city’s use of local data to address health and social inequities.

But Baguio’s smoke-free story was built over decades, not around a single ordinance or administration.

When it all started

The city’s earliest documented anti-smoking measure was Ordinance No. 433 in September 1966, which prohibited smoking inside theaters and movie houses.

In 1974, Ordinance No. 596 extended restrictions to public utility vehicles.

The city widened the coverage again in 1989 through Ordinance No. 24, which included public conveyances, theaters, assembly halls, hospital rooms and corridors, government offices, and classrooms.

Restaurants and eateries were eventually brought under local smoking regulations, while later amendments strengthened requirements such as posting anti-smoking signs.

By 2008, Baguio had adopted Ordinance No. 8, known as the Comprehensive Anti-Smoking Ordinance.

It prohibited smoking in public transportation, government vehicles, accommodation and entertainment establishments, public buildings, public places, and other enclosed areas outside private residences and certain private workplaces, while allowing designated smoking areas under prescribed conditions.

The rules had become broader. Enforcement remained the harder part.

City health officials continued to push for stronger regulations and tighter controls on tobacco sales, advertising, and newer nicotine products.

But the major shift came in 2017.

Turning point

The City Council passed Ordinance No. 34, Series of 2017, principally authored by then councilor Joel Alangsab.

The Smoke-Free Baguio City Ordinance amended the 2008 law and went beyond simply determining where a person could smoke.

It covered cigarettes and electronic cigarettes, prohibited smoking or vaping in covered public places, workplaces, and public conveyances except in duly approved designated smoking areas, restricted tobacco advertising and promotion, regulated sales, and sought to limit children’s access to tobacco.

It also provided the framework for the Smoke-Free Baguio Task Force.

This is why describing Baguio simply as a city where smoking is “totally banned” is inaccurate.

Smoking remains allowed in certain private spaces and in designated smoking areas that comply with city requirements. The ordinance instead made smoke-free public spaces the norm and placed stricter conditions on where tobacco and vaping products could be used, sold, and promoted.

The city formally launched the Smoke-Free Baguio campaign in November 2017 and intensified implementation in 2018.

Enforcement eventually moved beyond city hall, police, and the Public Order and Safety Division. Community and district task forces were organized, while barangay personnel and other local enforcers were trained to help monitor compliance.

Baguio also treated tobacco use as a public health problem, not merely an enforcement issue.

The program included information campaigns, inspections, smoking-cessation services, school and community initiatives, and partnerships with government agencies, civil society, and the private sector.

In November 2018, the Department of Health, Philippine Economic Zone Authority, and WHO launched the Revolution Smoke-Free campaign at the Baguio City Economic Zone, bringing the effort into workplaces and encouraging smokers to quit.

The results eventually began showing in the numbers.

City epidemiologist Dr. Donna Panes has reported a steep decline in cigarette smoking in Baguio, although published reports have used different survey years and datasets.

One city presentation placed adult smoking prevalence at 31.9% in 2014 and 8.9% by 2022.

Among young people, local tobacco surveys showed cigarette smoking falling from 28.13% in 2014 to 5.29% in 2023.

Enforcement figures also moved downward.

As we reported in Rappler in June, violations of the city’s smoke-free ordinance have generally declined from the high levels recorded during the early years of intensified enforcement, although authorities continue to catch violators and confiscate prohibited tobacco and vaping products.

Recognition soon followed.

In 2021, Baguio received a WHO Healthy Cities Recognition Award for its Smoke-Free Baguio campaign under the theme “Sharing Clean Air: Committed to multisectoral implementation of smoke-free laws.”

The award recognized not just the ordinance but the involvement of different sectors in implementing it.

Four years later, Baguio became one of six recipients of the 2025 Bloomberg Philanthropies Awards for Global Tobacco Control.

The city was recognized under the “M” component of WHO’s MPOWER tobacco-control framework, which focuses on monitoring tobacco use and prevention policies. Mayor Benjamin Magalong received the award during the World Conference on Tobacco Control in Dublin, Ireland, in June 2025.

Then, in May 2026, Baguio was named a recipient of the WHO World No Tobacco Day Award.

WHO cited the city government of Baguio for sustained leadership in keeping public places free from tobacco and e-cigarette use through consistent enforcement, public education, and partnerships with civil society and academic institutions.

The honor came as the city confronted a problem that barely figured in its early anti-smoking ordinances: vaping.

Magalong has pushed for a nationwide prohibition on vape products, citing their health risks, particularly to young people.

“We clearly and explicitly stipulated [that] we are highly recommending a total ban for vape because of the serious health issues,” he said in June after authorities confirmed that marijuana-laced vape devices had been found in a Baguio school.

Health officials have also raised concerns about electronic smoking devices being marketed to young people, sold online, passed among friends, or designed to resemble everyday objects.

In February 2026, the city destroyed about P5 million worth of confiscated cigarettes and vape products accumulated since August 2024, including products seized from schools.

Fewer cigarette smokers, in other words, did not mean the tobacco and nicotine problem had disappeared. It had changed.

Beyond smoke-free Baguio

By September, another WHO recognition showed how Baguio’s public health work had expanded beyond tobacco.

On September 1, the city received the “Data for Equity: Informing Action, Improving Health” award under the 2026 WHO Healthy Cities Recognition Awards during the 11th Global Conference of the Alliance for Healthy Cities in Sydney, Australia.

City Epidemiology and Surveillance Unit chief Donna Panes received the award on behalf of Baguio.

This time, the recognition was for the city’s barangay-level Livability Index, an initiative spearheaded by the City Planning, Development and Sustainability Office headed by Donna Rillera Tabangin.

The index maps disparities in health, social conditions, and access to basic services across Baguio’s barangays, allowing planners to see which communities face greater challenges instead of treating the city as one uniform population.

The findings are being integrated into planning, budgeting, and investment decisions so interventions and resources can be directed to communities where they are most needed.

That is precisely the kind of work the WHO award category was designed to recognize. The 2026 criteria emphasize using neighborhood-level and other disaggregated data to identify health inequities, guide policy and resource allocation, and turn evidence into concrete action.

For Baguio, there is a clear connection between the two Healthy Cities awards.

The 2021 recognition grew from years of gathering tobacco data, enforcing local policy, and bringing communities and institutions into the Smoke-Free Baguio campaign. The 2026 award shows the same evidence-based approach being used more broadly to understand how health and living conditions differ from one barangay to another.

Nine days after receiving the Sydney award, Baguio returned to where much of that public health story had begun.

At the second ASEAN Smoke-Free Awards on September 10, the city received the Gold Award, ahead of George Town in Penang, Malaysia, which received silver.

Baguio became the second Philippine city to win the ASEAN smoke-free gold after Iloilo City took the top award in the inaugural competition in 2024.

The gold does not mean the work is finished.

People are still caught smoking where they should not. Vape products have created new enforcement and health challenges, particularly among the young. Online selling and constantly changing product designs have made regulation more difficult than when Baguio’s first anti-smoking ordinance was written.

Still, the distance between 1966 and 2026 is worth remembering.

Baguio’s ASEAN gold did not begin with the 2017 ordinance, the launch of a campaign, or an international award.

It began with a much narrower rule six decades ago telling people not to smoke inside theaters and movie houses.

Today, the laws are broader, the evidence is better, and the challenge includes products that did not exist when the city started.

The basic idea remains remarkably simple: the air people share is also a matter of public health. – Rappler.com

World.title: 10 Filipino Artists Reimagine Democracy Across Philippine Islands through “Sprints”
World.content:
What does democracy look like when artists stop illustrating it as it is and start reimagining it as it could be? How can every person see and feel democracy as a lived experience daily?

From August 21 to 23, 2026, a dynamic mix of emerging, mid-career, and established Filipino illustrators and visual artists from across Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao came together for SPRINTS, a 48-hr challenge and creative bootcamp for artists in various cities around the world to imagine new possibilities for democracy through art.

This year’s global theme, Reimagining Democracy, asked a simple question: What if democracy could be different?

Rather than illustrating democracy through its familiar symbols and institutions, artists Cyrill Acuña, Jill Arteche, Alyssa Babasa, Maki Cabrera, Anjella Cruz, Ed Empemano, Ish Flores, Kieltokki, Kirsten Mago, and Ruer Torculas were invited to imagine new ways for people to participate, deliberate, decide, and shape the societies they live in. Over one productive weekend, they turned ideas into images, questions into visual narratives, and possibilities into something people could actually see.

SPRINTS in the Philippines was organized by DAKILA – Philippine Collective for Modern Heroism, in collaboration with global creative studio Fine Acts and the One World or None initiative. The Philippine edition held in the community space of Alon and Araw forms part of a global SPRINTS movement spanning more than 10 countries, bringing artists together around urgent social questions and giving them the space to respond through their own creative language.

The SPRINTS artworks are now being presented simultaneously across three creative spaces in the Philippines. Rather than being confined to traditional gallery spaces, the exhibitions use outdoor displays and banner formats to bring the artworks directly into public spaces and make them accessible to pedestrians and wider audiences.

LUZON — Commune, Metro Manila

VISAYAS — Arts and Design Collective, Dumaguete

MINDANAO — La Herencia, Davao

Together, these exhibitions form a kind of creative flag planted across the archipelago: a declaration from Filipino artists that democracy is not a finished picture. It is something we can question, redraw, and build again.

Elvin Macanlalay, Creative Director of DAKILA, on how else artists can express their perception of democracy.

“The outdoors, the banner material, and the overall exhibit design are also intended as a way to reimagine democracy. Particularly, with the idea of art having more open access to the public, in contrast to the traditional white-walled spaces which can unintentionally be exclusive,” Macanlalay added.

The public exhibition runs for the entire month of September and features works created by the 10 SPRINTS artists, alongside five collaborative works produced during the bootcamp. The exhibitions also feature additional works from homegrown artists at each location, including Red Genotiva and Noi Narciso from Davao, as well as guest artists from different cities and provinces, including Jonas Tugab, Cleo Manansala, and Airish Tayag.

Together, the exhibitions present not one singular vision of democracy, but many—bringing together different places, perspectives, experiences, and imaginations through simultaneous satellite exhibitions across the country.

“By bringing in this kind of art activation format in our country and intentionally contextualizing it on a local and community level, we have created a more grounding space to work on something genuinely close to most people’s lived experiences during a critical period wherein our democracy should be felt and not just remain as discussion points within the confines of high-profile symposiums, international convenings, and the like. SPRINTS demonstrates that artists can truly reimagine systems, spark dialogue, and make complex ideas more accessible and engaging,” said Ralph Eya, Artist-organizer and SPRINTS Coordinator in the Philippines.

All artworks created through SPRINTS are published under an open license on TheGreats.co, the global platform for free social-impact visuals. The works can be freely used and adapted for non-commercial purposes by activists, educators, nonprofits, journalists, and community organizations around the world, allowing these ideas to travel far beyond the exhibition walls.

“SPRINTS ultimately asks artists to do what artists have always done: look at the world we have been given, then dare to picture another one. True to working with One World or None, as a statement in its own name, this September 15, 2026, across Luzon, Visayas, and Mindanao, those pictures go one with the public,” Eya concluded.

The works invite audiences to look beyond democracy as ballots, elections, governments, and institutions, and toward the everyday spaces where people negotiate how they live together. Through their varied perspectives and visual languages, the artists imagine democracy as something more participatory, more deliberative, more human, and perhaps more possible than the versions inherited today.

Elvin Jay Macanlalay

DAKILA

elvin@dakila.org.ph

09666745544

ABOUT DAKILA



DAKILA is an organization of artists-activists, educators, and individuals building a movement of heroism toward social transformation. It fosters active citizenship by building one’s capacity to make change, organizing communities to be part of the movement for change, and leading advocacy campaigns that bring about strategic actions for real change.

World.title: FACT CHECK: Tito Sotto quote calling for VP Sara’s conviction without evidence is fake
World.content:
A similar false claim about Sotto supposedly calling for the rules to be bypassed to promptly convict Duterte surfaced in August

Claim: Senator Vicente “Tito” Sotto III called for the conviction of Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment trial even without valid evidence.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: Facebook user Jonathan Ornoza 2.0 posted Sotto’s supposed statement, labeled as “breaking news.”

The post reads, “Gusto ni Sotto i-convict agad si Sara kahit walang valid na ebidensya! ‘Wag na daw sumunod sa rules dahil ito daw ang nais ng taumbayan.”

(Sotto wants to convict Sara immediately, even without valid evidence! He says there’s no need to follow the rules because that is supposedly what the people want.)

The user then reacted to Sotto’s supposed remark: “Ang kapal naman ng pagmumukha mo… Kaya nga ginawa ‘yang rules na ‘yan para sundin, tapos kayo, di niyo susundin?”

(You got some nerve… Those rules were made to be followed, yet you won’t follow them?)

The post has 49,100 reactions, 14,900 comments, and 7,500 shares as of writing.

The facts: There are no public reports, statements, or interviews proving that Sotto said this.

“That’s fake news. I have never issued any statement about the impeachment court at all,” Sotto confirmed to Rappler through a message on Friday, September 18.

He added: “I have been exercising judicial ethics and restraint since day one. I have never even allowed any interviews.”

A similar false claim about Sotto supposedly calling for Duterte’s conviction without due process surfaced in August, which was already debunked. Fake quotes of Sotto related to the Senate impeachment trial have also been previously fact-checked.

Back when he was Senate president and preparing to receive the articles of impeachment from the lower house, Sotto had urged fellow senators to stay impartial, saying that the Senate should “follow the Constitution” and convene as an impeachment court upon receiving the articles of impeachment.

The Senate convened as an impeachment court in May. The trial is now on its 12th week since it began on July 6.

Conviction: Duterte was impeached by the House of Representatives in May 2026 on the grounds of alleged betrayal of public trust, culpable violation of the Constitution, bribery, graft and corruption, and other high crimes. (LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte)

Based on Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution, the conviction of an impeachable official such as the Vice President requires the concurrence of two-thirds of all of the members of the Senate. At the start of the impeachment trial, presiding officer Senator Chiz Escudero set the conviction threshold at 16 senators. However, the required vote count is currently under deliberation, with the Senate impeachment court consulting four retired Supreme Court justices to define the conviction threshold.

Three of the four former justices concluded that the number of votes is not fixed at 16, saying the two-thirds requirement does not automatically mean the denominator is 24.

The justices said senators who are absent due to “some legal impediment or restraints” should not be included in the vote count. Currently, Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained over separate plunder cases; Senator Ronald “Bato” Dela Rosa is evading an International Criminal Court arrest warrant; and Senator Loren Legarda has been on medical leave.

The senator-judges are set to hold a caucus on Monday, September 21, to discuss the disputed 16-vote threshold. – Eirene Manatlao/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Prosecution: Sara Duterte firms’ zero dividends a ‘mismatch’ from her net worth
World.content:
TRIAL. Securities and Exchange Commission Director Gerardo del Rosario takes the witness stand in the trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 21, 2026.

(1st UPDATE) 'Why is her worth so high if she is not receiving anything from these companies, or if these companies are incurring losses?' prosecution spokesman Zia Adiong says

MANILA, Philippines – The prosecution team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte examined Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) documents on Monday, September 21, to establish that companies associated with her declared no dividends, a business picture that does not align with her increasing net worth over the years.

Gencorp, one of the companies which Duterte said she is a stockholder according to her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), had reported sales of P1.04 billion from 2021 to 2024, but only a net income of P8 million. It had zero dividends.

Another company, Metro City Chow, posted sales of P309.01 million from 2017 to 2025, and a net loss of P3.15 million during the same period. No dividends were also declared.

“There is no income coming back to her. Why is this important? Because we will compare her corporate earnings and dividends as a shareholder against what she declares in her SALN. Why is her worth so high if she is not receiving anything from these companies, or if these companies are incurring losses?” prosecution spokesman Zia Alonto Adiong said in Filipino.

“The question of the public is: why are you doing business if you are continuously incurring losses? If you are continuously losing money, then why are your net worth and assets increasing?” Adiong added.

At least eight other companies tied to her or her husband also had no dividends declared, according to SEC documents.

Duterte declared a net worth of P71 million in 2022, the year she became vice president, but she has become wealthier since. Her net worth as of 2025 was P98 million.

Private prosecutor Erwin Matib also noted the repeated mention of Jaime T. Cruz in the SEC documents, although it has yet to fully articulate why this is relevant. Cruz was appointed special envoy to China in 2019 by then-president Rodrigo Duterte.

Play Video

The testimony of SEC company registration director Gerardo del Rosario is part of the ongoing effort by the prosecution to establish that Duterte had unexplained wealth.

Since last week, the prosecution has repeatedly pointed out that Duterte’s participation in businesses while in office is in violation of a constitutional provision that explicitly prohibits such a conflict of interest.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Jollibee extends ‘Forgotten Island’ film experience from the big screen to everyday moments
World.content:
The collab starts with sharing a song in the soundtrack by BINI and a teaser for exclusive Jollibee offers tied to the film

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Jollibee and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

Jollibee is marking a milestone with its global collaboration with DreamWorks Animation for the worldwide theatrical release of Forgotten Island on September 23.

At the heart of Forgotten Island are lifelong best friends Jo and Raissa, who discover a mysterious portal that transports them to Nakali, a fantastical island filled with mythical creatures inspired by stories from their Filipino families. When they discover that returning home could come at the cost of losing the memories of their friendship, Jo and Raissa must find a way to leave the island without forgetting each other.

Forgotten Island features Filipino and Filipino-American talent including Tony Award-winning Lea Salonga, global comedy star Jo Koy, Grammy and Academy Award-winning H.E.R., actress Liza Soberano, and co-writer and co-director Januel Mercado.

“Great stories and great food both have a way of bringing people together,” said David Beal, Jollibee Group global chief marketing officer and head of digital marketing. “With DreamWorks Animation’s Forgotten Island, we’re inviting friends and families to celebrate the joy of friendship—from watching the film to sharing a delicious Jollibee meal together. It is a simple expression of what Jollibee has always stood for: serving great-tasting food and bringing the joy of eating to everyone.”

The Filipino connection extends beyond the film with Filipino girl group BINI, who are also Jollibee endorsers, contributing the song “A Parallel World” to the Forgotten Island soundtrack. The upbeat electronic-pop track, which features English and Filipino lyrics, was released on July 23.

BINI also performed the song at the Forgotten Island panel during San Diego Comic-Con in July, further connecting the group and the film with audiences around the world. The music video for “A Parallel World” also features Jollibee, showing members of BINI enjoying their favorite meals and sharing candid moments while in the United States for the song’s recording and related activities.

“At Jollibee, we value partnerships that allow us to collaborate with world-class brands and create experiences that genuinely resonate with our customers,” said Dorothy Ching, vice president for marketing of Jollibee Philippines. “Our partnership with DreamWorks is especially meaningful because Forgotten Island brings together universal themes of friendship and family with Filipino-inspired storytelling. We are proud to be part of this global collaboration and excited to bring the spirit of the film to Jollibee communities around the world.”

The Jollibee and Forgotten Island collaboration brings together global entertainment, Filipino talent and storytelling, and Jollibee’s own spirit of togetherness, extending the experience from the big screen to everyday moments shared over a meal.

More elements of the collaboration are set to be revealed, including an exclusive Jollibee offer tied to the film. Details will be announced at a later date.

DreamWorks’ Forgotten Island arrives in theaters September 23.

For more information, visit https://www.jollibee.com.ph/ or follow Jollibee’s social media channels for updates. – Rappler.com

World.title: From Astana Events to Xi’an Rail Links, Kazakhstan Expands Tourism Reach
World.content:
ASTANA – Nearly 830,000 tourists visited Astana in the first half of 2026, a 12% increase from the same period last year, as Kazakhstan’s capital expands its tourism offering and strengthens international connectivity, including through a new tourist train linking China and Kazakhstan.

Of the total visitors to Astana, about 187,000 were foreign tourists, Deputy Mayor of Astana Yevgeniy Glotov said at the opening of the Kazakhstan Travel Forum 2026 in the capital on Sept. 18.

According to him, Astana is developing several segments of tourism, including business, cultural, medical and event tourism. The capital receives more than 1.6 million tourists annually, with visitor numbers growing by an average of 10–12% each year.

“Astana has long ceased to be a city that people visit only for work. More than 1.6 million tourists visit the capital every year, and this flow is growing by an average of 10–12% annually. Today, our task is to make sure that a guest who comes to Astana for a concert or business meeting stays here longer and returns again. Cities around the world are competing for this kind of tourist today, and Astana is actively participating in this competition,” he said.

Event tourism remains one of the city’s key priorities. International concerts, sporting competitions and major business and cultural events are being used to attract additional visitors and encourage them to extend their stays.

The city is also expanding its tourism infrastructure, with new attractions and international hotel brands adding to its offer.

Xi’an–Almaty tourist train strengthens China links

Meanwhile, Kazakhstan is expanding its railway tourism connections with China. An international tourist train operating on the Xi’an–Almaty route arrived in Almaty after departing from the Chinese city of Xi’an on Sept. 14. The route passes through northwestern China and Xinjiang along the historic Silk Road before crossing the Kazakhstan–China border at Khorgos.

Passenger transportation within Kazakhstan is provided by Passenger Transportation, which has established a special timetable for the international service to account for border procedures and the connection between the railway systems of the two countries.

“Developing tourist trains is of strategic importance to us. Railways make it possible to create comprehensive tourist routes, connecting cities, regions, historical and natural sites. Our task is to jointly develop this format with foreign partners, expand the geography of travel across Kazakhstan and create a quality tourism product for passengers,” said Anuar Akhmetzhanov, chairman of Passenger Transportation.

A cultural and sightseeing programme has been prepared for the Chinese tourists arriving in Almaty. The itinerary includes the Independence Monument, the 28 Panfilov Guardsmen Park, the Ascension Cathedral, the Central Mosque, Kok-Tobe, Shymbulak, the Central State Museum and other attractions.

The Xi’an–Almaty international tourist train was first launched by the Chinese side in 2025. In June 2026, the first service using Kazakhstan’s national carrier’s trains was operated. The current service is the second such trip this year.

World.title: B5+Italy Turns Italy’s Central Asia Strategy Into Working Platform
World.content:
The launch of B5+Italy in Astana matters because it gives Italy and the five Central Asian states a standing mechanism to turn last year’s summit diplomacy into investment, industrial partnerships, and regional economic cooperation.

The Central Asia-Italy Business Forum may look like another event in the region’s crowded calendar of international meetings. Its significance, however, lies in what it creates between high-level summits: a platform linking governments, businesses, and economic institutions around practical projects in energy, critical minerals, manufacturing, agriculture, transport, and the Middle Corridor.

B5+Italy is a direct follow-up to the first Central Asia–Italy summit, held in Astana in May 2025, which brought together Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and the leaders of the five Central Asian countries. Italy’s Foreign Ministry has presented the forum as a way to convert that political momentum into investment, industrial cooperation, and new opportunities for companies.

That shift from political declarations to an institutional mechanism capable of producing commercial results is why B5+Italy matters.

From summit diplomacy to economic infrastructure

The 2025 summit was an important political signal. It demonstrated that Italy sees Central Asia not as five separate markets, but increasingly as a region with common strategic and economic potential.

But political summits, however important, do not automatically generate commercial integration.

The more difficult question is what happens between summits.

This is precisely where B5+Italy could become consequential. The new platform is intended to facilitate regular dialogue between governments and businesses, support the preparation of joint investment projects, and expand direct contacts between companies from Italy and Central Asia. Priority areas include industrial production, critical minerals, energy, agribusiness, transport infrastructure, connectivity, and the Middle Corridor.

Italy already has a substantial economic presence in the region. Italian-Central Asian trade grew by 46.5 percent between 2019 and 2025, according to Italy’s Foreign Ministry. Rome increasingly sees Central Asia as a market of roughly 80 million people located at the crossroads of Europe and Asia.

The challenge now is to turn this growing interest into a deeper and more diversified economic relationship.

The real obstacle is not political will

There is no shortage of political support for stronger Italy–Central Asia relations. The more fundamental question is whether companies can operate across borders with sufficient predictability and manageable transaction costs.

For businesses, connectivity is not limited to railways, ports, and logistics corridors. It also means customs procedures, regulatory requirements, certification, investment protection, financing mechanisms, access to information, and the ability to identify reliable local partners.

This makes the simplification of procedures for business cooperation one of the most important issues on the agenda.

The launch of B5+Italy creates an opportunity to address precisely these practical barriers. If the platform can help companies navigate administrative procedures, identify partners, and move from initial discussions toward concrete projects, it could develop into something more significant than a traditional business forum.

The question should therefore not simply be how much Italy and Central Asia trade today.

The more important question is: what prevents that trade and investment relationship from becoming significantly larger?

A role for think tanks

There is also an important space between government and business that should not be overlooked: independent policy research, education, and skills development.

Italian officials have expressed interest in continuing the dialogue through a think-tank format that could bring together policymakers, businesses, academics, and experts from Italy and Central Asia. Such a forum could help identify common priorities not only in trade and investment, but also in research, education, and human-capital development.

This matters because the next stage of Central Asia’s economic development will depend not only on capital and infrastructure, but also on qualified people, technological expertise, and stronger links between universities, research institutions, and industry.

A structured expert dialogue could therefore provide an additional bridge between political ambitions and practical cooperation.

The next test: ministerial diplomacy

The next important step will be the planned ministerial engagement between Italy and the five Central Asian countries.

Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has already expressed his intention to organize a new ministerial meeting with the five countries in order to further strengthen dialogue and cooperation.

Such a meeting could help move the agenda from broad political support toward implementation: investment facilitation, trade procedures, connectivity, critical minerals, industrial partnerships, agriculture, technology, and energy.

It would also provide another opportunity to prepare the political ground for the next Central Asia–Italy summit, which is planned to take place in the Kyrgyz Republic in 2027. The decision to hold the next leaders’ meeting in the Kyrgyz Republic was included in the joint declaration adopted at the 2025 summit.

If this sequence develops as intended — business platform, ministerial dialogue, and then a second leaders’ summit — Italy and Central Asia will have created something increasingly valuable in international diplomacy: continuity between high-level political meetings.

Italy is part of a larger transformation

The significance of B5+Italy becomes even clearer when viewed against the wider transformation of Central Asia’s external relations.

The region has witnessed a rapid expansion of the C5+1 model, through which external powers engage the five Central Asian states collectively.

The latest example came only days before the Italy–Central Asia business forum.

On Sept. 16, South Korea hosted the first Central Asia–Republic of Korea summit, bringing together the leaders of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan with the South Korean president. The summit focused heavily on critical minerals, energy, supply chains, industrial cooperation, technology, and investment. More than 70 agreements and memoranda were reportedly concluded during the broader summit process.

The significance of the Korean example is not simply the number of agreements.

It demonstrates that the C5 format is becoming increasingly useful as an instrument through which external powers can engage Central Asia as a regional economic space.

This does not mean that Central Asia is becoming a formal bloc. The five countries retain different economic structures, national priorities, and foreign-policy interests. Bilateral relations will remain essential.

But the regional format is becoming complementary to bilateral diplomacy.

For external partners, it offers access to a larger regional market and a coordinated political dialogue. For the Central Asian states, it provides an additional mechanism for presenting regional priorities and attracting investment, technology, and expertise.

Competition is creating opportunity

The growing number of C5+1 initiatives also reflects a broader change in how the world perceives Central Asia.

The region is increasingly relevant to discussions about supply-chain diversification, critical minerals, energy security, transport connectivity, food security, and new trade routes between Europe and Asia.

Italy has a potentially distinctive role in this process.

It is not simply another external power seeking access to Central Asian resources. Italy has considerable industrial and manufacturing expertise, strong agricultural and engineering capabilities, logistics companies, and a large network of small and medium-sized enterprises.

At the same time, Central Asian economies are looking for partners capable of providing not only capital, but also technology, industrial expertise, and access to international value chains.

The potential complementarity is therefore considerable.

But potential alone is not enough.

The real test of B5+Italy will be whether it can help businesses overcome the practical barriers that currently stand between political agreements and commercial projects.

A quiet but important milestone

The Astana forum therefore deserves to be viewed as more than another business gathering.

Its importance lies in the institutional architecture being built around it.

The 2025 leaders’ summit created political momentum. B5+Italy creates an economic mechanism. The forthcoming ministerial dialogue can provide political direction. A possible think-tank track can help generate ideas and identify areas of convergence. And the planned 2027 summit in the Kyrgyz Republic can consolidate the progress made.

Taken together, these developments suggest that Italy–Central Asia relations are moving from episodic diplomacy toward a more continuous partnership.

The development is also significant for Central Asia itself.

As more global and middle powers return to the region with concrete economic proposals, the C5 format is gaining practical value. The question is no longer simply whether Central Asia can attract international attention. It is increasingly about whether the five countries can use that attention to build mutually beneficial projects, diversify external partnerships, and strengthen their collective economic position.

The launch of B5+Italy may have passed relatively quietly in the international media. But beneath the headlines, a more important process is underway: the gradual construction of a denser network of institutions linking Central Asia with the major economic centers of Europe and Asia.

For Italy, the task is to turn political interest into business reality.

For Central Asia, the task is to ensure that growing international competition translates into investment, technology, industrial capacity, skills, and greater connectivity.

And for the C5 format, the expanding number of external partnerships suggests that its most important phase may only now be beginning.

The authors are Sapargali Shalgimbayev, the president of the CFive Intellectual Platform, and Domenico Palmieri, the secretary general of the Italian Institute for Asia (ISIA).

The article is published as part of the partnership between The Astana Times and CFive think tank.

World.title: Making of World No. 1: Elena Rybakina’s Journey
World.content:
ASTANA – On Sept. 12, Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina defeated Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 in the US Open final to claim the third Grand Slam title of her career.

The victory ended Sabalenka’s 19-match winning streak at the tournament and completed a remarkable rise for Rybakina. A few days before that, she became the world No. 1, the 30th woman in WTA history to reach the top of the rankings and the first player representing Kazakhstan to do so.

Rybakina had technically secured the No. 1 ranking before the final, after defeating Zheng Qinwen in the quarterfinals. But winning the title made the achievement even more significant.

It was also an unexpected conclusion to a tournament that had begun with uncertainty. Rybakina arrived in New York after spending a week away from the court because of a left-foot injury. She had retired during the first set of her Cincinnati match against Iga Swiatek, and that tournament could have given her an earlier opportunity to reach the top of the rankings.

Instead, she reached No. 1 in New York.

“I don’t want to put too much pressure on myself,” Rybakina said before the final, explaining that regardless of the result, she would still have other opportunities ahead.

The Grand Slam

Before 2026, the US Open was Rybakina’s least successful Grand Slam tournament.

Across eight previous appearances, she had never advanced beyond the fourth round. This time, however, she defeated Thea Frodin, Jessica Bouzas Maneiro and Yuliia Starodubtseva before overcoming former champion Naomi Osaka.

Her quarterfinal against Zheng Qinwen became another test of her ability to recover. Rybakina lost the opening set but fought back to win the match.

The semifinal against Coco Gauff followed a similar pattern. After losing the first set 3-6, Rybakina won the next two 6-4, 6-4 to reach her first US Open final.

Three consecutive comeback victories were significant for a player whose game has often been associated with a straightforward formula: a powerful serve, flat groundstrokes and an aggressive style of play.

In New York, she demonstrated another side of her game: the ability to adapt, recover and win when a match does not follow her preferred script.

A tennis player almost by accident

Rybakina was born in Moscow on June 17, 1999. She initially tried several sports with her elder sister Anna, including gymnastics and figure skating. Tennis came later.

Because of her height, gymnastics and figure skating eventually became less suitable, and her father, who was interested in tennis, suggested that she try the sport. She was six years old.

Rybakina trained first at Dynamo and later at Spartak, where she worked with former Top-10 player Andrei Chesnokov and former world No. 100 Evgenia Kulikovskaya.

For years, she did not have an individual coach. Until the age of 15, she trained in a group of around eight players and later in a smaller group of four.

Her daily schedule also looked different from that of many young elite athletes. She spent roughly two hours on tennis and another three hours on physical preparation while attending a regular school rather than a specialized sports school.

This became an important part of her development. Rybakina was not raised through one of the highly structured tennis academies that produce professional players from an early age. Much of the work that would eventually turn her into an elite athlete came later.

From junior success to an uncertain future

Rybakina entered the ITF junior circuit in November 2013, at the age of 14.

Her strongest junior season came in 2017. By the end of that season, she was ranked No. 3 in the world among juniors. But her path was not always smooth.

At the 2016 US Open junior tournament, Rybakina fainted because of low hemoglobin and withdrew in the first round. According to her account, her family did not receive sufficient assistance from representatives of the Russian Tennis Federation at the tournament.

After the incident, her parents decided that she would no longer travel to tournaments without them.

That created another problem: the cost.

Professional tennis requires constant travel, accommodation, coaching and tournament expenses. Her family could not indefinitely finance that lifestyle on its own.

As a result, Rybakina and her family seriously considered another route of moving to the United States or Canada, studying at a university and playing college tennis.

For a teenager who would eventually become world No. 1, a professional tennis career was still far from guaranteed.

The decision that changed her career

In 2018, shortly before turning 19, Rybakina received Kazakh citizenship and switched her sporting representation from Russia to Kazakhstan.

The initiative came from her father, Andrey Rybakin, who was born in Almaty. He contacted the Kazakhstan Tennis Federation, which offered financial support in exchange for her representing Kazakhstan.

Rybakina chose that opportunity instead of pursuing university tennis in the U.S.

The change affected her career in practical ways. The support allowed her to travel to tournaments, build a professional team and most importantly, work with a full-time coach who could accompany her on the tour.

In February 2019, Croatian coach Stefano Vukov became her coach. He was the first coach in her career to regularly travel with her to tournaments.

Rybakina later described Kazakhstan’s support as crucial.

“They believed in me,” she said in an interview with the WTA. “I was not so good when they offered. So they believed in me and they’re helping me a lot.”

The decision therefore meant more than simply changing the flag next to her name in the rankings. It came at a moment when Rybakina had to decide whether tennis would remain an after-school activity or become her profession. With Kazakhstan’s support, she chose the latter.

The first signs of a breakthrough

Rybakina’s first major breakthrough on the WTA Tour came in St. Petersburg in 2018.

After winning her first WTA-level match, she moved up from around No. 450 to No. 268. The following year brought an even bigger step. In July 2019, Rybakina won her first WTA title in Bucharest, which pushed her into the Top 100 for the first time, at No. 65. She ended the season ranked No. 37.

Then came 2020. Rybakina reached five finals during the season, more than any other women’s player that year, and won the title in Hobart. By the time the COVID-19 pandemic interrupted the tennis season, Rybakina had risen to No. 17 and become the first Kazakh player to enter the WTA Top 20.

In 2021, she reached her first Grand Slam quarterfinal at Roland Garros, defeating Serena Williams on the way, and finished fourth at the Tokyo Olympics.

Rybakina was no longer simply a promising young player. She was becoming one of the strongest players on tour.

Wimbledon 2022: the title that changed everything

The biggest moment of her career came at Wimbledon in 2022. At 23, Rybakina became the first player representing Kazakhstan to win a Grand Slam singles title.

The victory also created a complicated situation because Wimbledon had banned Russian and Belarusian players following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Rybakina had been born in Moscow and had represented Russia as a junior, leading to considerable discussion around her nationality and sporting identity.

There was another unusual consequence: Wimbledon did not award ranking points that year. As a result, winning the tournament did not improve Rybakina’s ranking in the way a Grand Slam victory normally would.

She ended 2022 ranked No. 22 and did not qualify for the WTA Finals.

From Grand Slam champion to a Top-3 player

The next major step came in 2023. Rybakina reached the Australian Open final and then won two WTA 1000 titles, in Indian Wells and Rome. In June, she reached a career-high No. 3 in the WTA rankings.

But the following two years were less straightforward. Injuries and health problems affected her schedule, while changes to her coaching team added another layer of uncertainty.

She split with Vukov after the 2024 US Open and briefly worked with former Wimbledon champion Goran Ivanisevic. She later reunited with Vukov, who was subsequently suspended by the WTA for 12 months. Rybakina also worked with Davide Sanguinetti during this period.

While she had fallen to No. 11 in April 2025, the year of 2025 became another turning point.

At the 2025 WTA Finals in Riyadh, Rybakina entered the tournament as the final qualifier among the eight players. She then won the entire tournament without losing a match. The victory brought her back into the world’s Top 5 and gave her the biggest title of her career since Wimbledon.

2026: the season that took her to the top

Rybakina began 2026 by winning the Australian Open. Rybakina won 6-4, 4-6, 6-4 in a match against Sabalenka to claim her second Grand Slam title.

She later won in Stuttgart and reached the finals in Indian Wells and Toronto.

When she arrived in New York, she was ranked No. 2. The gap between Rybakina and Sabalenka at the top of the rankings had become one of the central storylines of the season.

Rybakina secured the No. 1 ranking after defeating Zheng Qinwen in the quarterfinals. But she still had two matches to play.

“You never know how long you’re going to stay. I want to win the titles still in tournaments, so all my thoughts are just for the next match,” she said.

That mentality carried her through the semifinal against Gauff and into the final against Sabalenka.

Rybakina’s victory over Sabalenka in the US Open final completed perhaps the most successful season of her career.

She became a three-time Grand Slam champion, won her first US Open and became the first world No. 1 in the history of Kazakh tennis.

Rybakina said she would like to win the French Open one day and complete a career Grand Slam. The achievement matters, she said, but she does not want to spend too much time thinking about it. There will always be another tournament, another opponent and another problem to solve.

That perspective is consistent with the story of her career.

Rybakina was not a child prodigy who was destined for the top from the beginning. She started tennis because other sports were not a good fit. She trained without an individual coach for years. At 17, she was still considering university instead of professional tennis.

Her career changed when Kazakhstan offered her the support needed to make professional tennis financially and logistically possible. From there, the progress came step by step and the ranking is only one part of the story. The girl who once played tennis simply because it was something to do after school had become the best-ranked women’s player in the world.

And, for Rybakina, there was still another match ahead.

World.title: Asian Games Open in Nagoya as Kazakhstan Targets Bigger Medal Haul
World.content:
ASTANA – The 20th Asian Games opened in Japan on Sept. 19, bringing together thousands of the continent’s top athletes. Kazakhstan is represented by 558 athletes competing in 35 of the 43 sports on the program, reported the Ministry of Tourism and Sports.

The opening ceremony was held in Aichi Prefecture and Nagoya, and the Games run through Oct. 4.

More than 15,000 athletes are expected to compete for medals in 469 events across 43 sports, spanning both Olympic and non-Olympic disciplines. Several competitions will also count toward qualification for the 2028 Olympic Games, either by awarding direct quota places or points toward Olympic rankings.

Paris 2024 Olympic judo champion Yeldos Smetov and national table tennis team member Sarvinoz Mirkadirova carried the Kazakh flag at the opening ceremony. Smetov is a three-time Olympic medalist, having also won silver at the 2016 Rio Games and bronze at Tokyo 2020, while Mirkadirova is a multiple Kazakh champion and medalist on the WTT Feeder circuit.

The scale of Kazakhstan’s delegation reflects a broader push ahead of the Games to strengthen the national team system. The ministry said foreign specialists with international experience and modern training methods had been brought into the preparation process, with the longer-term goal of developing domestic coaching expertise as well as improving results at major international competitions.

The country won 80 medals, including 10 gold, 22 silver and 48 bronze, at the previous Asian Games in Hangzhou, finishing 11th in the medal standings. Ahead of the competition in Japan, the ministry has set a target of 99 medals. Meeting that goal will depend on sports in which Kazakhstan has traditionally been competitive in Asia, including boxing, wrestling, judo, fencing and shooting. But several of the country’s leading medal contenders arrive in Japan with another layer of pressure, according to the National Olympic Committee press office. Many will be facing opponents they already know from Olympic finals, world championships and previous Asian Games.

Familiar rivals

One of the examples comes in men’s team épée, where Kazakhstan and host Japan have developed one of the continent’s strongest fencing rivalries.

Japan beat Kazakhstan in the semifinals of the 2018 Asian Games, while Kazakhstan took silver and Japan gold at the following edition. A few years later in the semifinals of the 2025 world championships, Japan edged Kazakhstan 42-41 before going on to win the title.

A year later, Kazakhstan won its first men’s team épée world championship, defeating Ukraine 45-40 in the final. It also won the 2026 Asian championship, with Japan finishing second.

That means the two teams arrive at the Asian Games as winners of the past two world championships.

Boxing

Boxing brings another major regional test, particularly against Uzbekistan.

Kazakhstan finished first at the inaugural World Boxing Championships in Liverpool in 2025 with seven gold medals, while Uzbekistan won six. Kazakh and Uzbek male boxers won in 10 weight categories at the tournament, setting up the possibility of several high-profile rematches in Japan.

Among them is Aibek Oralbay, who defeated Uzbekistan’s Jakhongir Zokirov in the over-90-kilogram final in Liverpool.

Aida Abikeyeva could also renew her rivalry with Uzbekistan’s Navbakhor Khamidova after the pair finished first and second at major international events over the past year.

Torekhan Sabyrkhan could again face Japan’s Sewonrets Okazawa after defeating him in the 70-kilogram world championship final in Liverpool.

Another major Kazakh medal contender is Nazym Kyzaibay, one of the most decorated athletes on the team. The Paris 2024 Olympic bronze medalist has repeatedly reached the podium at major international tournaments and took silver at the 2025 world championships while competing in the 48-kilogram division.

In Nagoya, Kyzaibay moves up to 54 kilograms, where she faces a particularly strong field. Her potential rivals include reigning world champion Huang Hsiao-wen of Chinese Taipei, Paris Olympic silver medalist Pang Chol-mi of North Korea, South Korea’s Olympic bronze medalist Im Ae-ji and Japan’s Tokyo Olympic bronze medalist Tsukimi Namiki.

Namiki also has a history with Kyzaibay: the Japanese boxer defeated her in the semifinals of the 2022 Asian championships, giving a potential meeting in Nagoya the added dimension of a rematch.

Olympic champions

Kazakhstan also brings considerable experience into the judo competition.

Smetov, the reigning Olympic champion in the 60-kilogram division, could again face Chinese Taipei’s Yang Yung-wei. Yang won silver at the Tokyo Olympics and gold at the previous Asian Games, while Smetov defeated him in the Paris 2024 Olympic quarterfinals on his way to the title.

Smetov is himself a former Asian Games champion, having won gold in Incheon in 2014.

Abiba Abuzhakynova gives Kazakhstan another strong medal opportunity in judo. She won silver at the previous Asian Games and has since added bronze at the 2024 world championships and silver in 2025, giving her three senior world championship medals.

Some of Kazakhstan’s most intriguing contests could come against Japanese athletes competing before a home crowd.

In Greco-Roman wrestling, Demeu Zhadrayev could meet Japan’s Nao Kusaka in a rematch of the Paris Olympic final. Zhadrayev took an early lead back then before Kusaka came back to win 5-2 and claim Olympic gold. Both return in the 77-kilogram division in Japan.

In breaking, Amir Zakirov could renew his rivalry with Japan’s Shigekix, or Shigeyuki Nakarai. Zakirov beat the Japanese star at the Breaking for Gold World Series in Kitakyushu in 2023, while Shigekix later won Asian Games gold in Hangzhou and became world champion in 2025. Both also competed at the Paris Olympics.

Medal chances

Kazakhstan’s medal ambitions extend beyond its traditional strengths in boxing, wrestling and judo.

Skeet shooter Assem Orynbay enters the Games after beating China’s Jiang Yiting at the World Cup in Almaty in May, where Orynbay hit 33 targets in the final, equaling the world record.

In athletics, former world champion Norah Jeruto could line up against Bahrain’s Olympic champion Winfred Yavi in the women’s 3,000-meter steeplechase. Yavi won the world title in 2023 and Olympic gold in Paris, while Jeruto was world champion in 2022.

Rhythmic gymnast Akmaral Yerekesheva arrives after a breakthrough first senior season. She won three medals at the 2026 Asian championships and finished sixth in the all-around at the world championships, putting her among Kazakhstan’s emerging medal prospects in Nagoya.

The men’s water polo tournament carries another long-running rivalry.

Kazakhstan won six Asian Games titles between 1994 and 2018, including one-goal victories over Japan in the finals in both 2014 and 2018. Japan reversed the balance in Hangzhou, beating Kazakhstan 15-13 in the group stage before winning gold, while Kazakhstan finished with bronze.

The two sides are drawn together again and are scheduled to meet Sept. 26.

Olympic Games official website describes China, Japan and South Korea as “three traditional powerhouses at the Asian Games.”

“Those three National Olympic Committees have won the most gold medals between them at every single Asian Games since 1978, with 1974 the last time one of those three NOCs did not win at least the third-most gold medals at the Games,” reads the website.

World.title: Kulans Released Into Wild in Ile-Balkhash Reserve
World.content:
ASTANA – A group of kulans has been released into the wild in the Ile-Balkhash State Nature Reserve as part of Kazakhstan’s efforts to restore the species’ population and return it to its historical range.

The animals were transferred from Altyn Emel National Park and released into their natural habitat, reported the Ministry of Ecology and Natural Resources. Specialists will monitor the kulans’ adaptation, movements and condition following the release.

The kulan, a wild relative of the domestic donkey, is native to the steppes and semi-deserts of Central Asia. In Kazakhstan, the species disappeared from most of its historical range in the first half of the 20th century, largely due to hunting and habitat loss.

Conservation efforts have gradually helped rebuild the population. In recent years, Kazakhstan has expanded reintroduction programs to several protected areas, including Ile-Balkhash and Altyn Dala.

In October 2024, 24 kulans were transported 2,139 kilometers from Altyn Emel National Park to the Altyn Dala Nature Reserve. The 50-hour journey was part of efforts to develop safer methods for relocating wild animals over long distances.

The Ile-Balkhash reserve has become one of the key sites for restoring native wildlife. The area is part of a wider ecosystem restoration project that includes the return of species alongside measures aimed at creating suitable conditions for the future return of the Turan tiger.

The reintroduction of kulans is intended to strengthen natural ecosystems as well as increase the number of animals in the wild. As large herbivores, kulans contribute to the functioning of steppe and desert habitats by influencing vegetation and forming part of the food chain.

The latest release marks another step in Kazakhstan’s broader biodiversity conservation strategy, which increasingly focuses on restoring species in their historical habitats and rebuilding entire ecosystems rather than protecting isolated animal populations.

World.title: Kazakhstan Eyes Cross-Border QR Payments as India’s UPI Offers Blueprint
World.content:
MUMBAI – Kazakhstan is moving toward expanding its domestic QR-payment infrastructure across borders, with India among 11 countries identified for potential cross-border QR-payment cooperation. The initiative comes as cashless payments continue to account for the overwhelming majority of transactions in Kazakhstan.

According to the National Bank of Kazakhstan, 84 million payment cards were in circulation as of Aug. 1, with debit cards accounting for 81.6% and credit cards for 15.5%. In July, transactions using cards issued by Kazakh banks reached 19.9 trillion tenge (US$44.4 billion), covering 1.3 billion transactions.

Non-cash transactions accounted for 17.6 trillion tenge (US$39.3 billion) and 1.3 billion transactions, increasing 8.4% in value and 7.5% in number compared with July 2025. Internet and mobile banking comprise 77.6% of the number and 89.6% of the value of non-cash payments and money transfers, while POS terminals accounted for 21.9% and 10%, respectively.

The figures provide a growing domestic base for Kazakhstan’s efforts to make QR payments interoperable across borders.

Kazakhstan launched its national Interbank Mobile-Payment System on July 19, allowing customers of participating banks to make real-time interbank transfers and payments using phone numbers and a single QR code. The system enables merchants to accept payments from customers of various participating banks without installing new equipment.

The next step is to make such payments work across borders.

India’s UPI model

India offers one example of how a nationally interoperable payment infrastructure can evolve into a cross-border service.

Speaking to foreign journalists in Mumbai on Sept. 16, Sonal Asnani, head of Asia Pacific at NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL), outlined how India developed the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) from a domestic payment infrastructure into a system with international applications.

UPI, operated by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), is a payment infrastructure rather than a standalone application or card. It connects banks, fintech companies and customers through a common framework, allowing users to make payments through different applications while maintaining interoperability.

“It’s not an application, it’s not a card. It’s a payment layer,” Asnani said, explaining the basic architecture of UPI.

According to Asnani, one of the key factors behind UPI’s expansion has been the division of roles across the ecosystem. The Reserve Bank of India acts as the regulator, NPCI operates the national payment infrastructure and establishes standards, banks hold customers’ accounts and funds, while fintech companies develop customer-facing services.

This model has allowed users to make payments through various applications while relying on the same underlying infrastructure.

From domestic payments to international use

NPCI created NIPL in 2020 to take Indian payment technologies and expertise to international markets.

One of its main areas of activity is cross-border merchant payments. Under UPI Global Acceptance, Indian users can make QR-based payments at participating international merchants directly from UPI-enabled applications.

Asnani noted that users can scan a participating local QR code and review the transaction amount, exchange rate, and applicable fees before completing the payment.

She said NPCI International currently works with 11 countries on international merchant-payment acceptance.

The model allows an Indian traveler to use a familiar UPI-enabled application abroad rather than relying exclusively on cash or international payment cards.

“For example, when I travel to other countries, I can scan the local QR with my UPI app and still make a payment,” Asnani said.

For Kazakhstan, which is developing cross-border QR arrangements with India and other countries, interoperability could provide a similar mechanism for travelers and merchants.

The practical question, however, is how two national payment systems can be connected while preserving their respective regulatory and technical frameworks.

Asnani highlighted that such partnerships require due diligence and compliance procedures, while the presence of an established QR-payment ecosystem in the partner country can make integration more straightforward.

“Wherever there is a high level of QR adoption, and there is a QR system, it becomes natural for us to collaborate,” she said, describing the factors considered when establishing international partnerships.

Beyond QR payments

NPCI International’s activities extend beyond merchant payments. The organization also works on cross-border person-to-person remittances and provides technology to countries seeking to develop their own domestic payment infrastructure.

Asnani said some countries have adopted elements of India’s technology to develop sovereign instant-payment or card systems rather than building such infrastructure entirely from scratch.

That approach differs from simply connecting two existing payment systems. It involves sharing technological infrastructure and experience with countries that are developing or upgrading their own national payment systems.

Kazakhstan has a well-developed digital payments ecosystem. The next step is to connect its existing infrastructure with international payment networks while ensuring seamless interoperability and maintaining regulatory oversight.

The potential use cases extend beyond tourism. Cross-border QR payments could facilitate transactions for travelers, small businesses and merchants. At the same time, interoperability between payment systems could also support broader economic and financial links between Kazakhstan and its partner countries.

The country’s growing domestic use of digital payments provides a substantial base for such expansion. In January-July, QR-code payments within Kazakhstan accounted for 2.34 billion transactions worth 11.8 trillion tenge (US$26.3 billion), according to National Bank data.

As Kazakhstan moves from domestic QR interoperability toward international connectivity, India’s experience offers one possible path. This involves building common infrastructure, allowing banks and fintech companies to compete at the customer level, and using interoperable standards to make the payment experience seamless for users.

World.title: News Digest: Rybakina’s US Open Triumph, Kazakhstan-South Korea Ties and Oil Export Strategy
World.content:
ASTANA – The Astana Times has selected articles from global media outlets covering Kazakhstan. This week’s foreign media digest highlights Elena Rybakina’s U.S. Open victory, strengthened Kazakhstan-South Korea cooperation, Astana Arena’s selection to host the 2028 UEFA Super Cup, and Kazakhstan’s efforts to diversify its oil export routes.

S. Korea, Kazakhstan sign MOU on preservation of historic sites linked to Korea’s independence movement

South Korea and Kazakhstan have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to help better preserve historical sites in the Central Asian country that are linked to Korea’s independence movement against Japan’s 1910-45 colonial rule, Seoul’s veterans ministry said Wednesday, Yonhap reported on Sept. 16.

“Under the MOU, the two countries agreed to systematically preserve the historical records and cultural value of historical sites related to Korea’s independence movement while also strengthening academic exchanges. There are 25 historical sites related to Korea’s independence movement in the central Asian country, according to the ministry,” reads the article.

Seoul Cyber University chairman receives Kazakhstan’s Order of Dostyk
