World.title: How Freo's former number one ticket holder has helped Brisbane's dynasty
World.content:
If the Brisbane Lions win a third straight AFL premiership on Saturday, they will be thanking a former number one ticketholder for the Fremantle Dockers.

Luc Longley, a three-time NBA champion with the Michael Jordan-led Chicago Bulls, knows what it takes to reach the top and stay there.

Longley, a Fremantle native, was also the Dockers' number one ticketholder in 2006 and 2007.

But a meeting the Olympian had with the Lions in July may be the catalyst for Fremantle's downfall this Saturday.

The Lions are in their fourth consecutive AFL decider, and are trying to complete three premiership triumphs in a row and join the list of all-time great dynasties.

Despite finishing third on the ladder and making it to the final day in September, the Lions' 2026 season has not been smooth sailing.

Brisbane lost their opening two matches of the season, conceded a record 86 points in the third quarter of their loss to GWS, were hammered by 76 points against Carlton, and lost the qualifying final by 53 points to an understrength Sydney.

But they have overcome all obstacles to be in another grand final, with several players telling ABC Sport of a meeting with Longley in July which has spurred them on.

Former NBA champion Luc Longley is from Fremantle, and was once the Dockers' number one ticketholder. (Getty Images: James Worsfold)

"The ability he had to share some of that wisdom and talk to us about what he went through, it was awesome," Lions star Cam Rayner said.

"Just being able to compare and bounce ideas off him and learn things from him about the ability to keep turning up and find that motivation again has held us in good stead."

The Lions had six wins and six losses through 12 games, but were on a five-match winning streak before meeting Longley ahead of their round 18 clash against West Coast in July.

Rayner said Longley's discussions with the team about keeping the desire to win, despite already experiencing success, resonated with the team as they strived for a third consecutive flag.

"The hunger to want to win and to continue to have that success. At the start of the year there were times that wasn't really there in our performances," he said.

"We were dropping in and out of games and struggling to really perform to the level that we could.

"You can't really question the hunger after the game last week. It's back to a level that it needs to be and it's exciting to bring it to this week.

"That's one of the messages Luc Longley brought to us, he said, 'If the game's not going to get you up, you're probably playing it for the wrong reasons'. I feel like that really resonated with a lot of the boys."

Longley was an important part of the Bulls' 1996-1998 championship run, without being the star player.

Michael Jordan was the star of the NBA, while Scottie Pippen, Dennis Rodman and Steve Kerr also enjoyed big-name status.

For experienced Lions' midfielder Jarrod Berry, speaking to a champion who was known for his team-first work ethic was exactly what he believed Brisbane's dynasty has been built on.

"He [Longley] was never the big dog, the star, the whatever. He got more satisfaction out of seeing his teammates succeed," Berry told ABC Sport.

"Our squad is so talented and we've got so many stars and whatever, but it's not necessarily those guys that are making the club so special.

"It's the other guys that are doing all the tough work and hard work and selfless stuff.

"It was really nice to highlight that. It's all about being generous to your teammates and doing it for them."

The Lions are attempting to become the sixth team to win three consecutive V/AFL premierships, and the first since Hawthorn, who did it from 2013-15.

The Lions won three premierships on the bounce in 2001, 2002 and 2003, then lost the 2004 grand final.

The only club to have won three consecutive flags twice is Melbourne, which did it from 1939–1941 and 1955–1957.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.

World.title: Forced job-cuts loom as Tasmanian government prepares to swing axe
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

At least 80 jobs have been identified to be abolished at Building Tasmania as part of its restructure and ongoing government efforts to shrink the state service.

The Tasmanian government announced during the May budget that it wanted to cut 250 Building Tasmania (formerly the Department of State Growth) jobs, primarily through voluntary redundancies.

On the weekend, the premier confirmed 111 full-time workers had taken redundancies. He reiterated his commitment that none would be forced.

But at an all-staff meeting on Monday, public service workers were told a number of jobs from each area had been identified to be abolished.

Despite the use of a slide show, which detailed things such as how many workers had taken redundancies so far and the operational efficiencies, the actual number of cuts planned for each area was only communicated verbally.

The Community and Public Sector Union (CPSU) and multiple sources have told the ABC they understand the number of positions to be abolished in the sector was roughly:

Building Tasmania — 32

Creative Industries, Sport and Visitor Economy — 23

Department of Premier and Cabinet — 5

Workers moving from Building Tasmania — 27

Corporate Services — 23

The ABC has asked the government to confirm the exact figures.

The staff the ABC spoke to left the meeting confused and still unclear about how many jobs would go or how it would work.

Staff do not know which jobs are being targeted but it is understood they will find out over the next few days, before the full restructure is revealed on Wednesday afternoon.

Staff shown slide show presentation

CPSU secretary Thirza White said the meeting was meant to provide certainty but created more confusion.

"There was quite significant frustration at that meeting today that despite being promised information and delaying the deadline for that information three times, that information was only provided verbally," she said.

"This is a really stressful time. People need to be given the information in a written format so they can go away and consider it.

"Now, instead over the next two to three days, people will be tapped on the shoulder and told they are potentially now an identified employee.

"It's not the way we should be doing this, and it makes a stressful situation even more stressful."

Ms White said it was a significant number of job losses.

"We have done some back-of-the-envelope calculations, and at a minimum we're looking at 80 roles being cut and likely north of a hundred roles," she said.

"These are huge cuts and agency leadership today did acknowledge that it's up to 10 per cent of the workforce in DPAC and Building Tasmania that will be directly impacted."

The slide show, seen by the ABC, addresses some of the many questions the workforce likely has.

Under the heading "When will I know if I have a job in the new structure?" there was text saying it is understood that workers are "keen to have certainty" about future positions.

"We expect many of you will know by mid-to-late October whether you have a confirmed position in the new organisational structure," the slide show said.

It also said just because staff could not see their position in the proposed structure it did not automatically mean their position was being removed.

Where are the cuts coming from in Tasmania's state budget? Treasurer Eric Abetz wants to find $1.47 billion in "efficiencies" in Tasmania's state budget. This is what's on the chopping block.

Ms White challenged Premier Jeremy Rockliff to keep his commitment of no forced redundancies.

"As recently as the weekend, the premier has publicly said that there will be no forced redundancies and yet the agency today started the process that does allow the agency to make forced redundancies," she said.

"Once a role is identified, then, after six months if can be made redundant forcibly. However, it does need the premier's signature.

"So, time will tell whether the premier's commitments around no forced redundancies are genuine."

Detailed proposed structures and change and consultation proposals will be released on Wednesday.

Labor on the attack

Labor Workplace Relations spokesperson Ella Haddad said the decision to put Treasurer Eric Abetz in charge was "causing chaos and confusion".

"Eric Abetz pointedly refused to rule out forced redundancies earlier this month," she said.

"The premier tried to yesterday, but today employees at Building Tasmania learned that over 100 jobs could be identified to be abolished in the coming days.

"The premier can try to soften the message as much as he likes, but nothing will soften the impact of Eric Abetz's blunt, $1.5 billion fiscal cleaver."

Consultation on redundancies will be open until October 9.

The government has been contacted for comment.

World.title: Footy fans filthy as airfares soar ahead of grand final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Return airfares to Melbourne have hit $6,000 ahead of Saturday's AFL Grand Final as Fremantle and Brisbane fans scramble for seats.

The eye-watering prices come despite airlines adding extra flights to meet the surge in demand.

Fremantle fan John Cooke said he knows of supporters paying $1,900 for a one-way flight from Perth.

"I've also seen people saying that you're better off getting flights to Europe or the US and spending a day shopping and sightseeing overseas and then coming back into Melbourne," Mr Cooke said.

John Cooke got in in early, but says airlines are ripping off fans. (Supplied: John Cooke)

The lifelong Dockers supporter booked his flights month ago and avoided the worst of the surge, but said many others were not so lucky.

"It's not like there are five or six different airlines all competing for airfare seats. They're pretty much all knowing that they're going to be full," he said.

" It's just profiteering. "

Lions fans are paying up in the hope of seeing their team claim a historic three-peat. (AFL Photos via Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Brisbane Lions fan Wendy Elson has also been tracking the fares.

Ms Elson has attended more than a dozen grand finals and has booked a one-way flight to Melbourne, but is still without a ticket home.

"I've been to 10 grand finals, so we're pretty good at working things out, but this year the flights have really hiked up. They're very expensive," she said.

Wendy Elson (left) is yet to work out how she'll get back home. (Supplied: Wendy Elson)

Ms Elson said prices jumped dramatically once the finals combination was announced.

"I said to my son, we may end up having to hire a car and drive home … or hitch a ride with someone," she said.

How airlines set the price

Griffith University aviation industry expert Justin Wastnage says airlines are using increasingly sophisticated dynamic pricing systems to maximise revenue from a limited number of seats.

"Airlines have a duty to their shareholders to maximise profits," he said.

Mr Wastnage said the major events could be factored into those systems and that airline booking systems analysed geographical information.

Airlines are using sophisticated dynamic pricing systems to maximise revenue from a limited number of seats. (AAP)

"If the booking platform knows your postcode and if it knows that postcode is within the territory of a home sporting club, it could even rank-jump those fares from searches from that sort of geographical area," he said.

Mr Wastnage described some of the less understood aspects of dynamic pricing as "dark arts".

"Some studies have suggested that if you book from a Mac computer, airfares could be about 15-20 per cent higher because there was an assumption that you're a higher revenue passenger," he said.

"Similarly with postcodes."

Fremantle fans chant their way from Melbourne's Federation Square to the MCG in 2013, the last time Fremantle reached the grand final. (ABC News)

Airlines add capacity

The airlines have responded to the demand by adding extra services.

Stronger protections for airline passengers The federal government has announced nearly $40 million to fund an overhaul of aviation consumer rights.

Qantas added 13 flights between Perth and Melbourne after Fremantle's preliminary-final win, with one-way fares advertised from $766.

Qantas and Jetstar also added seven Brisbane-Melbourne flights, while Virgin added 4,000 seats between Perth and Melbourne and another 1,000 from Brisbane.

Flight Centre said bookings to Melbourne from Brisbane and Perth were already up 126 per cent on the same time last year.

The federal government has announced nearly $40 million to fund an overhaul of aviation consumer rights.

These include a new watchdog and complaints system that could lead to compensation for disrupted passengers.

World.title: Mike Rann on 'maestro of the possible' 100 years after Don Dunstan's birth
World.content:
As South Australians commemorate 100 years since their most influential premier was born, a former political heavyweight has recalled his own entry to politics under the man's leadership.

Don Dunstan was SA's trailblazing Labor premier between 1967-68 and 1970-1979, a leader who championed social justice and the arts, and turned Adelaide into a national cultural centre that punched well above its weight.

He died in 1999 aged 72.

Mike Rann was a three-term premier for the state Labor Party between 2002 and 2011, making him the third-longest serving premier in the state's history.

Mr Rann said he had been studying Australian history and politics at university in New Zealand and found Don Dunstan to be somebody who "stood out" among a "fairly dreary lot".

He successfully applied to work in SA at the Unit for Industrial Democracy in the premier's department and at the age of 24 was notified that Mr Dunstan's speechwriter had resigned.

"Someone said to me, 'Look, you won't get the job, but he should get to know you, so why don't you apply for the position?'" Mr Rann told 891 ABC Adelaide.

Mr Dunstan ushered him into a room while wearing a white safari suit, before they sat down for a "charming" and "wonderful conversation".

"Then suddenly there was a tap on the door and his secretary said [former Australian prime minister] Gough Whitlam is here," Mr Rann said.

"So I'm being interviewed and terrified, and then I've got Gough Whitlam sitting there as well."

Mike Rann in 2008 during his time as SA premier. (ABC News)

Mr Dunstan had to step out for an ABC interview, leaving Mr Rann with Mr Whitlam, "who turned to me and said, 'Who the hell are you?'"

"I said I was from New Zealand and was applying for a job with Mr Dunstan.

"He said, 'You're wasting your time here, young man. Go east. Go east. Come to Sydney'.

"Dunstan came back and said the interview was concluded, with Gough still there, and then they asked me if I'd like to come out to dinner.

" I didn't think I would get the job but thought it would just be one of the great nights and stories to tell. The next day, I got the job. "

Mr Rann was appointed to be Dunstan's press secretary, speechwriter and head of the government's media operations for what he described as a "wild ride".

A true reformer

Emeritus Professor of Politics and International Relations at Adelaide University Clem Macintyre said Mr Dunstan's flagship reforms, first as attorney-general and then as premier, included the nation's first land rights and anti-discrimination laws for Aboriginals, the liberalisation of drinking hours in restaurants and pubs, and the decriminalisation of homosexuality — Australia's first jurisdiction to do so — in 1975.

Don Dunstan was also renowned for his outfits, such as the pink shorts he famously wore to parliament. (Supplied: Flinders University Library Dunstan collection)

"He was a transformative premier in South Australia in lots of ways and I think, arguably, set a lead for a number of other states as well in terms of social changes that were coming in the 60s and 70s," Dr Macintyre told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"In many respects, South Australia was a very conservative, inwardly-looking state in the 1950s into the early 1960s under the long-serving premier Tom Playford, who had built some very strong economic foundations.

"Then Dunstan, when he finally became premier in the mid-60s, really began to change the place and, particularly in that second term from 1970 onwards, initiated lots of reforms that really we still see signs of today."

Mr Rann said Mr Dunstan saw that a small jurisdiction like South Australia could be a pace-setter for reform both nationally and internationally and was not afraid to stick his neck out.

"Someone described him as the maestro of the possible, and that's how I saw it," he said.

"He was prepared to take risks, but he was also prepared to lead, rather than follow, and that's what South Australia was like in the 1890s."

After all, among other reforms, South Australia had been the first jurisdiction in the world to give women the vote in 1894, and the right to stand in parliament on equal terms.

"He wanted us to be a destination again, a place that attracted people from all over who were interested in actual reforms and doing things differently and better," Mr Rann said.

Queen Elizabeth II with former premier Don Dunstan while visiting Rundle Mall in 1977. (Supplied: University of Melbourne Archives)

A trained actor, Mr Dunstan was also a champion of the arts and raised money for and overlooked the opening of Adelaide Festival Centre, where the Dunstan Playhouse was later named in his honour, and established the SA Film Corporation.

He also closed a section of Rundle Street to cars and created Rundle Mall, which opened 50 years ago in 1976.

"He was very flamboyant and, while he was interesting, at parties, dinner parties, he would often be the shyest person there," Mr Rann said.

"But when he was on stage or on television, he had this incredible ability to sum up complicated arguments and punch them through."

Mike Rann, pictured during an event hosted by The Australia Institute last November, now chairs the UK board of the not-for-profit Climate Group. (ABC News: Steve Opie)

An exhibition, Don Dunstan: 100 Years, presented by the City of Norwood Payneham & St Peters, Don Dunstan Foundation and Centre of Democracy, is being held at The Gallery adjoining St Peters Library.

With personal items donated by those close to Dunstan, the council says visitors will be able to gain unique insights into his life, passions and personality, and "reflect on the ideas, courage and creativity of a leader whose vision helped shape modern South Australia and continues to inspire today".

The exhibition runs until November 7.

World.title: Man four times over limit breached AVO in crash that killed ex-partner
World.content:
A judge has told a NSW District Court that if a man had not breached an apprehended domestic violence order (AVO) against his ex-partner, she would not have died.

Rolong Stanley has pleaded guilty to aggravated dangerous driving near Orange that caused the death of his former girlfriend Justine Hammond in February last year.

The Orange District Court heard at the 31-year-old's sentence hearing today that he was at least four times over the legal blood alcohol limit when he lost control of his Holden Rodeo, rolled it, and crashed into a tree.

Rolong Stanley lost control of the car before it flipped on its roof and smashed into a tree around this bend. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

Ms Hammond, 42, had an AVO against Stanley since November 1, 2024, which was in force for two years.

Judge Penny Musgrave will also take into account that Stanley was driving an unregistered car with a defect notice, while he was disqualified from having a licence.

She told the court that the other offences linked to the main dangerous driving charge "placed pressure" on his sentence.

"Here we have a nuanced situation," she said.

" If he had complied with the AVO and not associated with the victim, if he had complied with the disqualification and not driven, this offence wouldn't have happened. "

Justine Hammond had an AVO against Stanley at the time of her death. (Supplied: Facebook)

Drink driving following afternoon at apple orchard

Ms Hammond and Stanley were drinking cask wine together inside the ute at a large apple orchard on Canobolas Road at 2pm on Sunday, February 9 last year.

Almost three hours later, Stanley drove off with Ms Hammond in the passenger seat south along Lake Canobolas Road, according to the agreed facts.

The document characterised the route as an "unmarked roadway" in "poor condition," with "patchy bituminous material".

Flowers were laid at the site of the fatal crash on Lake Canobolas Road in Orange, NSW. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

When Stanley took a slight right-hand turn, the tyres hit the grass nature strip.

He steered the car back onto the road before losing control and rotated the car clockwise.

It hit an embankment, rolled onto its roof and collided with a large tree.

Ms Hammond died at the scene from multiple injuries to her head, neck, chest, abdomen and upper limbs.

Stanley was extricated from the car by emergency services before he was flown to Westmead Hospital for further treatment.

Judge Musgrave said it was not only Ms Hammond who was put at risk by his actions.

"It's a Sunday afternoon on a day with clear weather," she said.

The speed limit along Lake Canobolas Road was 80 km/h at the time of the fatal crash, but has since been reduced to 70 km/h. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

"You've got Lake Canobolas, vineyards, orchards, restaurants … those vineyards are in swing — full on.

" That is not a lightly used road; within five minutes of the accident, someone has already come across it. "

Drinking 'major factor' in crash

A blood sample that was taken from Stanley while he was undergoing treatment at Westmead Hospital returned a blood alcohol limit (BAC) of 0.217 grams per 100ml.

That is more than four times the legal limit of 0.05, and above the threshold of a high range Prescribed Concentration of Alcohol (PCA) of 0.15.

The police investigation found his BAC was a "major contributory factor" in the circumstances of the collision, and ruled out the road's "poor" condition as an influence.

Crown prosecutor Craig Evans argued Stanley's moral blameworthiness, or whether he was responsible for wrongdoing, was "high or extremely high".

Police investigations found that the "poor, patchy bitumen" of Lake Canobolas Road was not a contributing factor to the crash. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

He told the court the offender had two previous drink driving offences on his record.

"He shouldn't have been driving and he knew it," he said.

Public defender Ian Nash said he believed the offending fell within a mid-range of objective seriousness.

"I don't think I can sensibly say it's in the low range," he told the court.

He said Stanley wanted the court to know he was sorry for his actions, and that he felt "sad and heartbroken."

Stanley tried to turn this corner before he lost control of the ute. (ABC News: Lani Oataway)

Mr Nash asked Judge Musgrave to consider his "impoverished upbringing" in Vanuatu, and his social and cultural isolation while working to send money home to his family.

"He was and is a man who comes from another world in many respects," he said.

Judge Musgrave will hand down the sentence next week.

World.title: Another indecent assault charge dropped against Alan Jones, amid trial
World.content:
Prosecutors have dropped another indecent assault charge against broadcaster Alan Jones, reducing the number of complainants midway through his lengthy criminal trial.

Mr Jones, 85, had pleaded not guilty to 20 counts of indecent assault and two of sexual touching in relation to six men, three of which have already given evidence in the NSW Local Court trial.

Prosecutors told the court on Monday they would no longer press one count of indecent assault in relation to Complainant F: a reporter who alleged Mr Jones touched him indecently in public.

The court has previously heard Complainant F was a younger man, working as a reporter, who alleged Mr Jones "touched and squeezed" his backside at a function in 2012.

It means Complainant F will no longer be part of the trial.

No reason was given in court for the decision to drop the charge.

It is the fourth time charges have been dropped or downgraded since September 2025, when the former 2GB host faced 44 counts relating to 11 complainants.

Mr Jones now faces 21 charges in relation to five male complainants, with alleged offences ranging between 2003 and 2020.

Evidence heard from three alleged victims

Three of the alleged victims have now completed their evidence, with dozens of witnesses also called in the trial.

Two of the men, a former emerging athlete known as Complainant J, and a former colleague of Mr Jones's known as Complainant C, told the court they were scared to speak up at the time of the alleged offending, because of his influence and power.

Last week the court heard from Complainant M, a prominent athlete, who said Mr Jones kissed him without his consent twice during their lengthy friendship.

The athlete said Mr Jones had been generous to him at times, but described his relationship with the broadcaster as something he "managed".

The prosecution has argued Mr Jones tended to act on a sexual interest in younger men.

But Mr Jones's lawyers have told the court the case is about "media rivalry", and have blamed their client's 2GB stablemate Ray Hadley for colluding with others to bring about complaints to "destroy" Mr Jones.

The court has heard the case is about "media rivalry" between Mr Hadley (pictured) and Mr Jones. (ABC News: Ethan Rix)

The fourth complainant, Complainant H, is due to begin their evidence on Tuesday.

That man, who is decades younger than Mr Jones, alleged the broadcaster slid his hand down his back and across his backside at an event.

The prosecution said the man did not initially complain to police, but reached out to Sydney Morning Herald journalist Kate McClymont when she first published other allegations against Mr Jones in 2023.

World.title: Wallabies eye Springboks scalp amid Dockers frenzy in Perth
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

This is how Wallabies flanker Carlo Tizzano wants this weekend to pan out: Fremantle saluting in the AFL grand final on Saturday and Australia beating world champions South Africa in front of a rocking Perth Stadium crowd on Sunday night.

Perth is abuzz with Flagmantle fever ahead of the Dockers' date with destiny against Brisbane at the MCG on Saturday.

It's little wonder the Wallabies' arrival in Perth has gone mostly unnoticed.

But rather than feeling a bit miffed, Wallabies players are keen to lap up the Dockers-inspired party atmosphere and hope they can add to the happy vibes.

Petaia in Wallabies squad Precocious outside back Jordan Petaia is back in the Wallabies squad for the first time since the 2023 Rugby World Cup as Australia brace for the Springboks.

Perth-born Tizzano is leading that charge.

"We're behind Freo all the way and hopefully they get a good win," he told AAP.

"The atmosphere here is crazy. You saw what Fremantle was like after their preliminary final win, and what a game that was.

"They're the minor premiers, so they've got a lot of momentum, and hopefully they win the grand final for the first time ever, and then we get the win on the weekend as well."

Like Fremantle, the Wallabies will start as underdogs when they face defending World Cup champions South Africa.

The Springboks beat Australia 30-12 in their last visit to Perth in 2024.

Tizzano was playing just his second Test on that wet and wild night, and although his team didn't come away with the win, the 26-year-old lapped up the experience of donning the Wallabies gold in front of family and friends.

Australia have won three and drawn one Test under new coach Les Kiss.

Taking into account the Wallabies' 57-10 win over Italy in Perth in Joe Schmidt's last match in charge in July, Australia are on a five-match unbeaten run.

Tizzano hopes the team can produce something special to take down South Africa, who arrive in Perth full of confidence following a 3-1 series win over New Zealand.

The Wallabies have included uncapped Western Force recruit Harry McLaughlin-Phillips in the 34-man squad.

But the biggest addition was the return of star back Jordan Petaia, who left the Queensland Reds in 2024 to pursue his NFL dream, and hasn't played for the Wallabies since the 2023 World Cup.

The Springboks arrive in Perth without Pieter-Steph du Toit and Damian de Allende after the veteran duo were released from the squad to spend more time with family.

AAP

World.title: No warning, 12-year-old guidelines and a long shift: The litany of problems before Joe Massa’s death
World.content:
NationalNSWHealthcare No warning, 12-year-old guidelines and a long shift: The litany of problems before Joe Massa’s death Rachel Rasker September 21, 2026 — 5:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The registered nurse who triaged a two-year-old who died at the Northern Beaches Hospital has told a coronial inquest she had no alert about his abnormal heartbeat, was working with 12-year-old guidelines and was finishing a long shift during which she had been assaulted. NSW State Coroner Teresa O’Sullivan is examining the litany of problems at Northern Beaches Hospital that led to Joe Massa going from playing peek-a-boo to entering cardiac arrest within a day. Joe Massa’s mother stroked a tiny pair of shoes as she gave evidence. The toddler’s death shocked Sydney and led to the hospital, which was previously run by the private operator Healthscope, to be transferred into public hands. His mother Elouise Massa’s advocacy following his death also led to “Joe’s Law”, which bans future public-private partnerships. Massa gently stroked a tiny pair of her son’s shoes as she gave evidence on Monday, the first day of the inquest. She said clinicians at the hospital were rude and did not listen to her concerns as Joe’s condition rapidly deteriorated.



Related Article Northern Beaches Hospital This life-saving equipment is standard across NSW hospitals. It was never installed at Northern Beaches Massa took Joe to the Northern Beaches emergency department about 7am on September 14, 2024, after she became concerned about his severe vomiting and dry retching overnight. “He looked terrible,” she said. “He could barely keep his head up, he was going in and out of consciousness, he was floppy.” She told the court she had “a mother’s instinct” that something was “very wrong”. Joe was triaged as a category three patient who required treatment within 30 minutes, despite having a “red zone” heart rate of 182 beats per minute.



The registered nurse who triaged Joe, Hilary O’Neill, said she saw the toddler at the end of a 12-hour overnight shift without a proper break, during which she said she was assaulted by a mental health patient, who threw her against an ambulance door. O’Neill said the only reference she had to assess Joe’s heart rate was a resuscitation guideline from 2012. The system informed her Joseph was one year old – he was aged 22 months – and she assessed his initial heart rate of 160-170 BPM as just above the normal range. She did not re-check the guide after he later recorded the higher heart rate. “There were no track or trigger systems in place to alert me that it was in the red zone,” she said.



The inquest heard that in the public hospital system, clinical software would have automatically flagged that the reading was outside normal parameters, and notified all staff who reviewed the patient file. O’Neill said if she had known Joe’s heart rate was in the red zone, she would have put him in category two, which would have resulted in him being given a bed on the ward with constant cardiac monitoring. Elouise Massa gave evidence at the NSW Coroner’s Court on Monday about her son Joe’s treatment at Northern Beaches Hospital. Kate Geraghty O’Neill also said she contacted the chief medical officer on duty and asked for a bed. She said the doctor told her that paediatric emergency nurses would collect him. However, the mother and son were instead left on a chair in the waiting room for two and a half hours, where Massa said she was instructed to continue a “sip and wait process” of rehydration.



Massa said trying to cradle Joe on her lap, fill a medical syringe with liquid from a cup of electrolytes, administer the fluid to Joe, note his intake on a form and set a new timer every five minutes was “near impossible”. She said her son was declining rapidly but that her repeated requests for a bed were denied, and the doctor on duty instead treated Joe in the waiting area: “I was pacing around with him in my arms ... petrified.” Loading The statement Massa created a few days after Joe’s death was a key point of reference throughout her testimony. She said she put together the record of events while “lying in bed crying” as a friend took notes.



“I knew instinctively Joe wasn’t cared for properly, and we knew it would be a wise idea to make notes, so down the track [I had] events freshly on paper.” Related Article Healthcare ‘Trust your gut’: Parents’ plea after toddler’s sepsis death The court heard Joe was given a bed by 9.51am, but was moved to the hospital’s resuscitation unit by 10.41am after a nurse raised concern about the toddler’s condition. Massa said the family was left alone in the resuscitation bay, during which time hospital staff said they were gathering a team together. “I was always by his side,” Massa said.



She said she called a friend whose husband was a doctor, and hung up at about 10.47am: “I was on the phone in utter despair, wanting to get out of this hospital, not knowing what to do.” It was at about this time that Joe went into cardiac arrest. He was given CPR and circulation returned about 30 minutes later. He was intubated and transferred to Sydney Children’s Hospital but suffered irreversible brain damage. Joe’s life support was withdrawn two days later. The clinicians involved in the boy’s treatment and a coalition of independent experts are expected to continue their testimony at the inquest in the coming days. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial as it happened: Former NSW police officer’s trial begins over alleged murder of Paddington couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies
World.content:
Good evening and thank you for reading our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s criminal trial.

The former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, on February 19, 2024.

Beau Lamarre-Condon in the NSW Supreme Court on the first day of his trial. Rocco Fazzari

He has also pleaded not guilty to one count of aggravated breaking and entering Baird’s home in August 2023 and stealing a mobile phone and wallet belonging to Baird.

A 15-person jury was empanelled on Monday for the trial, which is expected to run for up to 12 weeks. In the event all 15 jurors are still present at the end of the trial, a ballot will be conducted to reduce their number to 12.

Today, Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, delivered his opening address to the jury. This sets out the Crown’s case and is not evidence, but it is a guide to the evidence it expects to call in the months ahead.

Lamarre-Condon is entitled to the presumption of innocence and his barrister John Stratton, SC, will deliver an opening address on Tuesday after Hatfield.

During his opening this afternoon, Hatfield alleged that Lamarre-Condon developed an “an obsessive and jealous infatuation” with Baird after a short relationship that started in late 2022 and was ended for the first time by Baird in April 2023.

After a brief resumption of their relationship later that year, it was “firmly and irretrievably ended” by Baird in November 2023, the Crown alleges.

The Crown case is that the murder of Baird was premeditated but that he killed Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, to eliminate a witness to his crime. This is the Crown’s alleged timeline of events.

Late 2022 : The accused and Jesse Baird met and started a casual relationship.

: The accused and Jesse Baird met and started a casual relationship. April 2023 : Baird sent the accused a “sympathetic” message saying he wasn’t ready for a relationship.

: Baird sent the accused a “sympathetic” message saying he wasn’t ready for a relationship. May 19, 2023 : The accused allegedly used his authority as a police officer to obtain CCTV footage of Jesse Baird on a date with a man in Paddington.

: The accused allegedly used his authority as a police officer to obtain CCTV footage of Jesse Baird on a date with a man in Paddington. June 24, 2023 : The accused allegedly showed up uninvited to a meeting Baird had with two men.

: The accused allegedly showed up uninvited to a meeting Baird had with two men. August 17, 2023 : The accused allegedly breaks into Baird’s home and steals his mobile phone and wallet while Baird is home. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to this charge.

: The accused allegedly breaks into Baird’s home and steals his mobile phone and wallet while Baird is home. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to this charge. September 2023 : The accused and Jesse Baird re-start their relationship.

: The accused and Jesse Baird re-start their relationship. November 2023 : The pair break up for the final time after Baird allegedly discovers the accused had allegedly accessed his phone to delete messages and block people; and had posted a photograph on Instagram that falsely gave the impression Baird had sent him flowers.

: The pair break up for the final time after Baird allegedly discovers the accused had allegedly accessed his phone to delete messages and block people; and had posted a photograph on Instagram that falsely gave the impression Baird had sent him flowers. World.title: The secret relationship, the $40 million legal fight and the corporate cop’s latest case
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAppliances Opinion The secret relationship, the $40 million legal fight and the corporate cop’s latest case Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer September 21, 2026 — 5:37pm

September 21, 2026 — 5:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Well, you can’t say they weren’t warned. When luxury whitegoods retailer Winning Group appointed former Super Retail boss Anthony Heraghty as chief executive last month, they knew he came with baggage. Former Super Retail Group chief executive Anthony Heraghty. Photography by Joe Ruckli They knew he had conducted a secret relationship with the company’s head of human resources. They knew he had allegedly lied about the relationship to the board and the market. They knew that the board had burnt $40 million in legal bills seeking to defend his lie and destroy the reputation of two senior women who attempted to expose it. They knew he was eventually dumped by Super Retail Group for misleading the company. And they knew that, even as Heraghty’s appointment was announced, the corporate watchdog was still probing Super Retail Group’s handling of whistleblower complaints.



So Winning Group can hardly be surprised that, within weeks of Heraghty getting his feet under the desk, the decision to hire him spectacularly imploded. On Monday the Australian Securities and Investments Commission commenced legal proceedings against Heraghty in the Federal Court, alleging he breached his director’s duties and lied to the board and the market about the relationship. “ASIC alleges Mr Heraghty put himself in a position where his personal interests conflicted with his duties to Super Retail Group and that he failed to properly disclose and manage that conflict,” ASIC chair Sarah Court said. “The allegations in this matter raise important issues about governance, transparency and trust in the information provided to boards and the market.” Given the scale of Heraghty’s very recent fall from grace at Super Retail Group, it was utterly predictable that scandal would follow him to the new job. Predictable, at least, to everyone except Winning. The company did not address the $40 million elephant in the room when he was announced as chief executive in July. And after ASIC launched its legal action on Monday morning, it maintained stony silence. Just days earlier, however, Winning’s external public relations representatives were offering up interviews with Heraghty to celebrate subsidiary Appliances Online’s 21st birthday sale.



Evidently, Winning Group had put a lot of faith in the value of second chances. Or, at least, in the value of Heraghty’s ability to make it rain. Founded more than a century ago, the family-owned company is planning a $1 billion sharemarket float, and believed that Heraghty was the man to take them into that new era. It has also drawn some serious backers, with Ellerston Capital, the investment firm backed by wealthy families, taking a $100 million stake this year. Related Article Opinion

Appliances He lied about an affair and cost his company nearly $30 million. Now he has a new job Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Perhaps the Winning board felt Heraghty’s tawdry scandal was simply a personal matter that could be swiftly brushed aside. Infidelity does not contravene the Corporations Act, after all. But the corporate regulator has taken pains to make clear that it is not acting as the moral arbiter for executive conduct. “This case is not about private relationships but whether a director properly disclosed and managed conflicts of interest and met their duties to the company and shareholders,” Court said.



If ASIC is successful, Heraghty could face penalties in the seven figures. And it’s worth remembering that Heraghty is not only alleged to have misled the board and the market. His former company Super Retail Group led an aggressive campaign of lawfare against the two whistleblowers, former chief legal officer Rebecca Farrell and company secretary Amelia Berczelly, that left both hospitalised for stress. In an affidavit, Berczelly said she believed the company had “wanted to push me to kill myself, destroy my reputation, and bankrupt me as a means to silence me and punish me”. All of this has been well documented in dozens of news articles, of which Winning would be well and truly aware. It was a very big call to hire Heraghty in July, knowing full well the financial and reputational damage he had inflicted upon Super Retail Group. Winning viewed Heraghty as the man to help them scale new heights. Instead, he has dragged them into the muck along with him. They can’t be surprised this has now blown up. World.title: Platina reshuffles hand for high-stakes WA gold hunt
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Platina reshuffles hand for high-stakes WA gold hunt Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 21, 2026 — 5:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Platina Resources has spent the past three years giving itself quite the makeover, swapping its former scandium ambitions for a sharper WA gold focus and progressively sorting through its exploration hand to decide which cards are worth keeping. The transformation received a sizeable financial kick-start in 2023 when Platina sold its namesake Platina scandium project in New South Wales to mining heavyweight Rio Tinto for up to US$14 (A$19.7) million at current exchange rates, of which A$18.3 million has been received, giving the junior something every explorer covets: a decent war chest. Reverse circulation drill rig on site at Platina Resources’ Sunrise Bore project in the well-endowed Laverton greenstone belt, 44 kilometres south of the town of Laverton in WA. The proceeds have helped fund Platina’s gold push without repeatedly rattling the tin for fresh equity. Notably, the company is also entitled to a further US$2 (A$2.8) million from Rio, which is still due this year depending on a timing clause around the granting of Platina’s mining licence - now named Burra - to Rio. The result has delivered a sharper proposition, increasingly concentrated in Western Australia’s prolific Laverton gold district, where the company’s Sunrise Bore, Mt McKenna and Mt Morgans South projects now form the centrepiece of its strategy.



After completing a $1.15 million, largely scrip-based acquisition of the 11.59-square-kilometre Sunrise Bore gold project from private outfit Bravo Minerals in June, Platina wasted little time getting the rods turning. With the deal barely through the door, the company wheeled in a reverse circulation (RC) rig to give the ground its first taste of modern drilling since 1998, quickly putting runs on the board at its newest WA gold play. And if the early results are anything to go by, the company should certainly have plenty to smile about. The maiden 23-hole, 2863-metre campaign delivered a hefty 29-metre hit at 3.38g/t gold from just 11m, including an 11m slice grading an eye-catching 8.62g/t, backed up by hits including 18m going 1.12g/t and a broader 37m intersection assaying 0.43g/t. Hitting such promising numbers first up shouldn’t be a huge surprise given the company is hardly hunting in geological no-man’s-land. Sunrise Bore sits in serious gold company 45km south of Laverton. The broader district hosts AngloGold Ashanti’s multi-million-ounce Sunrise Dam operation 13 km away and Gold Fields’ 3.9-million- ounce Granny Smith mine. Closer historical deposits include Keringal at 450,000 ounces, Golden Delicious with 240,000 ounces and Jubilee, which produced 145,000 ounces of gold. Although proximity to a mine should never be taken for granted, those ounces show the surrounding greenstones and structures clearly know how to carry gold. Platina interprets Sunrise Bore’s mineralised zone as roughly 80m in true thickness and open down-dip, with a simple weighted average of current and historical intersections through the core area clocking in at 0.5g/t gold. There is an intriguing twist, though: the strong recent grades occur predominantly in oxide and could reflect supergene enrichment hiding a bigger orebody lurking below, making fresh-rock drilling an important priority.



Notably, plenty remains to test. The maiden drilling campaign covered only 200m of a broader 1.2km historically identified mineralised trend, which itself lies within a bigger 3.6km structural corridor. Impressive historical drilling included 78m going at 1.17g/t, featuring a 38-metre core of 2.13g/t, while another hole produced a 10-metre slice running at 5.31g/t within a broader interval of 20m grading 2.77g/t, reinforcing the prospect’s geological pedigree. After electing to pivot away from scandium and sharpen its focus on the Eastern Goldfields in 2023, Platina also set about clearing the decks of its other non-core assets, including Xanadu in the Ashburton, Challa near Sandstone and Brimstone near Kalgoorlie. Xanadu was sold to Kalamazoo Resources after disappointing follow-up results, with Platina retaining a one per cent royalty and a potential $500,000 milestone payment, while Challa was relinquished after further work failed to justify continued spending. The still-retained Brimstone was farmed out to NE Minerals, which can earn an 80 per cent interest by funding the project through to a decision to mine. For an explorer with money in the bank, the discipline to stop spending can be just as important as deciding when to start. Platina’s recent rationalisation looks a savvy piece of capital allocation: cut ground that failed to earn another dollar, preserve value where possible and redirect its own exploration firepower towards opportunities it believes can deliver greater scale. With the portfolio reshaped, the treasury well stocked and Sunrise Bore already putting runs on the board, Platina’s next chapter is now about turning its carefully assembled gold hand into genuine scale. Charged with doing exactly that is geologist Dr Paul Polito, who took over as managing director from Corey Nolan in July. Nolan oversaw much of Platina’s portfolio transformation and the assembly of its current Laverton position, leaving Polito with the task of finding out just how much gold potential lies within it.



Polito brings more than three decades of exploration, geoscience, mine geology and development experience, including senior roles with IGO and Anglo-American Exploration. His arrival marks another stage in Platina’s evolution, from assembling and pruning its exploration hand to determining whether the projects surviving the cut possess genuine discovery scale. Platina Resources Mt McKenna gold project 13 kilometres east of Laverton in WA. And Sunrise Bore is not the only card in the hand. Platina’s 174-square-kilometre Mt McKenna project, 13km east of Laverton and 20km northeast of Granny Smith, provides another major prong of the company’s gold push. Platina bought the gold project in September last year by acquiring 100 per cent of the shares in private vendor, Jasper Exploration. The deal comprised $320,000 cash, 20 million Platina shares and a 1.5 per cent net smelter royalty to Jasper. Platina can buy back half of that royalty at market value. Since the acquisition, the company has carried out significant drilling. A maiden 26-hole air core program in late 2025 for 6000m was followed up with an even bigger drilling blitz in 2026. More than 10,800m of air core drilling across 220 holes outlined a mineralised corridor stretching one kilometre at the Granite Well East prospect, with hits including 1m at 7.1g/t from 40m and 4m at 1.11g/t from 12m. The company says follow-up air core drilling is now planned.



At two of Mt McKenna’s other prospects, Black Rock and Granite Hill, drilling added a 4-metre hit going 4.69g/t from 16m. Additional gold and arsenic anomalism point to a north-northeast structure that could support gold mineralisation extending more than 800m. Several mineralised holes finished at or near the top of fresh rock, suggesting the shallow campaign has done its targeting job. Deeper RC drilling is now planned to determine whether the gold, structures and associated arsenic anomalism point towards something meatier lurking below. As a vote of confidence, Platina was awarded $109,200 under the Western Australian Government’s Co-funded Exploration Drilling Program to support a planned 13-hole RC program at Black Rock and Granite Hill later this year. The company has also recently added the 126.4-square-kilometre Mt Morgans South gold project to its Laverton hand, acquiring the ground from Genesis Minerals. Sitting 35km southwest of Laverton, the project lies in well-endowed gold country, close to Genesis’ Mt Morgans operations and its Westralia deposit, which hosts more than 1.4 million ounces of gold, while the nearby Jupiter deposit adds a further 740,000 ounces. Platina acquired the 18 tenements for $100,000 cash and five million shares, with another $550,000 payable if a JORC gold resource of at least 200,000 ounces is defined. The ground includes a stretch of the regional Celia fault, although the project remains earlier-stage, with a review of historical exploration data and soil sampling still required to generate compelling drilling targets, along with executing a heritage agreement.



Beyond Laverton, Platina’s Beete gold project, near Norseman, contains prospective structures along an extension of the Norseman greenstone belt and sits 10km south of the one-million-ounce Scotia gold deposit owned by Pantoro Limited and Tulla Resources. Although an air-core program provided modest initial results, the company plans to undertake an RC program across selected zones and around the historical 24.8g/t Beete mine, subject to finalising native title requirements. Rounding out the company’s assets is the Brimstone project, 40km northeast of Kalgoorlie, where Platina can keep a foot in the door while NE Minerals picks up the exploration tab. Under their joint venture agreement, NE Minerals can earn an 80 per cent interest by funding all exploration, evaluation and development expenditure through to a decision to mine, preserving Platina’s exposure without draining its own exploration kitty. Finally, its Jubilee project 15km east of Meekatharra in the prolific Yilgarn craton is subject to ongoing native title negotiations to establish a heritage agreement before the tenement application can progress. Platina entered 2026 with $11.4 million in cash and still held a healthy $8.6 million at the end of the June quarter despite ramping up exploration and completing a string of acquisitions, allowing it to make the leap into full-time gold exploration from a position of financial strength. The additional A$2.8 million still expected to drop into the till from Rio will provide another handy fillip. Three years after cashing in its scandium chips, Platina has tested projects, walked away when results did not warrant another dollar, preserved upside where it could and concentrated its own exploration spending around some of WA’s most heavily endowed gold country. Sunrise Bore has supplied the eye-catching numbers, Mt McKenna has generated targets demanding a deeper look and Mt Morgans South adds another sizeable piece of prospective Laverton real estate.



Now it falls to Polito and his team to play those cards. With a healthy treasury, promising early gold hits and plenty of targets still to drill, the challenge is to turn three years of careful portfolio reshuffling into the kind of discovery scale Platina has been positioning itself to chase. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: NRL axes top referee Ashley Klein after Eden Park blunder
World.content:
Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL axes top referee Ashley Klein after Eden Park blunder Christian Nicolussi Updated September 21, 2026 — 5:00pm ,first published 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Top referee Ashley Klein has been dumped for failing to award an escort penalty in the final minute of Sunday’s Eden Park epic. The NRL conceded the New Zealand Warriors should have been awarded a penalty – and the chance to send their game against Newcastle into extra point – when Tyson Frizell escorted Leka Halasima off the ball. Loading The Warriors contacted the NRL on Monday morning to discuss a number of contentious calls in their 12-10 loss to Newcastle, particularly why Frizell was not punished for blocking the path of a leaping Halasima. Ironically, the non-call on Frizell came after the NRL last week sent out a reminder to clubs still in the finals race that referees would clamp down on escorts after the Dolphins accused the Warriors of getting away with the same tactic in week one of the finals.



Klein did not penalise Frizell on Sunday, and the Warriors had already used their captain’s challenge, which meant they could not ask for the play to be reviewed by the bunker. Klein will not be selected to officiate either of the two preliminary finals this weekend. Newcastle celebrate a shock win at Eden Park on Sunday. NRL Photos Sources with knowledge of the situation not authorised to speak publicly confirmed Klein remained in contention to be the man in the middle for Sunday week’s grand final, but he will not feature this weekend. Adam Gee refereed the Roosters-Sharks semi-final on Saturday night, while Gerard Sutton and Grant Atkins, last year’s grand final referee, will be in contention for this weekend’s preliminary finals.



Warriors chief executive Cameron George confirmed he wanted an explanation from the NRL, saying on Monday: “It was disappointing because a warning was sent out to the clubs about [escorts] this week; it was extremely obvious that’s what occurred with [Frizell]. “Then to have no review or anything done by the referee, it was disappointing. We have to move on.” Referee Ashley Klein will not officiate either of this weekend’s preliminary finals after failing to award a penalty late in Sunday’s semi-final at Eden Park. Getty Images The bunker had minutes earlier ruled that centre Ali Leiataua had got a thumb to an intercept attempt, and Te Maire Martin was controversially ruled to have stripped the ball from Greg Marzhew in a tackle with more than one defender involved. As Warriors coach Andrew Webster said after the gut-wrenching loss: “I thought they were trying to find ways to take it off us.”



The same sources, however, confirmed the NRL was satisfied with both those bunker calls. The Frizell blunder ignited the debate about the bunker and what role technology should play in the NRL. It was only a couple of weeks ago South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett wanted it scrapped completely, given those operating the multimillion-dollar technology are not immune from human error. Fan frustration spilled over after the game with a handful of spectators throwing bottles in the direction of Klein. NRL investigators have already started analysing TV footage to identify the culprits. View post on X



“We had close to 49,000 fans, which meant we broke a record, and while I know we can all get frustrated, that behaviour is unacceptable and poor,” George said. “I know the stadium and the NRL are looking at it. Whatever action they take, we will support.” ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys added: “We began an investigation immediately on breaches of the NRL spectators’ code of conduct. “We had an investigator from the integrity unit at the actual game. If those fans are found guilty, they will be banned for a period of time. “It was a shame because the actual day was brilliant. I was there, and the atmosphere was so good.



Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Footy fans must pull their heads in after unruly crowd behaviour Tom Decent SMH chief sports writer “There will be no issues about Eden Park holding an Origin game there next year because of the actions of a few fans. Most of the fans were well-behaved all afternoon – we won’t punish 99.9 per cent of them because of the 0.1 per cent.” Such was the success of the Eden Park clash, V’landys said he was open to taking more events to Auckland, and pointed out there had been more than 80,000 fans

World.content:
Recommendation 2

That the NSW government, as part of its review of university enabling acts, consider amendments to the legislation to require university governing bodies to have regard to the wellbeing, health and safety of staff and students when exercising their functions and making significant strategic, organisational and operational decisions.

Recommendation 3

That, in order to better protect the psychosocial safety of staff and address fears of reprisal, the NSW government, as part of its review of the enabling acts, consider how the legislation can provide checks and balances on the very significant power held by heads of school, deans and other senior leaders.

Recommendation 7

That the NSW government consider establishing an independent external mechanism through which university staff can confidentially raise governance, integrity and maladministration concerns, with appropriate whistleblower protections.

Recommendation 8

That the NSW government amend the enabling acts for all NSW universities to strengthen representative governance by increasing minimum requirements for 50 per cent elected academic staff, professional staff and student representation on university councils.

Recommendation 11

That the NSW government amend the enabling legislation for each NSW university to require the establishment of an independent university council secretariat at each university, accountable to and operating under the direction of the university’s governing body rather than university management.

Recommendation 14

That, to improve transparency in university council decision-making, the NSW government require NSW universities to publish the minutes of university council meetings, including the rationale for major decisions affecting staff and students, subject to appropriate confidentiality requirements.

Recommendation 15

That the NSW government improve legislative provisions for transparency and accountability in university executive decision-making.

Recommendation 16

That the NSW government: require universities to disclose in their annual reports in a standardised format the process and considerations by which remuneration for their vice chancellors and senior executives is determined, including key performance indicators, bonuses, incentive arrangements, allowances, loan arrangements, reimbursements and other material non-salary benefits.

Recommendation 18

That the NSW government prohibit NSW universities from providing staff or student data to private third-party organisations for sector-wide benchmarking, analytics or comparative performance products unless the explicit informed consent of affected staff and students has first been obtained, in line with the National Health and Medical Research Council’s Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research.

World.title: No warning, 12-year-old guidelines and a long shift: The litany of problems before Joe Massa’s death
World.content:
NationalNSWHealthcare No warning, 12-year-old guidelines and a long shift: The litany of problems before Joe Massa’s death Rachel Rasker September 21, 2026 — 5:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The registered nurse who triaged a two-year-old who died at the Northern Beaches Hospital has told a coronial inquest she had no alert about his abnormal heartbeat, was working with 12-year-old guidelines and was finishing a long shift during which she had been assaulted. NSW State Coroner Teresa O’Sullivan is examining the litany of problems at Northern Beaches Hospital that led to Joe Massa going from playing peek-a-boo to entering cardiac arrest within a day. Joe Massa’s mother stroked a tiny pair of shoes as she gave evidence. The toddler’s death shocked Sydney and led to the hospital, which was previously run by the private operator Healthscope, to be transferred into public hands. His mother Elouise Massa’s advocacy following his death also led to “Joe’s Law”, which bans future public-private partnerships. Massa gently stroked a tiny pair of her son’s shoes as she gave evidence on Monday, the first day of the inquest. She said clinicians at the hospital were rude and did not listen to her concerns as Joe’s condition rapidly deteriorated.



Related Article Northern Beaches Hospital This life-saving equipment is standard across NSW hospitals. It was never installed at Northern Beaches Massa took Joe to the Northern Beaches emergency department about 7am on September 14, 2024, after she became concerned about his severe vomiting and dry retching overnight. “He looked terrible,” she said. “He could barely keep his head up, he was going in and out of consciousness, he was floppy.” She told the court she had “a mother’s instinct” that something was “very wrong”. Joe was triaged as a category three patient who required treatment within 30 minutes, despite having a “red zone” heart rate of 182 beats per minute.



The registered nurse who triaged Joe, Hilary O’Neill, said she saw the toddler at the end of a 12-hour overnight shift without a proper break, during which she said she was assaulted by a mental health patient, who threw her against an ambulance door. O’Neill said the only reference she had to assess Joe’s heart rate was a resuscitation guideline from 2012. The system informed her Joseph was one year old – he was aged 22 months – and she assessed his initial heart rate of 160-170 BPM as just above the normal range. She did not re-check the guide after he later recorded the higher heart rate. “There were no track or trigger systems in place to alert me that it was in the red zone,” she said.



The inquest heard that in the public hospital system, clinical software would have automatically flagged that the reading was outside normal parameters, and notified all staff who reviewed the patient file. O’Neill said if she had known Joe’s heart rate was in the red zone, she would have put him in category two, which would have resulted in him being given a bed on the ward with constant cardiac monitoring. Elouise Massa gave evidence at the NSW Coroner’s Court on Monday about her son Joe’s treatment at Northern Beaches Hospital. Kate Geraghty O’Neill also said she contacted the chief medical officer on duty and asked for a bed. She said the doctor told her that paediatric emergency nurses would collect him. However, the mother and son were instead left on a chair in the waiting room for two and a half hours, where Massa said she was instructed to continue a “sip and wait process” of rehydration.



Massa said trying to cradle Joe on her lap, fill a medical syringe with liquid from a cup of electrolytes, administer the fluid to Joe, note his intake on a form and set a new timer every five minutes was “near impossible”. She said her son was declining rapidly but that her repeated requests for a bed were denied, and the doctor on duty instead treated Joe in the waiting area: “I was pacing around with him in my arms ... petrified.” Loading The statement Massa created a few days after Joe’s death was a key point of reference throughout her testimony. She said she put together the record of events while “lying in bed crying” as a friend took notes.



“I knew instinctively Joe wasn’t cared for properly, and we knew it would be a wise idea to make notes, so down the track [I had] events freshly on paper.” Related Article Healthcare ‘Trust your gut’: Parents’ plea after toddler’s sepsis death The court heard Joe was given a bed by 9.51am, but was moved to the hospital’s resuscitation unit by 10.41am after a nurse raised concern about the toddler’s condition. Massa said the family was left alone in the resuscitation bay, during which time hospital staff said they were gathering a team together. “I was always by his side,” Massa said.



She said she called a friend whose husband was a doctor, and hung up at about 10.47am: “I was on the phone in utter despair, wanting to get out of this hospital, not knowing what to do.” It was at about this time that Joe went into cardiac arrest. He was given CPR and circulation returned about 30 minutes later. He was intubated and transferred to Sydney Children’s Hospital but suffered irreversible brain damage. Joe’s life support was withdrawn two days later. The clinicians involved in the boy’s treatment and a coalition of independent experts are expected to continue their testimony at the inquest in the coming days. World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial as it happened: Former NSW police officer’s trial begins over alleged murder of Paddington couple Jesse Baird and Luke Davies
World.content:
Good evening and thank you for reading our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s criminal trial.

The former police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, on February 19, 2024.

Beau Lamarre-Condon in the NSW Supreme Court on the first day of his trial. Rocco Fazzari

He has also pleaded not guilty to one count of aggravated breaking and entering Baird’s home in August 2023 and stealing a mobile phone and wallet belonging to Baird.

A 15-person jury was empanelled on Monday for the trial, which is expected to run for up to 12 weeks. In the event all 15 jurors are still present at the end of the trial, a ballot will be conducted to reduce their number to 12.

Today, Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, delivered his opening address to the jury. This sets out the Crown’s case and is not evidence, but it is a guide to the evidence it expects to call in the months ahead.

Lamarre-Condon is entitled to the presumption of innocence and his barrister John Stratton, SC, will deliver an opening address on Tuesday after Hatfield.

During his opening this afternoon, Hatfield alleged that Lamarre-Condon developed an “an obsessive and jealous infatuation” with Baird after a short relationship that started in late 2022 and was ended for the first time by Baird in April 2023.

After a brief resumption of their relationship later that year, it was “firmly and irretrievably ended” by Baird in November 2023, the Crown alleges.

The Crown case is that the murder of Baird was premeditated but that he killed Davies, Baird’s new boyfriend, to eliminate a witness to his crime. This is the Crown’s alleged timeline of events.

Late 2022 : The accused and Jesse Baird met and started a casual relationship.

: The accused and Jesse Baird met and started a casual relationship. April 2023 : Baird sent the accused a “sympathetic” message saying he wasn’t ready for a relationship.

: Baird sent the accused a “sympathetic” message saying he wasn’t ready for a relationship. May 19, 2023 : The accused allegedly used his authority as a police officer to obtain CCTV footage of Jesse Baird on a date with a man in Paddington.

: The accused allegedly used his authority as a police officer to obtain CCTV footage of Jesse Baird on a date with a man in Paddington. June 24, 2023 : The accused allegedly showed up uninvited to a meeting Baird had with two men.

: The accused allegedly showed up uninvited to a meeting Baird had with two men. August 17, 2023 : The accused allegedly breaks into Baird’s home and steals his mobile phone and wallet while Baird is home. Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to this charge.

World.title: The secret relationship, the $40 million legal fight and the corporate cop’s latest case
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesAppliances Opinion The secret relationship, the $40 million legal fight and the corporate cop’s latest case Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer September 21, 2026 — 5:37pm

September 21, 2026 — 5:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Well, you can’t say they weren’t warned. When luxury whitegoods retailer Winning Group appointed former Super Retail boss Anthony Heraghty as chief executive last month, they knew he came with baggage. Former Super Retail Group chief executive Anthony Heraghty. Photography by Joe Ruckli They knew he had conducted a secret relationship with the company’s head of human resources. They knew he had allegedly lied about the relationship to the board and the market. They knew that the board had burnt $40 million in legal bills seeking to defend his lie and destroy the reputation of two senior women who attempted to expose it. They knew he was eventually dumped by Super Retail Group for misleading the company. And they knew that, even as Heraghty’s appointment was announced, the corporate watchdog was still probing Super Retail Group’s handling of whistleblower complaints.



So Winning Group can hardly be surprised that, within weeks of Heraghty getting his feet under the desk, the decision to hire him spectacularly imploded. On Monday the Australian Securities and Investments Commission commenced legal proceedings against Heraghty in the Federal Court, alleging he breached his director’s duties and lied to the board and the market about the relationship. “ASIC alleges Mr Heraghty put himself in a position where his personal interests conflicted with his duties to Super Retail Group and that he failed to properly disclose and manage that conflict,” ASIC chair Sarah Court said. “The allegations in this matter raise important issues about governance, transparency and trust in the information provided to boards and the market.” Given the scale of Heraghty’s very recent fall from grace at Super Retail Group, it was utterly predictable that scandal would follow him to the new job. Predictable, at least, to everyone except Winning. The company did not address the $40 million elephant in the room when he was announced as chief executive in July. And after ASIC launched its legal action on Monday morning, it maintained stony silence. Just days earlier, however, Winning’s external public relations representatives were offering up interviews with Heraghty to celebrate subsidiary Appliances Online’s 21st birthday sale.



Evidently, Winning Group had put a lot of faith in the value of second chances. Or, at least, in the value of Heraghty’s ability to make it rain. Founded more than a century ago, the family-owned company is planning a $1 billion sharemarket float, and believed that Heraghty was the man to take them into that new era. It has also drawn some serious backers, with Ellerston Capital, the investment firm backed by wealthy families, taking a $100 million stake this year. Related Article Opinion

Appliances He lied about an affair and cost his company nearly $30 million. Now he has a new job Kishor Napier-Raman Senior Business Writer Perhaps the Winning board felt Heraghty’s tawdry scandal was simply a personal matter that could be swiftly brushed aside. Infidelity does not contravene the Corporations Act, after all. But the corporate regulator has taken pains to make clear that it is not acting as the moral arbiter for executive conduct. “This case is not about private relationships but whether a director properly disclosed and managed conflicts of interest and met their duties to the company and shareholders,” Court said.



If ASIC is successful, Heraghty could face penalties in the seven figures. And it’s worth remembering that Heraghty is not only alleged to have misled the board and the market. His former company Super Retail Group led an aggressive campaign of lawfare against the two whistleblowers, former chief legal officer Rebecca Farrell and company secretary Amelia Berczelly, that left both hospitalised for stress. In an affidavit, Berczelly said she believed the company had “wanted to push me to kill myself, destroy my reputation, and bankrupt me as a means to silence me and punish me”. All of this has been well documented in dozens of news articles, of which Winning would be well and truly aware. It was a very big call to hire Heraghty in July, knowing full well the financial and reputational damage he had inflicted upon Super Retail Group. Winning viewed Heraghty as the man to help them scale new heights. Instead, he has dragged them into the muck along with him. They can’t be surprised this has now blown up.
