World.title: Platina reshuffles hand for high-stakes WA gold hunt
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Platina reshuffles hand for high-stakes WA gold hunt Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward September 21, 2026 — 5:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Platina Resources has spent the past three years giving itself quite the makeover, swapping its former scandium ambitions for a sharper WA gold focus and progressively sorting through its exploration hand to decide which cards are worth keeping. The transformation received a sizeable financial kick-start in 2023 when Platina sold its namesake Platina scandium project in New South Wales to mining heavyweight Rio Tinto for up to US$14 (A$19.7) million at current exchange rates, of which A$18.3 million has been received, giving the junior something every explorer covets: a decent war chest. Reverse circulation drill rig on site at Platina Resources’ Sunrise Bore project in the well-endowed Laverton greenstone belt, 44 kilometres south of the town of Laverton in WA. The proceeds have helped fund Platina’s gold push without repeatedly rattling the tin for fresh equity. Notably, the company is also entitled to a further US$2 (A$2.8) million from Rio, which is still due this year depending on a timing clause around the granting of Platina’s mining licence - now named Burra - to Rio. The result has delivered a sharper proposition, increasingly concentrated in Western Australia’s prolific Laverton gold district, where the company’s Sunrise Bore, Mt McKenna and Mt Morgans South projects now form the centrepiece of its strategy.



After completing a $1.15 million, largely scrip-based acquisition of the 11.59-square-kilometre Sunrise Bore gold project from private outfit Bravo Minerals in June, Platina wasted little time getting the rods turning. With the deal barely through the door, the company wheeled in a reverse circulation (RC) rig to give the ground its first taste of modern drilling since 1998, quickly putting runs on the board at its newest WA gold play. And if the early results are anything to go by, the company should certainly have plenty to smile about. The maiden 23-hole, 2863-metre campaign delivered a hefty 29-metre hit at 3.38g/t gold from just 11m, including an 11m slice grading an eye-catching 8.62g/t, backed up by hits including 18m going 1.12g/t and a broader 37m intersection assaying 0.43g/t. Hitting such promising numbers first up shouldn’t be a huge surprise given the company is hardly hunting in geological no-man’s-land. Sunrise Bore sits in serious gold company 45km south of Laverton. The broader district hosts AngloGold Ashanti’s multi-million-ounce Sunrise Dam operation 13 km away and Gold Fields’ 3.9-million- ounce Granny Smith mine. Closer historical deposits include Keringal at 450,000 ounces, Golden Delicious with 240,000 ounces and Jubilee, which produced 145,000 ounces of gold. Although proximity to a mine should never be taken for granted, those ounces show the surrounding greenstones and structures clearly know how to carry gold. Platina interprets Sunrise Bore’s mineralised zone as roughly 80m in true thickness and open down-dip, with a simple weighted average of current and historical intersections through the core area clocking in at 0.5g/t gold. There is an intriguing twist, though: the strong recent grades occur predominantly in oxide and could reflect supergene enrichment hiding a bigger orebody lurking below, making fresh-rock drilling an important priority.



Notably, plenty remains to test. The maiden drilling campaign covered only 200m of a broader 1.2km historically identified mineralised trend, which itself lies within a bigger 3.6km structural corridor. Impressive historical drilling included 78m going at 1.17g/t, featuring a 38-metre core of 2.13g/t, while another hole produced a 10-metre slice running at 5.31g/t within a broader interval of 20m grading 2.77g/t, reinforcing the prospect’s geological pedigree. After electing to pivot away from scandium and sharpen its focus on the Eastern Goldfields in 2023, Platina also set about clearing the decks of its other non-core assets, including Xanadu in the Ashburton, Challa near Sandstone and Brimstone near Kalgoorlie. Xanadu was sold to Kalamazoo Resources after disappointing follow-up results, with Platina retaining a one per cent royalty and a potential $500,000 milestone payment, while Challa was relinquished after further work failed to justify continued spending. The still-retained Brimstone was farmed out to NE Minerals, which can earn an 80 per cent interest by funding the project through to a decision to mine. For an explorer with money in the bank, the discipline to stop spending can be just as important as deciding when to start. Platina’s recent rationalisation looks a savvy piece of capital allocation: cut ground that failed to earn another dollar, preserve value where possible and redirect its own exploration firepower towards opportunities it believes can deliver greater scale. With the portfolio reshaped, the treasury well stocked and Sunrise Bore already putting runs on the board, Platina’s next chapter is now about turning its carefully assembled gold hand into genuine scale. Charged with doing exactly that is geologist Dr Paul Polito, who took over as managing director from Corey Nolan in July. Nolan oversaw much of Platina’s portfolio transformation and the assembly of its current Laverton position, leaving Polito with the task of finding out just how much gold potential lies within it.



Polito brings more than three decades of exploration, geoscience, mine geology and development experience, including senior roles with IGO and Anglo-American Exploration. His arrival marks another stage in Platina’s evolution, from assembling and pruning its exploration hand to determining whether the projects surviving the cut possess genuine discovery scale. Platina Resources Mt McKenna gold project 13 kilometres east of Laverton in WA. And Sunrise Bore is not the only card in the hand. Platina’s 174-square-kilometre Mt McKenna project, 13km east of Laverton and 20km northeast of Granny Smith, provides another major prong of the company’s gold push. Platina bought the gold project in September last year by acquiring 100 per cent of the shares in private vendor, Jasper Exploration. The deal comprised $320,000 cash, 20 million Platina shares and a 1.5 per cent net smelter royalty to Jasper. Platina can buy back half of that royalty at market value. Since the acquisition, the company has carried out significant drilling. A maiden 26-hole air core program in late 2025 for 6000m was followed up with an even bigger drilling blitz in 2026. More than 10,800m of air core drilling across 220 holes outlined a mineralised corridor stretching one kilometre at the Granite Well East prospect, with hits including 1m at 7.1g/t from 40m and 4m at 1.11g/t from 12m. The company says follow-up air core drilling is now planned.



At two of Mt McKenna’s other prospects, Black Rock and Granite Hill, drilling added a 4-metre hit going 4.69g/t from 16m. Additional gold and arsenic anomalism point to a north-northeast structure that could support gold mineralisation extending more than 800m. Several mineralised holes finished at or near the top of fresh rock, suggesting the shallow campaign has done its targeting job. Deeper RC drilling is now planned to determine whether the gold, structures and associated arsenic anomalism point towards something meatier lurking below. As a vote of confidence, Platina was awarded $109,200 under the Western Australian Government’s Co-funded Exploration Drilling Program to support a planned 13-hole RC program at Black Rock and Granite Hill later this year. The company has also recently added the 126.4-square-kilometre Mt Morgans South gold project to its Laverton hand, acquiring the ground from Genesis Minerals. Sitting 35km southwest of Laverton, the project lies in well-endowed gold country, close to Genesis’ Mt Morgans operations and its Westralia deposit, which hosts more than 1.4 million ounces of gold, while the nearby Jupiter deposit adds a further 740,000 ounces. Platina acquired the 18 tenements for $100,000 cash and five million shares, with another $550,000 payable if a JORC gold resource of at least 200,000 ounces is defined. The ground includes a stretch of the regional Celia fault, although the project remains earlier-stage, with a review of historical exploration data and soil sampling still required to generate compelling drilling targets, along with executing a heritage agreement.



Beyond Laverton, Platina’s Beete gold project, near Norseman, contains prospective structures along an extension of the Norseman greenstone belt and sits 10km south of the one-million-ounce Scotia gold deposit owned by Pantoro Limited and Tulla Resources. Although an air-core program provided modest initial results, the company plans to undertake an RC program across selected zones and around the historical 24.8g/t Beete mine, subject to finalising native title requirements. Rounding out the company’s assets is the Brimstone project, 40km northeast of Kalgoorlie, where Platina can keep a foot in the door while NE Minerals picks up the exploration tab. Under their joint venture agreement, NE Minerals can earn an 80 per cent interest by funding all exploration, evaluation and development expenditure through to a decision to mine, preserving Platina’s exposure without draining its own exploration kitty. Finally, its Jubilee project 15km east of Meekatharra in the prolific Yilgarn craton is subject to ongoing native title negotiations to establish a heritage agreement before the tenement application can progress. Platina entered 2026 with $11.4 million in cash and still held a healthy $8.6 million at the end of the June quarter despite ramping up exploration and completing a string of acquisitions, allowing it to make the leap into full-time gold exploration from a position of financial strength. The additional A$2.8 million still expected to drop into the till from Rio will provide another handy fillip. Three years after cashing in its scandium chips, Platina has tested projects, walked away when results did not warrant another dollar, preserved upside where it could and concentrated its own exploration spending around some of WA’s most heavily endowed gold country. Sunrise Bore has supplied the eye-catching numbers, Mt McKenna has generated targets demanding a deeper look and Mt Morgans South adds another sizeable piece of prospective Laverton real estate.



Now it falls to Polito and his team to play those cards. With a healthy treasury, promising early gold hits and plenty of targets still to drill, the challenge is to turn three years of careful portfolio reshuffling into the kind of discovery scale Platina has been positioning itself to chase. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? Contact: mattbirney@bullsnbears.com.au

World.title: NRL axes top referee Ashley Klein after Eden Park blunder
World.content:
Breaking SportNRLNRL 2026 NRL axes top referee Ashley Klein after Eden Park blunder Christian Nicolussi Updated September 21, 2026 — 5:00pm ,first published 11:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Top referee Ashley Klein has been dumped for failing to award an escort penalty in the final minute of Sunday’s Eden Park epic. The NRL conceded the New Zealand Warriors should have been awarded a penalty – and the chance to send their game against Newcastle into extra point – when Tyson Frizell escorted Leka Halasima off the ball. Loading The Warriors contacted the NRL on Monday morning to discuss a number of contentious calls in their 12-10 loss to Newcastle, particularly why Frizell was not punished for blocking the path of a leaping Halasima. Ironically, the non-call on Frizell came after the NRL last week sent out a reminder to clubs still in the finals race that referees would clamp down on escorts after the Dolphins accused the Warriors of getting away with the same tactic in week one of the finals.



Klein did not penalise Frizell on Sunday, and the Warriors had already used their captain’s challenge, which meant they could not ask for the play to be reviewed by the bunker. Klein will not be selected to officiate either of the two preliminary finals this weekend. Newcastle celebrate a shock win at Eden Park on Sunday. NRL Photos Sources with knowledge of the situation not authorised to speak publicly confirmed Klein remained in contention to be the man in the middle for Sunday week’s grand final, but he will not feature this weekend. Adam Gee refereed the Roosters-Sharks semi-final on Saturday night, while Gerard Sutton and Grant Atkins, last year’s grand final referee, will be in contention for this weekend’s preliminary finals.



Warriors chief executive Cameron George confirmed he wanted an explanation from the NRL, saying on Monday: “It was disappointing because a warning was sent out to the clubs about [escorts] this week; it was extremely obvious that’s what occurred with [Frizell]. “Then to have no review or anything done by the referee, it was disappointing. We have to move on.” Referee Ashley Klein will not officiate either of this weekend’s preliminary finals after failing to award a penalty late in Sunday’s semi-final at Eden Park. Getty Images The bunker had minutes earlier ruled that centre Ali Leiataua had got a thumb to an intercept attempt, and Te Maire Martin was controversially ruled to have stripped the ball from Greg Marzhew in a tackle with more than one defender involved. As Warriors coach Andrew Webster said after the gut-wrenching loss: “I thought they were trying to find ways to take it off us.”



The same sources, however, confirmed the NRL was satisfied with both those bunker calls. The Frizell blunder ignited the debate about the bunker and what role technology should play in the NRL. It was only a couple of weeks ago South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett wanted it scrapped completely, given those operating the multimillion-dollar technology are not immune from human error. Fan frustration spilled over after the game with a handful of spectators throwing bottles in the direction of Klein. NRL investigators have already started analysing TV footage to identify the culprits. View post on X



“We had close to 49,000 fans, which meant we broke a record, and while I know we can all get frustrated, that behaviour is unacceptable and poor,” George said. “I know the stadium and the NRL are looking at it. Whatever action they take, we will support.” ARL Commission chairman Peter V’landys added: “We began an investigation immediately on breaches of the NRL spectators’ code of conduct. “We had an investigator from the integrity unit at the actual game. If those fans are found guilty, they will be banned for a period of time. “It was a shame because the actual day was brilliant. I was there, and the atmosphere was so good.



Related Article Opinion

NRL 2026 Footy fans must pull their heads in after unruly crowd behaviour Tom Decent SMH chief sports writer “There will be no issues about Eden Park holding an Origin game there next year because of the actions of a few fans. Most of the fans were well-behaved all afternoon – we won’t punish 99.9 per cent of them because of the 0.1 per cent.” Such was the success of the Eden Park clash, V’landys said he was open to taking more events to Auckland, and pointed out there had been more than 80,000 fans

World.title: Why vice chancellors may be forced to justify their pay packets
World.content:
Recommendation 2

That the NSW government, as part of its review of university enabling acts, consider amendments to the legislation to require university governing bodies to have regard to the wellbeing, health and safety of staff and students when exercising their functions and making significant strategic, organisational and operational decisions.

Recommendation 3

That, in order to better protect the psychosocial safety of staff and address fears of reprisal, the NSW government, as part of its review of the enabling acts, consider how the legislation can provide checks and balances on the very significant power held by heads of school, deans and other senior leaders.

Recommendation 7

That the NSW government consider establishing an independent external mechanism through which university staff can confidentially raise governance, integrity and maladministration concerns, with appropriate whistleblower protections.

Recommendation 8

That the NSW government amend the enabling acts for all NSW universities to strengthen representative governance by increasing minimum requirements for 50 per cent elected academic staff, professional staff and student representation on university councils.

Recommendation 11

That the NSW government amend the enabling legislation for each NSW university to require the establishment of an independent university council secretariat at each university, accountable to and operating under the direction of the university’s governing body rather than university management.

Recommendation 14

That, to improve transparency in university council decision-making, the NSW government require NSW universities to publish the minutes of university council meetings, including the rationale for major decisions affecting staff and students, subject to appropriate confidentiality requirements.

Recommendation 15

That the NSW government improve legislative provisions for transparency and accountability in university executive decision-making.

Recommendation 16

That the NSW government: require universities to disclose in their annual reports in a standardised format the process and considerations by which remuneration for their vice chancellors and senior executives is determined, including key performance indicators, bonuses, incentive arrangements, allowances, loan arrangements, reimbursements and other material non-salary benefits.

Recommendation 18

That the NSW government prohibit NSW universities from providing staff or student data to private third-party organisations for sector-wide benchmarking, analytics or comparative performance products unless the explicit informed consent of affected staff and students has first been obtained, in line with the National Health and Medical Research Council’s Statement on Ethical Conduct in Human Research.

Note: Recommendations have been edited for brevity.

World.title: 'It's certainly not safe for the patients': Six staff resign from  Pahīatua medical centre
World.content:
Six staff at the Pahīatua Medical Centre have resigned today, amid growing concern around extreme workloads and patient safety.

Almost 5000 patients depend on the clinic in the Tararua district.

But over the past two years, 81 staff have resigned from the Tararua Health Group, alleging unsafe workloads and dangerously long wait times for appointments and tests.

Registered nurse Mark Emmerson resigned along with five of his colleagues today.

He told Checkpoint he was "sick" at the decision, but also "relieved" the matter had come to the nation's attention.

"As nurses, we try. We will run ourselves ragged until to get the job done. But it's certainly not safe for the patients. It's not safe for the staff psychologically."

Audio player for " Six staff resign from Pahiatua Medical Centre over safety concerns " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1498378%2Fit-s-certainly-not-safe-for-the-patients-six-staff-resign-from-pahiatua-medical-centre

Six staff resign from Pahiatua Medical Centre over safety concerns Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

He said the clinic was a "pressure cooker" as there were limited clinicians.

"We have a nurse practitioner that works for us four days a week. We've got a nurse prescriber that is full-time, but she's leaving in two weeks."

He said a lot of experience had left Pahīatua Medical centre today: a phlebotomist of 15 years, an administrator of 21 years, three registered nurses including himself, and a nurse practitioner.

He said the clinic would "certainly not" function without them.

He said an acute clinic had been set up a few months ago, but patients were being seen there when it was not appropriate.

"We're getting ACC, we're getting working income renewals and all of that sort of thing just can't be done in an acute setting."

He stressed that the staff were not leaving the community behind.

"We have put out there that we are willing to work with other providers who recognise the importance of our community, recognise the importance of our staff and are willing to work with us towards providing essential primary health care in the area."

Locals rally outside Pahiatua Medical Centre in support of staff. Supplied

Tony Wai - chief executive of the Primary Health Organisation, which managed the clinic's contract - responded that he felt concerns could be addressed with a plan, but he was not sure what that plan would look like.

However, health advocacy group Patient Voice Aotearoa called for a review into every patient who had a screening test through Tararua Health Group.

Co-founder and spokesperson Malcolm Mulholland said the group serviced 9500 patients in the wider area.

He told Checkpoint a review was important to understand patients' status as a delayed cancer diagnosis resulted in negative outcomes for patients.

Audio player for " Major concerns over state of rural health services " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/health/1498378%2Fit-s-certainly-not-safe-for-the-patients-six-staff-resign-from-pahiatua-medical-centre

Major concerns over state of rural health services Checkpoint Download MP3 9m

He said the health minister and Health NZ were responsible.

"Ultimately it's up to the minister and Health New Zealand to intervene and say 'enough is enough; we're pulling the contract and we're going back to the community to see what best meets their needs'."

Mulholland said other regions were facing similar problems, citing Kirikiri as an example of where there might not be a GP within a couple of years.

In order to retain GPs in rural areas, he argued that Health NZ should hire practitioners directly.

"There's no middleman, there's no PHO, there's no business, there's no practice."

He said the approach would hand doctors more freedom as well.

World.title: Flooding occurred five times at Moa Point in months leading to the failure, new report reveals
World.content:
A newly-released report into the Moa Point failure reveals flooding occurred five times at the sewage treatment plant in the months leading up to disaster.

It also raises questions about the plant's alarm systems - including whether alarms were sighted but not acted on, and that others weren't programmed to trigger immediate pagers.

About 16 billion litres of raw sewage had spilled into the city's south coast since Moa Point catastrophically flooded on February 4.

The report from infrastructure consultancy firm Aecom had been withheld until now due to insurance discussions.

Its investigation did not identify a single sole cause of the flooding but found it was caused by a combination of technical and organisation factors.

The plant was undergoing critical upgrades to its ultra-violet disinfection channels at the time of the flooding. This reduced the plant's capacity to treat sewage from the community.

A Moa Point wastewater sign. (File photo) RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

With sewage diverted to a bypass pipe, heavy rain and increased flows on the night caused air bubbles in the bypass pipe choking the wastewater and causing it to flood.

But the report said overflows occurred in one of the UV channels twice in October 2025, twice in January and once on February 3 - the day before the disaster.

While these did not spill into the wider plant, they did flood one of the offline UV pipes.

The report noted by October 22 2025, crews were warned flooding could occur in storm events. In an incident report after the January 15 flooding, Veolia operators warned there was a risk of pumping into the short outfall pipe if flows exceeded 3200 litres per second.

A meeting was held between Wellington Water staff, Veolia and Stantec on February 3 to discuss the flooding incidents, where a Veolia staff member said the bypass pipe being used could only take 1500 litres per second, and there was a risk of overflow to the short pipe at Tarakena Bay if sewage flows passed 3000 litres per second.

Check LAWA signage on Wellington's South Coast. (File photo) Kate Pereyra/RNZ

"Veolia have explored options for ways to mitigate/eliminate this and found limited options", meeting minutes cited in the report said.

People raised the potential to limit flow into the pipe, the report said, but this was not taken up because it would result in discharging sewage into the short pipe close to the shore at Tarakena Bay.

The report said Fire and Emergency staff were the first to alert operations staff flooding had happened, shortly after 1am on February 4.

While two Moa Point alarms appeared to have been sighted by a duty manager at 12.19 am and 12.34 am, the report authors' said they were not aware of staff turning off pumps and equipment remotely.

Additionally, several critical alarms triggered before and during the flooding were not pager alarms, and weren't programmed to require immediate operator action.

A Veolia spokesperson said unlike the Crown Review, the AECOM report was not independent or a "complete view of the situation".

The spokesperson said the report explicitly excluded roles, responsibilities and contractural requirements that Veolia was not the contractor or controller of the UV filtration upgrade.

Untreated wastewater signs at Lyall Bay, Wellington. (File photo) RNZ / Krystal Gibbens

"The area was isolated and roped off. Our role was to provide advice and operate the broader plant. As noted in the Crown Review, Veolia alerted Wellington Water to concerns about the project."

The spokesperson said remote monitoring routines that had worked successfully for 28 years were being followed because the UV upgrade had been classified by Wellington Water as a business-as-usual process.

"On the night of the Moa Point incident, as soon as Veolia staff were onsite they initiated action in response to the emergency."

The AECOM report stated this incident was not the result of a single decision or operational failure. It was, as the Crown Review concluded, "the cumulative effect of longstanding weaknesses in asset stewardship, risk management, accountability, governance, and infrastructure resilience"."

Veolia said the plant was on track to be fully operating by February 2027.

"The well reported underlying issue that led to this event is the chronic underinvestment in water infrastructure that has persisted for up to 30 years."

World.title: Labour rules out changes to interest deductibility settings for landlords if elected
World.content:
Labour leader Chris Hipkins has ruled out any changes to interest deductibility settings for landlords, if elected.

The coalition government in 2024 reinstated landlords' ability to claim tax deductions for interest on residential investment properties.

Opposition parties decried the government prioritising "tax cuts for landlords" which cost around $2.8 billion over four years.

But Hipkins on Monday confirmed Labour would not change the policy, because it was committed to a capital gains tax instead.

"We did foreshadow when we announced a capital gains tax that that was changing our thinking around how we would look at interest deductibility in the future, and that has now been confirmed," he said.

"[Under Labour] landlords will ultimately be subjected to a capital gains tax when they sell their investment properties.

"If you were to make changes to interest deductibility, it would ultimately change then, potentially, the capital gains tax settings."

Hipkins said he also did not want to risk landlords hiking rents, because people were already struggling to pay them.

National criticises 'rank hypocrisy'

National's campaign chair Simeon Brown questioned how Labour would pay for its policies without the additional revenue.

He said the move demonstrated "rank hypocrisy".

"After three years of attacking 'tax cuts for landlords' and blaming them for the cost-of-living crisis, Chris Hipkins has performed an eleventh-hour u-turn and decided to keep the very policy Labour has spent years condemning," he said.

World.title: Chris Hipkins wants police to 'front up' and explain 'ongoing matter' with Rakesh Naidoo
World.content:
Labour leader Chris Hipkins says police need to "front up" and "explain what is going on", following comments by the Police Minister about Labour's top cop candidate Rakesh Naidoo.

It comes after Police Minister Mark Mitchell last week said there was an "ongoing matter" in relation to Naidoo, but would not say what it was.

On Monday, following questions from RNZ, Hipkins said he had "absolute confidence in Rakesh Naidoo".

"He has behaved with absolute integrity throughout this process."

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

Hipkins said Mitchell "should not be using his position as minister of police to make unsubstantiated insinuations against the character of a rival political candidate".

"Neither Mr Naidoo nor the Labour Party have any idea what is actually being alleged.

"The police need to front up here and explain what is going on."

In response, Mitchell told RNZ Hipkins "should not be commenting on something that has nothing to do with him".

"As I have said I am unable to comment any further as I am observing the rules around 6c of the Official Information Act.

"That is the response I gave when asked by media about Mr Naidoo. I have nothing further to add."

Naidoo's candidacy - announced in June - prompted public criticism from Police Commissioner Richard Chambers and minister Mark Mitchell, both claiming the superintendent should have declared his intentions earlier.

An internal review later concluded that Naidoo had complied with police policy, though noted it would have been "prudent" for him to have given his superiors more advance warning.

In response to media questions last week Mitchell said there were "two or three different facets to this situation".

"And they have dealt with one of them."

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

After the review's findings were announced, Mitchell confirmed to RNZ he had two phone calls with Chambers on 8 and 9 June.

"[The calls] were to discuss the situation, including the response to media queries, concerns the minister held in relation to the disclosure timeline, including pre-existing concerns regarding a sensitive briefing Mr Naidoo had attended with the minister prior to Mr Naidoo advising anyone at police of his political intentions."

Mitchell declined to release information in relation to the sensitive briefing under section 6 (c) of the Official Information Act.

Section 6 (c) relates to prejudicing the maintenance of the law, including the prevention, investigation, and detection of offences, and the right to a fair trial.

Mitchell's office confirmed to RNZ earlier this month the grounds for withholding under Section 6c of the OIA still applied.

Mitchell referred to the OIA again last week and said "the OIA is very clear it says there's matters that can't be disclosed because there's an ongoing matter".

RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

He said he was unable to comment further.

Hipkins said last week Mitchell had "crossed a line here".

"He is the minister of police, and he is using that office to spread claims about a Labour candidate who doesn't even know what the specific accusation against him is. You cannot use the power of the police portfolio to invent allegations against political opponents.

"Mark Mitchell should be ashamed of himself. Mark Mitchell should not be commenting, directing or be privy to police employment matters."

Police declined to comment last week.

RNZ earlier asked for comment on whether there was an investigation into Naidoo.

A police spokesperson said "we have no further comment on the matter".

Speaking to RNZ earlier for the first time since being recruited by Labour, Naidoo said he would not do anything differently with hindsight, pointing to a police review which cleared him of any wrongdoing.

In a sit-down interview marking his entry into the election campaign, Naidoo remained diplomatic about the criticism levelled at him by his superiors.

"In my view, they were expressing themselves based on the information that they had," he said.

World.title: 'My whole world stopped' - Nelson donors raise $30,000 for Nepalese woman's cancer surgery
World.content:
Donors have raised $30,000 for a Nelson-based Nepalese woman who needs life-saving surgery after a doctor discovered she had advanced thyroid cancer during a visa medical check.

Samira Basnet, 36, moved to New Zealand two years ago to study for her Master's degree in Management Studies at NMIT.

During a medical check-up for her post-study work visa application a month ago, the doctor noticed a lump on Basnet's neck and referred her for further tests.

"My whole world stopped when they said that it's like 90 percent thyroid cancer," she said.

Basnet said the diagnosis came as a shock because she had not noticed the lump, did not have any symptoms and otherwise felt fit and healthy.

"It's very hard because it's unexpected, no one expects like a big like shocking news like this," she said.

"It's not spread, that's the reason also I'm a little bit positive. It's curable, it's treatable, that's the thing that keeps me going."

Basnet is ineligible for publicly-funded healthcare because she is not a New Zealand resident and does not currently hold the required work visa.

She said friends and family had been affected by Nepal's deadly flood, including relatives who were still missing. The disaster meant she could not return to Nepal for treatment.

"My parents call me every single day because they are just worried if I'm okay or not," she said.

Basnet was referred to surgeon Dr Ros Pochin who said the cancer would continue to spread without treatment.

"Unfortunately, when I looked at her ultrasound and looked at her neck, I could tell that she had quite an advanced thyroid cancer," she said.

Pochin said the cancer had spread to Basnet's neck muscles and lymph nodes but could be cured with surgery and treatment.

"Even when you've got nodes involved, we think that the survival rate is at 90 percent-plus at 10 years."

Pochin said it was frustrating and upsetting to discover Basnet was not eligible for treatment, so she decided to do something about it.

"I see cancer patients every day and I'm used to telling people bad news but also saying how I'm going to fix it," Pochin said.

"To be honest, I really can't cope with telling somebody there's bad news and knowing that it's something that I could fix but not being able to fix it."

The surgery cost around $26,000 but Pochin and anaesthetist Dr Katie Ben were not charging for their time. Basnet would also need radioactive iodine therapy in Christchurch at an estimated cost of $15,000.

Pochin said the the Givealittle page she set up raised $30,000 in just four days.

"It was really heartening to see how much has been donated and when I've looked through the people, because I get notified for every donation, there are an awful lot of names that I imagine are Nepalese and the Nepalese community is doing it really hard already and yet here is everybody giving whatever they can," she said.

Nelson has the largest proportion of people of Nepalese origin among all regions in New Zealand as a result of the refugee resettlement programme.

The surgery to remove Basnet's thyroid and affected muscles and lymph nodes is booked for November.

Pochin said the surgery and treatment meant Basnet would not be a burden on the health system.

World.title: All Blacks captain Ardie Savea faces lengthy spell on sideline after surgery confirmed
World.content:
All Blacks captain Ardie Savea is facing a lengthy spell on the sidelines after it was confirmed he will undergo shoulder surgery.

The star loose forward dislocated his shoulder during in the third test against South Africa in Soweto earlier this month, which saw him return home early and miss the series finale in the United States.

Savea had already been ruled out for next month's Bledisloe Cup tests against Australia, now his involvement in the Nations Championship at the end of the year is in doubt after New Zealand Rugby on Monday confirmed the 32-year-old will require surgery.

NZ Rugby said a return-to-play timeframe for Savea will not be known until after surgery. However, with the rehabilitation time for shoulder surgery typically taking around six months, it is unlikely the All Blacks' skipper will return to the field before the end of 2026.

Savea's absence is another significant blow to an All Blacks side already dealing with a lengthy injury list.

Luke Jacobson has undergone surgery on an elbow tendon injury and is expected to be sidelined for four to five months, while Caleb Clarke's ruptured shoulder tendon is expected to keep him out for about five months.

The latest injury update also lists Anton Lienert-Brown (four to six weeks), Quinn Tupaea (one to two weeks), Anton Segner (one to two weeks), Cortez Ratima (one to two weeks) and Billy Proctor (four to six weeks) among those recovering from injuries sustained on tour.

Savea's injury occurred in the first half of the All Blacks' 29-24 defeat to the Springboks in Soweto, a match in which he scored two tries before being forced from the field.

World.title: Vet performs surgery on critically injured skink 'Kevin', who weighs less than 4 grams
World.content:
Audio player for " Vets operate on critically injured native skink " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._g.pKhUMkRnoOZwX4iq2fhLAqba5Rz0jb3mINKRqASmxf0/environment/1497171%2Fvet-performs-surgery-on-critically-injured-skink-kevin-who-weighs-less-than-4-grams

Vets operate on critically injured native skink Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

A vet at Massey Wildbase Hospital has operated on their smallest patient yet - a critically injured skink now known as "Kevin".

Veterinary resident Ingrid Brookshaw told Checkpoint the skink, who weighed less than four grams, had been attacked by a cat in Whanganui and was left with a serious puncture wound on its side.

The skink was a native species, a northern grass skink, which was listed as non-threatened, but Brookshaw said they did still face habitat loss and predation.

She said while he wasn't endangered, there were the immediate ethical implications as he was predated on by an introduced species.

He was about 4cm long and the biggest puncture wound he had was about 4 to 5mm in length.

"We want to help every individual that we can and we're a teaching hospital..."

Brookshaw said such surgeries would be good practice for when a critically endangered species did come through.

Performing surgery on such a small patient was definitely a challenge, Brookshaw said, and they had to get "a little bit creative" with their really small patients.

That included adapting the equipment used and making sure injectable drugs for pain management were diluted down to the right amount.

"We did a little bit of careful mathematics on the weekend for this little patient."

A surgical microscope was used to magnify the incision site, Brookshaw said, which allowed the team to keep their hands steady and get two tiny sutures in place.

"We were pretty lucky with the orientation of the wound that those sutures could be placed appropriately."

The little skink was recovering in hospital and would be there for a while, she said, as they didn't heal particularly fast.

"He's doing well, but not out of the woods yet - he's working hard and eating like a champion."

He was being fed a specialised puree diet which he was loving, Brookshaw said.

"We may have to watch his weight before he leaves!"

While she said they tried to avoid giving names to any patients as a "superstitious thing", Brookshaw admitted he looked like a Kevin.

World.title: The clause that may save Lions ace for AFL grand final
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The AFL tribunal chairman was blunt: the "good bloke" clause does not exist.

Instead, tribunal chair Jeff Gleeson KC turned to a fresh provision in the AFL's laws, centred on compelling and exceptional circumstances.

It is the clause that could save Brisbane's Lachie Neale from being suspended for Saturday's grand final.

The Lions will challenge Neale's one-game suspension for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan in last Saturday night's preliminary final.

Neale's gut punch on Ginnivan was graded intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact.

On video evidence, Neale is guilty.

"There's no point putting energy into it until we know the result," Neale's teammate Jarrod Berry said today.

"We'll be sitting tight and praying that he gets off. But if he doesn't, we'll face it when it comes."

Precedents this season have resulted in one-game bans to numerous players. The most recent just last week, when Adelaide's Max Michalanney was suspended for delivering an off-the-ball gut punch.

Neale facing grand final ban The Lions will contest a one-match suspension handed to Lachie Neale, which would rule the two-time premiership captain out of the AFL grand final.

But what may allow Neale, a dual Brownlow medallist to play in the premiership decider is the clause that saved Collingwood legend Scott Pendlebury from suspension in March.

"Exceptional and compelling circumstances" is certain to be the anchor of Brisbane's argument at Tuesday night's tribunal hearing.

The Lions will cite Pendlebury's hearing on March 17 this year.

The acts in the cases of Pendlebury and Neale are starkly different.

The Magpie great was charged with rough conduct for a bump on Adelaide's Josh Worrell.

His proposed one-match suspension was downgraded to a $3,000 fine with Gleeson enacting the "compelling and exceptional circumstances" clause.

Pendlebury's advocate Myles Tehan successfully argued the ex-Pies captain "stands in a class of his own", having never previously been before the tribunal in a 21-year AFL career.

"It's frankly difficult to imagine how it could not constitute an exceptional and compelling circumstance (to avoid a ban)," Tehan told the hearing.

"I should say this is not by any means a good bloke clause or a get of jail free card or anything of that nature."

Tribunal chair Gleeson then interjected.

"I might add, it never has been. It's misreported as being something to that effect from time to time," Gleeson said.

"But people who read the guidelines and listen to what the tribunal says will understand it's nothing to do with being a good bloke.

"It's to do with whether the circumstances are exceptional and compelling."

The relevant clause states: "Players will not automatically receive a reduced sanction for a good record. However, if a classifiable offence is contested or referred to the tribunal, a player with an exemplary record may argue that their good record constitutes exceptional and compelling circumstances".

Neale, a 320-gamer, is a dual Brownlow medallist; a dual premiership captain; a four-time All Australian; a four-time club champion who, like Pendlebury, has never been suspended.

His exemplary history gives the Lions cause to argue, and hope for a reprieve.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Fremantle legend in tears as AFL grand final honour revealed
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Fremantle pioneer Shaun McManus will hand over the AFL premiership cup to captain Alex Pearce if the Dockers break through for their maiden flag.

Part of the inaugural 1995 Dockers squad, McManus has been named as Fremantle's cup presenter ahead of Saturday's grand final against back-to-back reigning premiers Brisbane.

The Lions are yet to name their presenter after three-time premiership player Jonathan Brown did so for last year's decider win over Geelong.

McManus was brought to tears when he was told he was the club's cup presenter during a segment on Perth radio this morning.

Peter Bell was named the club's presenter for the eventual 2013 grand final loss to Hawthorn.

Dockers chief Simon Garlick described McManus as a perfect embodiment of the club's values.

McManus began his AFL career as a 19-year-old, going on to play 228 games across 14 seasons.

He captained the team alongside Adrian Fletcher from 2000 to 2001, and played alongside current coach Justin Longmuir.

"Shaun perfectly sums up what a Fremantle person is," Garlick said in a club statement.

"He had a remarkable career as a Fremantle player, but beyond that he has been a champion of this club since our humble beginnings back in 1995.

"Those early foundation years weren't easy, and as a 19-year-old he came in, showed great qualities which resulted in him being named captain at just 24.

"The courage he showed on field speaks for itself, but ever since retiring he's been a passionate and positive influence, someone who purely lives and breathes Freo.

"If we are good enough to get the job done on Saturday, it will be a great moment to see Shaun present the cup to Alex, and his old teammate Justin."

McManus is the ninth-highest game record holder in the club's history and was the second behind Shane Parker to reach the 200-game milestone.

Retiring after the 2008 season, McManus remained at the club as a player development coach and transitioned through various off-field roles.

The 50-year-old became a Dockers life member in 2004.

ABC Sport will have a live blog of the AFL grand final between Fremantle and Brisbane from the MCG on Saturday.

AAP

World.title: NRL set to act over 'embarrassing' referee abuse
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

The NRL has threatened to ban spectators who threw projectiles at referee Ashley Klein, with the league's integrity unit investigating the aftermath of Sunday's semifinal in Auckland.

Footage from after full-time in Newcastle's 12-10 win over the Warriors at Eden Park showed a raft of bottles, cups and rubbish being thrown at Klein as he walked from the field.

Projectiles thrown at ref as Knights win Projectiles have been thrown at the NRL refereeing crew following Newcastle's upset semifinal win over the New Zealand Warriors.

Klein had to be protected by security as fans abused the veteran referee and threw projectiles.

The NRL immediately launched an investigation into potential breaches of its spectators' code of conduct.

An integrity unit investigator had been at the ground.

"If found guilty, they [the fans] will be banned for a period of time from attending NRL games," ARL Commission chair Peter V'landys said.

Auckland police have since confirmed no arrests were made.

They said there were "no issues to note", other than two pitch invaders.

The Warriors exited the finals following the loss to the Knights. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

Sunday's crowd of 48,511 marked the largest ever for a rugby league match in New Zealand, after the NRL made the call to move the match from Mount Smart Stadium.

The spectator abuse came after two contentious calls went against the Warriors late in the match, including a decision not to penalise Tyson Frizell for an escort in the dying minutes.

Warriors great Shaun Johnson hit out at the response of spectators after the match, labelling it "embarrassing".

"It leaves a bit of a sour taste in your mouth [after] what has been an unbelievable night with the colours, the energy, the happiness and celebration," Johnson said on Sky NZ's coverage.

"But there is just no need for it. It's just embarrassing.

"Ashley Klein has probably refereed the best game of rugby league I have seen in a long time tonight.

Hawks fans facing bans Hawthorn supporters who threw bottles at umpires after a controversial finals exit face lengthy bans if identified by the AFL and Victoria Police.

"He didn't take any gamesmanship in terms of people laying down. He didn't let people approach him whingeing.

"He didn't make the game about him. He let the players come and play and they dictated the outcome."

Warriors coach Andrew Webster vented his frustration in the post-match media conference, highlighting a bunker strip call on Te Maire Martin and the decision not to penalise Frizell for a possible escort on Leka Halasima.

"The last one, [when] two points would have drawn the game, he [Frizell] is going across Leka, pretending to try and catch the ball, which they've told us you can't do," Webster said.

The incident came after AFL umpires also had bottles and cans thrown at them while leaving the MCG following Hawthorn's nine-point loss to the Brisbane Lions in Saturday night's preliminary final.

The AFL has condemned the behaviour and warned of minimum five-year bans for any fans found responsible.

AAP

World.title: Everything you need to know about the 2026 Brownlow Medal count
World.content:
The AFL's grand final week is here, and will begin as usual with the awarding of the Brownlow Medal tonight.

The best-and-fairest player of the 2026 season will be presented with the AFL's highest award at the end of the evening, with a first-time winner widely expected to be crowned.

The fashion on display beforehand on the red carpet will also be a big focus of attention.

Here is what you need to know about the AFL's night of nights.

What time is the 2026 Brownlow Medal?

The Brownlow Medal count will be held tonight, Monday, September 21, with the broadcast coverage starting at 7:30pm (AEST) and the count getting underway from 8pm.

Red carpet guests arrive from 5:15pm. The mark of the year winner will be announced at 8:35pm, and the goal of the year at 9pm.

How can I watch and follow the Brownlow Medal?

ABC Sport will be live blogging all the action with every vote from every round at abc.net.au.

The broadcast of the event from Melbourne's Crown Palladium will be on Channel 7 and 7Plus.

Who is the favourite to win the 2026 Brownlow?

Collingwood's Nick Daicos is the unbackable favourite.

As a demonstration of his favouritism, most bookmakers have listed him at $1.01 to win.

However, Daicos was also the strong favourite to win last season, before coming second to the Gold Coast's Matt Rowell by seven votes.

Other players in the discussion are Geelong's Bailey Smith, Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli and Carlton star Patrick Cripps.

Can umpires access stats when they give their votes?

Traditionally umpires haven't had access to game stats when they cast their votes directly after a match.

That has changed this year, after St Kilda's Nasiah Wanganeen-Milera was controversially deemed not the best player on the field in a game against Melbourne last season, despite being the clear star on the day.

This season umpires were given access to stats, including: kicks, handballs, disposals, marks, contested marks, tackles, goals, behinds, goal assists, score involvements, clearances, contested possessions, hitouts, kick-ins, intercept marks, intercept possessions and spoils.

Can the banned Sydney Swans players receive votes in the Brownlow?

Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Nick Blakey, Riley Bice and James Jordon were all banned from playing finals after breaching club standards.

The players were also deemed ineligible for the All Australian team, with Heeney and Warner both likely to have been named if not for the ban.

However, all players will be able to receive votes in the Brownlow, and all votes will count.

Heeney is considered a top 10 prospect in the award.

How does the Brownlow work?

Unlike other awards, the Brownlow Medal is decided by the votes of the umpires.

For every game of the home-and-away season (not counting finals), umpires award votes to the three best players on the field.

The best player is given three votes, the second-best two votes and the third-best one vote.

The votes are kept secret and are revealed round-by-round at the ceremony.

The player who ends with the most votes at the end of the season is crowned the Brownlow Medal winner.

The award is for the fairest and best players, so those who have been suspended for a week or more during the season are ineligible. Corey McKernan (1996) and Chris Grant (1997) are the most recent examples of ineligible players notching the most votes, while Jobe Watson won the medal in 2012 before having it rescinded in the wake of Essendon's supplements scandal.

In the event of a tie, the Brownlow can be shared, as was the case in 2003 when Adelaide's Mark Ricciuto, Collingwood's Nathan Buckley and Sydney's Adam Goodes shared the medal.

World.title: Kenyan breaks women-only half marathon world record by a second
World.content:
Tell us about your experience.

Kenya's Agnes Ngetich has taken a second off the women-only half marathon ​world record at the ‌World Athletics Road Running Championships in Copenhagen.

Ngetich stopped the clock at one ​hour, five minutes and 15 ​seconds.

She ​pushed to the front from the outset in the Danish capital and led through to the end, finishing 50 ​seconds ahead of compatriot Veronica Loleo, who ​claimed the silver medal.

Rebecca Lowe was the best-placed Australian, running a personal best of 1:11.38 to finish in 51st position.

"My coach believed in me and told me that I could do it, that I could win the gold medal," Ngetich said.

"So, I am very happy and very grateful to now hold the world half marathon record, too."

The previous world record was set by ‌Peres ⁠Jepchirchir, another Kenyan, in 2020.

The overall women's half marathon world record is held ​by Ethiopia's ​Letesenbet ⁠Gidey, who clocked 1:02:52 in 2021.

⁠Gidey set her mark at the Valencia Half Marathon, which involved both women's and men's races.

Ngetich also helped Kenya win the team half marathon in Copenhagen.

The 25-year-old's triumph was the ​latest major title she has won this year.

She was also ⁠victorious at the World Cross Country ​Championships in January.
